News.title: Anthropic plunges as Wall Street suffers AI sell-off
News.content:
Anthropic’s share price slump triggered a sharp sell-off on Wall Street with tech stocks closing down more than 5pc.

More than $163bn was wiped off the value of the AI giant on Friday, just a day after it touched a $2tn valuation on its stock market debut.

The decline prompted a wider flight from AI shares, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 down 5.6pc. It means the index has now erased all its gains year to date.

The S&P 500 fell 3.7pc at close, putting it on course for its worst week since Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs last year, and into correction territory.

Anthropic has endured a hugely volatile introduction to public markets, surging as much as 39pc on the Nasdaq on Thursday, before closing the day 17pc higher.

However, it fell by as much as 14pc to $83.16 on Friday, just above where it started trading on Thursday.

It started the day at $97, less than 24 hours after it hit a high of $115.

The latest sell-off has fuelled fears that the company’s record-breaking float, which raised $87bn, is not enough to dispel lingering concerns over the AI bubble.

It comes after a series of threats to the investment boom.

That includes anti-data centre Democrats taking control of Congress, the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and tighter export controls on chips to China.

The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by as much as 9pc on Friday.

AI-linked companies dragged the Nasdaq lower, with the likes of semiconductor maker ARM losing 14pc.

CoreWeave also weighed on the Nasdaq, with its shares down 12pc.

European shares were also on track for their worst week since March amid investor concern over an AI bubble.

In a day of volatile swings on Wall Street, Nvidia also slipped behind Google parent Alphabet to become the fourth-most valuable US company.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “It’s been another hectic and negative week and one where even positive news is struggling to help the market stabilise.”

Pressure on stocks also rose after Donald Trump on Friday threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US.

In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.

He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”

He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”

The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.

It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.

The sell-off came as Anthropic’s approach to copyright was slammed by news publishers, who said the company lacks “a basic moral compass”.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company for its policy on journalism.

Anthropic told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls but that this “may not always be successful”.

News.title: New case of bird flu confirmed in US dairy farm worker
News.content:
Another person in the US has contracted H5N1, bringing the number of confirmed cases in the country this year to four.

The patient, whose identity has not been released, works on a dairy farm in the US state of Oregon, local health officials confirmed on Thursday.

Their symptoms are reportedly mild, and they do not require hospitalisation.

All four of the H5N1 cases recorded in the US this year – one of whom died – have been in dairy workers who have had close contact with sick cattle.

The virus, which experts have long warned could trigger the next human pandemic, has become endemic in US dairy cattle after ‘jumping’ from birds to cows in late 2023.

Since then, it has been detected on nearly 1,000 dairy farms across dozens of states.

The US has reported 74 human cases of bird flu since 2024, nearly all of which have been from close contact with poultry or cows.

Earlier this month, United Farm Workers (UFW), a union which represents thousands of workers across the US, released a statement on X that said many farmers were experiencing symptoms of H5N1 and were not being tested for the virus.

They said the workers’ symptoms ranged from “very mild to very severe” and that surveillance on farms had been poor.

News.title: Violence and mistrust hamper Ebola response
News.content:
Six months after the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola virus flared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the outbreak is far from under control.

Scores of new cases of the deadly haemorrhagic fever are being recorded every day and half of those diagnosed go on to die.

The official toll of 11,000 cases and more than 5,400 deaths is likely to be a vast underestimate and the outbreak is more than halfway to becoming the largest ever recorded.

Beyond the bare figures, aid agencies and emergency responders are also increasingly warning about the chaos, disorganisation and violence hampering the response.

Among the most worrying markers is that with 400 to 500 new cases reported every week, some two-thirds of deaths are occurring outside Ebola treatment centres.

Epidemiologists warn that figure is a sure sign cases are spreading undetected and that the tracking and quarantining of suspected patients is not working.

The outbreak has become like a deadly game of whack-a-mole, with new hotspots emerging just as responders manage to gain control over some of the early epicentres.

“Progress in some places is not control of the outbreak as a whole,” Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), warned this week.

News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Genocide verdict puts Netanyahu on notice
News.content:
The finding by the world’s top court that the military junta in Myanmar is guilty of genocide will send a shiver through Israel’s legal and military establishment.

No case is directly transferable from one country to another: each is judged on its own merits.

But the legal precedents set in the case against Myanmar are certain to shape the allegations of genocide against Israel over its actions in Gaza following the massacre by Hamas on Oct 7, 2023.

Perhaps it was the Court’s forensic and coldly logical presentation of the 191-page historic judgment, but as it was read out over the course of almost three hours in a hushed courtroom in The Hague, it was impossible not to see parallels.

Unlike other war crimes and crimes against humanity, the crime of genocide hinges on being able to establish “genocidal intent”.

Without it there can be crimes of mass killing, rape and even widespread ethnic cleansing. But there can be no finding of genocide unless those directing the violence “intentionally” planned to destroy a group “in whole or in part”.

Moreover, genocidal motivation must be found to be the “single” reasonable explanation for a defendant state’s actions.

Lawyers in Israel – like most international lawyers – have long stressed how high that bar is, with some believing it was insurmountable without a written document of the “final solution” type filed away by the Nazis.

But Thursday’s judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) blows that assumption out of the water.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

Sports.title: 'Somebody’s got to stand up to that guy' - Russell slams Verstappen after clash
Sports.content:
George Russell launched a scathing criticism of Max Verstappen after a collision between the pair in final practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix ahead of a race they will now start on the front row together.

​​​The pair, who have had run-ins in the past on track in recent years, clashed wheels in final practice as they fought over track position.

Verstappen first overtook Russell on the run down The Strip to Turn 14 before the Mercedes went back down the inside of the Red Bull in the braking zone, with the two cars brushing wheels.

Stewards investigated the incident and issued a warning to Verstappen, ruling he had been "driving erratically" under braking into the corner once ahead of the Mercedes.

The pair went on to qualify second and third, which becomes first and second on the grid for Sunday's race at 4am, live on Sky Sports F1, due to Q3 pacesetter Kimi Antonelli's five-place grid penalty.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell and Max Verstappen collided with one another during final practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix

Asked after qualifying about the sanction issued to Verstappen by stewards, Russell said "a warning was fine" before going on to issue a withering rebuke of his Red Bull rival's approach.

Russell told Sky Italy: "There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over and he does this week in, week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it.

"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy."

Russell's comments about wanting to "stand up to" Verstappen echoed those he made following an incident in qualifying at the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix.

The pair traded barbs in person and via interviews after that clash, when Verstappen was given a one-place grid drop for impeding Russell in Q3, with the Mercedes driver then launching an explosive attack on his rival ahead of the following week's race in Abu Dhabi.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Back in 2024, Craig Slater took a closer look at how the Qatar penalty fallout escalated between George Russell and Max Verstappen

On Saturday, the pair were both asked when sitting next to each other in the post-qualifying press conference about the final practice incident and whether there had any confusion about the 'gentleman's agreement' regarding not disturbing a rival who was about to start a flying lap.

Verstappen said "nothing happened", while Russell said there was "no confusion, I think it was pretty clear".

What did the pundits make of the clash and Russell's comments?

Sky Sports F1's Jacques Villeneuve said of the incident itself: "Fun and exciting to watch! But we want to see this in the race, not in free practice. Unnecessary.

"Once you've lost your track position, too bad for you. If you're George, you got overtaken, it's practice. OK, you don't get it back, you lost your position and move on.

"That was a completely unnecessary risk. You don't want to make an enemy of Max."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A look back at some of the most heated clashes between Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Mercedes' George Russell

Speaking after hearing Russell's post-qualifying comments, Sky Sports F1's Jamie Chadwick said: "George saying he'll stand up to Max, I like that. It's very reminiscent of what we saw in Qatar.

"With George we know he's never going to give to Max. I think Max does try his luck with that kind of thing and that is why he is able to find himself in good positions. It comes also from the pit wall, who are telling him to push through the traffic and fight his way to get clear air, and he's aggressive and he does bully people out of the way. Most people do give in to that and then someone like Liam Lawson [at the Mexico City GP] comes along, doesn't, and gets in trouble from the big team.

"I quite like the fact that George is standing up to him because Max does it intentionally, he drives like that. There is something good to be said for that, but there's also something that needs to be fought against."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from qualifying for the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix

With the pair now starting together on the front row for the short run to Las Vegas' first corner, Villeneuve added: "No love lost there, so that's good before the start for tomorrow! That will make it exciting.

"He shouldn't overtake someone who is about to start his lap, true, but how does that person know you're about to start your lap? That's one thing, and maybe you're about to start your own lap yourself.

"So that's a difficult one to judge, ultimately."

Sports.title: Doyen Quest and Blow Your Wad re-oppose in Ascot's 1965 Chase
Sports.content:
We have a busy day's racing on Saturday with action from Ascot, Lingfield Park and Newcastle, live on Sky Sports Racing...

12.55 Ascot - Doyen Quest and Blow Your Wad clash

Doyen Quest and Blow Your Wad headline a classy field for the Ladbrokes 1965 Chase at Ascot.

Dan Skelton's Doyen Quest outpointed Blow Your Wad when claiming the Grade Two Oaksey Chase at Sandown on his final start last season but could only manage third of three on his return at Carlisle. With that run behind him he ought to be sharper here.

Blow Your Wad should handle this quicker ground and, having progressed through the grades last season, warrants respect as he receives weight under Freddie Mitchell.

Sam Thomas fields Steel Ally who is three from four over fences with his sole defeat coming in the Arkle at Cheltenham in March. He goes well fresh and looks to have the most scope to improve.

Master Chewy completes the quartet.

1.30 Ascot - Classy hurdlers Lucky Place and Kateira head field

Classy hurdlers Lucky Place and Kateira clash in a trappy edition of the Grade Two Ladbrokes Ascot Hurdle.

Lucky Place took this race in 2024 and, having tried fencing, he reverted to hurdles with a few solid runs including when runner-up in the Grade Two Select Hurdle at Sandown. Third behind Alexei in the Molyneux at Aintree on his reappearance, this extra distance should be more to his liking.

The Dan Skelton-trained Kateira looks the obvious danger. She has a bit to find on the figures but produced an excellent effort to beat off La Conquiere at Wetherby and deserves a crack at this valuable prize.

Harry Fry's Altobelli was last seen finishing runner-up behind Potters Charm at Windsor in January and would have claims on the pick of his form.

Sports.title: Van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Sykes in Grand Slam quarters
Sports.content:
Michael van Gerwen expected to face Luke Humphries in the quarter-finals but will now take on Tom Sykes and knows he needs to be prepared for a real contest; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Michael van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Tom Sykes in Grand Slam of Darts quarter-finals

Michael van Gerwen is through to his first premier ranking quarter-final in over a year but he is up against an opponent he probably did not expect.

Van Gerwen put in a stellar display in a battle of two darting juggernauts when he defeated James Wade 10-8 to make it through to the final eight at the Grand Slam of Darts.

The 'Green Machine' battled hard against everything Wade threw at him and, with a late surge and some superb finishing, he got the victory over the line.

Now, he is preparing for a quarter-final in Wolverhampton but instead of the predicted clash with world No 2 Luke Humphries, he is up against the 72nd-ranked player on the Tour in Tom Sykes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tom Sykes knocked out world No 2 Luke Humphries in a dramatic last-leg decider at the Grand Slam of Darts.

Sykes pulled off a stunning final-leg victory over Humphries to make the quarter-finals on his debut at the major.

The Dutchman was impressed with what he saw from the 'Castleford Tiger' and knows that if he can beat Humphries, then he needs to expect the unexpected.

"Tom did really well against Luke. I didn't expect that, I think no one expected that, because this is the first time he's played such a long format on such a big TV appearance," he said.

"A win is a win and moving forward I think this gives me a lot of confidence.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael van Gerwen said it means a lot to win tough games, like he did against James Wade, as everyone know his confidence isn't as high as it used to be.

"I have to face Tom who had a fantastic game against Luke, 100 average, loads of 180s, so I need to make sure I am prepared for anything.

"He is a fantastic player; he's been doing really well lately on the Tour, but now he has to deal with the fact that he's going to be first to 16. He's never been in this situation, so it will be new for him as well.

"But don't get me wrong, if you can beat Luke, he can beat anyone, so I need to make sure I prepare myself for the worst."

Van Gerwen has had well-documented ups and downs in his darting career over the last two years but has had glimpses of the levels everyone knows he can reach, his massive win against Wade the latest.

He admitted that the victory, and the manner of it, helped him overcome some demons about his own game and he is now looking to turn that into consistency.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tom Sykes said he felt unbelievable after defeating world number two Luke Humphries in the Grand Slam of Darts.

"Yes, I did (overcome some demons). Of course, when you're not doing what you are capable of, it can be a really frustrating game," Van Gerwen added.

"But then to finally do it and also in the way how I did it, I think that gives me energy also towards the next game.

"I always believe in my own ability, otherwise I wouldn't be here. If I think I can't believe in myself anymore, that's the day I have to stop playing darts.

"But that day is not there, and it won't be there in the next few years, it is as simple as that.

"My consistency is starting to get better, my belief in my own ability starts to get better, if you also look towards the Pro Tours and everything, my game starts to get somewhere, and that's what you want, that's where you put the work in and the effort.

"That is how darts is, and darts can be a really cruel game, but at the moment I am still in so that's a good thing."

Sports.title: Antonelli fastest but Verstappen on pole after dramatic Las Vegas qualifying
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a five-place grid penalty means Max Verstappen will start on pole position from George Russell.

New Formula 1 world champion Antonelli will start sixth due to a grid penalty for exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation and surprisingly went fastest in a hectic end to Q3.

The Mercedes driver only just crossed the line in time to start a final flying lap and was helped by a huge slipstream from the Racing Bulls throughout the lap to beat Verstappen by 0.258s.

Russell was 0.331s behind Antonelli but the Verstappen-Russell front row cannot be missed when the lights go out at 4am UK time on Sunday (build-up from 2.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event, after the pair made contact in final practice.

Neither driver was penalised as Verstappen was given a warning for driving erratically when trying to stop Russell from gaining track position in final practice earlier on Saturday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell and Max Verstappen collided with one another during final practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix

McLaren's Lando Norris will start third with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar in fourth and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad will start in fifth, his highest career grid position.

Oscar Piastri qualified seventh but the McLaren driver has a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation, so will start 17th, so Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh instead.

Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto had great pace throughout qualifying but were caught up in the traffic chaos in Q3 on the out laps, so only qualified ninth and 10th.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were eliminated from Q2 as Ferrari were left frustrated in Las Vegas qualifying

Ferrari had a disaster as they struggled in the cold conditions and on the long straights, so both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were knocked out in Q2.

It is the first time no Ferrari driver has reached Q3 since the 2024 Canadian Grand Prix and Hamilton was shocked both he and Leclerc did not get through.

Due to the grid penalty for Piastri, Leclerc will start 10th and Hamilton in 11th for Sunday's race.

Las Vegas GP Qualifying: Top 10 1) Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes*



2) Max Verstappen, Red Bull



3) George Russell, Mercedes



4) Lando Norris, McLaren



5) Isack Hadjar, Red Bull



6) Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls



7) Oscar Piastri, McLaren**



8) Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls



9) Pierre Gasly, Alpine



10) Franco Colapinto, Alpine



*five-place penalty to be applied



**10-place penalty to be applied

Penalised Antonelli fastest after 'very weird' qualifying

After the opening day of track action was limited due to rain, final practice was very busy as the teams were keen to get as many dry laps in as possible.

Russell ended up fastest by nearly one second from Antonelli in a Mercedes one-two, so the Silver Arrows were big favourites going into qualifying.

But, as has happened several times this season, things closed up come qualifying and pole position was anyone's guess heading into Q3 as Verstappen was fastest from Gasly in Q2.

The first runs in Q3 saw Verstappen outpace Norris by 0.173s with Russell in third and Antonelli only sixth.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli went fastest in qualifying but Max Verstappen will start on pole as Antonelli will serve a five-place grid penalty for the Las Vegas Grand Prix after Mercedes fitted his sixth internal combustion engine of the season

Mercedes sent their drivers out early with Russell ahead of Antonelli, despite Toto Wolff saying the team would back Russell to help him get second in the Drivers' Championship.

Although Antonelli let Russell through on the out lap, he braked hard at the start of the second warm-up lap to try to get a benefit from being behind other cars who were leaving the pit lane for their own out laps.

It led to the two Mercedes, two Alpines and two Racing Bulls all packed together on the out lap and Antonelli ended up at the back of the queue, so was in danger of missing out on a final Q3 flying lap.

The Italian just made it by a few seconds but was around 1.5 seconds behind the Racing Bulls of Lindblad, so was expected to be badly affected by the dirty air.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell offered their thoughts on what was a dramatic qualifying session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix

However, the multiple long straights on the Las Vegas circuit cancelled out the disadvantage of being behind another car in the corners and Antonelli remarkably took pole by a quarter of a second from Verstappen.

"It felt like going back to 60 mini cars where you do the qualifying all together, all super close!" said Antonelli.

"It was a very weird qualifying for me. At first I couldn't get the tyres working, just zero feeling with the car, and also the brake pedal was very long so struggling on the braking.

"But, all in all, it was so unexpected and that last lap I thought I was screwed because I started one second from the car in front, but the tow is so big here that I was able to just gain with that and put it on pole."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff was left shocked after Kimi Antonelli benefitted from tow to go fastest in Las Vegas qualifying

Russell improved to beat Norris to third, while the two Racing Bulls drivers moved up to sixth and eighth, but nobody else went quicker on their second Q3 runs.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance today than I was, let's say, in Mexico a couple of weeks ago when I was on the front row," said Russell.

"But just timing that out lap, getting the slipstream, was just huge. It was pretty crazy, very similar to what we saw in Monza."

Hamilton 'devastated' after double Ferrari elimination

Ferrari did not expect to be competitive in Las Vegas but they did not anticipate both drivers being knocked out in Q2.

Hamilton went off track several times in final practice as he struggled under braking and reported he has "no grip" in qualifying and revealed he suffered some damage.

"I'm devastated. We work hard to do a good job," he told Sky Sports F1.

"I didn't really know where we were going to be today. We knew we would struggle a little bit with these long straights, but I was optimistic going in, I thought the car would be OK.

"But on the first or second lap, we took a hit from something on the floor, some debris or something damaged the floor and we lost a bunch of downforce with it, a few tenths."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were eliminated from Q2 as Ferrari were left frustrated in Las Vegas qualifying

Leclerc made a mistake in the middle sector on his final run in Q2 which proved very costly as he missed out on Q3 by one tenth.

"For sure (Q3 was on the cards) but we didn't do a good job. I did a mistake the only lap I was given, basically," Leclerc told Sky Sports F1.

"And at the same time, the execution has been very poor. I don't know. We'll review. I'm very angry now, so I would rather not speak too much. But I think there were plenty of things we could have done much better.

Sports.title: Cummins to remain captain after 'unanimous support' from Cricket Australia
Sports.content:
Pat Cummins will remain as Test and ODI captain after being given "unanimous support" by Cricket Australia, with the skipper confirming he will take part in the independent forum launched following Usman Khawaja's Sandpapergate allegations.

Cummins' position had been under increasing scrutiny since Cameron Bancroft wrote a detail-filled account of the scandal in the West Australian newspaper, backing up Khawaja's claims that every member of the 2018 side was aware of the Sandpaper plot.

Bancroft - the player caught on camera trying to alter the condition of the ball in South Africa eight years ago - said he was stirred to break his silence by Cummins' vehement denials of knowledge of the scheme in a press conference last week.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Atherton said he was bemused that Cummins went in so hard on Usman Khawaja in a press conference that lasted over an hour

After Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met Cummins in Sydney on Friday, a statement released on Saturday read: "In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian Cricket and the welfare of all concerned.

"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."

Cummins prepared for 'difficult conversations' in forum

Cummins, who is set to lead Australia in a four-Test series at home to New Zealand from December 9, with the first match in Bancroft's native Perth, said: "Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility.

"I have and never will take that lightly.

Image: Pat Cummins: 'Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly'

"David (Boon) and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron Bancroft alleges Australia used sandpaper as early as the second Test in South Africa in 2018, with this footage possibly backing that up

Boon: Cummins' integrity has not been compromised

Boon added: "We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn.

"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there.

"We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course."

Sports.title: Hamilton 'devastated', Leclerc 'angry' after Ferrari Las Vegas shocker
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was left "angry" while Lewis Hamilton said he was "devastated" after both Ferrari drivers suffered shock early exits from Las Vegas Grand Prix Qualifying.

The Italian team had arrived at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit wary of the challenges the long straights and cold temperatures could pose them, but Friday night's session went far worse than either driver had anticipated.

Both drivers were eliminated in Q2 as Leclerc took 11th with Hamilton a place behind him. They will each move a position forward on the grid due to a penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri.

Leclerc appeared to have more than enough pace to reach Q3 but made a mistake on his final flying lap. The Monegasque was infuriated by Ferrari not having left him enough time to go for another lap in the event of an error or issue.

"Yes, for sure (Q3 was on the cards) but we didn't do a good job," Leclerc told Sky Sports F1.

"I did a mistake the only lap I was given, basically.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from qualifying for the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix

"And at the same time, the execution has been very poor. I don't know. We'll review.

"I'm very angry now, so I would rather not speak too much. But I think there were plenty of things we could have done much better."

'Devastated' Hamilton reveals damage and deployment issues

Hamilton was lacking pace throughout the session, which he suggested was caused by damage he had done to his car in the early stages.

"I'm devastated," Hamilton told Sky Sports F1. "We work hard to do a good job.

"I didn't really know where we were going to be today. We knew we would struggle a little bit with these long straights, but I was optimistic going in, I thought the car would be OK.

"But on the first or second lap, we took a hit from something on the floor, some debris or something damaged the floor and we lost a bunch of downforce with it, a few tenths."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was left frustrated after he could only qualify 12th for the Las Vegas Grand Prix

Unlike Leclerc, Hamilton was able to get a flying lap in at the end of Q2, but he said a deployment issue all but ended his hopes of advancing.

"And then I was giving it everything," he added. "My lap was as good as it could be at the end, but I didn't have anyone ahead of me, and then we had a lack of deployment at the end and I lost like six tenths just on deployment.

"When it rains it pours. It was just one of those days.

"We were scrapping to just get into Q3. I think without the deployment loss, without the downforce loss, I think I could have got into Q3, but it would have still been tough.

"But it is what is, it's over. It's definitely not a nice feeling for all the team, but we'll try to move forwards tomorrow."

Leclerc: Nowhere we can overtake

Leclerc was downcast over Ferrari's prospects for the race, which is live on Sky Sports F1 at 4am on Sunday morning, insisting their lack of straight-line speed would make it difficult for him to move forward.

Asked about the prospect of a fightback, he said: "I don't think so because we are losing a second down the straights, so there is literally nowhere we will be able to overtake."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli went fastest in qualifying but Max Verstappen will start on pole as Antonelli will serve a five-place grid penalty for the Las Vegas Grand Prix after Mercedes fitted his sixth internal combustion engine of the season

Sky Sports F1 pundit Jamie Chadwick said she could understand why both drivers would be frustrated by the team's execution during qualifying.

Chadwick said: "The thing that I don't understand, and I think this is where Charles refers to the execution, he had no margin to make a mistake on that last lap. That's frustrating for him.

"And then on Lewis' side, he was always on his own. If they're saying that they're losing a second on the straight, at least stack the odds in your favour to have a slipstream and give yourself the best chance."

Sports.title: Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?
Sports.content:
They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.

But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.

It was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.

If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.

According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.

They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.

View image in fullscreen Brighton’s £3.5m midfielder Yasin Ayari challenges Enzo Fernández, who cost Manchester City £125m. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?

On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.

“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”

Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.

View image in fullscreen Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO and deputy chair, next to a model that combines the three different stadiums the club has used in the city. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be said of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.

Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics company founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”

When I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.

When the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.

Later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”

One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.

‘The numbers have to be right’

Before Brighton’s victory over City, I met Mike Cave, the club’s sporting director, at the Lowry hotel in Manchester. A few of the Brighton players wandered around in club tracksuits. Cave wore a suit and tie and his hair was slicked back. He was telling me it was a big day without saying it.

Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear about how it informs your decision-making process, then it’s just a lot of data that doesn’t move the dial.”

The power of data is that it strips away emotions and preconceptions. When watching games, Hürzeler said he often identifies a player he thinks is performing well and texts Cave, only to learn that the numbers don’t support his impression. The conversation ends. “The numbers have to be right otherwise we have no chance of getting a player in.”

Conversely, the data identifies players he might not otherwise have considered – such as Diego Gómez, the Paraguayan signed from Inter Miami in 2024. Despite the strength of Gómez’s underlying numbers, the club had a free run at signing him. Cave suggested this reflected a misconception that players in MLS aren’t equipped to play in the Premier League. “What the data has allowed us to do is step away from some of those biases and just be clear on what the evidence tells us, to look at the signal rather than the noise.”

View image in fullscreen Diego Gómez joined from Inter Miami for a fee of around £12m. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

But identifying a player who can perform for Brighton is different from identifying one who will, Cave said. The club’s requirements are so specific that the data typically identifies only around five candidates, Hürzeler says, and fewer still are affordable. Of those remaining, the recruitment team and Hürzeler will speak to anyone with experience of them – players, coaches and sponsors – to learn more about their character and personality, and prepare dossiers. Together, they’ll identify a primary target and make a move. “It’s not like I get a list and then decide which players; it’s something we all decide together,” said Hürzeler.

As Barber explained: “The more we can find out about a player’s character the less risk there is of that player being rejected like a bad organ transplant.” There’s no exhaustive list of desirable characteristics, he added, but “coachability” is key. Brighton’s model hinges on players having the capacity to improve, and the best indication is their drive to do so. “The biggest element of coachability is attitude.”

Hürzeler asks himself: “What are they willing to give for their development? Are they willing to suffer?” He’s convinced this desire is innate. “These are things I can’t control.”

Brighton's Fabian Hürzeler on what the club looks for when signing players – video

Conversations with people around Gómez painted a picture of “a boy that is clearly trying to get absolutely everything out of his career”, said Cave. But sometimes the qualities Brighton are looking for aren’t so obvious. Whereas the data is objective, says Barber, references are “someone’s opinion”. It’s challenging to know how much weight to give a single person’s negative judgment, particularly when it conflicts with other opinions, without dismissing it altogether. “Sometimes when you want to sign somebody you can subjectively screen out the negativity because you want them, and the data says you need them.”

Beyond character, the team consider a player’s ability to settle into a new country, and whether their partner will, too. Once Brighton make an offer, the player is normally keen to join, in Barber’s experience, because they know it can lead to a move to “potentially bigger things”. The selling club is often receptive because there are rarely any other comparable offers on the table.

View image in fullscreen A young fan eagerly accepts Diego Gómez’s shirt after Brighton’s win over Brentford at the Amex. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

But this has been changing, says Barber. Brighton’s success means their interest in a player “alerts other clubs to that talent”, creating competition. Selling clubs, meanwhile, have reason to believe that the player “has the potential to be valued for a lot more”. Increasingly, then, Brighton are having to pay more, making “our ability to trade profitably ever harder”.

Even if a deal can be agreed, it doesn’t always represent good business. As Cave explained: “You’re dealing with human beings, in a complex system and a complex game, so you will never have a 100% strike record.”

View image in fullscreen Disbelief among supporters as Diego Gómez’s spectacular strike puts Brighton ahead against Brentford. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Keep, loan or send on

Asked what Brighton looks for in recruits, Gordon Greer, who played for the club from 2010 to 2016, was quick to answer: “high potential”. But that potential rarely means they’re ready to slot into the first‑team. Today, as Brighton’s pathway development manager, Greer’s job is to bridge that gap.

To understand how Greer does this, I joined him for coffee at the Lowry. He told me that he begins planning a player’s development while the club are still negotiating his signing. “In the buildup to us signing him, we’ll start to analyse him … what’s his strengths, what’s his weaknesses … where do we think we can help?” Once he’s met the player and understood their ambitions, he turns that assessment into a development plan.

To begin, Greer explained, he asked himself: “What are this player’s limiting factors to play for Brighton?” Sometimes the answer lies off the pitch. Hürzeler requires his players to speak English. It helps embed his playing principles by allowing the players to transmit them to each other. “We want to have a common language, so they can coach each other on the pitch,” he explained. Other times the shortcomings are more directly related to football, such as back‑post defending. A typical one is physicality; Hürzeler’s counter-pressing requires repeated sprints and many recruits would risk injury if they were thrown into the first team. “The game is so fast, and the intensity is crazy,” Jack Hinshelwood, who made his first‑team debut in 2023, has said.

One pathway for development is the under-21s team, Greer says, but the physical demands of the game fall short of those in the Premier League. Hinshelwood, who came through the under-21s, suffered a stress fracture in his foot after a few top-flight games. “You need time to adapt,” he said. In Greer’s view, the level doesn’t challenge most recruits enough for them to learn. “We want to put them in a position where they’re stretched enough that they’re uncomfortable but they’ve got enough success that they’re doing things that they enjoy.”

View image in fullscreen Jack Hinshelwood says Brighton’s counter-pressing game is ‘so fast and the intensity is crazy’. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

An alternative is the loan market. Since 2018–19, Brighton have agreed more than 20 loan deals in each campaign. Playing time is an important consideration when arranging a loan, Greer explains, because a player’s value can drop if they’re not playing often. But he also considers the location, manager, formation and quality of the pitch. Position is crucial, too. Sending a striker to a team near the bottom of their league, where they’re likely to be living off scraps, can see their confidence and value drop, but sending a defender into the same environment can accelerate their development with repeated defensive situations. “You’re trying to get to a point where they’re impacting the game.”

A successful loan addresses a player’s limitations. “You’re trying to expose someone to something totally different,” Greer added. In 2017, Ben White – now of Arsenal and England – was loaned to Newport County to improve the “urgency in his defending”.
