“The game model was end‑to-end, back-to-front, League Two, where you’re up against it,” Greer added. In 2024, Ibrahim Osman, shortly after signing from Nordsjælland in Denmark, went to Feyenoord, a possession-based team, to develop his technical game. “Physically, he was a beast, but he was quite untidy,” said Greer.

Throughout a loan, each player is continually reassessed. Those ready are brought into Hürzeler’s first team. If they’re not, another spell elsewhere might be arranged. But if their development has stalled for too long, they’ll be encouraged to leave permanently. That was the case with Leo Østigård, a Norway international signed from Molde in 2018. He was a skilled defender but he “wasn’t good enough on the ball”, Greer said. His development slowed down during a loan at Coventry, and then, at Stoke, it became “clear he wasn’t going to be for us”.

Rather than continuing to work on Østigård’s weaknesses, the club sought to maximise his strengths. A loan was arranged at Genoa, a defensive team where Østigård would shine. A year later, he signed for Napoli. “We tried everything but it didn’t work,” Greer said, “so we thought: ‘How do we create as much value as possible?’”

‘You’re allowed to make mistakes’

After speaking to Barber, I headed to Brighton’s training base, a short drive away from the Amex, to meet Hürzeler. Academy players milled around outside, while the first team was elsewhere preparing to face Getafe in the Conference League, a competition Brighton are being tipped to win.

I noticed a mural bearing the words: “Challenge the Establishment,” a reference to the so-called big six clubs. A member of staff pointed out that the mural had been Hürzeler’s idea, but the philosophy it exhibits has existed since Bloom took over the club in 2009. Brighton, the member of staff whispered to me, saw themselves as the “antidote” to big-spending clubs such as City.

Before Hürzeler and I sat down in the press conference room, another journalist asked him whether he thought Brighton could win the title. He dismissed the question. His focus was improving the team, he said. He suggested to me, however, that victories such as that over City were the fruits of his work developing the squad and an environment that allows talents to excel. “If you work with players for a longer time, you get used to each other and they get more and more of your principles.”

View image in fullscreen Fabian Hürzeler requires his players to speak English. ‘We want to have a common language, so they can coach each other on the pitch.’ Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Hürzeler tells me he relies on older players who embody these principles, such as Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross. At 33, Hürzeler is younger than both, and became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in 2024. When you’re developing raw talents from abroad, while constantly selling and bringing in new players, you need a core group to “build the right culture”. Hinshelwood told me he has experienced this first-hand: “I remember watching their habits every day, how they live their lives, how they’re training, what they’re doing in the gym, how they’re communicating, and I learned so much just by watching them.”

Hürzeler also emphasised the importance of tailoring the support players receive. “You can’t treat a player like Yankuba Minteh who is coming from [the] Gambia the same as a player like Lewis Dunk, who comes from England,” he said. He wants to cultivate an environment in which, as he put it, players, “no matter which age, no matter from where they are coming from, can express themselves”.

To that end, Hürzeler appointed Mike Anthony, who spent 14 years working with New Zealand Rugby, as head of player development and high performance – a new role. One of Anthony’s priorities, he said, has been giving the players more responsibility. Players and the coaches increasingly “lead the programme together”, with players invited to lead discussions.

“They don’t want to just execute things, they want to be valued, they want to be appreciated, they want to be heard by us coaches,” Hürzeler said. “If you don’t give them ownership and responsibility off the pitch, how can you expect them to take responsibility for their own execution on the pitch? It’s not possible.”

View image in fullscreen ‘Challenge the Establishment’: a slogan at the club’s training ground sums up Brighton’s ethos. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

A key part of his role, Hürzeler told me, is listening to his players. It helps them perform, and makes him a better coach. He was reminded of this in February 2025, when there were calls for him to lose his job after a poor run that included a 7-0 defeat at Nottingham Forest. James Milner and Danny Welbeck suggested he was overcomplicating his messaging around counter-pressing. Taking their advice on board, he made changes that helped turn things around. “It was definitely one reason why we turned around the results.”

Asked why Brighton have such a strong record for developing talent, Hinshelwood smiled: “You’re allowed to make mistakes, not effort mistakes, or applying yourself badly, but if you make a technical mistake you know you’ve got 10 other players who want you to try things,” he said.

‘Revolutions cost a lot of money’

Hürzeler also credited the club’s summer recruitment with this season’s success. Yet Brighton had sold Jan Paul van Hecke to Tottenham and Baleba to United, I pointed out. How could a club expect to improve while selling their best players?

Although he often tries to prevent departures by convincing Bloom not to sell, Hürzeler said he has no final say. “I can’t control whether a player gets a big offer and Tony wants to accept this offer.” But he’s come to see departures as an opportunity to revitalise the squad with new profiles. “When you sign for Brighton, you know that it’s part of the identity, so automatically you have the mindset that you have to deal with these things.”

View image in fullscreen Tony Bloom, who took over Brighton in 2009, in a club hat and tie. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Being transparent about the club’s model with coaches is a crucial component in their success, according to Barber, but even then it can create tensions. The decision to sell Caicedo was one reason De Zerbi departed, as was the Italian’s insistence on big-name signings rather than trusting the data. It’s no different with supporters, Barber said: “Sometimes when a big player leaves a club and the fans are blindsided by that, it creates this bigger sense of injustice, anger, disappointment.”

Barber also explains that he must go to great lengths to keep costs down. “The difference between what we bring in and what we spend is what we put out on the pitch.” The club’s use of experienced players such as Dunk is ultimately driven by financial constraints. They can’t afford to sign players in their prime, either in transfer fees or wages, so rely on players a little past their prime to counterbalance the inexperience of their younger recruits. “They’re providing that level of experience of a 27-, 28-, 29-year-old, albeit four or five years later, but at a much lower cost.”

Brighton also use data to identify and recruit coaches whose philosophy aligns with the existing squad, minimising the need to overhaul the squad to fit a new style of football. Hürzeler was identified in large part because the numbers showed he could build on the players he inherited. “Revolutions cost a lot of money,” Barber said. “If you can match the coach that you’re bringing into the squad that you’ve got, the cost of change is minimal.”

The final part of the model is knowing when to sell. Barber tries to have a replacement through the door before letting a player go. It becomes trickier to negotiate a fee for a replacement when the selling club knows Brighton have just sold a player for £100m. Barber told me he delayed selling Caicedo until he was confident Baleba could step up. “We felt Carlos had a lot of potential that we could help to realise quite quickly … he’s a quick learner and quite raw, but at the same time you could see rapid improvements in him.”

But other factors matter too, such as whether a player still has room to develop, and therefore increase his value further; the state of the market; and the risk that turning down an offer might jeopardise the chance of a future sale. “If there is a dearth of central midfielders at the moment, maybe now is the time to sell because there will be a significant premium because there are no other options.”

Barber adds that refusing to sell Caicedo to Arsenal in January 2023 was easier because other clubs wanted him in the summer. “Not doing the deal didn’t affect our ability to do the deal with Liverpool and then Chelsea the following summer.”

The price of success

In their last match before the November international break, Brighton beat Brentford and leapfrogged City. They’d progressed in Europe too: a goal from Malick Yalcouyé, a £6m signing from ​​IFK Göteborg, had beaten Getafe. Outside the ground, fans were dreaming of titles. Barber said he hoped they would not have to wait much longer. “We now need to take the next step and put some silverware on the table.”

But if Brighton are to compete for major trophies, I wondered, will they have to invest more heavily in players, and keep them in their prime? Can the club’s current model allow them to become part of the establishment, rather than simply challenging it?

The club are already adapting, says Barber. The signing of Vuskovic for a club record £46m demonstrates an appetite for talents better equipped to immediately contribute to the first team. “Those players are already at a level of transfer fee that we wouldn’t have contemplated, and 10 years ago we wouldn’t have even considered.” As Jamestown’s algorithm improves, Barber says, he’s hopeful it will become easier for the club to invest these sorts of sums in players, because the risk of getting the assessment wrong will be lower.

But Barber believes player trading is likely to stay as the core of the club’s strategy, partly because they are good at it, but also because they need the revenue. “There’s always going to be this gap [in commercial sales and ticket revenue] so the need for us to trade will always be there.” Even if they did decide to keep players such as Baleba and Van Hecke, would they be able to? As much as a title or two might make it easier to convince top players to stay, Barber said he struggles to envisage a time when they’ll be able to compete with the bigger clubs on wages.

View image in fullscreen Brighton fans hope the club’s run of form can lead to silverware. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

And even if Brighton could one day afford to retain their best players, would it make them less attractive to the next generation of recruits, who might no longer see the club as a stepping stone on the way to the so-called establishment? Could the club become so successful that the prices of their targets rise beyond what they can afford? Might the model self-cannibalise?

Hürzeler tells me he reflects on these same questions. “It’s interesting, this discussion, because these kinds of discussions we also have in the building.” When we spoke on the phone before the Hull match, I brought up Hearts, who have partnered with Jamestown and came close to winning the Scottish title in May for the first time since 1960, challenging the Celtic-Rangers duopoly. I asked whether this gave him the belief that Brighton could go one step further and break the big clubs’ stranglehold.

“Of course, you see this as motivation for what is possible,” he said. He revealed a belief that he can lift a trophy with Brighton, which is why he has extended his contract to 2029. “When I see the team now, they are so into it, they are so committed to it.” He just wouldn’t say when. “Will it be this season? I don’t know. Will it be next season? I don’t know.” Beyond that, he tries not to give it much attention. “These kinds of questions, we can answer them one day.”

Sports.title: Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury
Sports.content:
Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted and the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, said that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”

The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, the first leg of which takes place in Norway on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.

Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

View image in fullscreen Bayern Munich’s coach, Vincent Kompany, returned with his arm in a sling after dislocating his shoulder last month. Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters

Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

“I think this result was fair and Cologne deserved the point,” Kompany said after the game. “We have other worries now, I have to honestly say. We will all try together to make something strong out of this situation. FC Bayern does that time and again, and that’s what we want to do now too.”

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone when Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane stays down holding his lower leg after a challenge from Cologne’s Joël Schmied. Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters

Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

The hosts levelled 17 minutes later when full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return for the second half and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig. El Mala, recently called up by Germany, then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.

Now a point behind Bayern, Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first place if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.

This month Kane signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029, which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.

Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

Sports.title: Premier League news: Moyes demands more from Grealish, Iraola wary of United threat
Sports.content:
1. Moyes: ‘I want Jack to show more’ David Moyes has said he wants Jack Grealish to produce more for Everton as he prepares to reintegrate the playmaker into the squad. Grealish has missed Everton’s past four games mainly for disciplinary reasons having failed to report for training before last month’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle. His last appearance for the team was in the 2-0 loss to Chelsea on 17 October but he is fit and available for Monday’s visit to Brentford. “He has served his punishment and we will treat him as we were treating him before,” the Everton manager said. “We will get on with things. The team is doing really well at the moment and what I don’t want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn’t be.” The 31-year-old played in a behind-closed-doors fixture against Derby last week andalso apologised on social media for being unable to help the team, who won three of four matches in his absence. Grealish, however, had struggled to replicate last season’s form impact when joining on loan from Manchester City prior to his breach of discipline. And Moyes is demanding more. He added: “Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, more goals. There’s lots of things about him which we need and he’s good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need. I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we’re hoping to get that again.” The Everton manager has backed Jordan Pickford to respond strongly to the threat from James Trafford to his England place, following after the Leeds goalkeeper’s inclusion and impressive display in the Nations League win over Spain. “I don’t think it will have a great effect on him,” claimed Moyes. “If you’re playing for England you will always have other players chasing you. I still think Jordan Pickford is out there on his own at the moment. If anything, he’s getting better. It will be good for us now that he’s getting competition [with England].” Andy Hunter

2. United better than place in table, says Iraola Andoni Iraola has said Liverpool must disregard the latest turmoil at Manchester United and treat Sunday’s visitors like the team that thrived under Michael Carrick last season. Sunday will be the first time since March 1937 that United have faced Liverpool in a league game at Anfield while languishing in the relegation zone. Mauricio Pochettino could start his United reign bottom of the table should results on Saturday go against his new club. Iraola never lost in six league meetings with United as Bournemouth head coach. Before his first taste of the fixture with Liverpool, he insisted his north-west rivals are in a false position. “United finished third in the table last season. You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season,” Iraola said. “Now we have just started, it is just 10 games. For sure, they will be a lot higher in the table [soon]. We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third. “We have to look at ourselves because we need the points. We need to improve our home form. It is also a big game in terms of relevance. It’s Liverpool v Manchester United, this is the biggest one in English football, so we want to play well and we want to win.” Iraola was boosted this week by the returns of Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni to training after serious knee injuries, although the two defenders are not yet ready for consideration. “We think they will have two weeks on and off with the group,” he said. “Then it is going to be a matter of whether we organise something behind closed doors, 11 v 11, or they straight away play with the under-21s. Before they start playing with us they have to go through that.” Liverpool’s other long-term absentee, Hugo Ekitiké, remains on course to return in January from an achilles injury. Andy Hunter

3. Alonso concerned by growing injury list Xabi Alonso has admitted Chelsea’s injury list is a concern. The club have a lighter schedule after their failure to qualify for Europe but they are struggling to keep players fit and have a host of selection issues before Saturday’s home game against Leeds. The Brazil striker João Pedro is yet to return from a thigh injury, Reece James is unlikely to recover from knee surgery until the new year and the France centre-back Maxence Lacroix is out with a long-term hamstring injury. Alonso is having to adjust. Jorrel Hato is unavailable in defence with a back injury and the England Under-21 winger Jamie Gittens, who has made five league starts for Chelsea since joining for £51.5m in the summer of 2025, has been out since September. “It’s a concern,” Alonso said of the injuries. “Sometimes you can analyse them and find a reason but sometimes it is difficult to find a reason.” Alonso has made 24 changes to his lineup in his first 10 league games. “It depends on the context and adaptability. I adapt to the circumstances. With the injuries you don’t have a choice. Once you have the whole menu, you can select what you like and I know what I like from the menu.” Chelsea have failed to score in three of the four league games João Pedro has missed this season. They have also had to monitor Moisés Caicedo closely, with the midfielder minding a muscle issue. But Alonso wants his side to become less reliant on Caicedo and João Pedro. “We want to have a complete squad,” he said. “That’s the goal of any manager. We have built a good squad. We are a better team with them. But it’s not about making a big drama when someone is out.” Jacob Steinberg

Sports.title: Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino is obsessed with what he calls energia universal, a guiding life force that influences everything, touching on concepts such as karma. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.

Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.

“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.

Why are United turning now to a manager they have previously overlooked? Pochettino is not about to dwell on that because he is in dream-come-true territory. He will love how the United support stand behind their manager, especially in troublesome times. He will love the pageantry and event glamour of Old Trafford. And he will love having Ferguson in the crowd for the matches.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino had a good relationship with Kylian Mbappé when he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain. Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA

Pochettino first encountered him in January 2013 when, in his second Southampton game, he went to Old Trafford to face Ferguson’s United, who won 2-1. Pochettino has mentioned that this week. And the meal at Scott’s. And how he was at the Camp Nou for Ferguson’s finest hour: the 1999 Champions League final victory against Bayern Munich. Pochettino was an Espanyol player at the time, together with Toni Jiménez, who is part of his coaching staff, and they watched the first half from so-so seats before blagging their way into the directors’ box for the second period.

When Solskjær scored his iconic late winner, Pochettino and Jiménez celebrated wildly. They were caught up in the moment. It was the first time Pochettino felt a connection to United and he began to pay more attention to them. And Ferguson. Pochettino described him this week as “the best coach in the history of the sport” but it was not a soundbite of convenience. He has always maintained this and said so on the record after the lunch at Scott’s.

How can Pochettino position himself in terms of the Glazers and Ratcliffe? The first thing to say is that he does have experience of unpopular and/or difficult owners. At Spurs, Daniel Levy was forever maligned by the fans, and Pochettino had problems with the American ownership at Chelsea. Between times, the Qataris at PSG were not easy. Pochettino worked to build a relationship with Levy, regularly saying nice things about him in the press and famously including him on a staff-bonding trip to Argentina.

It featured white-water rafting and ended with Pochettino having to fish Levy out of the Manso River. A repeat of the adventure with Joel Glazer feels unlikely but Pochettino’s starting point at United has been to stress unity; the need to create chemistry with everyone, including “the directors and the owners”.

And so to Anfield, where Pochettino first managed with Southampton in September 2013 when his team won 1-0. He has not tasted victory in his eight subsequent trips; seven with Spurs, one with Chelsea, the record shows two draws and six defeats. No United fan expects anything this time but Pochettino considers it a great game to have. He will certainly learn a lot about his players.

Sports.title: Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet
Sports.content:
Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.

“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”

Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.

View image in fullscreen Dele celebrates scoring for Spurs against Arsenal in 2018. Photograph: Alex Morton/Getty

To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.

“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”

Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.

By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.

“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”

But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.

View image in fullscreen Dele Alli during his time with Como. He made one appearance, off the bench against Milan, and was sent off nine minutes later. Photograph: Paolo Bruno/Getty Images

He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”

When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.

In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.

His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.

In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

Dele, according to those close to him, is biding his time to get his next move right. He will be 31 in April and wants a suitable contract. He has spoken to a host of clubs, with interest from the Premier League and the Championship, and from the Middle East, where he has been tempted by the riches of the Saudi Pro League, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. There has also been interest from Major League Soccer and he has held talks with clubs in Brazil and Japan. It is believed he will join a club this season.

View image in fullscreen Dele on debut for England, a Euro 2016 qualifier against Estonia in October 2015. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

In preparation, Peters is also guiding Dele’s nutrition, though he does not require much guidance. “Del’s a weird one, because he doesn’t snack, he doesn’t eat unhealthily, he doesn’t have a Sprite or a Coke or whatever. He’s never really been that kind of guy. All he does is drink coconut water, and he’ll have a small lunch, or his cheat day will be a Nando’s or something.”

Happiness is his priority. He spoke candidly on Gary Neville’s The Overlap in 2023 about his struggles with mental health and an addiction to sleeping pills after revealing abuse as a child. “Because he’s had such a long time out, he’s like: ‘What’s another few months if it means that I’m going to find something I’m actually happy with?’” Peters says. The aim is to “carry on for as long as possible”.

For the time being, Dele’s days are simple. When not training, he goes for coffee or a swim, and he has taken up padel. “He’s very much a person that’s happy with the little things,” Peters says. “He’s always the person that’s positive, the one that, if the group’s down or whatever, is going to pick everyone up. He’s happy with what he’s doing. His main happiness is playing football, and that’s what he wants to do.”

Sports.title: Tom Brady in talks over buying Chelsea stake after Birmingham City exit
Sports.content:
Tom Brady is in discussions about buying a small stake in Chelsea. The NFL legend sold a minority share in Birmingham City this month after three years, a move sources said was to pave the way for investing at Stamford Bridge.

Brady was a guest of Chelsea when they won the Club World Cup in New Jersey last year and was seen celebrating with the players after their remarkable 3-0 final win over Paris Saint-Germain.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner is understood to have a good relationship with Behdad Eghbali, whose fund, Clearlake Capital, owns 86.5% of Chelsea after Todd Boehly and Mark Walter sold their shares in September.

Brady bought into Birmingham in August 2023, less than a year after his second and final retirement from the NFL, after the club’s takeover by Tom Wagner’s Knighthead Capital.

Brady was appointed chair of the club’s advisory board and had a prominent role in the 2025 Amazon Prime documentary Built in Birmingham: Brady & The Blues, which made headlines when he questioned the “work ethic” of Wayne Rooney, who was the manager.

In announcing Brady’s departure the club said: “Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.”

Brady owns a minority stake in the NFL team Las Vegas Raiders, which he purchased alongside Wagner.

Chelsea declined to comment.

Sports.title: Arsenal’s Lisa Baum: ‘I believe in us. I think it’s all about the small margins’
Sports.content:
Lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” says Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”

That win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

View image in fullscreen Lisa Baum celebrates after scoring 10 minutes into her Arsenal debut against Brighton. Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

“I believe in us,” says Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”

Overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

Quick Guide Taylor: Pro Ref says Liverpool goal against Arsenal should have stood Show The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, says Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield. The Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays showed the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL. Taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, said on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she says. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she says. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”

View image in fullscreen Lisa Baum, in action for Arsenal at Anfield, played for RB Leipzig last season. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

She started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a big fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent said she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

“Everything was just so quick,” she says of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”

The transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” says Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a big stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”

View image in fullscreen Lisa Baum with the wrist strap she wears in memory of her brother, Dennis. Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty Images

Look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

The brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she says. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”

Sports.title: Pat Cummins to remain captain despite Sandpapergate claims after Cricket Australia's unanimous vote of confidence
Sports.content:
Australian Test captain Pat Cummins will remain skipper of the team after a 'unanimous' vote of support from the Cricket Australia board.

Cummins said the backing, expressed during a meeting with Cricket Australia interim chair David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg on Friday, 'meant a lot', according to ABC News.

The show of support follows ongoing speculation over who knew about ball-tampering during Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa, with recent claims prompting questions about Cummins' leadership.

'It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility,' Cummins said in a statement on Saturday.

'I have and never will take that lightly.

'David and Todd have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this, and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.'

Australian Test captain Pat Cummins will remain skipper of the team after a 'unanimous' vote of support from the Cricket Australia board

It followed almost a fortnight of speculation about the Sandpapergate scandal after retired batter Usman Khawaja claimed in a newly released autobiography that the entire Australian team knew about the planfor ball tampering in South Africa in 2018

Cummins said the backing, expressed during a meeting with Cricket Australia chair David Boon (right) and chief executive Todd Greenberg (left) on Friday, 'meant a lot'

Mr Boon also published a statement regarding the vote backing Cummins, according to The Daily Telegraph.

'We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa,' he said.

'We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised.

'We are absolutely determined to steward Australian Cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn,' Boon said in a statement on Saturday.

'That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there.

'We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course.'

Earlier this week, CA announced that it would establish a forum for players and staff to share their accounts of the Sandpapergate scandal that rocked Australian cricket eight years ago.

It followed almost a fortnight after retired batter Usman Khawaja claimed in his newly released autobiography that the entire Australian team knew about the plan to use sandpaper in South Africa in 2018.

Pictured, Khawaja and Cummins during day five of the Third Test match in the series between Australia and India at Melbourne Cricket Ground in 2018

The aim of the 'circuit breaker', according to CA, is to allow players and staff involved in the events to share their experiences and perspectives.

Cummins said on Saturday that he would be in attendance but highlighted his focus was returning to upcoming matches.

'I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there,' the captain said in a statement.

'All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what's needed.

'Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority.'

Earlier on Saturday, fellow cricketer Josh Hazlewood had spoken out in defence of Cummins amid suggestions his captaincy might not survive the Sandpapergate saga.

The 35-year-old warned Code Sports that removing Cummins would divide the squad and described how there had been a 'bit of a pile on the last few days from different people'.

Looking ahead to Australia's first Test against New Zealand, which is scheduled for December 9, he suggested that if the team turned up Cummins wasn't the captain, then there could be fractures, saying: 'Honestly, I don't know how that would go.'

Cummins said on Saturday that he would be in attendance of the CA's forum, which has been set up to allow players and staff to share their experiences

It came after claims by Usman Khawaja, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft over the last fortnight that other members of the Australian team knew about ball tampering in South Africa eight years ago.

On Friday, former Australian fast bowler Mitchell Johnson suggested Cummins's 'personal brand' and role as captain may not survive the scrutiny he has faced.

'I believe Bancroft's account. It comes across as real and I could feel the words as he was saying them,' he wrote in the West Australian.

'The pressure on Cummins is now immense. I think he will still try to stand by what he has said. But I think the public pressure for Cummins to stand down as Test captain now will be too much.

'I just can't see how his captaincy and personal brand survives this.'

Cummins has repeatedly denied having prior knowledge of the plan to alter the condition of the ball during the 2018 Cape Town Test.

When he fronted the media on November 13, he also directly challenged Khawaja's claim that the team knew.

'When he says "We all knew", if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong,' Cummins said.

Cummins, Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon had previously addressed what they knew during the Cape Town Test in a joint statement issued on May 18, 2021.

The four said they 'did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball' until they saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

Sports.title: Josh Hazlewood breaks ranks to defend his captain Pat Cummins as Sandpapergate claims escalate
Sports.content:
Cricketer Josh Hazlewood has spoken out in defence of Pat Cummins amid suggestions his captaincy might not survive the Sandpapergate saga.

Cricket Australia is set to publicly back Pat Cummins to remain Test captain this weekend, despite claims by Usman Khawaja, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft that other members of the Australian team knew about the alleged sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago.

Hazlewood, 35, has warned that removing Cummins would divide the squad and described how there had been a 'bit of a pile on the last few days from different people'.

The comments were made in an interview with Code Sports on Saturday, during which the fast bowler was asked if he would consider leaving the team in protest if Cummins were removed.

'I think I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it,' Hazlewood said.

'I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

Cricket Australia is set to publicly back Pat Cummins to remain Test captain this weekend, despite claims by Usman Khawaja, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft that other members of the Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago

Josh Hazlewood (pictured with wife Cherina Murphy-Christian) has spoken out in defence of Cummins

'To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that is never going to happen again, I think is just a remarkable job. He's a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.'

Hazlewood warned that, if Australia turned up for the first Test and Cummins wasn't the captain, that there could be fractures among teammates, saying: 'Honestly, I don't know how that would go.'

He also denied knowledge of the sandpaper plan but said he sympathised with Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith, who were sanctioned over the plan.

'Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field? The answer is no,' he said.

'When it boils down to it I think those two points are crucial.

'Assuming everyone knows and actually knowing everyone knows, that gap is huge... That's a big chasm.'

On Friday, former Australian fast bowler Mitchell Johnson suggested Cummins's 'personal brand' and role as skipper may not survive the scrutiny he has faced.

'I believe Bancroft's account. It comes across as real and I could feel the words as he was saying them,' he wrote in the West Australian.

The ball-tampering plot came to light following the 2018 Cape Town Test

The debate over the scandal was reignited after Usman Khawaja suggested in his newly released book Sabr that the entire team may have known about the use of sandpaper

'The pressure on Cummins is now immense. I think he will still try to stand by what he has said. But I think the public pressure for Cummins to stand down as Test captain now will be too much.

'I just can't see how his captaincy and personal brand survives this.'

The debate reignited after Khawaja suggested in his newly released book Sabr that the entire team may have known about the ball-tampering plot rather than just those officially sanctioned by Cricket Australia following the 2018 Cape Town Test.

Khawaja claimed a player experimented with sandpaper on a ball in the Port Elizabeth dressing room. 'Everyone… was laughing their heads off,' he wrote, adding that Bancroft then volunteered to do it.

Cummins has repeatedly denied having prior knowledge of the plan to alter the condition of the ball during the 2018 Cape Town Test.

When he fronted the media on November 13, Cummins also directly challenged Khawaja's claim that the team knew.

'When he says "We all knew", if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong,' Cummins said.

But just days later, in a more than 4,000-word essay, Bancroft claimed he used sandpaper nearly every over in the final session and continued using it for the rest of the Test.

Khawaja claimed a player experimented with sandpaper on a ball in the Port Elizabeth dressing room

'I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers - Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh - about whether it was reverse swinging enough,' he wrote in The West Australian.

Bancroft said he also sought feedback from wicketkeeper Tim Paine. As the wickets fell, he recalled teammates telling him: 'Great work Bang. Keep it up.'

He claimed his use of sandpaper was discussed in front of the group the following morning and that he received encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff.

Cummins, Hazlewood, Starc and Nathan Lyon had previously addressed what they knew during the Cape Town Test in a joint statement issued on May 18, 2021.

The four said they 'did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball' until they saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

Following Bancroft's lengthy essay, Cummins' manager Neil Maxwell said on Thursday that the Australian captain remained firm in his position, which he has maintained since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Maxwell said Cummins had never wavered in his account of events over the past eight years.

He acknowledged that Cummins felt sympathy for Bancroft, who had endured significant difficulties in the aftermath of the scandal.

Cricket Australia said on Wednesday night it would take time to examine Bancroft's claims before making any further comment.

Maxwell also encouraged people to revisit Cummins' previous interview transcript, insisting the Test skipper had already addressed every question put to him, including those raised by Bancroft's latest comments.

He credited Cummins with helping transform Australian cricket, saying the young player who made a commitment to turn things around in Cape Town had spent the subsequent eight years working towards that goal.

Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann, who was in charge during the scandal, has also promised to address the allegations in the coming days.

Cricket Australia said on Wednesday night it would take time to examine Bancroft's claims before making any further comment.

In a statement, the governing body said it respected Bancroft's decision to share his account and recognised there could be different perspectives on the events of 2018.

It pointed to the independent forum it had established, which will give players and staff involved in the tour a confidential opportunity to provide their own accounts.

Cricket Australia will determine what information can eventually be released publicly after seeking independent advice, with Bancroft indicating he is willing to participate.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: The grubby antics of JJ Gabriel's entourage threaten to derail his career before it's begun. Man United insiders tell a revealing story about his acrimonious exit
Sports.content:
We should start with the video. It’s something to behold. Opening with a scene that depicts a young footballer being ushered through a crowd of faux reporters, there is a promise within the first five seconds of ‘epic news’ and ‘a rare discovery’.

It’s a little on-the-nose, but the messaging will only escalate. Soon we find ourselves staring at what appears to be a Ballon d’Or replica, before the director cuts to a moody shot of the footballer from behind as he stares at a wall of photographs.

Those images are showing a few of the staging posts in his brief career to date – signing for Manchester United aged 10, posing with a ball and, then, one of him preparing to come on as a substitute. A pair of Nike boots find their way in.

Finally, the lad shows himself and delivers a single line to camera: ‘I am epic.’

This came out at the start of the week. Our epic footballer? That would be JJ Gabriel, aged 16 years and one month, still in braces, and potentially the best you’ve not yet seen.

As you have likely heard, he really is that good. And as you will also know, the mechanisms of his exit from United ahead of an imminent deal with Real Madrid have been ugly.

JJ Gabriel, aged 16 years and one month, still in braces, and potentially the best footballer you’ve not yet seen

The video Gabriel released this week announcing his exit from Manchester United includes signing for the club at the age of 10 alongside Cristiano Ronaldo Jr (Source: Instagram/Jjnr10)

Finally, the lad shows himself and delivers a single line to camera: ‘I am epic’ (Source: Instagram/Jjnr10)

But let’s momentarily keep to that bizarre video, which has been watched almost two million times on Gabriel’s Instagram page, and from there we can raise the question of whoever thought it was a good idea.

This is where we should introduce Ali Barat, the owner of Epic Sports. He’s a big fish in the world of football agencies and the 31-second clip was advertising their latest coup: Gabriel had joined his group, which is timely because a move to Real is imminent and that will follow other big deals brokered by Barat.

They include Moises Caicedo to Chelsea for £115million, Noni Madueke to Arsenal for £52m and Dean Huijsen to Bournemouth for £12.6m, then on to Real Madrid for £50m more. He’s a significant figure with a changeable definition of what it means to be understated. Here’s an example from his company’s website: ‘While some agents seek the spotlight, Ali Barat is quietly reshaping the transfer market.’

Amusingly, it then goes on to describe Barat as a ‘super-agent’ twice in the same paragraph while declaring he is ‘not just closing deals, he is building careers, guiding legacies, and setting the standard for a new era of football representation’.

The ‘quiet’ part was possibly lost along the way. But ‘legacy’ is the word among that salad most worthy of fixation, because Gabriel has been steered to a series of pivotal decisions at an incredibly young age.

He is yet to play a single minute of competitive senior football but he is clear on what he wishes to become. Earlier this month, his handlers felt it prudent to place him in an interview with the Madrid-based newspaper Marca and Gabriel said: ‘My dream is to win a Ballon d'Or.’

Fair enough. He’s a teenager aiming high. Is it wise to say so? Maybe not, but he’s 16. Barat, the super-agent, has no such excuse. He’s 30 years older than his client and saw no harm in a video that invoked the Ballon d’Or to peddle an academy kid.

There’s less ambiguity in the wisdom of what Barat has done there. It reeks. It carries the stench of an agent who evidently doesn’t mind so much if the labels attached to Gabriel today stick for the remainder of his career.

Earlier this month, his handlers felt it prudent to place him in an interview with the Madrid-based newspaper Marca and Gabriel said: ‘My dream is to win a Ballon d'Or’

Gabriel's representative Ali Barat, who is 30 years older than his client and saw no harm in a video that invoked the Ballon d’Or to peddle an academy kid

I can remember when Mauricio Pochettino once made the blunder of placing Marcus Edwards, a Tottenham wonderkid, into the same sentence as Lionel Messi. His point was that he had some similar movement patterns, but the fact the lad was named mini-Messi in training didn’t help – it was a tag that endured.

Thankfully, Edwards has carved out a respectable career at Burnley via Sporting in Portugal, but Pochettino regretted the words as soon as they left his mouth.

That’s different to designing and releasing a video, of course. That’s different to a process involving some level of sign-off. That’s different to the grubby act of hyping a very young guy to a standard reached by only five Englishmen in history.

A question at this stage: where was Gabriel’s family when this was being decided? That’s somewhat loaded because there is chatter about how much of the United separation has been driven by Gabriel’s father, Joe O'Cearuill, formerly a professional himself for Brighton, Barnet and the Republic of Ireland.

I’d add that many of those noises have originated from within Carrington. It might simply be the bitter discourse of the jilted. But a recurring sentiment among some United staffers is that the father became difficult during the breakdown in relations.

These are lines we have heard before in football. But for once, United do not appear to have done much wrong. There was genuine care for the player. And if there is one thing they can guarantee, it is that young talents get a good chance, though evidently not enough to please Gabriel’s camp.

A demand for minutes against Azerbaijani side Sabah in the Champions League was a bad look; similar might be said with less force around reports that he changed his name from Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill for commercial reasons, feeding one of those blurry conversations about where the athlete ends and the product begins.

Gabriel’s early days with Epic and Barat and his content wing do not serve much encouragement on that front.

Gabriel's father Joe O'Cearuill was briefly in Arsenal's reserves before going on to play for Brighton, Barnet and the Republic of Ireland

United do not appear to have done much wrong. There was genuine care for the player. And if there is one thing they can guarantee, it is that young talents get a good chance

It is worth stating that the teenager at the heart of it all is not considered to be a bad sort. Far from it.

None of his ascent was accompanied by the worrying noises that followed another prodigy in Ravel Morrison – once described by Sir Alex Ferguson as having 'as much natural talent as any youngster we ever signed', but who made all of three League Cup appearances for United before a journeyman career through the Championship, Italy, Mexico, Sweden, the Netherlands, the US and the UAE.

One source has suggested Gabriel even cried when he said his goodbyes back in September.

It might be over-reaching to claim he has left the club against his own better judgment, but there is no doubt he has gambled hugely on Real Madrid.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is pretty handy and has found it tough there; Martin Odegaard is a far closer parallel to Gabriel having moved to Madrid aged 15, and he played 11 games in three seasons.

If the pathway was blocked at United, then what is it at a club who employ Vinicius Junior, Rodrygo, Yan Diomande, Arda Guler, Endrick, Brahim Diaz, Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe in Gabriel's positions?

A new language and surroundings are large hurdles for a young player, especially one whose ambitions are so public and grand. It won’t be a quiet arrival by any definition, even those found in the quirky dictionary of Ali Barat, and the pressure will be significant.

Hopefully such factors don’t impact upon an exciting trajectory. That would be an epic shame.

If United's pathway was blocked, then what is it at a club with (L-R) Vinicius Junior, Jude Bellingham, Rodrygo, Kylian Mbappe and plenty more in Gabriel's positions?

A new language and surroundings are large hurdles for a young player, and hopefully such factors don’t impact upon an exciting trajectory. That would be an epic shame

Welsh Rugby Union's 20,000 reasons to be ashamed

Among the joys of this job is being present at rare moments of sporting greatness. The Welsh win over the All Blacks last weekend was one such occasion and, for me, it was compounded by a subsequent email from a lovely chap named John Evans, aged 87 and from Tredegar in Blaenau Gwent.

John had watched the game on television, but was part of what must be a dwindling group who could say they were there the last time Wales had beaten New Zealand, at the Arms Park in 1953.

After detailing how he, ‘a small-bottomed outside-half’, had left himself with no view of the pitch at the back of the stand, John went on to recall that the crowd around him and a friend ‘decided to pass us over everyone’s head back down to the front’. He landed just in time to see Ken Jones score the winning try. His excitement in sharing a memory from 73 years ago was spelled out in block capitals.

One of the consequences of the ongoing shambles at the Welsh Rugby Union is that there were 20,000 empty seats at the Principality Stadium last weekend, mainly due to a combination of apathy and protest. Accordingly, there will be 20,000 fewer people with a great story to tell decades from now. While the WRU ponder their next blunders, they might wish to consider some of the above.

Sports.title: 'Some things Henry Pollock does, I wouldn't want our guys to do': The All Blacks coach behind 'no d***heads' mantra on how he's given New Zealand stars the 'edge' to take down England after Wales humiliation and a death in the camp
Sports.content:
'Some things Henry Pollock does, I wouldn't want our guys to do': The All Blacks coach behind 'no d***heads' mantra on how he's given New Zealand stars the 'edge' to take down England after Wales humiliation and a death in the camp

It was shortly after buying Chelsea that the club’s former owner Todd Boehly read a book on the All Blacks. Boehly was impressed by Legacy, which leant heavily on the philosophies of Gilbert Enoka – the architect behind New Zealand’s ‘no d***heads’ rugby philosophy.

Boehly, who was busy spending billions trying and failing to transform Chelsea into the best football team in the world, instructed his team to hire Enoka whatever the cost. But when he arrived at Stamford Bridge, Enoka discovered all the money in the world could not buy the one thing Chelsea desperately needed: a strong culture.

Having joined the All Blacks in 2000, working with everyone from Tana Umaga to Richie McCaw and Dan Carter, Enoka was used to excellence. He found life in the Premier League to be short of the high standards he’d experienced previously.

‘They had just signed Enzo Fernandez and we were living in the same hotel in Cobham,’ says Enoka, who recently returned to the All Blacks management team as mental skills coach and has had the task of picking up a team reeling from a humiliating first defeat by Wales for 73 years, ahead of Saturday’s Test with England at Twickenham.

‘Chelsea had a legacy but it just wasn't being nourished by the current custodians. John Terry was around the club – passionate, connected and wanting to do things – but everyone was just trying to get stability. They hired some people on horrendous money. They gave Graham Potter a five-year contract but 200 days into it, he was gone.

'Before 2007, every time an All Black coach had failed to win the World Cup, they were gone. In 2007, the chairman looked at Graham Henry, Wayne Smith and Steve Hansen and said: “These guys aren't bad coaches." He reappointed them and all of a sudden, we won the World Cup in 2011 and 2015.

Gilbert Enoka, the architect of New Zealand’s ‘no d**kheads’ philosophy, is back working with the All Blacks after stints with Chelsea and the England cricket team

New Zealand need picking up from their humiliation last weekend - a first defeat by Wales since 1953

'I believe the first English football club to genuinely adopt an All Black-esque type culture will get a significant advantage. Chelsea were hamstrung because they couldn’t get it right at the top. Players would turn up to meetings and no one would have a notebook. You come to a meeting here with the All Blacks and every single person will have a tablet or a book.

‘With the All Blacks, the legacy is more intimidating than any opposition. We leverage off that hugely. Whenever you're getting a group together in the All Black environment, you are engaging who they are, who they represent and how they want to be perceived.'

Sipping on a coffee and wearing his trademark flip-flops at the Lensbury Hotel in Teddington, Enoka is back in his most cherished environment, after New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie asked him to return in March.

‘Dave wanted to get people who had been through the traps a bit,' he says. 'The last two years haven't been pretty for the group. The results were OK but the culture was very challenging. My wife pushed me into it and said, “The jersey needs you”.’

This month’s tour has been particularly challenging. Five days before playing Scotland in their first match of the autumn leg of the Nations Championship, New Zealand’s long-serving head of security, Logan Cadwallader, died at the team’s hotel in Edinburgh.

The sudden loss brought last Saturday’s defeat by Wales into perspective, and Enoka is the man responsible for overseeing the team’s emotional recovery.

‘We've just been through the death of one of our colleagues, which rocked the group immeasurably,’ he says. ‘Something tragic happened inside our tent, so we spent some time helping them to understand what happens in the brain and in the body when you go through trauma.

'A lot of the guys said, "How can I concentrate on rugby when I've got a mate who's just died?” We gave them some tools and techniques to manage the inevitable waves that will come their way. We helped them understand you can grieve and you can reconnect with rugby at the same time. We had to give people time to cry, to talk, to share and to grieve. We're still going through it now.

Long-serving All Blacks head of security Logan Cadwallader (right) died at the team’s hotel in Edinburgh before the Test against Scotland this month

Enoka with Sir Graham Henry (left) and Steve Hansen (centre), the architects of the All Blacks' dominant 2010s era of success, at New Zealand training this summer

'Logan was a big part of us. The funeral has been held until December 8 when we’re back. Tragedy can fracture you or strengthen you. It's been tough and it’s tightened us up.

‘This is my 24th year with the All Blacks. I've been through everything. We lost to Wales last week. In that same Cardiff stadium, we lost to France in the quarter-finals of the 2007 World Cup – the worst result in history. All of a sudden, you climb the other mountain and four years later you're winning a World Cup by one point.

‘Losing to Wales hurt and we scrutinise every performance heavily. We run the stethoscope over the beast. We had to sit back and have some fairly free and frank conversations about why we weren't able to get across the line.

‘Your skillsets don't work if your mindset's not right. You never lose your skills, all you lose is access to them. And pressure does that. We had played against Scotland in a very tumultuous week for the group. At the end of that game, when everybody finished, there was a collective sigh.

'I can still feel us getting on the plane, leaving Edinburgh, feeling, “Wow, what a week”. So you then start saying: “Well, where was your mindset? Did you take mental breaks on Sunday and Monday?” Because your performance on Saturday starts with your mentality on a Monday.

‘You never accept defeat. You can drop your lip and you can feel sorry for yourself for 24 hours but after that, you've got to turn and look forward. We’ve not moved on but moved forwards with the lessons. Wales were passionate and played tremendously well, but we didn't live up to our standards. It has given us an edge. We’ll be a different beast this weekend, which is exciting.’

The All Blacks have welcomed back their big hitters for England. Their backline should be razor sharp thanks to the return of Damian McKenzie, Jordie Barrett and Will Jordan. However, without injured captain Ardie Savea, their pack does not have the same clout as the English.

Twelve months ago, England roared past Scott Robertson's New Zealand 33-19 at Twickenham. The Kiwis have an entirely new management team now but the memories remain fresh. Henry Pollock licked his lips throughout the Haka before England dominated the aerial contest.

Henry Pollock licked his lips during the Haka before last year's Test between England and New Zealand. 'People who don't understand the Haka will do exactly what Pollock did,' says Enoka

Enoka also had a stint with the England cricket team last summer as he had worked with fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum in the past

‘It’s interesting because the Haka is never about the person on the other side,’ says Enoka. ‘People who don't understand the Haka will do exactly what Pollock did. People who understand our culture will know the Haka is calling on our ancestors from all the aeons of time to come up through the earth, fill our souls and be with us in battle. It's all about the brothers either side of you.

'It’s nothing to do with that person over there. People that don't understand it will walk forward, get agitated and do all this other stuff. It doesn’t really matter to us what the opposition do.’

So, would Pollock meet the All Blacks’ cultural standards? ‘He’s a different personality, isn't he? We’re looking at the behaviours that enhance the legacy and the behaviours that are not in line. Some of the things he does, I wouldn't want one of our guys to do. I may not be right. But I've had 24 years inside this environment so I've got a reasonable idea of what it takes to make it tick.’

In many ways, Enoka, who also had a stint with the England cricket team last summer as he has worked with fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum in the past, is one of the founding fathers of the modern All Blacks aura.
