World.title: Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
World.content:
It has been more than three years since war erupted in Sudan, and its consequences continue to worsen. More people continue to be displaced and require basic humanitarian assistance to survive. On the surface, the conflict appears set to continue indefinitely.

At a recent Security Council briefing, a United Nations official noted: “The picture is bleak. … The parties continue to show no credible commitment to compromise or to pursuing a negotiated pause in fighting. They are not moving closer to dialogue.”

This assessment reflects the international consensus so much so that the United States has chosen in recent months to heap sanction upon sanction in a bid to “raise the costs of continued conflict” for the warring sides and force them into ceasefire talks. But what the view from New York and Washington misses and what became obvious after only a few days in Khartoum this month is that the conditions for a ceasefire are rapidly emerging from within the country.

A perfect storm of financial collapse, military advances and humanitarian catastrophe, along with growing civilian demands, is creating the long-elusive pressure for a ceasefire that could well take hold before the fourth anniversary of the war next April.

Khartoum, Sudan’s beleaguered capital, is no longer the ghost town that it was throughout much of the war. International flights now arrive regularly at the city’s modest airport from Cairo, Riyadh and Doha, carrying Sudanese looking to restart the lives the war put on hold and businessmen sensing a ceasefire on the horizon and angling to get in on the ground floor of the country’s rebirth. At one of the city’s leading business hotels, the lobby was buzzing with British, Swiss and Saudi business groups there to close deals on everything from mining to commodity trading to reconstruction.



But Sudan’s leaders don’t just see the opportunities; they are also feeling the pressure of an economy in freefall. The week I was there, the Sudanese pound fell to a then-record low of 9,000 to the US dollar, compared with a pre-war average of 600. (The exchange rate now exceeds 10,000.) Petrol queues stretched for blocks, even for those lucky enough to be able to afford to fill their tanks. Many of Khartoum’s returnees, more than 2 million of the roughly 3.8 million people who fled, are struggling to buy groceries and keep the lights on. Worse still, farmers can no longer afford fertiliser, leaving much of the country’s most productive cropland lying fallow.

A senior official acknowledged to me privately that the war economy, which enabled Sudan’s army to procure the weapons needed to turn the tide of the war, is now the greatest source of pain for the country’s population. The pressure on Sudan’s leaders to reverse the economic decline is real and is creating a new demand to end the fighting.

Friendly states like Turkiye and Saudi Arabia have pitched in, pursuing agreements to secure fuel supplies and rebuild energy infrastructure, but such support remains limited and temporary. Protests over transit costs recently broke out in Atbara, the northern city where protests against skyrocketing bread prices began in December 2018, helping to spark Sudan’s 2019 democratic revolution. Economic protests unified the country before and could do so again, and the military knows it.

Beyond the economy, it is the military’s battlefield gains that are creating the conditions for it to contemplate a ceasefire. Army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has promised to reclaim “every inch” of territory. He has succeeded in pushing back a new offensive in southeastern Sudan’s Blue Nile State and is advancing farther west in West Kordofan, where the army and its allied Joint Forces recently retook the strategic town of el-Khuwei and several surrounding areas, increasing the army’s control to roughly two-thirds of the country.

Fighting for control of the western region of Darfur, the only region almost entirely under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary, could be costly and time-consuming. But a year after the fall of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur State, to the RSF amid atrocities that a UN fact-finding mission said bore the hallmarks of genocide, efforts to retake the area would demonstrate that the military’s commitment to unify the country wasn’t just battlefield bravado. Making inroads in Darfur would also paint the RSF into a corner and give the army both tactical gains and a strategic advantage in ceasefire discussions.



The final reason why a ceasefire has become so urgent is the spiralling humanitarian crisis in the country, which has been at crisis levels for months but could well become catastrophic by year’s end. Adding to the internal displacement, restrictions on humanitarian access and lost food production is this year’s “Super El Nino”, which has disrupted Sudan’s annual rains and devastated whatever meagre harvest was expected.

With more than 40 percent of the population already facing “acute food insecurity”, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification hunger monitor, projections suggested that Sudan’s hunger crisis could deteriorate dramatically by mid-2027 when food shortages are expected to be at their most severe. The only way to avoid or even mitigate that outcome would be through a ceasefire in the coming months that enables a massive influx of lifesaving aid.

As conditions on the ground make a ceasefire more urgent, Sudan’s own plans for the day after the fighting are becoming clearer. With each ceasefire proposal the military rejects, public demand for a deal grows as people become increasingly exhausted by the war.

Talk of an inter-Sudanese dialogue, political reconciliation and eventually elections is also becoming more common, creating greater expectations that fighting should soon come to an end and responsibility for day-to-day governance and service delivery be transferred to civilians. While these efforts remain inchoate, the demand for them is building.

Ultimately, it is the attitudes inside Sudan that will create the momentum for peace, not the external pressures and punitive measures employed by the international community. As conditions for civilians inside the country continue to deteriorate and the military’s position stabilises, there is hope on the horizon that a ceasefire could be achieved. The international community should focus on supporting these internal conditions before the dire warnings about the economy and humanitarian situation become reality.

A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
World.content:
Politics is not for the faint-hearted, and debate and disagreement are integral to it. A number of politicians believe that the end justifies the means, but most know when they are approaching the red lines and when to stop.

Not Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s current prime minister. His repulsive response to the success of the Arab parties in last month’s general election unleashed his darkest racist demons.

Some might argue that this is simply another cynical tactic in his efforts to derail his political rivals’ attempts to form a government. Whether this is who he really is or simply a cynical politician at his core, governing through division makes little difference.

He is the prime minister, and his words and behaviour matter. When he legitimises and normalises this kind of language, he releases the racist genie from the bottle. Certain segments of his supporters may interpret it as a licence to resort to actual violence, and history has precedent for it.

Accusing all 19 elected members of the Knesset (MKs) representing predominantly Palestinian citizens of Israel, individually and collectively, of being supporters of terrorism and terrorists, while portraying those members of the Jewish/Zionist parties prepared to form a coalition with them as, for all intents and purposes, collaborators with those who support terrorism against Jews and seek the destruction of the “Jewish state”, amounts to declaring open season on them. In doing so, Netanyahu is abusing the protection afforded to him by his parliamentary immunity, making allegations for which there is not a shred of truth.



If anyone should know better, learn from his past mistakes and express profound remorse for such behaviour, it is Benjamin Netanyahu. No one is more closely associated with the atmosphere of incitement that preceded the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin on November 4, 1995 than Netanyahu.

Rabin became the principal target of the Israeli right’s hatred after signing the Oslo Accords – in other words, for demonstrating the courage to pursue a peaceful end to the conflict between Israelis and Palestinians. The religious-messianic right, including several rabbis, issued a ruling known as din rodef (the law of the pursuer) against Rabin, accusing him of “ceding parts of the Land of Israel to Gentiles”. Yigal Amir, Rabin’s eventual assassin, cited this ruling as justification for his heinous crime. Amir pulled the trigger, but those who orchestrated and fed the campaign of hatred against Rabin bear considerable responsibility too, at the very least morally.

Netanyahu, who was chairman of the Likud party and leader of the opposition at the time, not only failed to condemn this behaviour but notoriously participated in a protest in Jerusalem during which Rabin’s image was portrayed in a Nazi uniform. Rabin’s widow, Leah, later recalled: “There was a Likud rally in Jerusalem not too long ago. They put the figure of Yitzhak, my husband, in the uniform of a Nazi leader and Mr Netanyahu was there. He later talked against it, but he was there, and he didn’t stop it.”

She never forgave him for that. He never apologised or expressed regret.

Several months later, Netanyahu was elected prime minister. Perhaps, in his mind, this electoral victory exonerated him from any responsibility for creating the atmosphere that led to Rabin’s assassination. It may also have reinforced his belief that divisive politics pays off and can take him where he has always felt he belongs: The prime minister’s office.

Now, caught between a sense of entitlement to remain in power that appears stronger than ever and the fear that relinquishing office could jeopardise his efforts to prevent his corruption trial from reaching its conclusion, Netanyahu is allowing racial hatred to pour out of him unabated.

It began during the election campaign, when he foresaw that his chances of forming the next government were slim. It escalated dramatically on election day, when he once again resorted to his vile dog-whistle tactics in a last-ditch attempt to mobilise his supporters. He warned of surging Arab voter turnout and, by that, at least implicitly questioned the legitimacy of their votes compared with the Jewish ones, as they couldn’t bear their success. But that was only the beginning. The day after the election, Netanyahu and his ultra-right-wing partners turned up the volume, raising allegations of irregularities in Arab communities to advance a narrative of a “stolen” election.



Worse was to come. What should have been days of celebrating Israeli democracy, the swearing-in of the new Knesset, became another opportunity for Netanyahu to abuse his parliamentary privilege. Instead of delivering a speech that might have helped unite the nation after a bruising election campaign, he embarked on a jingoistic horror show.

He accused Gadi Eisenkot, whom President Isaac Herzog had tasked with forming a government because he enjoyed the support of a majority of MKs, and his political partners of seeking to establish a government dependent on parties that, according to Netanyahu, “agree that the Jewish state must be destroyed”. He went on to claim that these parties differed only over the kind of Palestinian state they wanted to see emerge from the ruins of the Jewish state: “Whether an Islamic state in the Muslim Brotherhood mould, like Hamas in Gaza, or a nationalist Palestinian state in the Fatah mould. That is the whole difference.”

This amounts to nothing less than portraying Arab political representatives as a fifth column or traitors, while depicting those prepared to form a government with them as collaborators with this supposed ambition, or as dangerously naive for failing to recognise it.

When Netanyahu and his political partners insist that their accusations are not directed at the Arab population, even though Arab citizens had voted in record numbers for these very parties only days earlier, they are either playing innocent or insulting the intelligence of both Arab citizens and the wider public.

Not so long ago, Netanyahu himself offered Mansour Abbas and his Ra’am party the opportunity to join his own government when it suited his political interests. Yet when his rivals contemplate doing precisely the same thing, he shamelessly incites against them.

Let us not forget that Netanyahu is the politician who legitimised the messianic far right and normalised sharing power with its representatives in government. He appointed Itamar Ben-Gvir, who had been convicted of incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organisation, as minister of national security. This is the same Ben-Gvir who first gained notoriety by stealing the emblem from the car of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, displaying it on television and declaring: “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him too.” Netanyahu is opportunistic and cynical to the very end, but by now the distinction between him and the Kahanist Ben-Gvir has become paper-thin.

The warning signs are there, written on the wall in capital letters. The incitement of 1995 helped create the atmosphere that led to Rabin’s assassination. The scale and intensity of today’s incitement could once again lead an extremist zealot to pull the trigger, this time against an Arab or Jewish politician seeking to work with Arab political representatives. It could also encourage attacks against Arab citizens, potentially escalating into widespread communal violence or even civil war, as extremists convince themselves that they are acting in accordance with their leader’s wishes to prevent the supposed destruction of the Jewish state.



Israel is on the brink of political violence. And Benjamin Netanyahu bears a very substantial share of the responsibility for bringing it there.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
World.content:
As negotiations over the formation of Israel’s next government approach their first deadline of December 6, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be seeking to exploit divisions within the opposition “change” alliance trying to oust him.

On Wednesday, he held an undeclared meeting with one of its leading figures, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, in a move that has prompted accusations that Netanyahu is attempting to fracture the bloc from within.

The meeting, which lasted two and a half hours, was described by Netanyahu’s office as a “security briefing”. Sources within the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, however, characterised it as a “strategic disaster”, according to Israeli media.

Bennett had not informed Eisenkot of the meeting in advance, sources told the outlet Ynet. During a subsequent gathering of opposition leaders, Bennett is reported to have argued that they should try to pursue the possibility of a unity government with Netanyahu, Channel 12 reported.

Bennett, a right-winger, is among several prominent figures in the opposition alliance who have previously served in Netanyahu-led governments. Eisenkot himself joined Netanyahu’s emergency unity government following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, serving as a minister without portfolio and a member of the war cabinet.

Avigdor Lieberman, meanwhile – another right-wing member of the opposition bloc – served as Netanyahu’s foreign minister and defence minister.

“Netanyahu is trying to break up the [opposition] bloc for change through Bennett,” a senior figure in the Eisenkot-led alliance told Ynet in an article referencing the numerous pledges by opposition leaders, including Bennett, never to serve within a Netanyahu-led coalition again.

However, given the broad array of ideologies among the coalition leaders, stretching from the hard-right policies of Lieberman to the relatively left-wing platform of Democrats’ leader Yair Golan, and many having previously worked with Netanyahu, it remains unclear how long the bloc can maintain its unity.



Bennett himself was once among Netanyahu’s closest political allies, serving in several of his governments before breaking with him in 2021, when the opportunity arose to form an alternative administration with centrist Yair Lapid. Bennett and Lapid subsequently assembled a cross-party coalition that ended Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office, with Bennett taking the premiership for the first half of its term. But he still shares many policy positions with Netanyahu.

So how cohesive is the opposition coalition, and what could be its potential breaking points?

Here’s what we know:

Is the change bloc united ideologically?

All of the bloc’s members supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – at least at its start – as well as its attacks on several regional states, including Iran and Lebanon.

In terms of domestic policy, however, there are marked differences between members of the alliance.

Both the bloc’s leader, former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, and Bennett’s electoral partner, Yair Lapid, are regarded as relatively centrist figures. By contrast, Bennett and Lieberman are firmly on the right, divided largely by their attitudes towards religion: Bennett is a religious nationalist, while Liberman is a staunchly secular politician with a background in Israel’s Russian-speaking community, increasingly at odds with Israel’s powerful religious political currents.

Standing apart is the left-wing Yair Golan, a supporter of a two-state solution with the Palestinians and an outspoken critic of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which he has accused the government of encouraging or tolerating.

Is the alliance under strain?

Yes.

Beyond the prospect of Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – continually attempting to undermine them, Eisenkot faces the formidable task of finding the additional 13 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. His bloc holds just 48 of the parliament’s 120 seats after the October 27 elections, leaving him dependent on bridging deep political divides among his allies if he is to form a government capable of governing.

Golan has already met political leaders from parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel and spoken enthusiastically about forming a government with their support. However, that suggestion has been rejected by the rest of the bloc, and has provoked fierce opposition, with right-wing protesters even threatening civil war at the prospect.

Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beytenu party holds seven seats, has been particularly emphatic in rejecting any government dependent on Palestinian support. However, his longstanding and highly vocal opposition to the de facto exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service appears to be softening in the face of another possibility: the 13 seats held by the ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism.



Lieberman’s willingness to compromise on conscription risks undermining one of his central electoral promises, as well as those of other opposition leaders, and could prompt a backlash from supporters.

Have the change bloc’s differences come out in the open?

In August, Bennett dismissed Eisenkot’s proposal to allow limited exemptions from military conscription that would cover the ultra-Orthodox as an “insane mistake”, warning that ultra-Orthodox politicians Aryeh Deri and Moshe Gafni would “run circles around” him. Eisenkot subsequently countered, accusing Bennett and Lieberman of engaging in “old politics” and damaging the opposition’s electoral prospects by refusing to agree that the largest party in the alliance should lead the next government.

Lieberman, just weeks before the election, branded Eisenkot “Gantz 2.0” – referring to former defence minister Benny Gantz, who joined Netanyahu’s government in 2020 despite campaigning against him – accusing Eisenkot of secretly pursuing a deal with Netanyahu and acting out of personal ambition. Golan, meanwhile, told Lieberman several days after the election that, if he was to continue to insist on a government that avoids conscripting ultra-Orthodox men, he was “welcome to form one with Netanyahu”.

What did change bloc leaders say about Netanyahu before entering the opposition?

Their previous assessments of Netanyahu have not always been so harsh.

In 2020, Bennett told reporters that, despite their personal differences, he respected Netanyahu “very much”, adding that Israel had “won a victory” by having him in office for so long and that he had “done great things” for the country.

Lieberman, meanwhile, told The Jerusalem Post in 2019 that he wished Netanyahu “only really good results” and hoped that he would be acquitted on the corruption charges that he has since cited, on numerous occasions, as evidence that the prime minister is unfit for office.

World.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
World.content:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

World.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
World.content:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

World.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
World.content:
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

World.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
World.content:
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," said France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.

Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."

But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.

Arguing that this COP was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their power to come from electricity by 2035.

This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn by 2035 - that has now been removed.

"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

World.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
World.content:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

World.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

World.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
World.content:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent AlpÃ¶ge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

World.title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
World.content:
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."

Kaplan disagreed.

"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.

Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.

He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.

Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.

The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (Â£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

World.title: Solomon Adeola’s chance to build Africa’s largest subnational economy, By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
Ogun’s moment is real, but it is not guaranteed. The state’s proximity to Lagos is an advantage only if it is matched by superior policy. If Adeola pairs ambition with discipline, treats private enterprise as a partner rather than a patron’s reward, and publishes his results for all to scrutinise, Ogun could do more than catch up. It could set the standard for what a Nigerian state can become.

As it stands, Senator Solomon Adeola’s clear mandate from voters, as the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate in Ogun State, is within reach. But he must begin preparing for what lies ahead. The most crucial issue for Ogun is job creation through private sector development, and that is precisely where Adeola should start once elected next year.

Now that the panic over his family background has subsided, he should stay on course with his plans for the state. Perhaps the strongest argument in his favour is that the onslaught of criticism he has endured since becoming the candidate to beat, much of it from the opposition and internal adversaries, has revealed his mettle. They seem to believe they can kill his candidacy by throwing shade or confusing the electorate.

I am not an Adeola acolyte. I have never met the man or anyone around him since I first wrote, a decade ago, projecting him as a future governor of Ogun. But I am as pro-Ogun development as I am pro-Nigeria’s greatness. His policy decision-making prowess can galvanise economic development through the private sector, provided it is deployed without the cronyism that stains Nigerian politics.

It was remarkable, then, that he reiterated this vision at Friday’s manifesto conference at the June 12 Cultural Centre, Kuto, Abeokuta. In “Governance That Works for Everyone: My Economic and Social Development Covenant with the People of Ogun State,” Adeola outlines infrastructure development, human capital, agricultural transformation and industrialisation as the bedrock of jobs and a stable economy. He might yet make history as the governor who builds the largest state economy in Africa.

Why the Private Sector Must Lead

The logic is simple arithmetic. The World Bank Group estimates that private firms provide roughly nine in ten jobs in developing countries. No state payroll, however generous, can absorb a young and growing population. Governments set the rules, build the roads and guarantee the contracts. Firms hire workers, buy inputs, pay taxes and compound growth.

Ogun already has a head start. It ranked second only to Lagos in Phillips Consulting’s 2025 State Performance Index, with analysts crediting its manufacturing base and position as a logistics corridor. The National Bureau of Statistics’ figures show its internally generated revenue (IGR) rising from ₦100.7 billion in 2022 to ₦140.1 billion in 2024, driven largely by land transactions, factory levies and logistics taxes. Private capital is also arriving: a $1.8 billion Lee Group industrial park on the Lagos–Ibadan Expressway is expected to host more than 29 factories and generate some 2,500 direct and indirect jobs.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Yet strength in revenue is not strength in fiscal health. Despite an impressive IGR, the overall fiscal performance index remains poor and debt is mounting. BudgIT’s 2026 State of States report puts Ogun’s total debt at ₦538.92 billion. That is the central tension of the next administration: Ogun cannot borrow its way to greatness. It must invest, regulate and incentivise its way there. Yes, skeptics will say that Ogun’s rise so far owes more to Lagos spillover and land-driven revenue than to broad gains in productivity. They have a point, and that is precisely why transformation, not restoration, must be the standard.

The California Lesson

California is the world’s fourth-largest economy, trailing only the rest of the United States as a whole, China and Germany. Its rise was not engineered by government spending alone. Private enterprise in technology, entertainment, agriculture and trade built it, on a foundation of public universities, ports, predictable regulation and secure property rights. The state’s role was to enable, not to crowd out.

Ogun can learn from this. It has ports and airports in its manifesto, a dense manufacturing belt, fertile land, and a large, youthful population. Most of all, it has the opportunity to take back what Lagos harnessed from it: people and land. Lagos grew by absorbing the overflow of Nigerian ambition. Ogun, sitting at its border with cheaper land and a wider expanse, can offer that ambition a better address.

What Transformation, Not Restoration, Demands

Restoration means repairing roads and clearing arrears. Transformation means changing the state’s economic structure. That requires five disciplined commitments.

First, reliable power. Adeola has promised 24-hour electricity in Abeokuta. A factory cannot plan around a generator. Dependable power is the cheapest incentive a government can offer, and the most credible.

Second, a frictionless investment climate. A one-stop approvals system, transparent land titling and swift dispute resolution would do more for investor confidence than any tax holiday. Capital goes where rules are clear and enforced.

Third, an end to cronyism. Contracts must be awarded openly and judged on merit. An economy built on political patronage rewards connections over competence and drives away serious investors. This is where Adeola’s reputation will be won or lost.

Fourth, deeper value chains. Ogun’s agricultural land should feed agro-processing plants, not just markets. Affordable credit for small and medium enterprises, which employ most Nigerians outside government, would let local firms grow into suppliers for the industrial parks rising around them.

Fifth, a skills pipeline. Factories need technicians, not just labourers. Aligning technical colleges and training programmes with the needs of industry would ensure that jobs created in Ogun go to Ogun’s young people.

Accountability is the Multiplier

Adeola has promised that his manifesto will be translated into measurable plans, with agencies assigned performance targets and regular public reporting. That promise deserves to be held to the letter. Investors do not merely read manifestos; they read audited accounts, delivery timelines and the consistency of policy from one year to the next.

Ogun’s moment is real, but it is not guaranteed. The state’s proximity to Lagos is an advantage only if it is matched by superior policy. If Adeola pairs ambition with discipline, treats private enterprise as a partner rather than a patron’s reward, and publishes his results for all to scrutinise, Ogun could do more than catch up. It could set the standard for what a Nigerian state can become.

The mandate is within reach. The harder work is deserving it.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving global businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: Lagos increases HIV response budget to N1.07bn
World.content:
The Lagos State government has increased its HIV response budget to N1.065 billion, up from about N791 million.

The 35 per cent increase is to strengthen prevention, testing and treatment services across the state.

Folakemi Animashaun, Chief Executive Officer of the Lagos State AIDS Control Agency (LSACA), disclosed this on Thursday at a news conference in Lagos to herald activities for the 2026 World AIDS Day commemoration.

World AIDS Day is commemorated annually on 1 December to raise awareness about HIV/AIDS, remember those who have died from AIDS-related illnesses and renew commitment to ending the epidemic.

Ms Animashaun also said the agency had begun distributing Antiretroviral (ARV) medicines procured by the state government to ensure uninterrupted treatment for people living with HIV.

She said the increased budgetary allocation and medicine procurement demonstrated the state’s commitment to domestic ownership and sustainability of its HIV response amid changing global funding conditions.

“Development partners have made invaluable contributions to HIV prevention, treatment, medicines, laboratory services and community programmes,” she said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“However, our goal is not to replace partnerships but to build a stronger foundation for them and ensure that essential HIV services remain protected whenever external funding arrangements change,” she said.

The LSACA chief executive said the state’s consolidated HIV testing records showed 387,558 negative results and 7,584 positive results.

She clarified that the figures represented reported test results and should not be interpreted as new infections or necessarily as unique individuals.

According to her, the maternal health programme recorded 156,122 new antenatal care clients and 156,109 negative HIV test results among pregnant and breastfeeding women.

She said community-based services also recorded 25,167 HIV tests among persons aged 15 years and above between January and October, with 1,166 positive results.

Ms Animashaun said the figures demonstrated the scale of the state’s interventions but stressed that the ultimate measure of success was the number of people linked to treatment, retained in care and achieving improved health outcomes.

“The significance of testing lies not only in identifying HIV but in connecting people to the services that protect their health and wellbeing,” she said.

Collaborations

Ms Animashaun said the state was strengthening collaboration with ministries, departments and agencies, healthcare institutions, development partners and community organisations to improve programme implementation, coordination and accountability.

She added that supportive supervision and data-quality activities had been undertaken to identify gaps in service documentation, referrals, programme reporting and continuity of care.

She said the agency was also promoting the integration of HIV services into routine healthcare, particularly maternal and child health, tuberculosis and other essential services.

She emphasised the importance of protecting the dignity and rights of people living with HIV, noting that stigma and discrimination remained significant barriers to accessing healthcare.

“No one should be afraid to seek healthcare because of their HIV status. No one should be denied dignity because of a health condition,” she said.

“Also, no one should be made to feel that their HIV status diminishes their worth as a human being.”

On sustainability, she disclosed that Lagos State had advanced the development of a 10-year HIV Response Transition and Sustainability Roadmap covering 2027 to 2036.

She said the roadmap would provide a framework for strengthening domestic financing, healthcare delivery, human resources, medicines and diagnostics, programme information, community participation and institutional accountability.

According to her, the proposed roadmap is expected to be formally launched by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu at the World AIDS Day Symposium scheduled for 1 December, subject to necessary approvals.

She said the symposium would also feature the formal presentation of antiretroviral medicines procured by the state government.

On HIV prevention, Ms Animashaun urged residents to know their status and access appropriate preventive services, including condoms, HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), where indicated.

She explained that people living with HIV who maintained effective treatment and an undetectable viral load could not transmit the virus sexually, a principle known as Undetectable Equals Untransmittable (U=U).

The LSACA boss urged residents to seek professional advice promptly if exposed to HIV, noting that some preventive interventions were time-sensitive.

World AIDS Day activities

Ms Animashaun said this year’s World AIDS Day activities, with the theme: “Ending AIDS Starts with Access: Equity, Ownership and Sustainability”, were designed to promote awareness, inclusion and community participation.

She listed the activities to include a fitness walk and awareness rally on 19 November, a novelty football match at Campos Stadium, Lagos Island, on 21 November, and an empowerment programme for people living with HIV on 23 November.

Others include a Jumat service on 27 November, a church service on 29 November, and the World AIDS Day Symposium scheduled for 1 December at Balmoral Event Centre, Lagos.

READ ALSO: Nigeria records decline in HIV treatment among pregnant women

Ms Animashaun urged the media to support efforts to correct misconceptions, challenge harmful stereotypes and promote accurate information about HIV prevention and treatment.

“Your platforms have the power to correct misconceptions, challenge harmful stereotypes, encourage people to seek testing and treatment, and help dismantle the stigma and discrimination that continue to prevent people from accessing care,” she said.

She called for responsible reporting that respected confidentiality and distinguished between new HIV diagnoses and new infections.

The LSACA chief executive acknowledged the contributions of the federal government, the National Agency for the Control of AIDS, UNAIDS, the United States Health Assistance Office, the Global Fund, and other implementing partners to the state’s HIV response.

She also commended the state government, healthcare workers, civil society organisations, community-based groups and networks of people living with HIV for their contributions.

She reaffirmed the state’s commitment to expanding access to HIV services, protecting existing gains and ensuring sustainable treatment and care for residents.

(NAN)

World.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa in three months
World.content:
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country’s latest crime statistics.

The statistics, released by the South African Police Service (SAPS) on Friday, showed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September.

About 131 of them were from Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg.

South Africa reported a series of killings in Ekurhuleni, a metropolitan municipality east of Johannesburg, Gauteng Province, between July and September 2026, in which 13 women were murdered and their bodies dumped in public spaces.

The victims were found in various locations, including Kempton Park, Tembisa, Boksburg, Olifantsfontein and Springs. Several were partially naked and had visible bruises and other injuries.

On Thursday, the police in Gauteng province said that eight suspects had been arrested.

Five women and a toddler were also killed in the Free State province on Wednesday. They were murdered by three masked men in the township of Botshabelo, according to the police.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The trio allegedly stormed a house in search of its owner, and when they realised he was not there, they “forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside.”

South Africa has a high femicide rate. The crisis is not limited to isolated incidents of murder by strangers: a substantial proportion of women are killed by current or former intimate partners.

According to the police minister, Firoz Cachalia, South Africa needs “greater efforts to protect women and children from violence.”

READ ALSO: 17 killed in separate South African mass shootings

South Africa also has a homicide crisis. It has perpetually dealt with a high rate of gun violence and homicide.

Two separate mass shootings last week led to the deaths of 17 people. Another 27 people were killed in separate attacks.

Between April and June, South Africa recorded around 5,427 homicides, mostly in its poor districts. The country reported an average of nearly 60 homicides a day.

World.title: Court orders removal of Tukur Ribadu as ADC governorship candidate
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja has nullified Tukur Ribadu’s emergence as the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate for Adamawa State and ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to restore Omar Suleiman as the party’s candidate.

Judge Obiora Egwuatu on Friday ordered the ADC to “forward Mr Suleiman’s details to INEC for publication as its governorship candidate.” He also directed the commission not to “recognise or publish” Mr Ribadu’s name as the party’s candidate.

The court also restrained Mr Ribadu “from parading himself as the ADC governorship candidate for Adamawa State.”

He made the order while giving judgement in a suit that followed the party’s decision to replace Mr Suleiman, who emerged as the winner of its governorship primary, with Mr Ribadu. Mr Suleiman challenged the substitution, insisting that he won the primary and that the party had no lawful basis to replace him.

Before considering the substantive dispute, Judge Egwuatu dealt with preliminary objections filed by the ADC and Mr Ribadu.

The ADC had asked the court to strike out the case, describing it as incompetent, statute-barred and an abuse of court process. Mr Ribadu also sought its dismissal for want of jurisdiction.

Among their arguments was that Mr Suleiman’s written address exceeded the page limit prescribed by the Federal High Court’s Election Proceedings Practice Directions. They said the address ran to 17 pages instead of the permitted 15.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But Mr Suleiman opposed the objection, arguing that the excess pages did not justify striking out the suit.

The judge acknowledged that the address exceeded the prescribed limit by two pages but refused to strike it out. He held that doing so would not serve the interests of justice.

The ADC also argued that the suit relied on a constitutional provision that did not apply to the party. Judge Egwuatu rejected the argument and said that he could not establish that the suit was incompetent at the preliminary stage.

The defendants further argued that the suit was statute-barred because Mr Suleiman failed to file it within the 14 days prescribed for pre-election matters under the Constitution.

They contended that he should have instituted the action earlier rather than wait until 6 August, when he filed the suit.

But the judge held that the action commenced within the constitutional time limit.

The defendants also argued that Mr Suleiman failed to exhaust the party’s internal dispute-resolution process before approaching the court.

The judge rejected this argument, reasoning that requiring the plaintiff to pursue the party’s internal process would have caused the 14-day constitutional period to expire. He held that Mr Suleiman was entitled to approach the court to protect his rights rather than allow the time limit to lapse.

No valid basis to replace him

On the merits of the case, the judge considered whether Mr Ribadu had challenged the primary election through the ADC’s appeal committee and whether the committee was properly constituted.

Mr Suleiman had argued that there was no properly constituted appeal committee and no evidence that Mr Ribadu appeared before such a committee to challenge the primary election result.

The ADC and Mr Ribadu maintained that an appeal was filed and that the committee reviewed the result before the party’s National Working Committee adopted its report.

According to their argument, the appeal committee submitted its report to the National Working Committee, which considered it and issued a resolution on 29 May.

Mr Ribadu also maintained that his name was submitted to INEC following the party’s decision to review the disputed result.

The judge examined documents from an earlier suit involving another aspirant, which Mr Suleiman relied on to support his position. The documents included processes filed by the ADC and statements by party officials who supervised the primary election.

He noted that the party’s processes in the earlier case did not disclose that Mr Ribadu had petitioned the appeal committee or that the committee had decided any such petition in his favour.

The judge also considered affidavits from the chairman and secretary of the ADC’s Adamawa State primary election committee and held that the officials denied that an appeal committee had been constituted to review the governorship primary.

The judge further relied on the primary election committee’s report, which stated that no petition had been received when it submitted its report. The report also recorded that no violence occurred at the election venue.

The court found no evidence that Mr Ribadu had successfully challenged the primary result through the party’s appeal process. It consequently upheld Mr Suleiman’s claim that he emerged as the winner of the primary and that the party had no “valid basis to replace him.”

Suleiman’s emergency and substitute

Mr Suleiman, a former managing director of the Nigerian Ports Authority and former Nigerian ambassador to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, won the ADC governorship primary in Adamawa State in May, defeating Mr Ribadu.

Reports of the primary election showed that Mr Suleiman polled 143,216 votes across the state’s 21 local government areas. Mr Ribadu came second with 56,801 votes, while another aspirant, Umar Uba, scored 20,343 votes.

In late May, the chairman of the party’s Adamawa State Governorship Primary Committee, Nicholas Msheliza, announced the results and declared Mr Suleiman the winner.

However, the party’s national leadership later endorsed Mr Ribadu as its candidate, despite Mr Suleiman’s victory at the primary. The decision prompted Mr Suleiman to take the dispute to court.

World.title: Somalia expels UAE ambassador, recalls envoy from Abu Dhabi
World.content:
Somalia has ordered the United Arab Emirates (UAE) ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and has withdrawn its envoy from Abu Dhabi, citing a violation of its sovereignty.

The African State announced the measure in a broadcast on the state-run news agency on Thursday, according to Reuters.

The Information Minister, Abdifatah Mohamud, said, “Measures will also be taken against anyone who cooperates ‌with the UAE in the invasion of Somalia.”

“All Somalis are urged to defend their country and unite against the open invasion of the UAE against the sovereignty, security, land and unity of Somalis.”

This move further heightens the tension between the states. This is the strongest measure Mogadishu has taken against Abu Dhabi since it annulled every agreement with the Gulf state in January. The cancelled agreements included seaport operations and security cooperation.

However, Somalia did not specify what provoked the expulsion.

But on Tuesday, Somalian President Hassan Mohamud accused the UAE of giving economic and political support to regional Somali governments to oppose the federal government.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said Abu Dhabi signed agreements related to the ports of Berbera in Somaliland, the breakaway region in northern Somalia that declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but remains internationally unrecognised.

It accused the UAE of signing agreements related to the ports of Bosaso in Puntland and Kismayo in Jubaland with regional administrations, not the federal government.

Somalia’s president also said the UAE helped to establish military bases and forces outside Somalia’s national command while the army is fighting the al-Shabaab armed group.

The UAE, which has helped fund and train Somalia’s military in the past and has backed ports and other commercial ventures there, has long denied meddling in the country’s affairs.

However, the UAE denounced what it called the Somali government’s “escalatory and hostile” approach towards it.

In a statement, the UAE foreign ministry said it regrets Somalia’s attempts to drag the UAE into its internal power struggles and noted that the actions could harm bilateral relations between the two countries.

World.title: The big three in Yalta-like summit to calm unsettled waters, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
US President Donald Trump touched down in Shenzhen, Southern China, like a rain-soaked chicken. His wings had this month been clipped by massive Democrat victories in the midterm elections. Not his usual swagger, as if he owns the world. He travelled for a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday, 19 November.

Trump had eliminated the Iranian leadership but failed to conquer the Iranians who today hold firm to the Strait of Hormuz, giving passage to only ships they grant permission. Nine ships which, a few weeks ago, tried to circumvent the Iranians were disabled.

The attacks on Iran had increased the global cost of oil and energy. Trump had also abducted a sitting President, Nicholas Maduro, and his wife right inside their bedroom in Caracas and introduced chaos in world markets with tariffs that can best be described as insane. Generally, he has made the world unsafe. Now, he was in China to see how a world he has contributed to set adrift can be anchored.

The excitable Trump seemed wowed by the reception he received when he touched down: “This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody… And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing.”

Trump said he and the Chinese and Russian leaders are uniquely positioned to reduce the world’s nuclear weapons stockpile and lessen the risks that they will ever be used. He said that the power of having such weapons can be intoxicating, which is why the US wants to deny Iran the ability to produce them. In 2026 estimates, the USA and Russia hold about 8,000 nuclear warheads, and China, 600.

Trump also condemned “rogue globalist organizations.” He named the International Criminal Court as one of those and also referred to the Russo-Ukrainian War.

He said the trilateral was history-making, adding: “Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements…We feel the opposite.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Host Jinping maintained his generally dignified composure. He did not react to claims by Japan and Taiwan about alleged Chinese and Russian aggression. He simply told Trump to “do the right thing” about Taiwan, over which China has historical claims.

Jinping agreed that nuclear weapons should be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, warning that there can be no victory in a nuclear war. On the importance of the meeting, he said: “History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil.”

On conflicts around the world, the Chinese President said: “China, Russia, and the United States should continue encouraging parties to conflicts to sit down and engage in talks, and resolve disputes through political and diplomatic means.”

Just before the trilateral, the US had imposed further restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, and the latter had pledged to retaliate. The Chinese leader had in response said: “We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment…China is a country of etiquette and has a tradition of reciprocating courtesy.” This tradition was seen in practice when participating leaders from countries like Australia, South Korea and Canada were welcomed at the airport by gaily dressed children, dancers and soldiers hoisting rifles. But the Japanese Prime Minister, Sanae Takaichi, who had in 2025 said Japan could deploy its military against China if it attacks Taiwan and threatens its territory, had no welcome party.

Putin arrived in China, ever confident. The attempts of the European Union, EU, to isolate him and his country had failed. Now, he sat at the centre of world politics and attention, and those who seek his isolation were absent. To take the shine off the trilateral meeting, forty European countries and partners had, the same day, gathered in Germany to remind the world that the Ukrainians need military and financial support and that they are ready for ceasefire guarantees. Along with Ukraine, they asked to be involved in peace talks since they are locked out of the trilateral. They failed to take the shine off. Rather, the world focused on China. The meeting of forty, including France and Britain, two Permanent Members of the United Nations Security Council, did not weigh on the same scale as the meeting of the three.

Putin pushed for the three to address energy security, global and regional issues. He emphasized that the three countries have “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including, obviously, the conflict in Ukraine.”

In his address to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, APEC, summit on the eve of the trilateral, he said: “It would be no exaggeration to say there has been a tectonic shift, and the Asia Pacific region is now the center of global economy, the main technological hub of the planet.”

In a little veiled reference to Western Europe, he said a new world order is emerging which the old order is trying to hold down: “Instead of adapting to this change, the former hegemons sometimes, to their own detriment, want to hold back the development of those who demonstrate development and progress.”

On the sanctions the EU had imposed on his country since the February 24, 2022 outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian War, Putin said: “Sanctions, tariffs, and export limitations still have an effect, but they are no longer capable of crushing the economies of competing countries.” He said following the sanctions, Russia shifted from the euro and dollar, and its payments in those currencies fell from 85 percent in 2021 to 9 percent: “We were denied the use of these currencies. And frankly speaking, those who did that punished themselves, essentially.”

The Shenzhen Conference, in some respects, was like the Yalta Conference, Crimea, of February 4–11, 1945, when then US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the world after the defeat of Nazi Germany. They agreed on war crime tribunals, denazification and the establishment of the United Nations with veto rules for the big countries. But this time, Britain has slipped from that position of preeminence, and its place has been taken by China. The Soviet Union has also disintegrated, and its old position has been inherited by Russia. There was also no nuclear race. The Yalta Conference dissolved into the Cold War with Britain and the US on one side. The Shenzhen Conference may hold occasionally, but China and Russia are likely to remain allies, and the US may eventually return to its old European allies.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: How American billionaires bought the politicians and the narrative, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
Perhaps the most consequential achievement of these billionaire-backed movements is not that they have persuaded ordinary people to admire billionaires. It is that they have persuaded ordinary people to defend political and economic arrangements that disproportionately enrich billionaires, frequently at the expense of their own material interests.

Ask an average Nigerian to name his five favourite American presidents, and there is a reasonable chance Donald Trump would make the list. The irony is almost farcical. Here is a man whose administration has pursued immigration policies that disproportionately targets people from countries like Nigeria, and who once infamously dismissed African nations as “shithole countries.” Yet, inexplicably, he commands the admiration of people he has repeatedly disparaged.

One might dismiss this as an extraordinary manifestation of political Stockholm syndrome, but such an explanation would be woefully inadequate. Something considerably more sophisticated has unfolded. An extraordinarily well-financed and meticulously choreographed media ecosystem has persuaded millions of people, including audiences far beyond America’s shores, that a coterie of billionaire plutocrats are, in fact, godly men engaged in a noble crusade to rescue Christianity from an encroaching army of secularists, liberals and cultural heretics.

Those who interrogate their motives or challenge their ambitions are promptly recast as adversaries of faith, family, tradition and civilisation. It is a remarkable feat of political engineering: persuading people to become enthusiastic defenders of arrangements that may ultimately imperil their own interests. This is what happens when the manufacture of political narratives becomes more influential than the realities of people’s lived experiences.

I grew up in Nigeria at a time when CNN was regarded as the gold standard of international journalism. Its pronouncements carried an almost unimpeachable authority. Today, however, one encounters Nigerians who casually dismiss the network as a purveyor of fake news. Did CNN suddenly abandon the principles of journalism? Not necessarily. Someone has simply executed an extraordinarily effective campaign to persuade them that it has.

This is not to suggest that CNN’s journalism is infallible or that its reporting should be immune to scrutiny. The more consequential question is what has supplanted it as an authoritative source of information in the minds of many of its former audiences. Increasingly, it is a motley assortment of right-wing American broadcasters, ideological commentators and conservative media outlets that cloak themselves in the language of Christianity, while peddling a profoundly distorted political agenda.

And that distinction is crucial. Winning the messaging war does not necessarily require establishing that one’s opponent is dishonest. It requires cultivating sufficient suspicion to make the opponent inherently untrustworthy. Once that objective is achieved, facts become negotiable, evidence is filtered through ideological allegiance and accountability is reduced to an exercise in partisan interpretation.

To understand how this transformation occurred, we must interrogate the increasingly symbiotic relationship between stupendous wealth, religious mobilisation, political power and media ownership.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

America’s capitalist system has produced individuals whose personal fortunes rival the economic output of entire nations. In much of the developing world, such extraordinary wealth frequently confers something approaching immunity from the law. The fabulously wealthy can suborn institutions, purchase influence and comport themselves as though ordinary legal and moral restraints were designed for lesser mortals. America was supposed to be different. One of the defining accomplishments of its democratic tradition, at least in principle, was the insistence that even the most affluent and politically consequential citizens remained answerable to institutional authority.

Yet an increasingly assertive class of billionaires has grown impatient with precisely those constraints. Why should regulators scrutinise their commercial empires? Why should investigative journalists excavate their business dealings? Why should courts circumscribe their ambitions? Why should democratic institutions obstruct their pursuit of whatever they desire?

Their strategy for dismantling these impediments has been deceptively straightforward: acquire political leverage, commandeer the public narrative and systematically weaken the institutions that stand between concentrated wealth and unrestrained power.

The Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision in 2010 substantially advanced this undertaking by removing restrictions on independent political expenditure by corporations and unions. Subsequent legal developments facilitated the emergence of super PACs, which can raise unlimited sums from wealthy individuals and corporations. Billionaires no longer needed to acquire politicians through crude, transactional arrangements. They could finance the political infrastructure that renders politicians beholden to their interests.

The strategy is remarkably ingenious. One need not persuade ordinary citizens that billionaires deserve greater power if one can convince them that the gravest threats to their liberty emanate from journalists, immigrants, feminists, liberals and minorities. Public resentment is redirected away from economic exploitation and towards manufactured cultural antagonisms. Citizens are encouraged to wage interminable battles over identity while the architects of their economic circumstances pursue their interests with remarkably little interference.

But influencing electoral outcomes was merely the opening salvo. They required something more durable and consequential: the capacity to manufacture consent. Enter the media.

Elon Musk’s acquisition of Twitter, subsequently rechristened X, was marketed as a crusade to liberate free speech from ideological censorship. Whatever one’s assessment of that justification, the transaction placed an extraordinarily influential global public square under the dominion of one of the world’s wealthiest individuals. It illustrated how concentrated private fortunes could be converted directly into control over the platforms through which millions consume information, participate in political discourse and construct their understanding of the world.
