In the case of the Chatsworth pensioner, her 69-year-old husband went to withdraw their monthly grant from the ATM, only to find the account empty. They dutifully reported to the local SASSA office with a certified three-month bank statement.



When they were finally assisted, the elders were told to return with the husband’s banks statements, marriage certificate and all rates documents. An investigation into SASSA grants suspended was only intensifying …

The South African Social Security Agency alleged that a credit bureau had detected ‘undisclosed additional income,’ which sounds menacing. Turns out it was a mere R500 paid in January from her brother and sister-in-law. They’d asked for her banking details and sent some money after a hospital stay.

GIFT FROM HIS CHILD

A R2000 deposit from a man’s son to help pay rent for the month triggered all sorts of trouble. Image: File

Next, a 65-year-old man from Merebank reported that his grant had stopped suddenly. Owing R1 500 in rent, his child in Johannesburg deposited R2 000 so he could pay his landlord. Like before, SASSA wanted to see three months’ bank statements and all other documents.

The agency’s callous response to SASSA grants suspended was: “It can suspend, increase or decrease a grant under Chapter 5 of the Social Assistance Act. And it will notify beneficiaries of a review date at least 30 days ahead. Any beneficiaries who don’t comply risk suspension.”

As The South African explained in an earlier article, you can appeal within 90 days of SASSA grants suspended through the Department of Social Development (DSD).

ONE-TIME DEPOSITS ARE SURELY ALLOWED?

Nevertheless, in October 2026 the agency did clarify that a single deposit isn’t automatically treated as irregular income. Its argument is that money in a bank account doesn’t lead to suspension. But failing to cooperate with a review can lead to longer-term harm:



Keep records of any once-off deposits from family. Who sent it and why?

Make sure contact details are up to date and respond to review notices as soon as possible.

Always take three months of statements, plus a letter explaining one-off deposits.

Ask for a written reason if SASSA grants suspended or reduced.

Remember that you can appeal within 90 days if you are unhappy.

Finally, if you are in financial trouble and need a one-off deposit from a family member or friend, be sure to get it in cash or not in the bank account you register with the agency.

But what do you think? Let us know if you have an SASSA grant suspension stories/lessons to share. Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs expected starting XI vs Mamelodi Sundowns
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs and Mamelodi Sundowns will lock horns in the semi-final of the Carling Knockout Cup this Sunday.

Amakhosi finished last season without silverware and will be eager to change that this campaign. Having already missed out on the MTN8, the Carling Knockout Cup presents Fernando Da Cruz with another opportunity to bring home a trophy.

The Soweto giants are just two wins away from lifting the cup and giving their supporters something to celebrate.



How could Kaizer Chiefs line up against Sundowns?

Brandon Petersen is expected to start in goal after recovering from injury last month.

At right-back, Reeve Frosler is likely to occupy the position. With Miguel Inacio unavailable, Da Cruz could revert to a back-three formation, with Zitha Kwinika returning to the starting XI.

Thabo Moloisane and Rushwin Dortley are expected to partner Kwinika in central defence, while Bradley Cross could operate on the left side.

In midfield, Sibongiseni Mthethwa is likely to start alongside Lebohang Maboe, with the duo tasked with controlling the middle of the park.

Kaizer Chiefs looking to extend unbeaten run against Sundowns

Further forward, Wandile Duba is expected to lead the attack, with Mduduzi Shabalala operating in a free role behind him. Pule Mmodi could provide width on the flank.

Amakhosi will head into the encounter with confidence, having gone unbeaten against Sundowns in their last four meetings.



The last time the two sides met in a cup competition, Chiefs emerged victorious with a 2-1 win in 2025. They will hope to produce another memorable performance when the two giants meet again on Sunday.

World.title: PICTURE: Rassie Erasmus front and centre in Springbok photo
World.content:
There is no doubt that the clash between Rassie Erasmus’ Springboks and Ireland on Saturday is going to be an absolute spectacle as two leading rugby rivals go head-to-head in Dublin.

The Springboks will of course be without Rassie Erasmus as he begins his six-Test suspension, but it is worth remembering that his ban only relates to all matchday activities.

It means Erasmus was still freely available to work with the team in the lead up to the match, and on Friday the team held it’s traditional captains’ run and team photo.



So, as usual, the Springbok coach was front and centre – and all smiles – in the team picture shared on social media. The side was seen in their alternative kit, wearing a white jersey and white socks, with green shorts.

Rassie Erasmus will soon have to step away from the Springboks

Saturday’s battle between the Springboks and Ireland kicks off at 18:40 (SA time), and although Erasmus will be out of the picture, assistant coach Mzwandile Stick said the team remained fully focused on the task at hand.

“It’s been great to have Rassie with us throughout the whole week,” Stick said. “His energy levels, his spirit, the energy amongst our squad.



“I think we’re in a good space, we’re well prepared, we know what’s coming, and there’s one thing that I know about Ireland: they’re a very well-organised team, in the sense of how they operate as a team.

“So it’s going to be a tough challenge, but I think these are the games that we look forward to. We love him, we appreciate him, and no one is going to break us, I can tell you that for sure. So we’ll be prepared for it,” he added.

Siya Kolisi said they’d also be driven by the motivation of playing for South Africa, especially after last weekend’s disappointing defeat to France.



“We know what it does to the country, how happy the mood is when we win, and when we lose, it gets tough. People care a lot about it, and so many people go out of their way to make sure they get to watch us.

“It’s a privilege and an honour that we don’t take for granted, because we know how many people would love to sit where we sit today.”

World.title: Tributes pour in following Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka’s death
World.content:
Tributes continue to pour in for former deputy president Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, who died aged 71 on Friday, 20 November 2026. Image: X/The Presidency

President Cyril Ramaphosa has paid an emotional tribute to former deputy president Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, describing her death as a heartbreaking loss for South Africa.

Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and former head of UN Women, died on Friday, 20 November, aged 71.

Ramaphosa said Deputy President Paul Mashatile had informed him of her passing.



“Our hearts are really, really sad and broken for having lost such a very dynamic woman leader in our country,” Ramaphosa said.

RAMAPHOSA MOURNS PHUMZILE MLAMBO-NGCUKA

The president described Mlambo-Ngcuka as a patriotic South African who devoted her life to public service and advancing women’s rights.

He praised her contribution to the United Nations, where she served as Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN Women.

Ramaphosa said she championed the rights of women not only in South Africa and Africa but across the world.

“She remained truly committed to the upliftment and empowerment of women in our country and on the African continent,” he said.

He also remembered her dedication during her time as deputy president.



Ramaphosa said South Africa had lost a leading voice in the fight for women’s empowerment.

The president said he would convey his condolences to her husband, Bulelani Ngcuka, and the family upon his return home.

President Ramaphosa reacts to the sad passing of former deputy President Phumzile Mlambo Ngcuka#sabcnews pic.twitter.com/slW2gGkrqV — Sherwin Bryce-Pease (@sherwiebp) November 21, 2026

UNITED NATIONS MOURNS ‘ONE OF ITS OWN’

The United Nations has also paid a moving tribute to Mlambo-Ngcuka, who led UN Women from 2013 to 2021.

UN Resident Coordinator in South Africa Nelson Muffuh described her death as a devastating loss.

“South Africa has lost an extraordinary daughter and leader, and the United Nations has lost one of its own,” the organisation said.

The UN recalled Mlambo-Ngcuka’s appearance at its Day commemoration in Pretoria on 27 October, just 24 days before her death.

It praised her courage, humanity and lifelong commitment to equality, justice and the rights of women and girls.

UJ MOURNS ITS CHANCELLOR

The University of Johannesburg, where Mlambo-Ngcuka served as Chancellor since 2022, also expressed its grief.

Vice-Chancellor and Principal Professor Letlhokwa Mpedi described her passing as an immeasurable loss.

“Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka’s passing is an immeasurable loss to the University and to our country,” Mpedi said.

He praised her contribution to education, social justice, human rights and women’s empowerment.

UJ said her legacy would continue through the Dr Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka Annual Lecture on Women and Leadership, inaugurated in August 2026.

POLITICAL LEADERS PAY TRIBUTE

ActionSA president Herman Mashaba joined the tributes on Saturday, recognising Mlambo-Ngcuka’s decades of public service.

In an official statement, Mashaba said her contributions to South Africa’s development and the advancement of equality would be remembered for generations.

The ANC also mourned its former leader, describing her as a dedicated servant of the people.

Mlambo-Ngcuka made history in 2005 when she became South Africa’s first female deputy president under former president Thabo Mbeki.

She held the position until 2008 before later taking her advocacy for women’s rights to the international stage.

Her death comes as South Africa marks its nationwide Women’s Shutdown on Saturday, highlighting the continuing fight against gender-based violence and femicide.

Acting President Paul Mashatile announced her death on Friday evening.

The family has requested privacy during this difficult time.

World.title: WHO lives here? SASSA scammers target trusting elders
World.content:
SASSA scammers going door to door in Belgravia Road, Athlone, Western Cape, are going viral in a video across social media. The man in question is videoed asking residents where elderly pensioners live. He reportedly says he is from a Bellville-based direct marketing company and “wants to tell beneficiaries about a special promotion.”

BEWARE SASSA SCAMMERS

There’s arguably nothing untoward about that, a direct marketer going door to door to drum up business. However, that’s until SASSA Western Cape spokesperson Shivani Wahab weighed in. She confirmed that the agency, “views the matter in a very serious light.”

She reiterated that the South African Social Security Agency, “has no affiliations, partnerships or agreements with direct marketing companies. And it doesn’t authorise any outside company to canvass door-to-door or ask for recipients’ addresses. Therefore, any individual claiming to represent SASSA for marketing purposes is acting fraudulently,” she concluded.



WHAT SASSA SCAMMERS ARE AFTER

To take advantage of trusting elders for a small grift is the lowest of the low. Image: File

Identifying where pensioners live is just the first step for the SASSA scammers. Once they’ve got ID numbers, bank details or signature, they sign the victim up to a host of unauthorised products. SASSA has warned beneficiaries previously these can be funeral-policies, short-term loans, airtime or shopping vouchers.

The trick from the SASSA scammers is that these deductions are relatively small to avoid detection. R30 here and there, can go unnoticed for months. The agency CEO has said bogus financial institutions are increasingly targeting vulnerable beneficiaries. SASSA scammers also use time pressure, saying elders will lose out if they don’t sign up now.

WHAT ABOUT INTERNAL SASSA FRAUD?

Nevertheless, the agency is fighting SASSA fraud internally as much as it is externally. The Auditor-General found R1.33 billion was paid to ineligible beneficiaries in 2025/26. That makes R30 a month to an elder not even a drop in the ocean.



Of the 105 600 beneficiaries reviewed from April to June 2026, 56 807 grants were suspended as fraudulent. Of course, the agency says not every suspension means fraud. SASSA admits that some discrepancies do have innocent explanations, like a family member helping with a bill. But the scrutiny is always the same …

HOW SASSA SCAMMERS WORK

Inside assistance often helps sidestep agency verification software. Image: File

In general terms, SASSA scammers obtain names and ID numbers (directly or from data leaks). Where possible they will open accounts in their names, done with throwaway phones and fraudulent applications, often with inside assistance. Once the application slips through verification, money can be moved out of accounts quickly. As such, here’s how to protect yourself against potential SASSA scammers:

Don’t open the door to unverified visitors. Unless arranged, SASSA will never come to your house.

Never share your ID, cards, PIN, OTP or banking details with anyone.

Don’t sign anything. When in doubt, show the document to a trusted relative first.

Ignore any pressure. “Sign now or lose your grant,” is a red flag.

Check your bank statement monthly for deductions you don’t recognise.

REPORT IT

SAPS: 10111 or your nearest station

or your nearest station SASSA toll-free: 0800 601 011

National Anti-Corruption Hotline: 0800 701 701

But what do you think? Have you been propositioned before by SASSA scammers? If so, how did you handle it? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: LIVE SCORING: Springboks vs Ireland in Dublin
World.content:
All eyes will be on the Aviva Stadium on Saturday night when the Springboks – without the presence of banned Rassie Erasmus – take on Ireland in what will undoubtedly be a hostile atmosphere in Dublin.

Battles between these two teams have recently been filled with plenty of fireworks, and considering the headline-grabbing nature of the build up to this Test – it’s sure to be one of the most enthralling and intense international matches of the year.

As it is, heading into Saturday’s final round of pool fixtures, five teams – New Zealand and South Africa in the South, and France, England, and Ireland in the North – can still reach the inaugural Nations Championship Grand Final at Twickenham next weekend.



If the All Blacks beat England in the earlier game on Saturday 16:10 (SA time), the Springboks will then likely need to target a bonus-point win in Dublin in order to finish top of the southern standings, adding yet another subplot to proceedings.

Ahead of kick off, the Springboks have been forced into a late team change after Ruan Nortje was ruled out with injury, and so Franco Mostert will join the returning Eben Etzebeth in the second row.

Meanwhile, Ireland’s injury problems at No 8 have prompted coach Andy Farrell to select regular hooker Dan Sheehan at the back of the scrum as he also regains the captaincy.



This is one match not to be missed. The battle at the Aviva Stadium kicks off at 18:40 (SA time) and will be broadcast live on SuperSport.

World.title: ‘It helps but is not enough’: SASSA pensioner reveals her month-end reality
World.content:
Close-up of a man holding an empty wallet, symbolising financial crisis and hardship. Image: Pexels

A retired SASSA grant recipient in Gauteng says her Older Persons Grant runs dry every month, even though she has never had a problem with the agency itself.

The pensioner shared her experience in The South African’s SASSA grant survey and asked to remain anonymous. She has received the grant for five years.

grant leaves nothing by month-end

The Older Persons Grant increased by R80 to R2 400 in April 2026. For this pensioner, the money disappears before the next payment arrives.



By the end of each month, nothing remains of her grant.

She uses her grant for a mix of needs, including food, household bills and daily essentials. The cost of living and rising food prices top her list of financial worries.

No complaints about SASSA, but the grant falls short

Unlike many grant recipients, she has nothing negative to say about how SASSA runs things. She describes her grant experience as straightforward and rates the agency’s communication with recipients as very good.



Smooth service, however, does not put more food on the table. When asked what one thing she would change about SASSA, she chose to increase the grant amount.

Her message to fellow South Africans summed up her experience.

“It helps but is not enough,” she said.

Pensioner unaware of extra government support

She has never applied for any government support beyond her grant because she did not know what else was available. Her answer points to an information gap that may leave other pensioners without help they could qualify for.



For now, she continues to stretch every rand of her payment, knowing it will run out before the month does.

Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: Manhunt underway after six fatally shot in Worcester
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - Western Cape police have launched a manhunt for the search of perpetrators of a shooting incident in Worcester on Saturday.

Six people were shot dead while three were wounded in the early hours of the morning.

According to the police, six men entered a yard in the Zweletemba informal settlement with their faces concealed. Shots were fired and four men and two women were killed at the scene.

Three others were transported to a medical facility after sustaining serious gunshot wounds.

"No resources will be spared in ensuring the perpetrators are brought to book," said Provincial Commissioner Sizakele Dyantyi.

World.title: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka dies at age 71
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Former UN Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN Women, Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka has passed away at the age of 71.

Acting President Paul Mashatile made the announcement on Friday.

Mlambo-Ngcuka served as deputy president under former president Thabo Mbeki from 2005 to 2007. She also served as Minister of Minerals and Energy from 1999 until 2005.

She also served deputy minister of trade and industry from 1996 until 1999.

Mlambo-Ngquka is survived by her husband Bulelani Ngcuka and her five children.

Mashatile has conveyed his condolences to the family on behalf of the President Cyril Ramaphosa who is in the US.

He said more details will be communicated to the public in consultation with the family.

World.title: Cummins' manager hits out at 'hysteria' around Sandpapergate
World.content:
MELBOURNE - Australia captain Pat Cummins' manager has hit out at the "hysteria" whipped up by the festering "Sandpapergate" scandal as Usman Khawaja said there was no reason for Cameron Bancroft to lie.

The Test skipper has come under huge pressure since Khawaja and then Bancroft claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018.

Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Bancroft -- who used the sandpaper -- were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.

Cummins strenuously denied he was aware of what was going on in a lengthy press conference a week ago, comments that have since come under scrutiny.

He has kept his head down since, and his manager Neil Maxwell described the criticism of him as "hysteria unfounded in reality".

"When you go through it all calmly and in detail, Pat's eight-year-long position and 68-minute Q&A (press conference) stands up," he said in a statement to Australian media.

"There is no serious case he was an architect of ball-tampering or knew sandpaper was going on the field.

"It's also true that the players who were suspended paid far too high a price," he added, referring to Smith, Warner and Bancroft.

"Year-long bans for ball-tampering that players in other countries did and were suspended for just a few games -– they have always been right to feel aggrieved by that."

The retired Khawaja reignited the controversy in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by close friend Warner.

After Cummins' denials, Bancroft dropped a bomb in a newspaper column by also claiming "it was the whole team" while saying he felt "angry and betrayed" by the skipper.

Smith has so far stayed out of the furore.

World.title: Johannesburg Water closes bulk meters
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Johannesburg Water is temporarily closing seven bulk supply meters as it moves to stabilise critically low storage levels.

The utility says increased demand and hot weather have placed pressure on its networks.

It's left some areas with intermittent supply, low pressure or no water at all.

READ | Making Sense | Joburg Water Crisis: Are Restrictions Enough? | 20 November 2026

The affected systems include Oakdene, Eikenhof, Wilford Shaft, Orlando Power Station, Foresthill, Maraisburg and Roodepoort.

The closures will run for 24 hours from 4pm Friday until 4pm on Saturday.

Johannesburg Water says supply may take time to recover after the meters are reopened, and alternative water supply will be arranged where necessary.

World.title: Massive Nigeria's tiny coffee sector wants a shot
World.content:
LAGOS - Richard Ali grew up with the aroma of coffee wafting through his house in central Nigeria as his father, an accountant, worked late into the night, drinking powdered, instant stuff from Maxwell House and Nescafé.

It was not until years later, travelling on the other side of the continent, that Ali had a taste of "coffee, coffee -- brewed coffee".

"I have to bring this to Nigeria," he thought, and he started looking into importing beans from Rwanda.

Ali later discovered he did not have to: coffee has been growing in Nigeria for more than 100 years.

A wave of entrepreneurs in Africa's most populous country are turning towards the oil-producing nation's other black gold -- an uphill task in a place full of tea and instant coffee, and little sense of homegrown java as a daily staple or part of a wider cultural patrimony.

But roasters say they have found a market -- and sense of national pride -- to tap into, even if Nigeria's beans are not well-known.

"We need to grow more coffee, whether for the domestic market, which is expanding, or the global market, which is now considering Nigerian coffee," Ali, founder of Tigray Coffee, which launched in 2021, told AFP over a cup of Nigerian brew, light with slightly chocolatey notes.

- Agricultural investments -

In Ethiopia, hundreds of years of cultivation have bound coffee to local culture, while Uganda and Ivory Coast have become modern export powerhouses.

Nigeria produced 1,808 tonnes of beans in 2024 according to statistics from the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization -- a paltry sum compared to Kenya's 49,500 tonnes that same year.

The first seeds hit the ground in Nigeria in the 19th century, after coffee was introduced by British colonists.

World.title: Shelton into ATP Finals last four, France's Fils eliminated
World.content:
TURIN - Ben Shelton qualified for the semi-finals of the ATP Finals on Thursday after Arthur Fils lost the first set of his match against world number one Alexander Zverev.

Earlier American Shelton beat Spaniard Rafael Jodar 7-6 (10/8), 7-5, a win that meant Fils had to beat German Zverev in straight sets to snatch second place in the John McEnroe Group.

Fils went a set behind in 35 minutes, with Zverev taking the lead 6-4 and was eliminated after losing 6-4, 7-6 (8/6).

Zverev has yet to lose a set in Turin and over the weekend will face the second-placed finisher of the other four-man group, the winner of Friday's game between Daniil Medvedev and Frances Tiafoe.

Zverev seemed to struggling with an ankle injury late in the match, having torn ligaments in the joint at the French Open in 2022.

"The ankle unfortunately is a topic for me that probably will stay until the end of my career with the injury I had four years ago," he said.

"I'm going to do everything I can with the physio and with my team to be ready on Saturday and to be painfree on Saturday," he added.

Shelton joins Zverev, who is guaranteed to win the group, and Carlos Alcaraz in the last four.

The American, 24, had to work hard against Jodar who held two set points in the first set tie-break. After clinching a hard-fought opening set that lasted over an hour, Shelton quickly broke Jodar's serve in the second.

Trailing 3-1 and then 4-2, the 10th-ranked Spanish newcomer mounted a comeback.

The 20-year-old levelled at 4-4 and then took a 5-4 lead but eventually wilted, losing three consecutive games and falling to his third defeat of the week in his debut at the elite season-ending event.

World.title: 'The Altruists' dramatises the love story behind the FTX collapse
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - The spectacular fall of cryptocurrency platform FTX caught the attention of screenwriter Graham Moore, but the thing that really hooked him was the romance behind the 2022 scandal.

Four years later, Moore has brought a dramatised depiction of the events to Netflix in "The Altruists," a new series out now starring Anthony Boyle as FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner as his love interest, Caroline Ellison.

"Here was this guy who'd claimed to be the kind of great ethical white knight of crypto, being possibly revealed to be a fraud," Moore said of Bankman-Fried at a press event for the show.

But as Moore dug into the story further, he realised "it wasn't a story about crypto, and it wasn't a story about finance, and it wasn't just a story about Sam. It was also really a story about Caroline Ellison and their relationship."

Crypto wunderkind Bankman-Fried met Ellison at a trading firm in 2015, where they bonded over a mutual interest in effective altruism, a philosophy that aims to guide philanthropy for the greatest possible good.

Ellison later joined Alameda Research, an investment firm started by Bankman-Fried, and the two began a torrid relationship.

"Over the course of this six-year, on-and-off-again, dramatic, romantic relationship, they kind of turned each other into people who ended up doing the exact opposite of the thing they set out to do," Moore said.

- The rise and fall of a crypto star -

Bankman-Fried would go on to start FTX in 2019, which rocketed to being the second largest cryptocurrency platform in the world, valued at more than $30 billion at its peak.

He would become a billionaire before the age of 30, but Bankman-Fried's fall came as quick as his rise with the collapse of FTX in the autumn of 2022, exposing serious financial mismanagement and more than $8 billion in debt.

The couple came under the microscope of the courts, and Ellison would eventually testify against Bankman-Fried for a lighter sentence.

World.title: Government to fast-track plan to tackle scourge of GBV
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Government says it wants to speed up the rollout of President Cyril Ramaphosa’s plan to fight gender-based violence.

This comes amid alarming crime statistics, which found that around 9,200 rape cases were reported between April and June this year.

Thousands of GBV cases are believed to go unreported.

Minister in the Presidency for Women and Youth Sindisiwe Chijunga reflected on the President's four-point plan to deal with gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF) in the country.

READ | From broken streetlights to stalled cases: Ramaphosa outlines four GBV immediate

She said a model presented to them will be used by government to ensure that the four-point plan is implemented.

After this presentation, Sindisiwe said they convened an interministerial committee meeting, to which Gauteng also presented.

“[The meeting] was attended by premiers from all provinces, and at a national level, the model was adopted to be the model that will be used by all provinces,” she said.

The four measures announced by Ramaphosa in September consisted of deadlines ranging from 60 days to 90 days.

Chikunga said they remain committed to these deadlines.

World.title: Accountability test: Koome's Judiciary faces questions over delays and productivity
World.content:
President William Ruto during his State of the Nation Address at Parliament, Nairobi. November 18,2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

For the first time in Kenya’s history, judges and magistrates have been placed under the public spotlight, with the Judiciary publishing individual performance records showing how many judgments, rulings and cases they have handled.

In a landmark transparency move, the Judiciary has disclosed the individual output of judges, magistrates, Kadhis and Small Claims Court adjudicators in its 2025/2026 State of the Judiciary and Administration of Justice Report.

World.title: Ruto defends IEBC, challenges rivals to present alternative policies
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his tour of the Western region. [PCS]

President William Ruto has launched a scathing attack on opposition leaders over their demands on the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), accusing them of attempting to interfere with the electoral agency because they fear losing the 2027 General Election.

The President challenged opposition leaders to allow IEBC to prepare independently for next year's elections, saying they should instead focus on identifying their presidential candidate, developing a manifesto and presenting alternative policies to Kenyans.

Ruto accused his competitors of attempting to play the roles of both contestants and referees by seeking to influence decisions on the procurement of election materials and equipment.

He spoke a day after opposition leaders walked out of a meeting convened by IEBC, alleging bias by the commission.

“Please give IEBC a chance to arrange the elections next year. The people of Kenya will decide. You go and first look for your candidate, find your policies, agenda and plans and sell them to the wananchi. We shall meet at the ballot,” said Ruto.

Speaking during his development tour of Western Kenya, Ruto questioned why opposition politicians were concentrating on determining how IEBC should procure election materials instead of preparing to face voters.

“How can somebody who is in a competition want to decide where the pitch will be, who the referee will be and where the ball will be placed? Leave IEBC alone. Those who will vote are the citizens, and they are the ones who will decide,” he said.

The President accused his opponents of lacking a clear political agenda and capacity to deliver, claiming their campaigns were centred on slogans and personal attacks against him.

He challenged them to explain what they would do differently in agriculture, education, healthcare, infrastructure and employment rather than mobilising Kenyans around the slogan 'Kasongo Must Go'.

“The reason why my competitors cannot develop a plan is that they have no capacity. The reason why they have no agenda is that they have no knowledge. The reason why they cannot develop anything is that they know they have no capacity to deliver on anything that they will say,” he said.

His remarks were echoed by Kakamega Governor Fernandes Barasa and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula, who rallied Western Kenya leaders behind his re-election bid and defended IEBC against what they termed unnecessary political pressure. President William Ruto during his tour of the Western region. [ Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Speaking in Butere, Barasa said the region's political leadership, including Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, Cabinet Secretary Wycliffe Oparanya, Wetang'ula and trade unionist Francis Atwoli, was united behind Ruto's development agenda.

“IEBC will conduct the elections according to the law. Opposition leaders should leave IEBC alone and allow it to do its work,” he said.

Wetang'ula maintained that IEBC was independent of both the government and the opposition and should be allowed to conduct its work without interference.

“IEBC is independent of the government and independent of the Opposition. You stand there to do your work fairly, truthfully and equally,” he said.

He added: “Just as Arsenal supporters cannot dictate what uniform the referee should wear, the referee's responsibility is to ensure the game is played fairly and the winner emerges through a legitimate process.”

The exchanges underline the growing political contest over the management of the 2027 elections, with the government side accusing the opposition of undermining the electoral agency before campaigns gather momentum.

Beyond the political exchanges, Ruto used his Western Kenya tour to highlight development projects, saying his administration was committed to correcting years of neglect and unequal distribution of national resources.

He also announced plans for a second phase of the Nyota programme targeting an additional 200,000 young people, each expected to receive Sh50,000 to establish or expand businesses.

The government is also targeting 100,000 college graduates for internships from January, with each expected to receive a monthly stipend of Sh20,000.

Ruto's tour comes amid growing competition for Western Kenya's support ahead of the 2027 General Election, with emerging opposition alliances seeking to challenge his influence.

World.title: Ruto sustains attacks on Gachagua, dares Opposition to name 2027 flagbearer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto launches Matisi-Bokoli-Milani-Teremi road in Webuye West on November 19, 2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

President William Ruto has challenged Opposition leaders to name their presidential candidate and unveil a clear political agenda, accusing them of wasting time hopping from one hotel to another and holding meetings in private residences in search of a flagbearer and campaign manifesto.

The President said the Opposition was yet to settle on a flagbearer or agree on a common agenda despite the clock ticking towards the 2027 General Election.

He dismissed the rival camps' political engagements as endless consultations and manoeuvres, arguing that their leaders were more preoccupied with political meetings than developing policies to convince Kenyans.

Speaking in Bungoma during his development tour of Western Kenya, Ruto challenged his opponents to stop what he termed political confusion and present an alternative development agenda, insisting he was ready to face them in the 2027 contest.

"These people do not have a candidate. They are struggling, moving from one hotel to another and from one person's house to another, trying to find an agenda and a manifesto before they can start campaigning. Time is running out, yet they are still struggling to agree on an agenda," he said.

Ruto also launched a fresh attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, accusing him of promoting tribalism and hatred while questioning his remarks about relocating to Texas, United States.

The President mockingly referred to Gachagua as "Mr Chuki wa Texas", questioning why he would allegedly acquire a house in the US while engaging in politics that could divide Kenyans and fuel hostility.

"Mr Chuki wa Texas has gone to buy a house in Texas. He wants to know whether he will flee our country after spreading tribalism and hatred, dividing people and turning them against each other, before boarding a plane to Texas and leaving others to deal with the consequences," Ruto said.

He accused the former Deputy President of attempting to turn communities against one another for political gain, warning that he would not allow anyone to undermine national unity through ethnic mobilisation.

Ruto said he was ready to confront his political opponents directly but insisted that political competition should not become an avenue for spreading hatred and inciting Kenyans against one another.

The President also questioned Gachagua's allies over their reported visit to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) offices in Kizirani, accusing the Opposition of picking unnecessary fights with the electoral agency ahead of the 2027 General Election.

He suggested that politicians who begin questioning the electoral commission before elections could be preparing grounds to reject the results should they lose.

"Whenever you see someone picking a fight with IEBC, that person is already looking for an excuse to fail. Now they are coming up with all sorts of excuses, asking whether it is IEBC that votes. Is IEBC responsible for the votes?" He posed.

Ruto urged politicians to stop harassing the electoral agency, maintaining that the power to elect leaders rests with Kenyans and not the commission.

"I want to tell Kenyans to stop harassing IEBC. IEBC does not have votes. The votes belong to the people of Kenya," he said.

The President maintained that his administration was focused on delivering development, challenging the Opposition to explain its alternative plans on electricity connectivity, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

He questioned what the Opposition considered its development agenda, dismissing what he described as recycled political slogans and simplistic promises.

The President particularly took issue with promises centred on providing porridge to Kenyans, questioning whether such pledges could constitute a credible national development agenda.

He urged voters to interrogate the policies and development track records of politicians seeking their support instead of being swayed by political rhetoric and personal attacks.

The latest attack marks an escalation in political exchanges between Ruto and his rivals as competing camps intensify mobilisation ahead of the 2027 General Election.

It also comes amid efforts by Gachagua and other Opposition figures to consolidate their political formations and build a formidable challenge to Ruto's re-election bid, with Western Kenya emerging as a key battleground.

World.title: Ruto lists measures to lower cost of living, put more money in Kenyans' pockets
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his State Of The Nation Address at Parliament, Nairobi. November 18th, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

President William Ruto has outlined a raft of government interventions aimed at reducing the cost of living, increasing household incomes and creating more employment opportunities for Kenyans.

Addressing Parliament during the 2026 State of the Nation Address on Wednesday, Ruto said his administration had prioritised lowering the cost of essential goods and services while increasing earnings across key sectors of the economy.

“Our economic proposition was simple: Reduce the cost for families and increase the income from what they do,” he said.

On food prices, the President cited the government’s fertiliser subsidy programme, which has reduced the price of a 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from Sh7,500 in 2022 to Sh2,000 this year.

He said the government had distributed 38.5 million bags of subsidised fertiliser to farmers, contributing to an increase in maize production from 44.3 million bags in 2022 to 71 million bags last year.

Consequently, maize imports declined from 9.9 million bags to 3.3 million bags, while the average price of a two-kilogramme packet of sifted maize flour dropped from a high of Sh230 in September 2022 to Sh152 in September this year.

Ruto also highlighted gains in the tea, coffee, dairy and sugar industries, saying government interventions had helped improve production and increase farmers' earnings.

He said the Cherry Advance Revolving Fund had disbursed Sh15.07 billion to 684,000 coffee farmers, while tea export earnings increased from Sh163 billion in 2022 to Sh187 billion in 2025.

In the dairy sector, milk production rose from 4.5 billion litres to 5.52 billion litres, while average earnings for farmers increased from Sh32 to Sh60 per litre last month.

Sugar production, he added, increased by 60 per cent between January and October, with cane crushing rising by 57 per cent. The industry is projected to produce more than 900,000 tonnes by the end of the year, with Sh1.2 billion in bonuses expected to be paid to sugarcane farmers.

On healthcare, Ruto said the Social Health Authority (SHA) was designed to ease the financial burden of medical expenses on households through a shared health financing system.

In education, he said the government had employed 100,000 teachers and was preparing to recruit an additional 20,000 to address staffing shortages and reduce the burden on parents who pay teachers hired through Boards of Management.

He added that 23,000 classrooms had been constructed, while 1,600 laboratories were being built and equipped.

The President said the annual education allocation had increased from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.

"These investments improve the quality of education while progressively reducing the need for Kenyans to finance education," he said.

On affordable housing, Ruto said more than 313,000 homes were at different stages of construction across the 47 counties, with over 1.37 million Kenyans registered on the Boma Yangu platform and more than 18,000 homes already allocated.

He said households could work towards homeownership through monthly payments starting at Sh4,000, which he argued would help ease the burden of rent.

The housing programme, according to the President, had also generated more than 1.1 million employment opportunities and reserved orders worth over Sh61 billion for Jua Kali artisans.

On employment, Ruto said 350,000 Kenyans had secured jobs through the digital economy programme, while another 707,000 had obtained employment abroad through international labour mobility initiatives.

He also cited the Hustler Fund, saying more than seven million Kenyans had established credit records through the programme, with cumulative borrowing reaching Sh94 billion.

Under the NYOTA programme, more than 133,000 young entrepreneurs had received training, mentorship and Sh50,000 each in start-up capital, he said.

The President further announced proposed tax measures aimed at increasing disposable incomes, including exempting workers earning Sh32,333 or less per month from Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

Other proposals include scrapping stamp duty on land transactions valued at Sh1 million or less and removing the 25 per cent import duty on mobile phones.

On pending bills, Ruto said the government had approved the settlement of 28,726 verified claims amounting to Sh27.8 billion, covering debts of Sh50 million and below dating back to 2005.

He added that Sh18 billion owed to public universities and another Sh16 billion owed to public and private hospitals under the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) had been approved for payment and were undergoing Treasury processing.

“These are not isolated interventions, but parts of one comprehensive undertaking,” Ruto said.

He maintained that the government's economic strategy was anchored on reducing household expenditure, increasing incomes and expanding opportunities for Kenyans.

World.title: After 22 years of waiting, woman welcomes quadruplet boys
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Samuel Langat speaks to journalists outside St Clare's Kaplong Mission hospital in Sotik Subcounty, Bomet county after his wife Lily Langat gave to quadruplets at the hospital. [Kiprono Kurgat, Standard]

After 22 years of waiting to become a mother, a woman has welcomed quadruplet boys in a rare and joyful birth that has brought immense happiness to her family.

Lily Langat delivered the quadruplets through a Caesarean section at St Clare’s Kaplong Mission Hospital in Sotik Sub-County on November 14, 2026.

The four boys arrived after more than two decades of waiting for a child in what the family described as a double blessing.

The 43-year-old mother could not hide her joy, saying the arrival of the four babies was an answer to years of prayer.

“I am very grateful to God for giving me four babies at once. This is a great blessing to my family. I thank the hospital staff for ensuring I got to see these bundles of joy,” she said.

“I have been praying and waiting upon God to give me double for the trouble. I have been childless for a long time, and God could not have given me a better gift than this,” she added.

She said she had been looking forward to the moment after doctors informed her early in the pregnancy that she could be carrying quadruplets.

Hospital staff celebrated the successful delivery, describing it as a rare occurrence at the facility.

A nurse who spoke with The Standard said the mother and her four newborns were in stable condition.

“We were delighted to deliver the babies. The mother faced some difficulties because of the combined weight of the four babies, but both she and the newborns are now stable,” she said.

The nurse said the babies had been placed in the nursery for observation and were doing well.

“This is a rare case in this hospital. We have had twins before, but this is different. None of the babies has developed complications so far, and we expect them to be discharged once they are fully stable,” she said.

She added that the mother was also recovering well and was expected to be discharged once doctors were satisfied with the condition of the newborns.

Lily's husband, Samuel Langat, appealed to well-wishers to support the family as they prepare to raise the four children.

“Raising four babies at once is no easy task. I am calling on well-wishers to lend a helping hand as we begin this extraordinary journey,” he said.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges,” he added.

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, although the likelihood varies depending on several factors, including maternal age and fertility treatment.

The birth marks a remarkable new beginning for the Langat family after 22 years of waiting for a child.

World.title: TSC picks Cheptumo Ayabei as new Chief Executive Officer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Teachers Service Commission headquarters in Nairobi. [File, Standard]

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has picked Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, making him the first person with a disability to head the commission.

Ayabei emerged top in interviews conducted on Monday, beating four other candidates, including the commission’s acting chief executive, Dr Evaleen Jesang Mitei, to become the country’s top teachers’ employer.

His selection ends a prolonged search for a substantive head of the commission, which has operated under acting leadership since the departure of former CEO Nancy Macharia in June 2025.

Ayabei, who hails from Baringo County, is currently TSC’s Director of Finance, having served at the commission for more than two decades. He joined the institution in 1999 as a Finance Officer before rising through the ranks to become Director of Finance in 2009.

His elevation marks a significant milestone for the representation of persons with disabilities in the country’s public institutions.

Ayabei was the first candidate to face the selection panel at 9am at the commission’s headquarters in Upper Hill, Nairobi. He was followed by Mitei at 10am, Robert Odette at 11am, Lawrence Ngai Kaburu at noon and Farah Abdi Saman at 1pm.

The five candidates were shortlisted from 124 applicants who responded to a fresh  issued on September 29. Applications closed on October 30.

Ayabei holds a Bachelor of Education degree in Mathematics and Economics from Kenyatta University and a Master’s degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Stirling in the United Kingdom. He is also a Certified Public Accountant.

Before joining TSC, he worked at the Ministry of Education between 1990 and 1999.

He takes over at a critical time for the commission, which oversees the employment, deployment, promotion and discipline of teachers across the country. He will inherit mounting pressure over teacher shortages, recruitment, promotions, transfers and the management of the teaching workforce.

The recruitment process had faced legal challenges, with a petition filed at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Kisii seeking to halt the exercise.

The case, filed by Evans Morara Nyangongo under Cause E038 of 2026, challenged the fresh recruitment and raised questions about Mitei’s participation in the process while serving as acting CEO and seeking the substantive position.

Nyangongo sought to stop the commission from proceeding with the appointment until the issues raised in the petition were determined.

However, the court dismissed both the application and the suit, with no orders as to costs, clearing the way for the interviews.

In its defence, TSC maintained that the decision to advertise the position had been made collectively by the commission’s board and not by the acting CEO.

In a replying affidavit, TSC chairman Jamleck Muturi John maintained that Mitei had neither participated in the board’s deliberations on the recruitment nor influenced the process.

The fresh recruitment followed an earlier court decision that nullified the previous exercise over procedural irregularities, forcing the commission to restart the search for a substantive chief executive.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: For Xi and Putin, the Trump trilateral was a win for a new world order
World.content:
From an airy government villa in the hills of southern China on Thursday emerged an image, perhaps, for our times: the leaders of China, Russia and the US standing shoulder-to-shoulder, proclaiming themselves the stewards of world peace.

For Trump, the moment was a well-timed photo-op – a diplomatic flex for a president who revels in such spectacle and whose party is reeling from a major loss in the US midterm elections.

But for Xi and Putin, the meeting is more likely to go down as a vindication of their vision that the world is undergoing a fundamental rebalancing of power – in their favor.

In opening remarks before the roughly 90-minute meeting between them, Trump said he was honored to sit next to the two and framed the trio – the world’s three largest nuclear powers – as uniquely placed to work together for a “safer future.”

“No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them,” said Trump. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”

Chinese leader Xi Jinping sits between Russia’s Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump during their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday. Sergei Bobylyov/Sputnik/Reuters

But for talks that ended with a handful of vaguely worded outcomes – and no evidence that the US president and commander-in-chief of the world’s most powerful military had tried to hold Putin to account for his illegal invasion of Ukraine – that “different course” appears to be one that plays to the objectives of Moscow and Beijing.

Xi and Putin have long looked to push back against a world order they see as unfairly dominated by the US and its values.

A brief exchange caught on camera in 2023 during a state visit by the Chinese leader to Moscow captures that ambition. There, as he shook Putin’s hand, Xi was heard saying: “Together, we should push forward these changes that have not happened for 100 years.”

To that end, they have tightened their own partnership and built out non-Western international blocs engineered to help usher in a “multipolar” order that favors their interests.

For Xi and Putin, all this is underpinned by a shared view: that the East is rising as the West declines – and the age of American superpower comes to an end.

And what better illustration of that shift than sitting around a table in China’s futuristic tech hub of Shenzhen with a US president hailing them both as friends?

A new world order

Headlines across Chinese state media the day after the summit were in no doubt about its significance.

The state’s lead news agency hailed the meeting as a “new starting point” for a “new model of relationship among major powers.” That new model, explained the article, is one based on “mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, dialogue and consultation.”

For China’s leadership, those are buzzwords key to the country’s unimpeded rise on the global stage, essentially insurance that the US won’t look to meddle in what Beijing sees as its business – especially when it comes to its territorial claims on the self-ruling and democratic island of Taiwan.

And during the summit, with Trump to his left and Putin to his right, Xi pressed that point, using that time, according to Chinese media, to spell out China’s conditions for the three to get along.

At the top of that list? “Respect one another’s sovereignty and territorial integrity” – and stay out of one another’s internal affairs.

World.title: Video: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper targeted in Houthi strike
World.content:
Saudi Arabia announced on Friday that it thwarted a fresh aerial attack launched by Yemen’s Houthi movement targeting the Kingdom’s territory.

According to the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, air defense forces successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward the Kingdom’s southern region.

Simultaneously, Saudi Civil Defense reported intercepting explosive-laden drones in the south, prompting emergency warning alerts across several cities—including Jazan, Abha, and Khamis Mushait—before authorities later declared the threat had passed.

According to Reuters, Saudi Arabia’s southern provinces bordering Yemen have faced recurring cross-border missile and drone attacks by the Iran-aligned group, frequently targeting military installations, airports, and critical energy infrastructure.

Friday’s barrage comes less than 24 hours after a Houthi strike targeted Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper—which houses the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF)—on Thursday.

The conflict in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthi movement seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military coalition to intervene in March 2015 to restore the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

While UN-brokered truces and bilateral de-escalation talks had significantly reduced cross-border hostilities over recent years, renewed regional tensions have periodically triggered flare-ups along the Saudi-Yemeni border and deep inside the Kingdom.

World.title: Noor’s journey: Exploring faith, memory, and selfhood
World.content:
A few days ago, Kuwait kicked off its premier cultural celebration. On the morning of Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the Kuwait International Book Fair opened its 49th edition, setting the stage for a ten-day literary showcase running through November 28.

Over this period, visitors can navigate hundreds of Arab and international publishing houses, browsing and acquiring works whose pages have traveled across borders to find a temporary home in the “Bride of the Gulf,” offering avid readers a rare window into diverse worlds of thought.

During my first visit to the fair, my attention was immediately captured by a novel titled

A few days ago, Kuwait kicked off its premier cultural celebration. On the morning of Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the Kuwait International Book Fair opened its 49th edition, setting the stage for a ten-day literary showcase running through November 28. Over this period, visitors can navigate hundreds of Arab and international publishing houses, browsing and acquiring works whose pages have traveled across borders to find a temporary home in the “Bride of the Gulf,” offering avid readers a rare window into diverse worlds of thought.

During my first visit to the fair, my attention was immediately captured by a novel titled Hijab Mumazzaq (A Torn Veil), written by Ali Abdelghani. Initially, it was the cover art that drew me in, even before I registered the title. Once I picked it up and read the name on the jacket, I knew I had to buy it—compelled to immerse myself in its prose, uncover the meaning behind A Torn Veil, and follow “Noor’s Journey” to its conclusion.

The novel traces the trajectory of Noor, a young man raised in a strict religious environment whose worldview was shaped early on within the halls of an Al-Azhar institute. In his consciousness, the image of women became deeply entangled with inherited teachings on faith, society, and the human body. While he initially appears preoccupied with discovering the world and the people around him, it soon becomes clear that his true quest is directed inward—even if he remains blind to that reality.

His crisis begins when he crosses paths with Rasha, a childhood acquaintance whom he had long idealized through the lens of his own imagination. The moment of their reunion exposes the vast chasm between a real human being and the construct fabricated by the mind, triggering the first fractures in his internal belief system.

From there, the central conflict unfolds as Noor embarks on a turbulent psychological odyssey. Along the way, desire collides with fear, memory clashes with reality, and personal identity wrestles with social authority. As he attempts to reshape the world around him to match the vision he seeks, he finds himself drifting further away from his original self and the devout upbringing that defined him. Each time he believes he is closer to understanding others, he uncovers deeper, more enigmatic layers within his own psyche.

Hijab Mumazzaq is a novel about identity, perception, and the urge to transcend society’s rigid boundaries. At its core, however, it is an introspective journey of a man searching for his authentic face behind the masks he has worn for so long—leading inevitably to the hardest question of all: Was he searching for the truth, or merely for an illusion he invented for himself?

To be, or not to be: that is the question.

Author’s biography

Nermin al-Houti is an associate professor of the Department of Criticism at the Higher Institute of Dramatic Arts in Kuwait.

She holds a PhD in Philosophy of Literary Criticism and is a graduate of the Higher Institute of Dramatic Arts.

Houti is a member of the Association of Writers and the Journalists Association, and is also part of the literary arbitration committees on theater or poetry in Kuwait and other Arab countries.

She has authored numerous newspapers and magazines articles and several books on significant theatrical works examining women’s issues, the latest of which is “The Women in Ismail Abdullah’s Theater”.

She has been chosen as a panelist in various significant cultural events and has participated in multiple seminars across the Arab region.

World.title: KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP appointed to advance Angola’s  international tourism investment strategy
World.content:
Looking to diversify its economy beyond traditional commodities, Angola is launching an ambitious international campaign to court foreign capital for its burgeoning tourism sector. To spearhead this global outreach, the Angolan Ministry of Tourism has appointed KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP—the foreign direct investment (FDI) advisory arm of the German-based KLEBER GROUP—as its international investment partner.

The appointment marks a strategic evolution in a partnership that began in 2025, expanding KLEBER GROUP’s existing mandate from destination branding, travel trade engagement, and local capacity building into direct capital mobilization. Under the new remit, KAPITAL will identify global institutional investors, cultivate strategic relationships, and bridge the gap between international financiers and Angola’s public and private stakeholders to accelerate commercially viable hospitality projects.

Central to this drive is Investe Turismo, the ministry’s flagship national strategy designed to unlock private sector participation. The government will take its pitch directly to global financial capitals via an international roadshow, kicking off in London on November 26, 2026. There, Tourism Minister Márcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel and Jucimar Afonso, Secretary of State for Tourism Asset Management and Concessions, will unveil Angola’s priority tourism assets and curated investment opportunities. Additional roadshow stops, investor roundtables, and bilateral meetings across key target markets will follow throughout 2027.

“Tourism is Angola’s green oil,” Minister Márcio Daniel stated, framing the sector as a cornerstone of the nation’s economic transformation. “Through Investe Turismo and major public infrastructure commitments, we have created the conditions for international capital to build the next generation of hotels, resorts, and travel experiences in Angola. We are now taking these opportunities directly to investors in leading financial hubs, starting with London, in search of long-term partners whose investments generate jobs, transfer skills, and deliver lasting benefits to our communities.”

To de-risk private entry and lay the groundwork for development, Luanda has backed its rhetoric with substantial state capital. The government recently approved a €449 million public investment package—externally financed by Japan’s Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG)—earmarked for critical infrastructure upgrades at the Cabo Ledo tourism hub and along the country’s coastal tourism corridor.

The push comes amid clear signs of sector momentum. According to joint data from UN Tourism and the Angolan Ministry of Tourism, international arrivals surged by 28 percent in 2025 to reach 223,140 visitors. Government figures further indicate that tourism generated approximately $667 million in revenue and supported more than 9,000 jobs last year.

Julia Kleber, CEO of KLEBER GROUP, emphasized the untapped potential awaiting early movers in the southern African nation. “Angola’s tourism sector is on a clear upward trajectory, offering compelling opportunities across hospitality, infrastructure, and nature-based tourism,” she said. “Through KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP, we are connecting the country’s strategic priorities with international capital, operational expertise, and long-term partners to turn these projects into reality.”

About KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP

KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP is the dedicated investor relations and foreign direct investment (FDI) advisory unit of KLEBER GROUP, specializing in international capital attraction, destination and hospitality development, strategic investor engagement, and investment facilitation.

By connecting destinations, governments, and tourism enterprises with global investors, financial institutions, and strategic partners, KAPITAL positions high-potential opportunities, bridges access to capital, and drives long-term economic growth. Combining specialized investment advisory with KLEBER GROUP’s global tourism expertise and established network across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, the unit transforms destination development ambitions into bankable realities.

About KLEBER GROUP

Operating across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), and Africa, KLEBER GROUP pairs global reach with deep local market intelligence at the intersection of travel, luxury, and lifestyle. The group advises public and private sector clients across both inbound and outbound markets—spanning emerging, established, and luxury destinations, alongside hospitality, aviation, and tourism brands.

Through integrated market representation and strategic consultancy covering public relations, communications, marketing, travel trade, MICE, and investor relations—including FDI advisory via KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP—the firm delivers multidisciplinary expertise tailored to each client’s specific goals. Underscoring its long-standing commitment to the African continent, KLEBER GROUP also founded the Voice4Africa initiative.

Institutional investors, financial institutions, hospitality groups, and developers interested in attending the London showcase or requesting further details can contact Varun Kapur, Director of KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP, at [email protected].

World.title: Urgent US warning in Kuwait to prepare for airspace closures
World.content:
The United States has issued an urgent US warning in Kuwait, calling on American citizens in the country to stay away from US-affiliated sites and facilities. The advisory also urges travelers to prepare for sudden flight cancellations and potential airspace closures amid escalating security tensions and recent attacks targeting American interests across the Gulf region.

In an updated security alert, the US Embassy in Kuwait advised Americans to exercise extreme caution and maintain a low profile. Citizens are encouraged to closely monitor official flight updates from Kuwait International Airport and major airlines in anticipation of widespread regional aviation disruptions that could occur with little or no advance notice.

Travel advisory and contingency plans

Alongside the US warning in Kuwait, the US State Department has maintained its Level 3 travel advisory for the country, which officially urges citizens to “reconsider travel” due to heightened security risks. Officials strongly recommended that anyone planning to travel to or from the Middle East prepare immediate contingency plans that do not rely solely on commercial air travel.
