World.title: Infant mortality rates shoot up as aid dries up
World.content:
GOVERNMENT and UNICEF have raised concern over the spike in mortality rates and stunted growth among children under five years following the withdrawal of aid by major international donors.

In a joint statement marking commemorations of the World Children’s Day, both parties called for renewed investment in children’s healthcare to protect the gains made over the last few years.

“Rising newborn and infant deaths underline just how fragile these gains are, and this has come at a time when donor funding is dwindling, putting health, education and food security services under mounting pressure,” the statement read.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Drone Solutions to open CAAZ-approved training school in Bulawayo
World.content:
THE City of Bulawayo is set to become a regional hub for drone pilot training after Drone Solutions Training Institute (DSTI), formerly Drone University, got the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe (CAAZ) approval to establish a satellite training school.

The project is expected to bring specialised drone training closer to farmers, businesses and aspiring pilots in Matabeleland, reducing costs associated with travelling to Harare for training, accommodation and subsistence.

In a statement, Drone Solutions said the approval was granted under its Approved Training Organisation Certificate No.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Solar Boom Shifts From Mega-Projects to Small-Scale Systems - IEA
World.content:
Nigeria, alongside Algeria, Kenya and Senegal, added more than one gigawatt of solar capacity each in 2025, highlighting the growing adoption of solar energy across African economies

Africa's solar energy boom is increasingly driven by small-scale installations as imports of photovoltaic (PV) equipment surge. Countries, including Nigeria, are expanding solar deployment to address persistent electricity shortages, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.

The World Energy Outlook report, published by the IEA on Thursday, said solar PV imports to Africa have increased since 2017, with most of the increase coming from China, where imports have grown 28-fold.

The surge has contributed to an eightfold increase in installed solar capacity across the continent, reflecting growing adoption of solar energy as an alternative to conventional electricity sources.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

While utility-scale solar projects dominated Africa's solar market a decade ago, smaller installations are increasingly emerging as the main driver of growth, reflecting a shift toward decentralised energy systems as households, businesses, and industries seek alternatives to unreliable electricity supply.

Nigeria, alongside Algeria, Kenya and Senegal, added more than one gigawatt of solar capacity each in 2025, highlighting the growing adoption of solar energy across African economies.

The shift comes as solar imports continue to expand, with trade data indicating that Africa imported approximately 26 gigawatts (GW) of solar PV equipment in 2025 alone, compared with reported installations of about 10 GW.

Since 2020, imports of solar PV equipment from China to Africa have reached about 60 GW, while recorded installations across the continent have amounted to less than half that volume.

The IEA said the disparity raises questions about the pace of solar deployment, the accuracy of installation data and the extent to which imported equipment is being stockpiled, re-exported or deployed in installations missing from official statistics.

According to the agency, the gap between imported and recorded installed solar capacity stood at approximately 35 GW over the past five years.

It attributed the discrepancy partly to equipment remaining in inventories for extended periods, installations not being captured in official statistics and possible structural inconsistencies in trade and deployment data.

Around 15 per cent of solar imports are also solar cells rather than finished modules, some of which could be supplying Africa's emerging solar manufacturing industry.

Although solar module production capacity across Africa remained limited in 2025, Egypt and Ethiopia have since emerged as leading producers, while several other countries, including Nigeria, are pursuing ambitious plans to expand domestic manufacturing.

The rapid adoption of solar technology highlights the growing pressure climate activists are placing on world leaders at the ongoing climate talks in Turkey to phase out fossil fuels and transition to renewable energy equitably and justly.

Nigeria's emerging solar market

In recent years, households and businesses across Nigeria have increasingly adopted solar systems as an alternative energy source amid unreliable electricity supply and rising energy costs.

Repeated grid collapses, ageing infrastructure, metering gaps, gas supply shortages, mounting debts and estimated billing have undermined electricity delivery across the country, despite decades of investment in the sector.

The removal of the petrol subsidy in 2023 by President Bola Tinubu's administration further intensified the cost-of-living crisis, as petrol prices rose sharply, increasing the cost of running generators for households and businesses.

These pressures, alongside persistent electricity shortages, have strengthened the appeal of solar energy as consumers seek more reliable and affordable alternatives to grid electricity and petrol- and diesel-powered generators.

Nigeria's growing solar market reflects increasing efforts to reduce dependence on the national grid, particularly among households, businesses and industries grappling with unreliable electricity supply and rising energy costs.

The growing availability of imported solar panels and related equipment has helped expand access to alternative energy systems, while the country continues to explore opportunities to strengthen local manufacturing and supply chains.

The expansion of small-scale solar systems is also reshaping Africa's energy landscape, shifting growth beyond large utility-scale projects to distributed installations that serve consumers directly.

A decade ago, solar PV deployment was largely concentrated in utility-scale projects in relatively mature markets such as Egypt and South Africa.

Today, the market is increasingly driven by smaller installations, with Algeria, Kenya, Nigeria and Senegal each recording more than 1 GW in solar capacity additions in 2025.

The report noted that South Africa remains a major contributor to the continent's solar expansion, accounting for more than one-third of total capacity additions over the period examined.

As Nigeria's adoption of solar energy systems continues to grow amid unreliable electricity supply and rising petrol and diesel prices, energy experts have called for increased local manufacturing, affordable financing and stronger regulation to unlock the sector's economic potential.

Solar expansion outpaces official records

Despite the rapid growth in imports, questions remain about how much solar equipment is actually being deployed across Africa and how accurately governments capture the expansion in their energy statistics.

The IEA said newly developed tools combining satellite imagery and remote sensing have provided fresh evidence that a significant share of imported solar equipment is being deployed in utility-scale and distributed installations missing from official records.

Close 

Across Africa, the analysis identified more than 50 per cent more utility-scale solar capacity than governments had officially recorded.

However, even after accounting for the underreported installations detected through satellite imagery, the additional capacity remains insufficient to explain the volume of solar equipment imported, leaving a gap of nearly 30 GW.

The discrepancy suggests that Africa's solar market may be expanding faster than conventional energy statistics can capture, although the extent of equipment stockpiling, re-exportation and unrecorded deployment remains uncertain.

Outlook

In the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), Africa's installed solar capacity is projected to increase sixfold over the next decade, signalling further expansion of the continent's solar market.

The growth is expected to build on an increasingly diverse range of projects, from utility-scale installations and industrial energy systems to smaller distributed solar systems serving households and businesses.

Beyond large-scale solar farms, the accelerating adoption of smaller systems could reshape how Africans access electricity, particularly in countries where grid reliability, affordability and access remain major challenges.

For Nigeria, the trend offers opportunities to expand energy access, reduce reliance on diesel-powered generation, strengthen domestic solar manufacturing, and accelerate the transition to a more reliable electricity supply.

World.title: Sudan: West Kordofan - Intensified Conflict and Deadly Oil Pollution
World.content:
For nearly a decade, civil society groups in the oil-rich areas of West Kordofan State have raised environmental and health concerns linked to the oil sector, where local communities say industrial chemicals and petroleum residues, including oil leakages, have triggered an ongoing health crisis.

The current conflict between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has compounded the problem further, especially now that it is flaring up in West Kordofan State, these local groups told Ayin.

Since the war began, oil extraction facilities have been in the crosshairs of the warring parties. The destruction of pipelines, poor infrastructure maintenance, and lack of environmental oversight, local residents told Ayin, have only made conditions worse. "We have observed a severe deterioration in the situation since the war began," says one local civil society actor who has been documenting it. The source requested anonymity for security reasons. "There is no maintenance, and, in addition, there has been deliberate destruction, theft, and--in many areas--explosions at the oil wells," the source added. The civil society source, along with industry experts and aid workers, describe how weak safeguards in the oil extraction industries in West Kordofan used prior to the outbreak of the war in April 2023 have all but disappeared.

Oil pollution in wartime



From late October, the fight over oil-rich West Kordofan has intensified between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). On November 5, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and allied groups launched a multi-pronged offensive from El-Obeid, marking their return to West Kordofan State after more than a year. Advancing southwest, the SAF coalition successfully recaptured the administrative hub of Al-Khuwai and its surrounding villages by November 13, ending an RSF occupation that had been in place since May 2025. The SAF and its allies are now continuing their westward push toward Al-Morkib and El-Nuhud, directly threatening major RSF strongholds in the region.

Despite the SAF's recent territorial gains in the northeastern section of the state, the RSF continue to control an estimated 85% to 90% of West Kordofan, including major strongholds and oil hubs like Al-Fula, Abu Zabad, Babanusa, Al-Muglad, and the Heglig complex. Earlier this month, the RSF announced plans to revive oil extraction operations in three sites within the state, potentially aggravating the pollution problem further. The RSF have dispatched a technical delegation to inspect the Neem, Defra and Kanar oilfields as part of preparations to restore production, according to local news reports.

According to one local civil society organisation, the areas of concern are the residential areas near the Heglig oil field, specifically the Al-Barzaya and Al-Zurga areas. "While the entire region is a source of deep concern for us, these areas (near the Heglig oil fields) are particularly worrying due to their high volume of oil flows, combined with the destruction of oil wells and pipelines," the civil society actor said.

Deteriorating health

According to the local civil society organisation, which continues to document and confirm cases of oil explosions at wells and ruptured pipelines, there is a correlation between oil pollution and deteriorating public health. "There has been a sharp rise in cases of foetal deformity; (we) have consistently noted that women from oil-producing regions have a high rate of giving birth to children with deformities," the civil society actor said. The same source told Ayin there are growing cases of infertility and forms of cancer that may also be linked to the pollution. The ongoing insecurity, however, has prevented the organisation from conducting definitive tests to see if there are direct links between the pollution and illness. "Often, these health issues are only diagnosed once individuals leave the oil-producing regions," the same source said. "We frequently hear that someone who went elsewhere to see a doctor has been diagnosed with cancer."

In other cases, residents have attempted to seal off damaged oil wells or repair ruptured pipelines and get injured in the process. "It is particularly concerning that the parties to the conflict - who should be responsible for these areas and their maintenance - show a lack of interest and focus on the matter."

A decade-long complaint

A local humanitarian worker told Ayin that local groups began investigating suspected environmental damage since 2016, focusing on problems associated with oil extraction and processing. During the rule of former president Omar al-Bashir, senior officials received their complaints, but the groups struggled to secure government support. The humanitarian actor attributed this difficulty partly to the influence of former oil minister Awad al-Jaz and the close relationship between the oil sector and the security institutions of the former regime.

Following the 2019 revolution, local activists protested outside the Ministry of Oil in July of the same year. The then oil minister, Adel Ali Ibrahim, received representatives of the communities, who called for an environmental assessment of the consequences of oil production. According to the source, the activists questioned whether Chinese oil companies operating in the region were adequately adhering to quality and environmental protection standards. A committee was formed and field surveys took place in 17 oil-processing sites, including Sharaf, Helaid and Baleela, the same source added.

The committee documented cases of congenital abnormalities, skin conditions, eye irritation among children, sexual health problems among men and infertility - all symptoms with suspected links to local oil production. The humanitarian actor said they identified more than 20 children with physical or congenital abnormalities and also reported cases of paralysis, blindness and eye inflammation.

The accounts raised serious questions about environmental exposure and public health in oil-producing areas but did not identify a direct correlation to the oil operations taking place. Testing that link would require medical examinations, environmental sampling and epidemiological evidence.

The oil industry's view

Industry insiders describe a different picture. An environmental quality-control expert with previous experience working at Sudanese oil refineries said the sector has an established system for environmental monitoring, reporting and remediation, although implementation varies between companies. The expert said oil operators are expected to monitor emissions against predetermined limits, report incidents to the relevant ministry and take corrective action when measurements exceed permitted thresholds. The Ministry of Oil's health, safety and environment department also conducts inspections, although these may be infrequent, the expert said.

The existence of monitoring procedures, however, does not establish that environmental standards are consistently met or that communities' complaints have been adequately addressed. Assessing how effectively the system operates would require access to monitoring results, inspection records, incident reports and remediation assessments.

The expert also warned against attributing miscarriages, infertility or cancer to oil operations without specialist evidence, arguing that unsupported claims could weaken the credibility of legitimate environmental concerns.

Mohamed Ibrahim, an oil supply chain and operations management expert who spoke to Ayin, identified the wording of Sudan's petroleum agreements as one area requiring closer scrutiny. He argues that environmental provisions in contracts are often too general and depend heavily on existing national legislation rather than setting out sufficiently detailed operational requirements.

"One of the problems with contracts in Sudan is that environmental provisions are drafted in very general terms and rely on Sudan's environmental laws and terminology," Ibrahim said. "This raises questions about whether petroleum agreements clearly define companies' environmental obligations."

Close 

Wastewater and gas flaring

Oil extraction produces more than crude petroleum. Depending on the field and extraction process, operations can also generate associated gas and contaminated water, both of which require appropriate treatment or disposal.

Ibrahim identified the handling of produced water - toxic, underground water brought to the surface during oil extraction - as a major environmental challenge. If dumped into the open, such toxic wastewater devastates local agriculture, poisons groundwater, and acts as the primary driver for public health crises linked to the oil industry.

Gas management presents a separate problem, Ibrahim said. In some countries, associated gas is routinely burnt through flaring, while others with strict regulations require operators to explore alternatives. Where flaring is permitted, its environmental effects depend in part on operating conditions, emissions and the controls in place.

"Gas flaring must also be governed by specific studies and measurements, because excessive flaring causes environmental pollution. Measurements should be conducted by an independent third party to ensure transparency and provide reliable information," he said.

Evidence and transparency

For residents of West Kordofan, the central issue remains whether oil production is being conducted in a way that protects their health, livelihoods and surrounding environment. Imagery and footage shared with Ayin provide visual evidence of oil leaks in parts of West Kordofan, but the extent of contamination, its origins and its potential effects on nearby populations require further investigation.

Nearly a decade after local groups began raising concerns, these complaints remain unheeded and will only increase as signs of conflict-induced damage to oil fields in West Kordofan take place.

World.title: Sudan: In War-Torn Sudan, Mothers Worry About Empty Plates and Lost Childhoods
World.content:
The World Food Programme can't "outfeed conflict," says WFP's chief Luke J. Lindberg on his first official visit to Sudan, where years of conflict and aid cuts risk deepening one of the world's biggest hunger crises.

Samia has the dreams of any Sudanese mother. To see her five children educated. To put three square meals on the table. To go back to her old life of farming before war tore it apart.

Today, her new normal is a sandy displacement camp in the south-central Sudanese city of Kosti. Home is a white tent affixed with rickety poles. Now the family's main breadwinner, the 37-year-old mother tries to put food on her children's table by working in the local market.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Some days, when work is good, I can give them a good meal," Samia told World Food Programme (WFP) Executive Director Luke J. Lindberg, during his recent visit to Goz El Salam displacement camp where she now lives. (For their protection, WFP does not use last names of war-displaced people.) "When work is not good, I make kisra (a fermented flatbread) for breakfast, and for lunch maybe lentils."

"We are doing our part to make sure we're delivering, and it's time for world leaders to step up and do their part and end this war." - Luke J. Lindberg, WFP Executive Director

As Sudan wraps up another year of brutal conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions, many like Samia are simply fighting to stay alive. Across Sudan, more than 19.5 million people face acute hunger. More than 4 million women and children are acutely malnourished.

And at a time when the war risks deepening one of the world's biggest hunger crises, humanitarian aid is shrinking for lack of funds. That includes WFP assistance that in August fed 4 million people. Since then, we have been forced to cut nearly a million people from our food and nutrition support.

But vanishing assistance is only part of the problem.

"The World Food Programme can't outfeed the conflict," Lindberg said during his visit to Sudan earlier this month-- his first field mission since becoming WFP chief. "We are doing our part to make sure we're delivering, and it's time for world leaders to step up and do their part and end this war."

Fleeing war, finding hunger

WFP is delivering in places like Goz El Salam, where lines of cloth tents are pitched in a sea of sand. More than 28,000 displaced people now shelter here, many having fled fighting in the central Kordofan region and Darfur to the west.

Workers unload bags of WFP sorghum, vegetable oil and pulses from trucks ahead of distributions for the camp's most vulnerable residents. For Samia and her family, it will be their first WFP support - and, as funds run short, it's uncertain how long it will last.

"I hope the World Food Programme can continue providing assistance, so we can feed our children and keep them in school," she says. "So they can have a better future."

Samia and her five children arrived at Goz El Salam in April, after fleeing heavy fighting in her South Kordofan hometown of Dilling. Her husband stayed behind with other family members.

"There is nobody supporting us financially," Samia says. She and her children rely on what little she earns at the market. Times have become so lean, she adds, that her oldest son works there as well, pushing goods with a wheelbarrow.

"I do not want him to work with me," Samia says, hoping someday "he can stay in school and continue studying with his siblings."

A mother's wish for her children: food, peace and school

Across the dusty Goz El Salam camp there are many stories of hardship. Another mother of five, Noor, spent months running from war with her family. Like Samia, she, too, hails from the Kordofan region.

Her face creased with worry, Noor describes how she buried her husband after he was killed in the fighting. How a charity gave her the funds to cross into South Sudan, where she and her family found refuge for a few months and sold tea for a living. How they finally earned enough to return to Sudan - and the relative safety of Goz El Salam.

Like many, Noor's family now depends on WFP food assistance to live. And like for many, it is not enough.

Close 

"In the morning I give them tea with milk. Otherwise, they go to school two or three times a week with nothing in their stomachs." - Noor, a displaced mother who lives at Sudan's Goz El Salam displacement camp

"In the morning I give them tea with milk," Noor says of her three youngest children who go to one of the camp's schools taught by volunteers. "Otherwise, they go to school two or three times a week with nothing in their stomachs."

For her part, Samia still hopes to go back home to Dilling. Back to farming and peace. "We farmed many things," she recalls of the distant days without hunger.

"My children had enough food and drink, and they were in school," she adds. "They did not lack anything."

WFP's food and nutrition support in Sudan is made possible thanks to donors including the African Development Bank, Austria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, the European Union, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Kuwait, Lithuania, Monaco, Norway, Private Donors, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Nations, the United States of America and the World Bank.

World.title: Africa: TrustAfrica Announces New Board Leadership as It Prepares to Enter Its Third Decade
World.content:
Dr. Abdoulie Janneh was elected Chair of the Board of Directors of TrustAfrica.

press release

TrustAfrica has announced a significant transition in the leadership and composition of its Board of Trustees, following the 43rd meeting of the Board, held in Dakar, Senegal, on 9–10 November 2026.

After eight years of distinguished service as Chair of the Board of Trustees, Ms Coumba Toure has stepped down from the position she had held since October 2018. Her tenure spanned a defining period in TrustAfrica’s evolution, including navigating the turbulent years of the COVID-19 pandemic, significantly expanding the organisation’s programme portfolio, strengthening its institutional systems and resource base, and deepening partnerships with regional institutions and leading Pan-African civic and philanthropic networks.

During this period, TrustAfrica expanded and strengthened a number of flagship initiatives, including the African Philanthropy Conference, co-organised with the Centre on African Philanthropy and Social Investment (CAPSI) at Wits University and several other Pan-African networks; the African Social Movements Baraza; the Harambee-Ubuntu Pan-African and Feminist Philanthropies Initiative, jointly led by TrustAfrica and Urgent Action Fund-Africa; the reimagining of governance and democracy work under the West Africa Democracy Fund; the Africa Youth Panel and NextGen Initiative; and the Global Africa Reparations Caravan.

These advances have strengthened TrustAfrica’s ability to fulfil its mandate of reinforcing African agency in addressing the continent’s most pressing challenges, deepening solidarity, and advancing people-centred transformative change across Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Board elected Dr Abdoulie Janneh as its new Chair. A respected African statesman and development leader, Dr Janneh previously served as Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) and as Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations. His extensive experience in African development, governance and international cooperation will help guide TrustAfrica as it enters its third decade.

TrustAfrica also welcomed three distinguished leaders to its Board of Trustees:

Dr Hippolyte Fofack, former Chief Economist and Director of Research and International Cooperation at the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank). He currently holds the inaugural SDSN Parker Fellowship at Columbia University in New York, is a Distinguished Fellow at the Global Federation of Competitiveness Councils (GFCC), and serves as a Research Associate at Harvard University’s Center for African Studies.

Dr Adeyemi Dipeolu, former Economic Affairs Adviser to the President of Nigeria. He is an Adjunct Professor at the Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance at the University of Cape Town, a Fellow of the Development Leadership Dialogue Institute at SOAS University of London, and a member of the AfCFTA Trade and Industrial Policy Advisory Council.

Ms Ainka Sanders Jackson, founding Executive Director of the Selma Center for Nonviolence, Truth and Reconciliation in Selma, Alabama, USA, and Co-Executive Director of the Selma Bridge Crossing Jubilee, one of the largest annual civil rights commemorations in the United States. An inaugural Obama USA Leader, she has contributed to national and international conversations on racial and economic equity, nonviolence, democracy and social justice.

The addition of these three leaders brings to TrustAfrica’s Board a wealth of experience spanning African economic transformation, public policy, development, racial and economic justice, civil rights and international cooperation. Their appointment reinforces TrustAfrica’s commitment to harnessing the knowledge, expertise and resources of Global Africa, encompassing the continent and its diaspora, as well as friends of Africa around the world, to advance the continental transformation agenda and contribute to building the Africa we want.

The Board also confirmed 1–2 April 2027 as the new dates for TrustAfrica’s 20th Anniversary Conference in Abuja, Nigeria.

Under the theme “Sustaining African Agency, Building the Future We Want,” the high-level 20th Anniversary Conference will bring together TrustAfrica’s partners, current and former leaders, civil society actors, intellectuals, policymakers, philanthropists and friends from across Africa and other regions of the world. The conference will provide an important opportunity to reflect on two decades of work, celebrate the communities and partnerships that have shaped TrustAfrica’s journey, and collectively consider the challenges and possibilities facing Africa in the decades ahead.

As TrustAfrica marks twenty years of work and prepares for its next chapter, we express our profound appreciation to all our partners and supporters, and to all those who, over the past two decades, have served as Board or staff members.

We extend our sincere gratitude to Ms Coumba Toure for her dedicated leadership and eight years of service as Chair of the Board. Her contribution has been invaluable to the institution and to our collective efforts to strengthen African agency and advance a more equitable and just continent.

Close 

We warmly welcome Dr Abdoulie Janneh as Chair of the Board, alongside Dr Hippolyte Fofack, Dr Adeyemi Dipeolu and Ms Ainka Sanders Jackson as new Trustees. Their experience, leadership and commitment will enrich TrustAfrica’s work as the organisation enters its third decade.

We look forward to bringing together our partners, friends and wider community in Abuja on 1–2 April 2027 for TrustAfrica’s 20th Anniversary Conference, an important moment to celebrate what we have built together, reflect on our shared journey, and collectively imagine the future we want.

Dr Ebrima Sall

Executive Director

TrustAfrica

Dakar, Senegal

About TrustAfrica: TrustAfrica is an independent African foundation headquartered in Dakar, Senegal. For two decades, the organisation has worked to strengthen African agency and advance equitable development through grantmaking, knowledge production, convening, advocacy, and support for movements, institutions and networks working for social, economic and political transformation across the continent.

World.title: Nigeria: Atiku Loses Court Case Challenging Tinubu's 2027 Poll Eligibility
World.content:
Atiku and ADC had asked the court to declare Mr Tinubu unqualified to contest the election and compel INEC to remove his name and that of the APC from the list of candidates and political parties for the 2027 presidential poll.

The Federal High Court in Abuja has dismissed an application by former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) to amend their suit challenging President Bola Tinubu's eligibility to contest the 2027 presidential election.

Judge Inyang Ekwo on Friday ruled that the proposed amendments sought to introduce new facts into the case after the 14-day period prescribed by the Constitution for filing pre-election matters had expired.

He held that introducing fresh facts through an amendment would materially alter the original case.



Mr Ekwo ruled that he saw "no merit in this application, and it is hereby dismissed." Hence, the judge ordered the parties "to move to the substantive case."

Atiku and ADC instituted the suit on 14 August, challenging Mr Tinubu's eligibility to contest the 2027 presidential election.

The plaintiffs sued Mr Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress (APC) and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), alleging that the APC submitted a forged National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate to INEC in support of the president's nomination. They alleged that the certificate bore the name "Tinubu Bola Adekunle" rather than Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

At the 13 October hearing, Atiku's lawyer, Joseph Silas, moved an application filed on 10 September, seeking permission to amend the originating summons. The plaintiffs said they had noticed errors in their original court processes, including the description of INEC Form EC9A as Form CF001.

They also sought to provide clearer copies of some exhibits, set out particulars of the alleged fraud and include a written deposition by Atiku. They maintained that the proposed amendments would not introduce new issues or additional reliefs but were necessary to present their case properly.

But Mr Tinubu, through his lawyer, Wole Olanipekun, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), opposed the application. He argued that the proposed amendments would introduce a new case rather than correct errors and that the substantive suit was statute-barred.

The APC, represented by Akin Olujinmi, SAN, also urged the court to reject the application. Similarly, INEC's lawyer, Alex Izinyon, SAN, argued that the proposed amendments would introduce a fresh cause of action and attempt to cure defects after the constitutional deadline for filing pre-election cases had expired.

After listening to the parties, Judge Ekwo fixed 20 November (today) for ruling on the application.

'Pre-election matters are sui generis'

While ruling on the application, the judge agreed with Mr Tinubu, INEC and APC that the amendments would introduce new facts.

Mr Ekwo described pre-election matters as "sui generis", meaning they are a special category of cases with their own procedural requirements. He said the nature of such cases required parties to "present all relevant facts, documents and materials when they commenced their actions."

Referring to Section 285 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, the judge noted that the event forming the basis of the suit occurred at the beginning of August, while the plaintiffs commenced the action on 14 August. He acknowledged that the suit was filed within the 14-day constitutional period but the plaintiffs could not use an amendment to introduce fresh facts after that period had expired.

"it is not the law that incomplete facts, documents or materials can form a suit in a pre-election action," noted the judge.

The judge also acknowledged the amendment provisions in the Federal High Court's Pre-Election Practice Directions 2026 but explained that they were not intended to allow parties to introduce material changes or reframe their cases after the constitutional period had expired.

Mr Ekwo therefore questioned the plaintiffs' claim in their affidavit supporting the application that the amendments introduced no new facts or issues and sought no additional reliefs.

He specifically identified paragraphs 8, 9 and 10 of the proposed amended affidavit as containing facts that were not in the original affidavit. He also identified proposed changes to paragraph 14, as well as material alterations to other parts of the affidavit.

He concluded that the plaintiffs had misinformed the court about the nature of the proposed amendments and that the application consequently lacked credible evidence.

Background

Atiku and ADC had asked the court to declare Mr Tinubu unqualified to contest the election and compel INEC to remove his name and that of the APC from the list of candidates and political parties for the 2027 presidential poll. However, the substantive suit has yet to proceed to a full hearing since it was filed.

Close 

It first came up before Judge Ekwo on 1 September. The plaintiffs' lawyer, Joseph Onu, told the court that they had been unable to serve Mr Tinubu with the originating summons and other court processes. When Mr Tinubu's lawyer, Omosanya Popoola, offered to receive the documents on his behalf, Mr Onu declined without a written undertaking confirming that he was authorised to accept them.

The disagreement over service stalled the proceedings, prompting the judge to adjourn the case until 28 September. The court later granted the plaintiffs permission to serve Mr Tinubu through the APC, the second defendant in the suit, within seven days.

Meanwhile, Mr Tinubu and the APC filed a joint counter-affidavit around 9 September, urging the court to dismiss the suit as incompetent and arguing that the plaintiffs lacked the legal right to institute it.

They denied submitting any forged certificate to INEC for either the 2023 or 2027 presidential elections. They also said the NYSC had never denied issuing the discharge certificate to Mr Tinubu.

World.title: South Africa: Cachalia Drops Apartheid Truth Bombs As Latest Stats Show '60 Killed Daily in SA'
World.content:
South Africa's latest official crime statistics show that over three months, 5,590 people were murdered in the country. Referencing gang killings and violence, Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia reminded Parliamentarians that apartheid's legacy still affected these crimes and that the most affected areas needed development, not just heightened policing.

Acting National Police Minister Firoz Cachalia wants a serious discussion about critical issues underpinning gang violence - and this will involve uncomfortable truths about apartheid's corrosive legacy.

"It is not about blaming apartheid," Cachalia explained on Friday, 20 November 2026, as South Africa's latest official crime statistics were released.

"But it is also important not to pretend we didn't have that history... In this country, your chances in life are based on where you are born."

Cachalia addressed these realities while the South African Police Service (SAPS) presented its latest official crime figures covering the three months from the start of July to the end of September this year.

He spoke slowly with what sounded like a hint of frustration - and intense feeling.

'60 killed daily'

The latest SAPS figures provide a glimpse of what crimes have been prevalent and where.

According to these latest statistics, over the three months between July and September, there were:

5,590 murders nationally, an increase from 5,427 over the previous three months and lower than the 5,794 murders recorded between July and September last year.An average of 60 people killed in the country daily.261 gang-related murders, with the majority, 208, in the Western...

World.title: Africa: Ignore Fake Graphic Claiming Nigerians Have 120 Days to Leave South Africa
World.content:
This viral graphic appears to announce the "breaking news" that Nigerian nationals living in South Africa must leave by February 2027 or face legal action. It includes a photo of Democratic Alliance's Helen Zille and claims the "order" was issued by the Bloemfontein High Court. But the graphic is fake, and no such announcement has been made.

Ignore fake graphic claiming Nigerians have 120 days to leave South Africa

IN SHORT: A viral graphic appears to announce the "breaking news" that Nigerian nationals living in South Africa must leave by February 2027 or face legal action. It includes a photo of Democratic Alliance's Helen Zille and claims the "order" was issued by the Bloemfontein high court. But the graphic is fake, and no such announcement has been made.

A graphic formatted to look like a breaking news announcement is circulating on Facebook in South Africa in November 2026.

The graphic claims Nigerian nationals have 120 days to leave South Africa, starting on 15 November.



It reads:

All Nigerian nationals to vacate South Africa within 120 days; Starting from Sunday The 15 Nov-15 Feb 227. Business Owners to sell their businesses, Property owners to pack and Exit the Republic of South Africa Failure to leave South Africa within 120 days may lead to serious legal challenges that may include jail time and outstanding fines ... Nigerians are flooding South Africa 'Johannesburg' with drugs and 97.08% of Nigerians are feeding innocent South African souls with dangerous and poisonous drugs - says Helen Zille.

It also features Helen Zille's photo and further claims that the "ruling and order has been issued and finalised by the Bloemfontein High Court".

Zille is a prominent politician and high-ranking member of the Democratic Alliance (DA), South Africa's second-largest political party.

The graphic was first posted on Facebook by a page named Randy Empowerment Center, which appears to regularly post graphics and videos that are often flagged by Meta as generated using artificial intelligence tools. It also posts videos and graphics of politicians and other content, often framing them as "breaking news".

Earlier in 2026, Africa Check debunked a similar graphic with a "deadline" for foreign nationals to leave South Africa. It appeared during a surge in anti-migrant sentiment, especially on social media, along with protests, displacements and killings of suspected migrants in some parts of the country.

This graphic claiming Nigerians have 120 days to leave the country is also fake. Here's how we know.

Fake graphic, false claims

We found no evidence that such a notice was issued through the official accounts and communication platforms of Zille, the DA, or the South African government.

Rather than an official channel affiliated with a party or the government, the Facebook page that initially posted the notice describes itself as a "digital creator". It does not appear to be a credible source.

Close 

The graphic is also visually inconsistent with a legitimate official announcement; it includes grammatical errors, odd punctuation and the words "Randy Empowerment Center" in large letters across it.

The page also doesn't provide a source for the claim or when and where Zille may have made the attributed statement. Such a lack of detail suggests the graphic is fabricated.

A keyword search also brought up no credible media reports to support the claim. Such a major announcement would've made headlines, especially given South Africa's history with xenophobia.

We also searched through the 2026 rulings of the Bloemfontein high court, which is in the Free State province, and found nothing related to the claim.

The graphic is fabricated and makes false claims.

For more useful tips, read our guide to verifying breaking news events.

World.title: Uganda: Uganda Restricts Cross-Border Movement, Public Gatherings Amid Ebola Threat
World.content:
Nairobi — Uganda has imposed fresh restrictions on public gatherings and cross-border travel in 34 high-risk districts bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) as authorities intensify efforts to prevent another Ebola outbreak.

The measures include a ban on concerts, festivals and political rallies without clearance from the Ministry of Health, alongside mandatory 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation for Ugandans returning from the DRC.

The government has also tightened passenger screening at airports, introduced stricter monitoring of hotels and schools, and restricted the movement of humanitarian workers and bodies across its borders.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The restrictions, which took effect immediately, follow concerns over continued movement between Uganda and the DRC, including through unofficial crossing points that could facilitate the spread of the deadly virus.

In a public health advisory issued on November 19, Uganda's Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Diana Atwine said the National Task Force on Epidemic Preparedness and Response had approved the additional interventions following an assessment of the risks posed by the outbreak in the neighbouring DRC.

"With the current heightened surveillance, the ministry has observed continued movement of people across our borders, including through ungazetted crossing points, which has increased the risk of the disease entering Uganda and spreading to our communities and to other countries," Atwine said.

She emphasised that the new directives were additional safeguards, with previously announced restrictions remaining in force.

Under the new guidelines, authorities in the 34 designated border districts have been instructed to monitor new arrivals and people relocating into their communities. Local leaders, particularly Local Council chairpersons, must be notified immediately of new arrivals and movements into the affected areas.

Organisers of mass gatherings will also be required to obtain written authorisation from the Ministry of Health before holding concerts, festivals, political rallies or similar events in the designated districts.

The government has warned that individuals who illegally cross into the country, as well as those who facilitate unauthorised border movements, will face legal action.

Ugandans arriving from the DRC will undergo mandatory health risk assessments before being placed under 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation.

The restrictions also extend to humanitarian operations, with aid workers required to obtain clearance from the Director General of Health Services before undertaking cross-border movements.

The transportation of bodies into or out of Uganda will similarly require prior government authorisation.

At Entebbe International Airport, authorities have introduced enhanced screening and infection prevention measures for both arriving and departing passengers.

Travellers will be required to complete passenger locator forms before boarding to facilitate contact tracing, while airlines and other transport operators risk sanctions if they knowingly transport passengers without proper authorisation or documentation.

Uganda has also tightened controls in the education and hospitality sectors. Day scholars travelling between Uganda and the DRC in the designated border districts will no longer be permitted to cross under the new restrictions.

Boarding students who may have been exposed to the virus must undergo 21 days of quarantine in designated facilities before returning to school.

Hotels and other accommodation facilities have been directed to maintain accurate guest registers, verify visitors using valid identification documents and provide the records to health and security authorities when required.

Schools, hospitals, transport terminals, places of worship and other public facilities have also been instructed to provide handwashing facilities and strictly observe infection prevention and control measures.

To strengthen public awareness, radio stations operating in the affected border districts have been directed to dedicate at least two hours every month to Ebola prevention campaigns.

Kenya's Ebola threat

Uganda's heightened surveillance comes as Kenya approaches the end of its Ebola monitoring period following an outbreak linked to a traveller who passed through Uganda after arriving from the DRC.

Kenya confirmed its first case on October 6, involving a man who had travelled from the DRC through Kampala before arriving in Nairobi. The patient died on October 5, becoming the index case in the country's outbreak.

Health authorities subsequently identified eight secondary infections, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to nine. All infections were linked to a single transmission cluster, with no evidence of wider community transmission.

The outbreak claimed two lives, including the index patient and his 65-year-old mother.

Kenya is now working towards a possible declaration of being Ebola-free around December 23, provided no new infections are detected.

The 42-day countdown began on November 12, following the discharge of the last patient and the completion of the mandatory 21-day monitoring period for the final contacts on November 11.

The 42-day period represents twice the virus's maximum incubation period of 21 days and is the standard requirement for declaring an Ebola outbreak over.

Uganda's latest restrictions also reflect its own experience with the disease earlier this year, when it recorded 20 confirmed cases between May and June 2026.

The infections comprised 15 imported cases from the DRC and five secondary infections among contacts, with two deaths reported.

Uganda declared its outbreak over on July 28, with the World Health Organisation following on August 27 after the country went 42 days without recording a new confirmed infection.

Close 

However, the continued movement of people across its border with the DRC has kept the threat of fresh infections alive.

By mid-November, the DRC had reported more than 11,300 confirmed cases and over 5,500 deaths, making it a major source of concern for neighbouring countries.

The World Health Organisation has assessed the risk of further spread within the DRC as very high, while the risk to countries sharing land borders with it remains high.

Atwine has urged communities to remain vigilant, warning that Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood and other body fluids of infected people, individuals who have died from the disease, or infected animals.

Symptoms include sudden fever, headache, muscle pain, weakness, vomiting, diarrhoea and unexplained bleeding.

She advised the public to avoid contact with anyone displaying suspected symptoms and to refrain from handling bodies of people who have died from unexplained illnesses.

"Wash hands regularly with soap and clean water," she advised.

Members of the public have also been urged to report suspected infections immediately to the nearest health facility or contact the Ministry of Health through its toll-free line, 0800 100 066.

The Permanent Secretary said the ministry would continue issuing updates as the situation develops.

World.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

World.title: New drug combo shrinks tumors in most patients facing aggressive cancer type
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Pairing an experimental pill with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or halted growth in most patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, according to early clinical trial results presented Friday at a major international cancer conference.

The findings, shared at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium in Barcelona, come from a phase ½ trial testing a daily oral medication called daraxonrasib, along with two standard intravenous chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel.

The trial focused on 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had already spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for their advanced disease.

PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENT BEN SASSE SEES 'MASSIVE' TUMOR REDUCTION WITH EXPERIMENTAL NEW DRUG

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat because more than half of patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread, research shows.

In major clinical trials for metastatic pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy alone shrinks tumors in about 23% to 42% of patients, but the disease typically begins growing again after five to six months, and most patients survive between 8 and 11 months.

According to National Cancer Institute data, only about 3% of patients with distant-stage disease live five years past diagnosis.

In the new study, which tracked patients for a median follow-up of 18 months, tumors shrank in 60.7% of cases, including 8.2% where they disappeared entirely on scans. Overall, the combination stopped tumor growth in 90.2% of participants.

FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer worsened, almost double the timeframe typically seen with standard chemotherapy, and 76.6% were still alive at the one-year mark, the study found.

"We are now seeing not only substantial tumor shrinkages, including complete responses, but also durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year," study lead Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, said in a press release.

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are driven by a faulty gene called RAS, which allows tumors to keep growing. Daraxonrasib is designed to turn off that growth signal, something scientists long thought was impossible to fix with medication.

Dr. Elena Garralda, chair of the symposium and co-director of the clinical research program at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology in Spain, who was not involved in the research, said the results show that RAS-targeted drugs can be combined with existing treatments at the start of treatment to potentially achieve longer-lasting benefits.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Side effects included rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts linked to chemotherapy, most of which were manageable with standard care.

Only 5% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects tied to daraxonrasib.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers emphasized that the findings carry some limitations.

Because this was an early-phase, single-group study involving 61 people, all participants received the experimental combination. Without a direct comparison group of patients receiving standard chemotherapy alone, doctors cannot yet confirm how much better the new regimen performs or whether it definitively extends overall survival.

The findings also apply strictly to metastatic pancreatic cancer, even though RAS mutations drive several other cancers, including certain lung, colorectal and gynecological cancers. Separate studies would be needed to test whether the combination works in those diseases.

CLICK HERE TO 

The trial was funded by Revolution Medicines, the California-based developer of daraxonrasib.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

To determine whether these early findings translate into a durable survival benefit, researchers have launched a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial, called RASolute-303, which directly compares daraxonrasib — both on its own and combined with chemotherapy — against standard chemotherapy alone.

World.title: 'Enough': Protesters decry antisemitism after Hunter College student event including Jewish group is canceled
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A crowd gathered Thursday outside Hunter College to protest after the school's student government seemingly canceled an event due to the participation of a Jewish organization.

On one side of the street, pro-Israel protesters chanted "enough is enough" and waved American and Israeli flags as speakers addressed the crowd. Across the street, a group of counter-protesters gathered waving Palestinian flags while yelling chants of their own.

Passersby also shouted, some in support and others yelling "Free Palestine" and "F--- Israel."

JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS

Organizers behind the Stand with Jewish Students at Hunter rally included the Israeli American Council (IAC), Students Supporting Israel (SSI) and #EndJewHatred.

On flyers advertising the rally, they criticized the college's administration for not doing enough in response to what they saw as an act of antisemitism.

"We're saying enough to the marginalization of the Jewish community. We're saying enough is enough to discrimination against Jewish students. And we're saying enough is enough to this obsessive hatred of all of the symbols of Jewish life, whether it's Hillel on campus or the State of Israel," IAC CEO Elan Carr told Fox News Digital, referring to a chapter of the Jewish student group.

Michelle Ahdoot, director of programming and strategy at #EndJewHatred, told Fox News Digital the cancellation of the event demonstrated a problem that went beyond Hunter College.

"When a multicultural event is canceled simply because Jewish students are included, we have a serious problem that goes far beyond one event at Hunter College," Ahdoot said. "The very purpose of multiculturalism is to celebrate diversity and inclusion, not to allow certain groups to decide who is welcome and who is not.

"Any student organization has the right to choose not to participate," he continued. "But when an elected student government responds by canceling the entire event rather than standing up for the inclusion of Jewish students, it sends a dangerous message that Jewish participation is somehow unacceptable."

The Cultural Arts Night was scheduled to take place Nov. 16 but was canceled just days before. Hunter College Undergraduate Student Government (USG) flyers promoting the event showed that clubs involved included Students for Justice in Palestine, the Peruvian Student Association, Hunter Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and Hunter Hillel, according to screenshots posted online.

Hillel International is a Jewish organization that can be found on college campuses across the globe. It describes itself as "a space for all kinds of Jewish students — a place where they feel welcomed and included." While its vision includes helping students make "an enduring commitment to Jewish life, learning and Israel," it is focused on Jewish life and culture, hosting holidays and holding events.

FIRE ALARM DISRUPTS NORTHWESTERN 'OCTOBER 7' PLAY BASED ON MASSACRE SURVIVOR TESTIMONY

Rita Levine Rabin Hillel at Hunter College said in a statement on Instagram it was "looking forward" to the event and that it "had no role in the decision to cancel."

"Antisemitism has no place at Hunter College. Jewish students should never be singled out, scapegoated, or made to feel unwelcome because of who they are and the anti-Semitic response online to the cancellation notice has been egregious and inappropriate," the statement read.

Ilya Bratman, who serves as executive director at Hillel at Baruch College in New York City, said the cancellation of Cultural Arts Night was a clear case of antisemitism and a sign that things could escalate.

"This is so obvious, and antisemitism has nothing to do with Israel. And that's what the main thing you have to say very loudly. This is about Jew hatred and exclusion," Bratman told Fox News Digital. "It's the first step in the process, which begins with physical exclusion of Jewish students from campuses.

"And that is what happened in the 1930s. We know this. This is a slower process here in American campuses, and I believe this is going to keep going if we don't step up in a very serious way to stop it."

Hunter College USG announced the cancellation on Nov. 14 in a statement from Hunter College USG President Sumaiya Ahmed and Vice President Ahmad Waraich. The two student leaders claimed that "lapses in communication kept the details of this event from reaching the people at the top."

"We hear what the student body has said, and we have made the decision to cancel the event as it doesn’t align with our values or the values of the students we represent as the Hunter Community. We apologize to the clubs and students who were affected by this instance," a statement posted on Instagram read.

After the announcement, speculation about the reason for the event's cancellation grew, with some pointing to pressure from anti-Israel activists who objected to Hillel's involvement. While this was not directly addressed, Hunter USG appeared to deny it in a subsequent statement in which it said that the event was canceled over "safety concerns."

BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES

Hunter College is a public institution in the City University of New York (CUNY) system, making allegations of discrimination particularly serious since public schools are legally barred from discriminating based on religion or national origin.

Hunter College told Fox News Digital it was "deeply troubled by reports that some student groups pulled from the event because of Hillel’s participation" and said it was investigating the issue.

"There is no place for discrimination and harassment in our college community. We have policies in place to safeguard that principle and will not hesitate to enforce them," the college said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

Michal Mari, who is president of SSI at Hunter College, told Fox News Digital during the rally that the environment at the school has been "tough" for Jewish students. She said Jewish students had seen calls for violence against their community, including statements calling to "bring the war home" and "globalize the intifada."

Mari believes the cancellation came after clubs dropped out of the event due to Hillel's participation, which she said was "blatant discrimination against Jewish students on campus."

"I've had professors turn their backs to me while I was speaking to them because they found out that I was wearing a Star of David or that I've been to Israel," Mari told Fox News Digital. "So, it's certainly not the most divided, but it's a place where there's work to be done."

Mari addressed the crowd at Thursday night's rally along with a number of other pro-Israel and Jewish speakers, including Shai Davidai, Ari Ackerman, Shabbos Kestenbaum and Rami Matan Even-Esh (also known as Kosha Dillz), among others, including Hunter College students.

Jayne Zirkle, who serves as director of communications for #EndJewHatred, said the organization was "incredibly proud" of the students who chose to speak publicly despite the pressures they face on campus.

"Their courage matters, and they deserve to know they are not standing alone," Zirkle said.

Davidai, a former Columbia University professor, told Fox News Digital he attended the rally to bring attention to what he saw as the "symptom" of a bigger issue.

"The symptom of canceling an event because a Jewish organization is part of it, that is a problem. And, by the way, it's a problem not just for Jews, it's a problem for everyone. Because when you cancel an event, everyone, Jewish or non-Jews, don't get to go to that event," Davidai said.

LEO TERRELL TAKES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S ANTISEMITISM FIGHT NATIONWIDE ON 15-CITY TOUR

While Davidai focused on the broader cultural fallout on campus, Kestenbaum, a former Harvard Divinity School student who sued Harvard over campus antisemitism, framed the issue around civil rights law and public funding.

"You cannot violate civil rights law. Colleges don't get to pick and choose which statute of the Civil Rights Act they want to subscribe to. There is one standard for all universities across the country, and if those universities insist on discriminating against students because of their ethnicity or because of their religious identity, that is illegal," Kestenbaum told Fox News Digital.

Kestenbaum is not the only one who has brought up the possible legal issues with canceling the event. New York City Council Member Eric Dinowitz publicly called for a civil rights investigation.

"[Hunter College] USG cancels a multicultural arts event because it did not align with its 'values.' It appears to be yet another chapter in the troubling history of antisemitism at CUNY and Hunter," Dinowitz wrote on X. "That's why [CUNY] must immediately launch a Title VI investigation."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Along with calls for institutional and legal accountability, speakers at Thursday night's rally encouraged students at Hunter College not to retreat from campus life and stay silent.

"Every student at Hunter or anywhere else, if you speak up, and when you speak up, we've got your back," Davidai said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"We've got your back with numbers. We've got your back with legal support. We got your back on social media. We have got your backs. But it's up to you to speak up, because if you don't speak up then, you know, the word doesn't come out."

Mari echoed the message, saying that the Jewish community at Hunter College was ready to rally behind those who choose to speak out.

"Courage isn't lack of fear but acting in the face of fear," Mari told Fox News Digital. "You have a community behind you. The Jewish community, especially, is one that is always behind you."

Hunter USG and Hunter Hillel did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

World.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous’ penalties on companies that build data centers overseas
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he plans to restrict U.S. companies from building data centers overseas — the latest instance of the president embracing the construction of massive tech facilities that a majority of Americans oppose.

Back in Washington after a trip to Asia, Trump said the restrictions were necessary to prevent AI infrastructure from leaving U.S. shores.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump told reporters in the White House briefing room.

“We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country,” he said.

He added that the U.S. would tax any company that attempted to build a data center abroad.

“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” he said.

The comments signaled a potential new headache for the artificial intelligence industry, on a day when stock markets tumbled and not even the record-setting IPO this week of Anthropic could soothe investors’ fears about the sustainability of AI stocks.

They were also the latest example of Trump’s forceful advocacy for AI data centers, a position that puts him squarely at odds with the majority of Americans.

“You ought to take advantage of the data centers,” Trump said Friday. “Make them pay you. Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don’t shut them off.”

Trump has previously attacked state and local efforts to roll back data center construction, saying in August that they should only be stopped if communities “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” Trump wrote in a social media post.

During this year’s midterm elections, data centers proved a key sticking point for voters, who overwhelmingly supported candidates who promised to curb their proliferation.

On Wall Street, the massive wins by Democrats who pledged to rein in data centers put a fresh dent in an already-ailing AI stock trade, as investors digested the prospect that tech companies’ computing resources would be further crimped.

Since Nov. 4, the S&P 500 has declined approximately 9%, though a confluence of other factors has also contributed to the brutal sell-off.

President Donald Trump at a press briefing with AI executives at the White House on Sept. 29. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

It is not clear how Trump’s foreign data center ban would be implemented; a White House representative did not immediately reply to a request for comment Friday.

Trump admitted that he had not yet told his staff about the plan.

“I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump mused. “I’m telling them now — they’re here, many of them are here — and we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can’t. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it.”

World.title: FBI investigating potential breach of its crime database
World.content:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, two people briefed on the matter told NBC News Friday.

The FBI’s National Crime Information Center is used to connect federal, state and local authorities so that important law enforcement information is available nationwide.

The FBI had no comment as of Friday night.

CNN reported the matter earlier in the evening.

While the FBI has not addressed who may have breached the system in this case, the agency did announce an investigation in September of a notorious hacking group that claimed it had stolen data on agents through the agency’s job portal.

The breach this week follows an apparent cyberattack at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, as employees were informed Thursday that one of its systems had been targeted.

USDA officials with knowledge of the matter said that a system the agency uses to pay farmers was hit by the breach, though as of Friday, no other systems were targeted. Officials raised alarms that the hackers could find a way to access more sensitive information due to the breach.

Alongside the reported breaches, outages affecting both private and public sectors over the last several days have raised concerns about the nation’s cybersecurity.

An internal classified computer network used by the National Security Agency endured a multi-day outage after it first went down Tuesday due to a technical problem, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. As of Friday, the outage has been resolved, sources said.

Sources told NBC News that the network went down while maintenance was being performed. They said that there was no sign that the outage was caused by a cyberattack.

Addressing the widespread tech outages, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said Wednesday that evidence showed that the tech outages were not caused by cyberattacks, though he warned that AI could have played a role in the systems’ vulnerabilities.

Amid rising concerns about the outages, a White House official confirmed to NBC News Thursday that White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was leaving his role.

Cairncross was directly involved with the White House’s deliberations on AI policy, including its move to direct Anthropic to take down its two most powerful AI systems over the summer due to national security concerns.
