World.title: Trump formally ends minting of the penny after nearly 250 years of production
World.content:
Washington is officially done with spending a pretty penny on penny production.

President Donald Trump on Friday signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act, which formally directs the federal government to stop minting the penny.

Both the House and the Senate passed the measure by voice vote, meaning no notable opposition.

“It costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny,” the bill’s author, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Sept. 29 on X a day after Senate passage. “This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production — it’s common sense!”

The government stopped making pennies in November 2025, nine months after Trump called for the Treasury Department to stop production, writing at the time that the process was “so wasteful!” Stephen Hilger / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The U.S. Mint last year put the immediate annual savings of discontinuing penny production at $56 million.

The government stopped making pennies in November 2025, nine months after Trump called for the Treasury Department to stop production, writing at the time that the process was “so wasteful!” However, the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector versions to be produced in “limited quantities.”

The penny can still be used as legal tender “for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues,” according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence “for as long as possible.”

The new measure also provides a procedure for stores and businesses that accept cash payments to round their prices to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents.

And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint’s currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.

Congress passed the Coinage Act in 1792, and the U.S. Mint began producing the penny, known officially as the cent, the following year.

It wasn’t until 1909 that it was given its modern-day face, featuring President Abraham Lincoln. Stephen Hilger / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

In its nearly 250 years in production, the penny has had multiple facades. It wasn’t until 1909 that it was given its modern-day face, featuring President Abraham Lincoln.

The first penny, produced in 1787, had a sundial design created by Benjamin Franklin. After the U.S. Mint took over, the penny was slightly bigger and included the image of a woman representing Liberty on one side and 15 chain links on the other.

The next penny debuted in 1857, taking on a smaller shape and displaying a flying eagle design on one side and a wreath on the other. It also changed from being 100% copper to 88% copper and 12% nickel. Two years later, an “Indian Head” design was added to one side.

The most recent design from the U.S. Mint was issued in 2010, featuring its “Union Shield” theme. It shows a shield on the tails side of the coin to represent “Lincoln’s preservation of the United States as a single country,” the U.S. Mint wrote.

World.title: Iraqi security forces deploy in Iran-backed militia stronghold
World.content:
JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq — Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, on Friday under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran’s most powerful Shi’ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi this week ordered security forces to move against the heavily armed Kataib Hezbollah, which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars in Jurf al-Sakhar.

The hardline Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United States, has rejected the smuggling accusations, which have led to arrests that prompted fears of an armed response. The group is among those that have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

A convoy of vehicles flying Iraqi flags headed into Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday and soldiers took up positions in the center after senior security officials told a press conference that government forces would protect the town.

Members of the Kataib Hezbollah group stood near their group’s flags.

“From Jurf al-Sakhar, we begin asserting state authority across all of Iraq, confronting corruption and weapons beyond state control,” Zaidi told government troops who entered the town, speaking from a military operations center in Baghdad.

“Our decision is firm: No weapons outside state authority, no weapons but Iraq‘s, no decisions but Iraq‘s, and no flag shall fly higher than the Iraqi flag.”

Under the arrangement, brokered by Shi’ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq, a major oil producer and ally of both the US and Iran.

“God willing, things will be safe and secure with the presence of the security forces,” said resident Mohamed Ali.

Senior Iranian representative visited Baghdad, sources say

The deal will include the opening of a security headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar on Saturday to oversee the handover. Iraq‘s energy police have begun securing an oil pipeline in Jurf al-Sakhar, the state news agency reported.

“Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi Armed Forces prove that they are the nation’s shield, safety valve, and the guardian ensuring security stability for the Iraqi people,” Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, told the press conference.

Reflecting the sensitivity of the situation, Iraqi Shi’ite political figures said Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataib Hezbollah.

So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad.

Any direct confrontation with Iran’s heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky.

After one of Zaidi’s predecessors ordered a similar crackdown on those armed groups five years ago, the prime minister’s Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt.

President Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck U.S. troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia & the United Arab Emirates. Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty

Refusal to disarm

US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February.

Kataib Hezbollah and other militias, all of whom report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, have refused to hand over their weapons to the state.

Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, the umbrella group of hardline Shi’ite armed organisations supported by Iran.

Kataib Hezbollah quickly developed a reputation for deadly attacks against military and diplomatic targets during the US-led counterinsurgency war and sectarian conflict of the 2000s, using snipers, rockets, mortars and roadside bombs.

Wide Iranian sway in Iraq

Since the 2003 US-led invasion toppled Iran’s arch-enemy, longtime Sunni leader Saddam Hussein, Tehran has steadily expanded its influence in Iraq through close ties with heavily armed Shi’ite militias and political parties.

Iraqi security officials say the militias’ arsenals include assault rifles, machineguns, anti-tank guided missiles, mortars, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missile capabilities.

Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though Kataib denies this and says it is dedicated to security.

Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters.

It forms several battalions in Iraq‘s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and subsequently recognized as an official security force.

Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF. While it is technically under the command of Iraq‘s prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command.

World.title: Man found guilty of starting deadly Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
LOS ANGELES — Almost five months after a first trial ended in a mistrial, a jury found a man guilty of starting what would become the devastating 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles that displaced thousands of people and became the most destructive wildfire in the city’s history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted Friday on both federal counts against him: destruction of property by means of fire, and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

Sentencing was set for March 17. Rinderknecht faces a minimum of five years and a maximum of 40 years in prison, prosecutors said.

The Palisades Fire, which began Jan. 7, 2025, was fueled by winds gusting up to 100 mph that fed on the very dry conditions.

It killed 12 people, destroyed over 6,000 homes and other structures, and caused $25 billion in damage, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.

“The question at the time was who was responsible. And now we have the answer to that question,” Essayli said after the verdict.

It was the second federal trial for Rinderknecht, who prosecutors alleged set a brush fire early New Year’s Day 2025 that was quickly contained by firefighters, but which continued to smolder and — seven days later — erupted into the Palisades Fire.

“The strongest evidence was the defendant’s own testimony,” one of the jurors, who gave his name as Cameron and who said he was initially the only juror who voted to acquit, told reporters outside the courthouse after the verdict.

The juror said Rinderknecht said that he was on the hill the night of the first fire, that he didn’t smell a fire or see fireworks and that it was a clear and calm night.

The sun is seen behind smoke above charred structures and vehicles after the passage of the Palisades Fire in Los Angeles on Jan. 8, 2025. Agustin Paullier / AFP via Getty

“No one else was on the hill that day or night and happened to be smoking,” the juror said. “Everything kind of started to point to one conclusion — especially if there was no one else on that hill,” he said.

Rinderknecht’s first trial in Los Angeles federal court ended in June with a mistrial after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of an acquittal.

His retrial began with jury selection on Nov. 2, and a panel comprising six men and six women began deliberating his fate on Wednesday.

Prosecutors alleged that Rinderknecht, a former Los Angeles resident who was an Uber driver at the time, started the prelude to the Palisades Fire, a much smaller blaze known as the Lachman Fire.

Named after a nearby street, this blaze was detected by environmental sensing platforms at 12:12 a.m. on Jan. 1, 2025, and was extinguished by firefighters after burning roughly five to eight acres of dense brush.

But even though firefighters doused the flames, the “holdover fire” continued to smolder underground and was reignited a week later by the Santa Ana winds and grew into the monstrous Palisades Fire, prosecutors said.

World.title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by deepening tech rout
World.content:
Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.

Both the S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic.

Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

"It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak.

Anthropic can't buck the market

Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO.

Shares of Nvidia, considered practically synonymous with the AI boom, are falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 13% in late Friday trading.

The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its co-founder and former CEO. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has shed more than 25% of its value.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%.

World.title: Jonathan Rinderknecht found guilty in Palisades Fire case
World.content:
A Los Angeles County jury has found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of starting a blaze that erupted into the deadly and destructive Palisades Fire in 2025.

The verdict comes nearly five months after a deadlocked jury caused a mistrial.

In his first trial, he faced two counts of arson and a third count for timber set afire. After the mistrial, federal prosecutors secured a superseding indictment, charging him with one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson.

He faces a minimum of five years and a maximum of 40 years in federal prison.

The Palisades Fire, fueled by life-threatening winds and hot conditions, burned more than 23,000 acres of land in the Pacific Palisades, Malibu and the Santa Monica Mountains. According to Cal Fire, 12 people were killed, and more than 6,800 structures were destroyed.

It was fully contained on Jan. 31, 2025 — 24 days after it started. It is the third most destructive fire in state history.

"Nearly two years ago, the Palisades Fire devastated our city, taking innocent lives, destroying thousands of homes, and changing so many lives and Los Angeles forever," LA Mayor Karen Bass said. "So many are still struggling to rebuild. For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Case against Rinderknecht

The case against Rinderknecht argued that he maliciously started the Lachman Fire near the Pacific Palisades neighborhood in LA at midnight on Jan.1, 2025. That fire eventually grew into the deadly Palisades Fire several days later.

The DOJ said that through their investigation, law enforcement agencies determined that the Palisades Fire was a "holdover" fire and was a continuation of the Lachman Fire. Firefighters responded and suppressed it, but it continued to smolder and burn underground before reigniting on Jan. 7, 2025.

Rinderknecht, 29, a Florida resident, had picked up a shift as an Uber driver during the early morning hours of Jan. 1, 2025, when prosecutors allege he started the Lachman Fire. The blaze burned an area of the hills in the Palisades that was covered with heavy vegetation.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht called 911 multiple times and initially fled the scene but returned to the area after seeing fire engines pass by. Rinderknecht's defense agreed with prosecutors that he called 911 multiple times but maintained the argument that he was simply a witness to the fire.

"No matter what the government's theory is, the evidence will show Jonathan did not start the Jan. 1 fire," defense attorney Steve Haney said during the first trial.

The DOJ said during an interview with law enforcement on Jan. 24, 2025, Rinderknecht allegedly lied about where he was when he first saw the Lachman Fire. Geolocation data from his phone confirmed that he was just 30 feet away from the flames as they began to spread, prosecutors said.

They also argued that Rinderknecht was agitated and angry when he started the fire.

Juror No. 3, who identified himself as Cameron, said after delivering the verdict that he initially believed Rinderknecht was not guilty. He said the other jurors believed he was guilty.

"I took the time, almost two days, to sit there and just look at everything over and over again," Cameron said. "I personally felt comfortable saying, without a doubt, specifically, that he was who started it."

Jonathan Rinderknecht's father, Joel Rinderknecht, disagreed with the jury's decision and said much of the prosecution's case was a "false narrative."

"It really just demonstrated that the ends justified the means," Joel Rinderknecht said. "They want him to be convicted, and it didn't matter."

Prosecutors said they combed through 1.5 million digital forensic points and collected more than 17,000 pieces of evidence. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli decided to retry the case based on the strength of the evidence.

"[The jury] came back and they held him accountable for the entire thing because that's consistent with the evidence," Essayli said. "We're happy with this jury. They did the right thing."

World.title: Detonation of unstable explosives in Iowa paused indefinitely by court
World.content:
The U.S. Army's plan to detonate five tons of unstable explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa has been put on indefinite hold by a federal court Friday.

The U.S. Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit Thursday.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter challenged the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency that allowed the detonation to happen. They argued the residents in Iowa had extremely short notice to prepare and take safety precautions, and that the evidence the EPA used to determine this was the best course of action for safety and health had not been made public and therefore could not be evaluated.

The court issued a single-sentence order granting an administrative stay of the EPA's permit "until the emergency motion for stay is ruled upon by this court."

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon CT on Friday, then was initially delayed until Monday. Since the stay does not set a date, this delay is indefinite until the entire case is heard and ruled upon.

The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people four hours west of Chicago, has been housing 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in munitions since World War I, a total of about 5 tons of material.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati said.

According to the EPA, the lead azide had deteriorated during storage, allowing it to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock. With that volatility came the risk that they could explode when being moved or during storage.

Toxic dust particle cloud could impact farms, homes, playgrounds

Acting Secretary of the U.S. Army Adam Telle said the military had determined the safest way to dispose of the lead azide would be through a "controlled detonation." That detonation would create a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles.

Preliminary maps based on Friday weather conditions showed a potential airborne plume stretching north across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River and possibly into far northwestern Illinois. Thousands of people live along the plume's original projected track, and there are also sources of groundwater, river water and farms in the area. Because the toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces, there are concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.

Residents in Middletown were asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday under the original detonation plan. The Army also warned residents of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows.

Lawmakers asked Army to delay detonation

A bipartisan group of elected officials from Illinois and Iowa sent a letter to the Pentagon and EPA, asking them to delay the detonation and find safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."

World.title: Teen becomes viral chef after stepping up when his mom had cancer
World.content:
He has no culinary training and has never worked in a restaurant. Yet 18-year-old Joey Charney of Augusta, Georgia, has become a famous chef, with more than 2 million followers.

"While I am very happy to be in the situation I'm in, I'm not happy of the reason that I'm there," Joey Charney told CBS News.

In August, Jennifer Charney, a stay-at-home mother of eight, lost her 10-year battle with breast cancer.

Over all those years, as Jennifer Charney's illness progressed, the kids had to step up — to do many of the things their mom used to do. Joey Charney, the youngest son, offered to do the cooking for all those hungry mouths — even though, at the time, he didn't know much about food preparation.

"I was able to ask her a bunch of questions — or she could just smell like, 'Oh, it's burning,'" Joey Charney said. "And she would sit here and yell at me from her bed. And I was like, 'I got it! I got it!'"

Along the way, he documented his cooking journey on social media, candidly sharing the ups and downs of feeding his family.

His videos have drawn an outpouring of support from followers, who offer praise and cooking advice, just like the mom he so misses.

"Oh, yeah, I mean I miss everything about her, but her cooking especially," Joey Charney said. "It was really good. I can't get her Parmesan chicken the same way."

This week, Joey Charney cooked a couple of whole chickens, practice for what may be his most important meal yet.

"This will be our first Thanksgiving without her," Joey's dad, Chris Charney, said. "That's going to be a big change."

This Thanksgiving, over the course of many courses, home chefs across America will carry on tradition, inherited from ancestors and passed down to children, sometimes far too early.

But the Charneys say they will still have much to be thankful for this holiday — like their brother, who saw a need to feed his family and served it.

"He has filled a big void — been a blessing," Chris Charney said.

World.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
World.content:
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

Sponsor Message

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

Sponsor Message

Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

Sponsor Message

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.

Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

World.title: The latest from Trump's press conference
World.content:
The latest from Trump's press conference

Transcript

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

President Trump returned to Washington after his three-day trip to Asia and took questions from the White House today. The trip included the first ever three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But there was little in the way of agreements on key global issues.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength.

CHANG: Well, all of this raises questions about the staying power of Trump's America-first approach and America's future role in the world. Joining us now is NPR White House correspondent Franco Ordoñez, who is in the room, and we have NPR national security correspondent Greg Myre. Hello to both of you.

FRANCO ORDOÑEZ, BYLINE: Hello.

GREG MYRE, BYLINE: Hi, Ailsa.

CHANG: All right. So, Franco, did the president make any news in this press conference?

ORDOÑEZ: Yeah, I mean, not really. I mean, it was really a very meandering talk, starting off with highlights of his first two years in office. And then he probably spent about 30 minutes talking about his time abroad and, you know, recounting his relationship with Xi and Putin. He did say, though, that he and Xi had made some agreements about putting in guardrails - that's the word he used - with artificial intelligence, which he calls super intelligence. Here he is there.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

TRUMP: It's not artificial intelligence. It's not artificial. It's super. Problem is, it may be too super. So President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us, 'cause there really is no third place.

ORDOÑEZ: Now, of course, details are scarce, but the idea of guardrails is notable because Trump has pretty - previously, at least, been pretty allergic to any restrictions on developing AI. I mean, he has repeatedly said he's wanted to maintain a U.S. advantage over China.

CHANG: Right. OK, well, Greg, Trump had some things to say about chip sales to China and the whole Nvidia fallout, right? What struck you about his answers there?

MYRE: Yeah, I mean, Trump says he wants the U.S. to keep the lead in AI, as Franco just noted. And he also said he won't allow U.S. companies to build AI data centers outside the U.S. However, Trump is the one allowing Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China. Nvidia's Jensen Huang lobbied Trump last year and persuaded the president to allow these sales. And just yesterday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released a list of requests this year by Nvidia and another chipmaker, AMD, to sell chips to Chinese company - companies. As of May this year, the Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips, and they include big names like Alibaba and Tencent. And those two companies are also on a Pentagon list of Chinese firms that are linked to the Chinese military. So what does Trump actually want here? Does he want Nvidia to keep selling those chips to China, or does he want to block those sales?

CHANG: Good questions. Well, Trump was also asked about the whole change in leadership over cybersecurity, right? What did we learn there?

MYRE: Yeah, Trump fired the White House Cybersecurity Director Sean Carncross, and at the press conference today, he said, I don't think that person was good enough. Now, he's being replaced by Kirsten Davies, who's been the chief information officer at the Defense Department. And this is certainly an important position, but it's a policy position, not a hands on operational position.

The agency that's really important here is CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which deals with election security and protecting government networks from cyberattacks. And this agency has not had a director since Trump became president almost two years ago. Now, as it happens, Trump's nomination to lead the agency, Michael LoSapio, had a Senate confirmation hearing yesterday. He was grilled by Democratic senators. He was asked who won the 2020 presidential election. He refused to answer. He was asked if the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021, and he said he didn't think it was an attack. So it's not clear that he'll be confirmed, but whoever winds up in this position will be in charge of election security in 2028.

CHANG: Interesting. OK, Franco, back to this meeting with Xi and Putin, which was designed to demonstrate American power, right? Do you think it also may have opened the door for allies to turn away from the U.S.?

ORDOÑEZ: Yeah, I mean, very much designed to demonstrate American power, but I also think it does show that power and influence are not the same thing. I mean, Trump was asked today if Putin, who he called his friend, was also America's friend.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

TRUMP: I can't speak to America.

ORDOÑEZ: You know, he really couldn't answer that. But he did continue to make the case that his relationship with Putin would reap benefits for America, though we haven't really seen that yet. You know, the war in Ukraine continues to rage on. But we are seeing allies start to build alliances with other nations as, you know, confidence in the U.S. falters, and they look to reduce their dependence on the U.S.

CHANG: Well, great. What about progress when it comes to Iran? Did anything come out of this trip on that front?

MYRE: The short answer is no. There's no indication the war, now nearly nine months old, was discussed in any great detail on the trip. Trump did mention it briefly at the news conference. He said what he said many times before - Iran can't have a nuclear weapon and that Iran does want to make a deal. The one significant development in recent days has been increased Iranian attacks on oil tankers and Gulf countries.

CHANG: OK, Franco, real quick on domestic politics. Now, Trump was up there with Vice President Vance - right? - and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Anything strike you about what either of those men said?

ORDOÑEZ: Well, I mean, both men offered really glowing support for the president. And Vance, who obviously remained in Washington for the trip, said he missed the president and even joked that he felt like he was in the movie "Home Alone."

CHANG: (Laughter).

ORDOÑEZ: Whereas Rubio was able to talk more authoritatively about his work and just came across as a more consequential figure. The issue for both, though, is that their association with Trump, who is, frankly, very unpopular now.

CHANG: That is NPR's Franco Ordoñez and NPR's Greg Myre. Thank you to both of you.

ORDOÑEZ: (Inaudible).

MYRE: Sure thing, Ailsa.

World.title: Rising seas have forced this Quinault village to relocate
World.content:
Rising seas have forced this Quinault village to relocate

The Quinault Indian Nation has moved its largest village away from rising seas and tsunamis

Transcript

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

All up and down the West Coast, massive waves have been pounding the seashores. But it's not just Pacific storms that are kicking up the surf. Next week, the season's first king tides arrive. That's the informal name for the highest predicted tides of the year. Now, the people of Taholah - that's a village on the coast of Washington state - they know that they need to get out of the way. John Ryan from member station KUOW reports on their efforts to relocate to higher ground.

(SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING)

JOHN RYAN, BYLINE: I'm at the mouth of the Quinault River on the Pacific Ocean. It's almost high tide right now. Surf is pounding the village of Taholah's big rocky seawall. These high tides will be getting higher in the months and years ahead. That's why the Quinault Indian Nation has been working for more than a decade to relocate the tribe's main village.

Quinault elder and Army veteran James DeLa Cruz lives right behind that seawall. It's no longer high enough to hold back the ocean.

JAMES DELA CRUZ: When them tides come, there's 3 feet of water in my yard, so I had to have a boat tied to my back porch if I wanted to escape.

RYAN: Part of DeLa Cruz's house is up on stilts that let him look over the seawall at the ocean that he loves.

DELA CRUZ: I wholeheartedly don't want to move, but I understand the need for it.

RYAN: DeLa Cruz and his neighbors along the seawall are slated to get the first homes in a new inland neighborhood currently under construction.

(SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING)

RYAN: Lia Frenchman is one of those neighbors.

LIA FRENCHMAN: When we have the full-size tides that come with the winter king tides, our street, our house is just shaking for hours. There's just so much power behind that water, has the whole ocean behind it.

RYAN: Frenchman says people in the coastal village of Taholah seem most concerned about the risk of a tsunami, but steadily rising sea levels have made the danger of inundation real as a warming ocean keeps expanding.

FRENCHMAN: The fact is, is it did not use to flood every year like it does right now, and that's definitely climate change (laughter).

RYAN: Frenchman says her home is never really dry, with moldy closets that defy cleaning.

FRENCHMAN: It's so clear when nature is showing you that you shouldn't be somewhere anymore (laughter). We need to listen to that.

RYAN: Coastal cities around the country are threatened by rising seas. New Orleans sits below sea level and is dangerously exposed. Cities in Florida frequently suffer flooding during high tides. Tribal communities in Alaska, Louisiana and Washington are intentionally pulling back from the sea rather than trying to fend it off. Relocating the Quinault Nation's main village has been a long push. So when the tribe got the go-ahead this fall to install the first modular homes in the new neighborhood, they held a celebration.

UNIDENTIFIED PEOPLE: (Vocalizing).

ALYSSA JOHNSTON: It's been a long time coming.

RYAN: Alyssa Johnston is managing the relocation project.

JOHNSTON: Every single king tide season that came, I was just thinking and hoping that we would be along further than what we were.

RYAN: She expects the first four families can move inland in January. Another 32 homes are to be built next year. King tides could hit record heights before then. A second even higher round of king tides is expected Christmas Eve. Oceanographers say extreme El Niño conditions could boost West Coast sea levels by as much as a foot by then.

JOHNSTON: That's what makes me not sleep at night.

RYAN: Relocating a village isn't easy, but Taholah residents have accepted that it's time to leave. Quinault Council Member Kaylah Mail's house has been in her family for four generations.

KAYLAH MAIL: That's going to be a little bit difficult to let go, but I have my 12-year-old to think about, too. Like, that's my worst fear is to be in a situation where I can't keep him safe.

RYAN: Mail says it's frustrating that more homes aren't available yet.

(SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING)

RYAN: The Quinault Nation has spent more than $40 million to get its new neighborhood started. To finish it, the tribe will need hundreds of millions more.

For NPR News, I'm John Ryan in Taholah, Washington.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

World.title: Trump's impact on an Ohio steel plant
World.content:
Trump's impact on an Ohio steel plant

The giant steel plant in Middletown, Ohio planned to switch away from using coke, a refined form of coal. The switch would have cut hazardous air pollution — and greenhouse gas emissions. But that plan has changed under President Trump

Transcript

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

In Middletown, Ohio, a big steel mill is the city's largest employer and the biggest source of local air pollution. Under the Biden administration, the mill had planned to clean up its operations by shifting away from coal, but that has changed under President Trump. Middletown is now one example of the administration's efforts to boost fossil fuels. The Allegheny Front's Reid Frazier reports.

REID FRAZIER, BYLINE: Donna Ballinger stands outside her house in Middletown, Ohio.

(SOUNDBITE OF HORN HONKING)

FRAZIER: Through a thicket of trees, she points to the Middletown Works, a steel mill which rises several stories above her home.

DONNA BALLINGER: And it runs 24/7. You don't get a break.

FRAZIER: The plant makes steel the traditional way - using coke, a refined form of coal. That process emits a lot of air pollution, including carbon dioxide, which contributes to climate change. It also releases lots of soot, which drifts down onto Ballinger's neighborhood.

BALLINGER: It's the fallout that's on everything we own, cars, property, kids' toys. You can't touch anything. You can't open your windows.

FRAZIER: That soot is bad for human health. According to the EPA, the tiny particles are linked to higher rates of heart and lung problems, including asthma. Ballinger eventually got so fed up with the air quality, she began working with the local Sierra Club to try to force the plant to clean up.

Then a few years ago, the steel mill did announce plans to cut its air pollution. Its owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, said it would convert to a new steelmaking process that doesn't use coal. Instead, it would switch to using natural gas or hydrogen. That would cut both the plant's local air pollution and its carbon footprint. That's important because the steel industry is a major source of climate pollution. CEO Lourenco Goncalves told investors at the time, hydrogen was the solution.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

LAURENCO GONCALVES: We believe hydrogen will be the true game changer for the decarbonization of steel.

FRAZIER: The Biden administration agreed. It awarded the Middletown Steel Mill $500 million as part of its climate agenda. But then Donald Trump came into office promising to boost fossil fuels like coal. Soon after, Goncalvez told investors the hydrogen project was off. Middletown is also the hometown of a major figure in the Trump administration.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

JD VANCE: It is great to be home. It is great to be back in Middletown, Ohio.

FRAZIER: In August, Vice President JD Vance came to town and spoke at the steel plant where his grandfather once worked. He announced a change. Instead of supporting a switch to hydrogen, the Trump administration would help the company reinvest in coal-based steelmaking.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

VANCE: Cleveland-Cliffs is making today, right here in Middletown, Ohio, a $1 billion investment in transformational manufacturing right here in our home.

FRAZIER: The Department of Energy and Cleveland-Cliffs didn't respond to questions for this story. Chris Pistorius studies steelmaking at Carnegie Mellon University. He was disappointed by the change.

CHRIS PISTORIUS: It's maybe not entirely surprising, but it's definitely unfortunate.

FRAZIER: Pistorius had hoped the Middletown project could be a model showing the steel industry how to adopt hydrogen. It's a relatively new technology, he says.

PISTORIUS: We really need a few big demonstrations like these to show that, yeah, it works the way we think it should and we can make the same steel grades. So this would have been a really excellent demonstration of that.

FRAZIER: In Middletown, city officials didn't want to answer questions about the plant's decision. The mill is the town's biggest employer with over 2,000 workers. Sheila and Kenneth Stephens Jr. live a few blocks from the plant. The retired couple both voted for Donald Trump. Sheila Stephens said she'd like for the plant to be cleaner, but Middletown depends on the mill, which many call by its old name, AK Steel.

SHEILA STEPHENS: I think this town would be a ghost town if AK shut down 'cause it's the main supporter of this, and about everybody around here works there, so...

FRAZIER: A few blocks away, Donna Ballinger, the Sierra Club organizer, says she's angry the hydrogen project fell through.

BALLINGER: Why wouldn't you want to make it safer for everyone to be able to breathe cleaner air? Why wouldn't you want to do that?

FRAZIER: Who does she hold responsible for the ongoing air pollution? The company, the state and the federal government. I blame them all, she says.

For NPR News, I'm Reid Frazier in Middletown, Ohio.
