World.title: BARITA SEEKS $9.3B IN FRESH FUNDING
World.content:
BARITA Investments Limited is returning to the public bond market with plans to raise up to $9.3 billion through a combination of Jamaican- and US-dollar-denominated securities, as the investment company seeks to strengthen its balance sheet and secure funding for new investment products.

In a prospectus published on Tuesday, Barita outlined a three-tranche bond offer comprising two US-dollar instruments and one Jamaican-dollar instrument, with interest rates ranging from 7.25 per cent to 10.50 per cent and repayment periods of two to five years.

The company is seeking to raise US$10 million in each of the two US-dollar tranches, with the option to increase each to US$15 million if demand permits. The Jamaican-dollar tranche targets $3 billion, with provision to increase the amount to $4.5 billion.

Investors in the first tranche will earn annual interest of 7.25 per cent over two years, while the second tranche offers 10.50 per cent over three years. The third tranche carries an interest rate of 8.25 per cent over five years.

Barita intends to use the proceeds to strengthen its capital base, improve liquidity and support the development and introduction of new investment products as it works to diversify its earnings.

“Continued emphasis on disciplined risk management, recurring income generation and balance sheet resilience, alongside selective participation in emerging investment and capital market opportunities, should support Barita’s competitiveness and long-term earnings growth,” the company stated in its prospectus.

Although Barita outlined the broad purposes of the fundraising, it did not specify how much would be allocated to each activity. Transaction costs associated with the offer are expected to remain below $200 million.

“We will strengthen liquidity and diversify our funding sources. With policy rates higher in Jamaica and the United States, we will manage the maturity and repricing of assets and liabilities and adjust funding terms where appropriate to protect net interest margins,” said Barita chairman Mark Myers in the company’s fourth quarter report ending September 30.

The bond offer also enters a market recently buoyed by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited’s $63.50-billion acquisition of the remaining minority shares in Scotia Group Jamaica Limited (SGJ), a transaction that has returned a substantial amount of capital to investors and potentially created fresh demand for investment securities.

Barita has been actively deploying capital into different opportunities over the last year. This included the acquisition of Barita Fund Managers Limited (formerly JN Fund Managers Limited) in January for $3.81 billion. The acquisition expanded Barita’s assets under management by at least $52 billion and contributed $789.5 million to Barita’s net operating income (NOI) and $60.2 million to net profit.

Barita also acquired Key Homes Limited from MJR Real Estate Holdings Limited in December 2025 as it brings some of its real estate plans to its balance sheet. The consideration for this deal was a series of debentures over five years valued at US$111.53 million ($17.63 billion). Key Homes owns a 101 acre property known as Windsor Estates in St Ann. This acquisition contributed $897 million in fair value gains to Barita’s NOI and increased its investment property balance to $20.23 billion.

The investment firm reported a 136 per cent increase in its net operating income from $8.70 billion to $20.47 billion for its financial year ending September 30. The bulk of this improved earning capacity was attributed to $13.27 billion in gains on its investment activities. Accordingly, Barita raked in $4.68 billion in realised gains and $8.59 billion in unrealised gains, with $7.09 billion arising in the fourth quarter.

Although revenue generation improved during the year, operating expenses doubled from $4.64 billion to $10.78 billion, which included $2.38 billion in credit loss provisions for amounts in doubt. There was also a sevenfold increase in the loss from its associate during the year.

Despite the higher costs, Barita’s profit before tax grew 126 per cent to $8.85 billion while net profit doubled from $3.01 billion to $6.03 billion. These figures are unaudited and subject to final review in the upcoming audited financial statements by newly appointed auditor PwC.

“We are tightening control of technology, administrative and transformation spending, simplifying processes and using targeted automation to lower the cost of serving clients. This work goes hand in hand with modernising our systems and improving digital service. Our aim is to improve operating leverage so that more of our revenue growth translates into earnings,” Myers explained on the 2027 objectives.

Barita’s balance sheet moved by 32 per cent to $196.17 billion, reflecting the benefits of its Barita Fund Managers and Key Homes acquisitions. The investment firm’s pledged assets reached $116.28 billion as it continued to grow its repurchase agreement (repo) book with its clients.

Equity increased by four per cent to $36.59 billion as Barita recorded unrealised losses on some investments and proposed a $3.25 billion dividend to be paid on November 30.

The investment firm is working to develop some of the real estate properties under its alternative investment portfolio. Three of the sites held by MJR Real Estate are in active pre-development, with demolition work completed former Ice Factory on Harbour Street and former Eden Gardens property on Lady Musgrave Road. MJR Real Estate is owned by the Barita Real Estate Unit Trust.

“Over time, we expect completed developments to broaden the portfolio’s sources of return through proceeds from sales and recurring income from leasing and operations, complementing the Group’s securities and asset management businesses,” Myers noted.

This is the company’s second public bond offer following its June 2025 bond listing where it raised $4.74 billion and US$20 million from investors. Tranche I and tranche III from that listing are scheduled to mature in June 2027, with US$10.22 million and $1.37 billion payable to investors, respectively.

Barita intends to apply to list the different tranches on the JSE’s Bond Markets. Barita currently has five securities listed on the JSE Bond Market and two securities on the JSE USD Bond Market.

Investors seeking to purchase tranches I or III must subscribe to a minimum of US$1,500 and apply in multiples of US$100 for higher amounts. The tranche II offer requires a minimum of $50,000 and increments in multiples of $1,000 for higher amounts. Applications can be made on Barita’s Boss website or through selling agents such as Jamaica Money Market Brokers Limited (JMMB), Barita Fund Managers, Proven Wealth Limited or VM Wealth Management Limited. The offer opens on November 25 and is scheduled to close by December 29.

World.title: UK will take its time setting out Brexit options, says minister
World.content:
Andy Burnham pledged in September to set out “options” to fix the U.K. relationship with the bloc — which he said could include rejoining its single market, customs union, or even the EU itself.

But speaking in Brussels on Friday, the prime minister suggested the process could take longer and signaled the start of an “informal brainstorming process” with the European Union to conclude at the next U.K.-EU summit near the end of 2027.

It comes after rumbles of Cabinet discontent over the policy shift and speculation the prime minister may be taking a more cautious approach to avoid spooking his own government allies.

Defending the length of the process, Falconer said there was “a lot of variation” in the different relationships Britain could have with the EU and detail to work through.

“People say, ‘Oh, the options are obvious’ … but I think most people would struggle to describe the precise difference between the different arrangements,” he said.

Burnham has said he will be led by the public on the issue and told reporters in Brussels on Friday that he would “not be running ahead of public opinion on the issue.”

World.title: The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals
World.content:
British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive.

Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers.

“That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,” RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.” EU renewables groups have made the same point.

The tech industry



The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel.



The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit.



The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID.



Of the more political parts of the agreement, the Youth Experience Scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene.

The City

While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry.

World.title: Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy
World.content:
A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.”

This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling.

Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa.

They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme.

David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what.

Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.”

World.title: France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership
World.content:
The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7.

The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said.

If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year.

In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets.

“I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.”

Fewer politicians

A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency.

World.title: Latvian leader calls for closure of EU borders to all Russians
World.content:
Latvia was among the 11 countries that signed a Swedish-led letter in June urging Brussels to restrict visas for Russians. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner suggested to POLITICO in October that the European Commission could present a proposal next year.

Kulbergs warned that Russia’s hybrid attacks on NATO’s eastern flank were intensifying. “The situation is escalating,” he said, adding that Latvian and Estonian special forces had arrested eight people on Estonian soil last weekend who had “concrete instructions to attack a production facility in Estonia that supports Ukraine.” Russia, he said, “is behind this.”

He called the coming months “a winter of truth,” arguing that Russia was striking Ukraine’s water, heating and power supplies because it was making little progress at the front, while also trying to sway public opinion in Germany and elsewhere. “Putin wants the Germans to be frightened and to demand that their government stop supporting Ukraine,” he said.

Kulbergs dismissed fears that Thursday’s summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen amounted to a new Yalta as “an exaggeration,” arguing that the Russian leader had been humiliated. The Yalta summit in February 1945, where U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin shaped Europe’s postwar order, is widely seen as having left much of Central and Eastern Europe under Soviet domination.

Kulbergs urged larger countries, especially Germany, not to give in to war fatigue. “It is entirely possible to be pro-European, to support Ukraine vigorously, to stand up to the aggressor — and still win an election by a large margin,” he said.

The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

World.title: French billionaire hunter takes fight global after California tax defeat
World.content:
Zucman sees fresh hope in the results of the U.S. midterms, in which a string of Democrats campaigning to tax the ultra-rich won their races.

“Now our party has a choice to make: Are we going to stand with the working class or the tech lords?” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is flying in for the Paris gathering. “The same inequality is fueling anger and distrust not only in America, but also in France and around the world,” he told POLITICO.

Khanna and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) are due to speak at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue off the Champs-Élysées loaned for the occasion by Emmanuel Grégoire, the socialist mayor of Paris.

Left-wing leaders from Italy, Brazil, Spain and the U.K. are also expected to attend. A “Paris Manifesto” published Friday calls for a minimum tax on the largest fortunes, protections for independent media and rules for artificial intelligence.

The question is whether anyone outside the theater will buy into Zucman’s ideas. His signature proposal, a minimum annual tax of 2% on the largest fortunes, was rejected by the French Senate last year.

“It’s a real program to save our democracy,” said Eva Joly, a former French investigating judge who jailed the boss of oil giant Elf in the 1990s and later served as a European lawmaker for the Greens. Zucman “carries it brilliantly,” she told POLITICO.

World.title: EU warns against COP31 becoming a ‘fossil fuel summit’
World.content:
The draft document calls on countries to scale up carbon storage and capture technologies (CCUS) to meet a specific target, and includes a pledge to raise the share of electricity in global energy use to 35% by 2035 — including power generated using fossil fuels.

France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has heavily criticized the inclusion of CCUS targets.

“When it comes to carbon capture, we’re completely opposed — and this is a real red line — to any figures, any targets, or any quantified objectives,” French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut told reporters on Friday.

Dated Nov. 19, the letter asks Australia and Turkey, who are jointly presiding over this year’s global climate talks, to address these demands.

“The EU always prefers an ambitious negotiated outcome but cannot accept agreement at any cost,” the letter warned.

World.title: Tusk: Russian cruise missile incursion into Poland seems ‘intentional’
World.content:
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Trump said that “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” referring to previous incidents.

“To put it mildly, I don’t always agree with the American side’s assessment and interpretation of these incidents,” Tusk said in the press conference.

He added that U.S. officials have access to the wreckage from Friday’s incursion. “I think that in this particular case, no one will try to pretend anymore that this was just an innocent accident,” Tusk said.

Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the objects fell at three locations in southeastern Poland: Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz. The object found at Nowy Lipowiec was a Russian Ch-101 cruise missile, he said. A second object was also believed to be a missile, Kosiniak-Kamysz added, while the third was probably a jet-powered drone.

Tusk pointed to a possible connection to military exercises by the “coalition of the willing” in nearby Nowa Dęba. Led by France and Britain, the drills involve 11 countries preparing to deploy a multinational force to support Ukraine after a ceasefire.

“We can’t rule out the possibility — and this is a hypothesis — that the provocation was also connected to the exercises taking place in Poland,” he said.

World.title: Chronic loneliness linked to higher dementia risks in new study
World.content:
People who are almost always lonely may be at higher risk of developing dementia, according to a new study that tracked ageing adults over three decades.

 

There is no current cure for dementia, which affects 57 million people worldwide. But a combination of genetic and lifestyle factors, such as exercise, alcohol and smoking, can affect people’s risk of developing the condition. According to an expert group convened by the Lancet, social isolation is another risk factor.

Researchers from the University of Bordeaux set out to measure that risk. They found that older adults who were chronically lonely had a 38% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who never felt lonely.

Notably, occasional loneliness was not significantly linked to dementia risk, according to the study, which was published in the journal Aging & Mental Health.

“This distinction is critical,” said Karine Pérès, one of the study’s authors and a senior researcher at the Bordeaux Population Health Centre.

“While most people experience loneliness at some point in their lives, it is when loneliness becomes chronic and persistent that it may increase the risk of developing dementia,” she said.

The researchers analysed data for 3,777 older adults who were tracked from 1988 to 2018. They classified people as “never lonely,” "occasionally lonely” or “chronically lonely” based on four research visits over an eight-year period. Then they looked at whether the participants developed dementia over the next 20 years.

Roughly one in three people who were never or occasionally lonely went on to develop dementia, compared to about 49% of the chronically lonely group, the study found. Most people in the study did not experience regular loneliness.

Loneliness and social isolation aren’t exactly the same. Loneliness is subjective, and people can experience it even if they live with family or regularly see other people, the Bordeaux team said.

“This vulnerability may also stem from unsatisfying relationships, caregiving burdens, or lack of meaningful activities,” said Yvanna Simon, the study’s lead author.

The study has some limitations. It relied on one question to measure loneliness, rather than a comprehensive assessment, and the researchers may not have accounted for all factors that could influence the relationship between dementia and loneliness. But the findings are in line with previous, bigger studies that found a similar link between dementia and loneliness in midlife and old age.

The Bordeaux researchers recommended that health care workers screen their patients for loneliness and encourage more social activities. More inclusive public spaces that welcome people of all ages could also help, they said.

According to Alzheimer’s Research UK, staying socially engaged in old age can help keep parts of the brain active and reduce changes in the brain that are linked to dementia. But the nonprofit emphasised that no one factor causes dementia on its own.

For example, people who are chronically lonely may also get less exercise and eat a less healthy diet, which may contribute to heart disease and diabetes. Those conditions, in turn, raise the risk of dementia. Social interactions are just another layer.

“Lack of social interactions limits cognitive stimulation, while unresolved social stress leads to an accumulation of biological wear and tear over time,” Pérès said.

World.title: Putin a 'killer,' Zelenskyy says after Trump calls Russian leader his 'friend'
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has branded Vladimir Putin a "killer" after Donald Trump referred to the Russian leader as his "friend" earlier this week.

 

"For us, he is an enemy. And of course, for us, he is a killer. And I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer," Zelenskyy told CNN in response to a question about Trump's comment, while also warning that such descriptions could ease pressure on Putin.

Trump called Putin a "friend" as they met on the sidelines of a trilateral meeting with China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week, and he continued to talk up their relationship during a press conference at the White House on Friday.

"I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That's a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That's a good thing. And our country is safe because of that," he told reporters.

"You're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he went on, adding that both Zelenskyy and Putin wanted to end the war but "don't know how."

Asked whether Putin was a friend of the US, Trump replied: "I can't speak to America."

It comes after Russian forces launched a major wave of strikes against Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning, killing at least seven people in Kyiv and damaging key bridges across the Dnipro River.

Zelenskyy said Russia had fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles during the assault, which he called "one of the largest attacks" of the war so far.

"Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives. Energy facilities, logistics – bridges across the Dnipro, railway infrastructure," he wrote in a post on social media.

The attacks followed Putin's warning that there would be "no negotiations" on a partial ceasefire with Ukraine following Ukrainian strikes on his prized Crimea bridge this week, which destroyed a large part of the structure.

World.title: Europe braces for cold winter as polar vortex flips. Can heat pumps help lower energy bills?
World.content:
Europeans brace for what could be a particularly cold winter this year, after an unusually early sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) flipped the polar vortex.

 

The polar vortex is a ring of westerly winds that keeps freezing polar air locked over the North Pole about 30km above the Earth’s surface.

Sometimes, large atmospheric waves can disrupt this circulation, causing the winds to weaken significantly or even reverse direction. This can cause temperatures in the stratosphere to rise rapidly.

As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere, which extends from the ground up to an average altitude of about eight to 15 kilometres.

Europe’s dwindling gas supplies

According to market intelligence provider Montel, forecasters warn that this "heightens the odds of colder temperatures”, more storms, wind and heating demand on the continent over the next month.

However, analysts say this would need to be a “repeated event” to have a sustained effect throughout the winter, as single SSW events are “short-term in nature”.

A severe cold spell could put gas supplies under even more pressure, following warnings from the EU that it may have to curb its gas consumption by seven per cent this winter as stocks hit record lows for this time of year.

Dwindling gas reserves, primarily driven by the war on Iran and subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel shipping routes – are also set to worsen ahead of a full ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from January 2027.

The unusually early SSW “might make people a bit nervous”, says Klaas Dozeman, energy forecaster at Brainchild Commodity Intelligence, adding that “most meteorologists remain puzzled on what the effects will be over the coming weeks”.

Can heat pumps save households from spiralling energy bills this winter?

Green technology is cushioning Europe from the ongoing fossil fuel crisis, providing more households with energy security and lower bills.

Solar power, for example, has already saved the EU €44.6 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the US-led war on Iran, which started on 28 February.

But as the days get shorter and darker, it is heat pumps that will offer relief from spiralling energy prices.

Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume.

Each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.

Europe’s heat pumps provide as much heat as the LNG carried by more than 200 tankers, according to an analysis from the European Heat Pump Association published in June*.

This is double the amount that arrived in the EU in 2025 from the Middle East and around seven per cent of the EU’s total annual imported LNG – avoiding €9.7 billion in import costs last year.

“Every heat pump installed is another bolt in the door of European energy security,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA.

“LNG is the most expensive energy source and comes from unreliable suppliers, and heat pumps can drastically reduce our need for it.”

Despite myths suggesting that heat pumps do not work in cold countries, which Euronews Earth has debunked here, new research has found that when used effectively, air source heat pumps could help heat homes on a typical winter day for as little as £1.84 (approximately €2.20) a day.

Heat pumps more efficient than gas boilers

The study, from British property developers Barratt Redrow, found that heat pumps can be more efficient than traditional gas boilers because they keep a more constant temperature rather than relying on spikes of heat.

"Heat pumps will run during the cold but consume a lot more power,” Jean-Paul Harreman, Director at Montel, tells Euronews Earth.

“The efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler, but if power prices go really high, high costs might still be seen during the worst of the cold. However, that is usually only part of the winter, so a price spike should not be confused with an annual total cost.”

Heat pump sales rose 13 per cent last year, hitting 2.9 million in 21 European countries. This brings the total stock to 29.3 million.

When asked whether heat pumps could help the EU’s dwindling gas supply, Harreman said: “A little yes. We see electrification of heating happening in many countries, but the overall impact on demand is not that large.

“Industrial demand destruction plays a bigger role.”

Industrial demand destruction is a sustained or permanent drop in industrial consumption of energy caused by prolonged high prices or supply constraints.

*EHPA’s data is based on 21 EU member states. You can read the full analysis here.

World.title: Seeking snow and ski this winter? Try these lesser-known destinations in Asia
World.content:
When it comes to planning a winter getaway, the chances are you might be thinking of heading to Europe's Alpine destinations in France, Switzerland or Austria.

 

But if you fancy a mid- to long-haul trip away from the continent, Asia has much to offer with snow-covered mountains, ski slopes and a host of resorts worth exploring.

From the landscapes of South Korea, Vietnam, Lebanon and beyond, these destinations deserve a place on your radar for skiing, snowboarding and other winter adventures.

Karakol in Kyrgyzstan Vlada Shcherb/Unsplash

Karakol Ski Resort, Kyrgyzstan

Kyrgyzstan is definitely worth adding to your winter travel bucket list. Picture fresh powder as far as the eyes can see, amid sweeping views of conifer forests.

On the outskirts of Karakol, a Kyrgyz destination for adventure, the Karakol Ski Resort sits at an altitude of 3,040 metres above sea level in the Tian Shan mountain range, which sprawls across the country, as well as China, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It is also the highest ski resort in Central Asia.

The season usually runs from late November through to April, with the high season being from 31 December to 10 January. During the winter, daytime temperatures rarely drop below -5C, alongside many sunny days.

Aside from the mild climate, there are an array of residences, from hotel rooms to chalet cottages, within the vicinity.

Mzaar Ski Resort, Lebanon

Self-styled as being “above the ordinary”, the Mzaar Ski Resort is perched above the mountain village of Kfardebian and overlooks the breathtaking Lebanese peak, Mount Sannine.

On offer are 115 kilometres of slopes, 19 lifts and a summit at 2,465 metres, making it the largest ski area in the Middle East. Aside from skiing and snowboarding, the winter season is ideal for ziplining over the mountain or riding aboard a snow groomer.

After a long day outdoors, the resort's wellness area is replete with sauna and cold plunge facilities. While there is an outdoor pool, the indoor one is a year-round option for guests to have a swim and unwind.

Accommodation options include the InterContinental Mzaar Mountain Resort & Spa, which has direct access to the 80km Mzaar Ski Domaine, and L’Escale Du Mzaar, which is just 40m from the first chairlift and has chalets and a ski shop.

O2 Ski Resort, South Korea

This resort in South Korea offers speedy rides 1,420 metres above sea level.

Located in the city of Taebaek, O2 Ski Resort has 16 slopes and six lifts, including one which goes up to the top of Hambaek Mountain, where visitors can take in sweeping views.

Facilities include an extreme park, half pipe and a 136m-long snow sledge, with snow made from Han and Nakdong river sources.

Via the gondola, visitors can head to the resting spot at the highest peak, Eutteum Maru, which overlooks the Baekdu mountain range. Beogeum Maru also offers skiers a place to rest, and is easily accessible to novice visitors as it sits between the beginners' slopes.

Sapa, Vietnam

While Southeast Asia isn’t famed for its snowy landscapes, you should also add Vietnam to your winter must-visit lists.

When the temperature drops over the Hoàng Liên Sơn mountain range – the country's highest peaks – frost and the occasional dusting settle over rice terraces.

In Sapa, the town can transform into a snowy sight from December to late January – occasionally extending into early February. During this time, the air becomes crisp, the mountains become capped by snow and the waterfalls also freeze over.

Vietnam Airlines recommends travellers to add Fansipan Mountain to their Sapa itineraries, which stands at 3,143 metres. The country's highest snow-capped peak is accessible via the Sun World Fansipan Legend cable car.

The carrier also suggests paying Bát Xát Commune a visit, as it receives some of Sapa's heaviest snowfall during the winter. The remote retreat's rice terraces and forests become pearly white landscapes during this time.

Meanwhile, Thác Bạc, or the Silver Waterfall, which is on the outskirts of Sapa, is a 200-metre cascade that frequently freezes.

Shahdag Mountain Resort, Azerbaijan

On the outskirts of Gusar city in Azerbaijan’s Greater Caucasus mountain range, the Shahdag Mountain Resort takes its name from Mount Shahdag, which stands 4,243 metres above sea level. This ski and snowboarding playground features 45 kilometres of pristine terrain, including a selection of 37 slopes and a network of 20 lifts.

Winter paintballing, mountain trekking, snow tubing as well as horseback riding are some of the other activities on offer at the resort during the winter. Visitors are also spoiled for choice when it comes to dining with more than 20 venues among five hotels.

At the backdrop of all this are pristine glaciers, deep ravines, stunning canyons and a variety of flora, fauna and wildlife.

Shymbulak ski resort in Almaty, Kazakhstan Matti Blume/Wikimedia Commons

Shymbulak Mountain Resort, Kazakhstan

The Shymbulak Mountain Resort is located in the gorge of Trans-Ili Alatau, within the city limits of Kazakhstan's cultural hub, Almaty. The resort itself sits at an elevation ranging from 2,200 metres to 3,180 metres above sea level.

With a total of 10 lifts, adventure travellers are treated to slopes with a total length of up to 20 kilometres and elevation difference of up to 920 metres for both beginners and experts.

The resort features a range of accommodation options, including the Nero Bianca high mountain chalets, which features its own sauna.

Meanwhile, the Le Mont boutique hotel welcomes guests, including those with four-legged companions. It has a viewing platform, with the panorama of Almaty and snow-capped peaks on display. Other options include Shymbulak Resort Hotel and Tenir Eco Hotels.

Zao Onsen Ski Resort, Japan

The Zao Onsen Ski Resort in Yamagata sits amid mountains and vast wilderness, offering a winter playground where the longest run is more than 10 kilometres long.

The Japanese resort features 32 lifts, ropeways and a gondola that goes up to the 1,661-metre summit station. Experienced skiers can enjoy ski jumps, while there are also routes that run through forests for skiers and snowboarders alike.

At the top lifts, keep an eye out for what the locals call "Juhyo", or snow monsters, that the area is known for during the peak of winter in February.

A combination of Siberian winds and heavy snowfall turn the Alpine trees into giant, monster-like figures. There's even a Zao Snow Monster festival where snow monster mascots entertain visitors.

World.title: Soil degradation could cost the EU up to €509 billion over its next budget, campaigners warn
World.content:
Damaged soils could drain €286 billion to €509 billion from the EU economy over the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget if yearly losses continue at today's pace, Save Soil estimated on Thursday.

 

The global campaign group wants the next Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the EU's farm subsidy system, to reward farmers for proven gains in soil health instead of leaving them to bear the cost of restoration.

Save Soil was launched in 2022 by Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru and his non-profit Isha Foundation to push governments into adopting policies that protect and restore soils.

Its estimate builds on research by the European Commission's in-house science service, the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which puts the yearly cost of soil degradation in the EU at €40.9 billion to €72.7 billion.

Save Soil multiplied that by the seven years of the next long-term budget currently being discussed in Brussels.

The range covers erosion, contamination, compaction and soil carbon losses, among other damage, and the JRC has noted the bill could double if costs such as biodiversity loss, floods, droughts and health effects were added.

Farm budget talks

In July 2025, the Commission proposed ring-fencing at least €300 billion for farmers' income and crisis support from 2028. On 26 October, EU agriculture ministers agreed their stance on the CAP rules but left funding to the wider budget talks.

Agriculture negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye, ended without a meaningful outcome, with a decision pushed back to 2027.

"Europe is debating hundreds of billions in agricultural support while soil degradation is already imposing enormous costs on its economy," Rico Rau, the lead author of the group's COP31 report, said in a statement.

"The next CAP should not simply compensate farmers for the pressures they face. It should help them rebuild the productive asset their livelihoods depend on," he added.

Risks to the food industry

According to the Commission, 60% to 70% of soils in the EU are unhealthy, weakening their ability to support farming, hold water and cope with extreme weather.

Poorer soils can cut yields, raise costs and make supply chains more fragile, Save Soil warned. The EU's food and drink sector alone turns over €1.5 trillion a year and employs 4.8 million people, according to industry body FoodDrinkEurope.

Save Soil wants the CAP to pay for measurable soil health gains and to reward farmers whose land is already healthy.

It also called for the Soil Monitoring Law, the EU's first soil law, to provide consistent evidence without duplicating measurements and paperwork. The law took effect in December 2025 but sets no binding restoration targets.

Its other two proposals are for the EU's carbon farming certification scheme to reward verified environmental benefits, and for public bodies to use their buying power to secure steady demand for sustainably grown food.

"If we want to ensure food security, farming has to be lucrative," Sadhguru stated in comments shared by the group, adding that governments must make farming profitable or farmers’ children will not take it up.

World.title: Five EU countries plan to send migrants to Rwanda. Is it legal?
World.content:
Five EU countries have unveiled this week a deal to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

 

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece will kick off this plan in 2027, with around 100 single men who cannot be deported directly to their home countries being sent to Rwanda.

The agreement is enabled by the EU return regulation, which entered into force last month. This marks the first time a group of EU member states have used the framework to send irregular migrants to a so-called “return hub.”

Article 14 of this law says that deals to deport migrants can only be made with countries that respect human rights, and many have expressed doubts about whether that is the case for Rwanda.

FILE: Syrian migrants arrive at main train station in Copenhagen - 2015 AP Photo

Freedom House, a US-based organisation which measures freedom around the world, gives the country a score of 7 points out of 40 in political rights and 14 out of 60 in civil liberties. Overall, they label Rwanda as “not free.”

The country also received a score of 0 out of 4 on judicial independence, raising questions about whether migrants not receiving proper treatment in Rwanda would be able to challenge their situation in court freely.

The United Nations Human Rights Council has also said this year that Rwandan authorities “suppress opposition and dissent, prosecuting political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders.”

Meanwhile, Amnesty International notes that Rwanda may be implicated in war crimes because of its support of M23, an armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that is allegedly responsible for summary killings and gang rape. War crimes are amongst the worst possible human rights violations.

The EU Parliament itself has proposed to suspend agreements with Rwanda because of these allegations.

Opponents also point to a precedent: a deal between the UK and Rwanda to send people there while their asylum requests were being processed (so not the same as the EU-Rwanda deal, but similar) was blocked by the UK Supreme Court because it found a real risk that Rwanda would send refugees back to the countries they had fled, which is forbidden by international law.

Rwanda’s government has pushed back and says that human rights are respected in the country and that an independent monitoring mechanism, to which the 5 EU countries have committed, will ensure that.

The parties also say that the UN Refugee Agency will have a role in making sure human rights are protected.

World.title: Germany: Berlin student protest targets rearmament and compulsory service
World.content:
Young protesters took to the streets of Berlin beneath the city’s television tower to oppose soaring defence budgets and the possible return of compulsory military service, chanting "Never again conscription" as smoke flares billowed above the march. Carrying signs emblazoned with "Hands off my future" alongside GTA VI-inspired posters proclaiming Generation Z’s readiness to push back, demonstrators warned that Germany’s drive to bolster its armed forces threatens their personal freedom and life choices. "We’re trying to resist this because it’s our future," one participant said.

 

The protest coincided with a broader day of youth-led demonstrations across Europe, with rallies also unfolding in Rome, Frankfurt and London. While local grievances differed, young crowds voiced shared anger at political leaders whom they accused of sidelining their generation’s priorities amid rising military expenditure and mounting global challenges.

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: US judge jails Indian national in foiled Sikh separatist murder plot
World.content:
Skip next section US judge jails Indian national in foiled plot to kill Sikh separatist, New Delhi denies involvement

11/21/2026 November 21, 2026 US judge jails Indian national in foiled plot to kill Sikh separatist, New Delhi denies involvement

Gupta paid $15,000 to a person he thought was a hitman, but turned out to be an undercover US agent Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

Nikhil G.*, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he said in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.

Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited the suspect in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.

The defendant paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.

Prosecutors also said the defendant had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.

His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.

"There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she said. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.

India-Canada row over Sikh killing has Punjab on edge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.

Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay."

Sikhs for Justice (SFJ) wants an independent Khalistan state and has been banned by India Image: David R. Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

World.title: Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
A 30-year-old man has been convicted of causing one of the most destructive wildfires in the history of Los Angeles. The verdict came after the case was retried.

A US-French man has been convicted on federal arson charges connected with the 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles, California, which killed 12 people and devastated the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.

The weeks-long blaze destroyed some 6,800 homes and other structures, causing estimated property losses of $150 billion (€136.7 billion).

What was the man convicted of in the Palisades fire case?

A US District Court jury in Los Angeles found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025.

While the fire was initially suppressed, it continued smoldering underground and reignited days later amid fierce winds to become the highly destructive Palisades Fire.

The fire caused widespread devastation Image: AGUSTIN PAULLIER/AFP/Getty Images

The man is set to be sentenced on March 17. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that he could face up to 40 years in prison.

The man was arrested in October 2025, and already faced one trial five months ago that ended with a hung jury. The judge declared a mistrial in June, prompting federal prosecutors to retry the case under modified charges.

Prosecutors said security camera footage and location data from the defendant's cellphone showed he was the only person nearby when ​the January 1 blaze began in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.

At both trials, they characterized the man, a former Uber driver, as a loner who held a deep resentment against society, and particularly the wealthy.

The Palisades area is an affluent Los Angeles neighborhood Image: Ethan Swope/AP Photo/picture alliance

The defense argued that the initial blaze could have been caused by fireworks, while prosecutors said there was no evidence that any had been set off in the area.

In March, the man denied in a court declaration that he had willfully started any fire, though he declined to testify in ⁠his own defense at either trial.

Double fire disaster

The Palisades blaze erupted almost at the same time as another wildfire that broke out in Eaton Canyon, some 30 miles (48 km) to the east.

That fire, believed to have been ignited by sparks from an electrical transmission tower, killed 19 people and devastated the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.

Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster ever seen in Los Angeles County.
