World.title: Bosnia Federation’s PM and Interior Minister Indicted Over Police Appointments
World.content:
Nermin Niksic. Photo: BIRN.

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Federation entity Prime Minister, Nermin Niksic, and six others have been indicted on charges colluding to commit a criminal act, abuse of office and influence peddling, the Federation prosecution said on Friday.

The indictment, filed by the Special Department of the Federation Prosecutor’s Office for the Suppression of Corruption, Organised and Inter-Entity Crime, POSKOK, also names Federation Interior Minister Ramo Isak, former Federation Police Administration chief Vahidin Munjic, Muhamed Ohranovic, Arijana Huseinovic Ajanovic, Ervin Musinovic and Mirela Bubalo.

According to the prosecution, the alleged offences took place between April 2023 and August 2024 in Sarajevo Canton and Mostar.

Niksic and Isak are accused of abusing their positions to appoint Munjic as head of the Federation Police Administration, FUP, and subsequently extend his mandate, allegedly in violation of Federation law. The prosecution says Munjic did not meet the legal requirements for the position.

Isak, as Federation interior minister, and Niksic, as entity prime minister, are accused of proposing and signing government decisions that enabled Munjic to take charge of the FUP.

The indictment alleges that Ohranovic, a FUP police officer, and Huseinovic Ajanovic, head of the Federation Prime Minister’s Office, acted as intermediaries in granting and extending Munjic’s authorisation. They are also accused of intervening in the appointment of Munjic’s relative as acting director of the state-owned BH Post.

Bubalo, a department head in the office of the Federation Interior Ministry, and Musinovic, an inspector responsible for overseeing security agencies, are accused of using their positions to facilitate employment at the FUP.

Isak is also accused of exceeding his authority in August 2024 by assigning Munjic to head the FUP Criminal Investigation Department, allegedly allowing him to continue directing the police administration until November 2025.

The indictment also covers alleged irregularities involving promotions and recruitment within the FUP, as well as the unauthorised disclosure of confidential information about prosecutorial checks and investigations.

The prosecution has requested that Niksic be barred from performing his duties as Federation PM and Isak from serving as Interior Minister. It has also proposed prohibiting both men from holding other official positions within the Federation government or senior posts in its institutions.

It has sought an extension of an existing ban preventing Huseinovic Ajanovic from performing official duties within the Federation government, as well as a ban preventing Musinovic from holding any official position within the FUP or the Federation Interior Ministry.

Security measures involving the seizure of items have also been proposed for Munjic, Huseinovic Ajanovic, Musinovic, Ohranovic and Isak.

For the trial, the prosecution has proposed hearing more than 60 witnesses and presenting over 500 pieces of material evidence.

The indictment has been submitted to the Special Department of the Federation Supreme Court for confirmation.

World.title: Week in Review: Protests, Hopes and Reality Checks
World.content:
Albania is moving towards local elections in May 2027 in an unusual atmosphere. Both traditional parties of power – the ruling Socialists and opposition Democrats – are gearing up for the fight.

This is not unusual. But the protests that have rocked Albania for more than half a year have shown that voters are keen to get rid not only of the Socialists but the Democrats as well. Serbia’s protesting students successfully squeezed out both the ruling and opposition parties. Can a similar force do the same in Albania?

World.title: Serbia Formally Drops ‘Violent Overthrow’ Case Against Student Protesters
World.content:
Court proceedings against nine students accused of calling for a violent change to Serbia’s constitutional order were formally concluded on Friday at Belgrade’s Palace of Justice, after the prosecution dropped the charges due to insufficient evidence.

After leaving the Palace of Justice, the students said the proceedings had been legally unfounded and politically motivated.

“It is not enough that the proceedings have been discontinued. We should never have had to wait a year and a half for justice. Justice must not depend on the will of those in power, but on the law. We would like this to mark the beginning of a new chapter – one in which the rule of law is restored to institutions and the state is returned to the people,” one student, Dimitrije Stefanovic, said after the court session.

Ivana Milenkovic, another defendant, called for accountability for all those who she said had participated in the arrests of her and her colleagues in an “unlawful and humiliating manner”.

“From plainclothes police officers to prosecutors, no one can or should be above the law. As the saying goes, let justice take its course. After all, they know very well what they did,” Milenkovic said outside the Palace of Justice following the hearing.

The nine students were arrested on June 29, 2025, a day after a major anti-government protest in Belgrade. They were accused of planning to radicalise the protests during meetings at the Faculty of Civil Engineering and the Faculty of Philology earlier that month.

Ahead of the protest, secretly recorded conversations from these meetings were broadcast on pro-government television channels. According to the prosecution, the students had discussed plans to blockade several state institutions, among other locations.

On September 11, 2026, the Higher Court in Belgrade ruled that evidence obtained through secret surveillance by Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA, had been collected unlawfully and should be excluded from the case. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in October.

On November 9, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said it had dropped the charges.

According to the prosecution, the excluded evidence constituted a significant part of its case, and the remaining material was insufficient to support a justified suspicion that the students had committed the alleged offences.

The students’ lawyer Aleksandar Radojicic, told N1 TV on Friday that it was rare for prosecutors to drop charges and that he hoped this would mark “the final act of the drama that the outgoing regime created against the children”.

Radojicic added that the judiciary had “shown integrity”, but there was still a “bitter taste” because they had not been able to hear the truth in the courtroom.

World.title: Former Ally of Albania’s PM Rama Denounces Ruling Party’s Governance
World.content:
Then Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali at a press conference in Tirana, February 2026. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA.

Former Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali, once a close ally of Prime Minister Edi Rama, spoke out publicly against her own Socialist Party in a TV interview on Thursday evening after she was reportedly dismissed from all party structures at the Socialists’ general assembly on November 14.

“I joined the Socialist Party, as a reformist force to change Albania; but what is the value of that today?” Spiropali, who was also speaker of the Albanian parliament between 2024 and 2025, said in the interview with Top Channel TV.

The Socialist Party came to power in 2013 and Spiropali was a key figure until March this year, when she refused to follow Rama’s line on the scandal around Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Infrastructure Belinda Balluku, who was charged with interfering with public procurements and corruption.

The Special Anti-Corruption Prosecution called on parliament to remove Balluku’s immunity to allow for her arrest.

Reportedly, one day before the parliamentary vote on Balluku’s immunity, Rama ordered his MPs to vote against the prosecution’s request. However, Spiropali did not participate in the vote.

In the interview with Top Channel’s ‘Top Story’ programme, Spiropali described the Balluku incident as “the worst example of governance by our political force”, and said the now-ousted minister was “the latest victim of a model that must change”.

“This is what I believed when I chose not to go to parliament to vote on the immunity issue,” she said.

Interviewer Grida Duma asked Spiropali how Balluku could represent the “worst example” and also be a victim.

Spiropali responded: “At a time when power becomes so personalised that all filters and internal checks within a political force vanish, and it is now abundantly clear that political courage has disappeared, that there is no longer any willingness to raise issues for discussion within party forums, and that no one confronts significant matters concerning governance or the Socialist Party, then, inevitably, a pattern emerges defined by phone calls, text messages, arbitrary personal choices and grave errors.”

Spiropali claimed that Balluku still maintains some power within the party because all its internal democratic mechanisms have failed.

She declared: “We can no longer continue with people in political forums who are using the Socialist Party as a shield for their own personal predicaments. The Socialist Party is not a bunker where they can hide.”

Asked if she had personally come under political pressure, she said: “From morning till night.” Asked by whom, she replied: “By Belinda Balluku and the institutions of this state.”

Balluku has not responded publicly to these allegations. She has however denied wrongdoing in the corruption case. Rama has made no comment on Spiropali’s interview so far.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechs, Slovaks Mark Velvet Revolution but Both Find Unity Elusive
World.content:
Russian drones hit close to Hungarian border; Orban used taxpayer money for sport trips

The war in Ukraine is getting closer to Hungary’s borders. On Tuesday, Russian drones struck Transcarpathia, Ukraine’s westernmost region – only 30 kilometres from the Hungarian border – and home to a significant Hungarian ethnic minority. While no casualties have been reported, the attacks caused infrastructure damage, and one of the drones exploded near the railway station in Mukachevo. In response, PM Peter Magyar announced the suspension of railway traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for two days. The attack was immediately seized on by the opposition Fidesz party, which accused the Tisza government of adopting Brussels’ “pro-war politics” and putting the security of the Hungarian minority at risk. “Peter Magyar’s government has abandoned its pro-peace policy and chosen to support the war instead of neutrality. This policy poses a threat to Hungary,” Fidesz wrote in a statement. The Hungarian government condemned the attack. Foreign Minister Anita Orban warned that “this is not the first air attack on Transcarpathia, and unfortunately, it will certainly not be the last,” expressing solidarity with the Ukrainian people. Russia also targeted Transcarpathia in 2025, but attacks on the region have been rare. Meanwhile, Russia’s ambassador to Hungary complained, in an interview with Demokrata, a Fidesz-aligned publication, about what he described as unfriendly steps taken by Hungarian diplomacy, including the expulsion of 10 Russian diplomats. He nevertheless expressed hope for mutually beneficial relations, saying that their future would depend on the Magyar government. He also issued a not-so-subtle warning about potential serious financial and legal consequences should the Hungarian government terminate its contract with Rosatom to construct the Paks II nuclear power plant. The project has been under review for several months.

This week it emerged that the Foreign Ministry under the previous government spent more than 280 million forints (about 760,000 euros) on sport-related trips for Orban and his retinue over the past decade, 444.hu reported. The revelations show that the former prime minister, a devoted football fan, financed most of his trips using taxpayers’ money via the Foreign Ministry’s budget. The report by 444.hu, based on data obtained by the publication through a lawsuit, found that the largest chunk, 180 million forints, was spent on accommodation, followed by transport at 79 million forints, airport VIP lounge services at 8.3 million forints, and miscellaneous expenses – taxis, parking, restaurant bills etc – another 10.3 million forints. These figures do not include trips made using a military aircraft or private jets, meaning the total public cost could be considerably higher. The most expensive trip was to Qatar in December 2022, where Orban attended the World Cup semi-final and final. Those two events cost taxpayers 131 million forints, of which 126 million went on accommodation. The second most expensive jaunt was to the 2016 Rio Olympics, costing 70.7 million forints, including 32 million for accommodation, flights, restaurant bills, sightseeing and other expenses. Other trips also raised questions about the use of public funds. Orban’s October 2017 visit to Switzerland for a World Cup qualifier cost nearly 2.5 million forints, including 1.3 million for a single night at the luxury Les Trois Rois hotel in Basel. Orban also attended Hungary’s World Cup qualifier against Ireland in 2025. Government offices and the Hungarian Football Federation had issued contradicting information about who paid for that trip, but the newly obtained records make clear that taxpayers covered the 14 million forints outlay. A subsequent trip to Portugal cost a further 7.9 million forints. The investigation into the football-related trips and their costs is part of a series by 444.hu about lavish spending habits of Orban and government delegations.

World.title: Russian Despatch: Without Vucic, Moscow Faces a Very Different Balkans
World.content:
November has turned into a month of frenetic diplomatic activity for Russia.

Moscow has not only resumed trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington on the settlement of its war against Ukraine, but also managed to expand the agenda to cover how the new security architecture of the whole of Europe should look after the end of hostilities.

And on Thursday, the leaders of Russia, the United States and China held an unprecedented trilateral meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China.

There are serious doubts that any of the above undertakings will produce tangible results, but their optics have largely overshadowed a major setback Moscow suffered in the Balkans - the fall of Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic, widely seen as a rare European ally for Russia.

World.title: EC approves Bulgaria’s final payment request under NextGenerationEU
World.content:
The European Commission said on November 20 that it has partially greenlighted Bulgaria’s fifth and final payment request for 1.82 billion euro under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) of the bloc’s NextGenerationEU post-pandemic economic recovery plan.

Bulgaria submitted the payment request on September 30, the deadline set by the European Commission, which aims to wind down the NextGenerationEU programme at the end of this year.

The Commission said that its assessment found that Bulgaria “has satisfactorily completed 53 out of 59 milestones and targets set out in the Council Implementing Decision.”

As such, the EC said that it would withhold part of the funds requested, but did not give an exact figure, noting only that it would be “proportional.”

Speaking to reporters in Sofia after the announcement, Deputy PM Atanas Pekanov, the Cabinet’s senior official tasked with securing RRF funds, said that Bulgaria was slated to receive more than 1.7 billion euro under the fifth payment request.

The policy areas in which Bulgaria pursued reforms and investments tied to this payment request include decarbonising the energy sector, strengthening the anti-corruption framework, enhancing the sustainability of transport and improving social inclusion and healthcare, the EC said.

The disbursement of the payment can be made after the Economic and Financial Committee, a body composed of senior officials from national administrations and central banks, the ECB and the EC, has issued an opinion on the Commission’s preliminary approval. It has four weeks to do so.

This is the second large RRF payment request received by Bulgaria this year, following 1.1 billion euro granted by the EC in June.

Due to years of political instability and short-lived governments, the country has lagged behind other EU member states in making the requests, raising the prospect that it could miss out on a significant amount of the 6.17 billion euro allocated to it under the RRF.

Pekanov said that this year’s two payment requests would take the amount received by Bulgaria under the RRF to between 98.7 per cent and 99 per cent of the allocated funding.

World.title: Bulgarian Parliament elects 11 members of Supreme Judicial Council
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly voted on November 20 to appoint 11 members of the country’s Supreme Judicial Council (SJC), the body tasked with the appointment of senior magistrates in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

Parliament held individual appointment votes for all 21 nominees. Vote tallies showed that the candidates that secured appointment were uniformly backed by the governing Progressive Bulgaria, alongside the opposition We Continue the Change (WCC) and Democratic Bulgaria.

The three parliamentary groups have a combined 168 MPs, enough to meet the qualified two-thirds majority of 160 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, required for the appointment of SJC members.

Most successful candidates, save three, were also backed by the opposition GERB and Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF) parties. Only pro-Kremlin party Vuzrazhdane, whose sole nominated candidate was not elected, voted against all successful appointments.

Of the 11 members of the SJC appointed by MPs on November 20, seven were nominated by Progressive Bulgaria and two apiece by WCC and Democratic Bulgaria.

The council has 25 members and is presided over by the Justice Minister, who is not, however, a member of the SJC. Of the 25 members, 11 are elected by Parliament, 11 by magistrates and three are members ex officio – the country’s prosecutor-general and the heads of the two high courts, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Supreme Administrative Court.

The 11 members elected by magistrates are voted by their respective branches – six by judges, four by prosecutors and one by investigators. This last one is part of the prosecutors college of the SJC, as the National Investigative Service is subordinated to the prosecutor’s office in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

MPs similarly elect six members of the SJC to the judges college and five to the prosecutors college.

The current SJC line-up, often criticised as being unduly under the influence of MRF leader Delyan Peevski – who is subject to US sanctions under the Magnitsky Act – has been in office nearly five years past the expiration of its five-year term.

That is because Bulgaria’s pollical instability since 2021, which saw eight parliamentary elections in five years, resulted in fragmented parliaments, some of them very short-lived, that had little appetite for tackling the issue of electing SJC members.

World.title: EU, UK in ‘landmark deal’ on food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions
World.content:
The European Union – United Kingdom summit on November 20 produced a “landmark deal” on food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions, but negotiations on university student fees – with the EU wanting its students to pay the same as British students in the UK – are to continue.

The joint statement, announced at a joint news conference by European Commission President António Costa, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, is part of efforts to “reset” the relationship between the bloc and Britain, 10 years after Brexit.

Costa said: “A strong partnership between the European Union and the United Kingdom is a strategic investment in Europe’s security. But it is also an investment in our shared prosperity, in innovation, competitiveness and resilience. Because there can be no strong defence without a stronger economy”.

“There is much more we can achieve together. We are not competing against each other, we are building win-win solutions together,” Costa said.

The European Union is a union of sovereign nations which respects sovereign natures, he said: “We respected the sovereign decision taken by the British people in 2016”.

“And I recall the words of the European Council after the referendum. We regret but we respect. And we will equally respect whatever decision the United Kingdom takes about the future of its long-term relationship with the European Union,” he said.

“Of course, we follow with great interest the debate you have relaunched about our common future. And as you know, we remain open to have the closest possible relationship between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”

Von der Leyen said: “We know the world around us is changing fast, making a closer and stronger partnership between the European Union and the UK the more important. And indeed, the spirit of our cooperation is win-win. Our economies are deeply connected.”

“Last year, we agreed on an ambitious agenda, and today we are delivering. First, we are bringing our people closer together. From next year on, the United Kingdom will once again take part in Erasmus+,” Von der Leyen said.

She said that negotiations had been concluded on a youth experience scheme. “It will allow 100 000 young people from each side to spend up to three years in each other’s countries. To work, to study, to volunteer, to simply travel.”

Von der Leyen said that negotiations had been concluded on an agreement on food and other agricultural products: “This is a big success. It is a two-way street”.

“For our businesses on both sides of the channel, it means easier trade and lower costs. And for our consumers, it means more choice and more affordable food, so lowering the living costs. We have also concluded negotiations to link our carbon markets.”

“The agreement will cut emissions, and it will generate investments in cleaner industries. It will help us advance our shared climate goals. Work also continues towards the United Kingdom’s participation in our electricity market,” Von der Leyen said.

Burnham said: “We’re 10 years on from Brexit, but I think we can all confidently say this is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe”.

“The agreement that we’ve reached together is a win-win. And it is in tune with public opinion in the UK. People can see the status quo isn’t working,” Burnham said.

“It’s not good enough for Britain. Three quarters of people say that they favour closer ties with Europe, according to the most recent polls. And that is because we’ve had a decade of drift, too much division, low growth in the economy, and higher prices in the shops,” he said.

“They want a better deal than the hard Brexit we ended up with. And today, together, we have delivered that better deal. As I say, it will be good for people in Britain, and good for people in Europe,” Burnham said.

“It directly addresses the biggest challenges of our times, and the biggest worries that people have. The cost of food. The cost of energy. The lack of growth in the economy, and the cost of doing business. The levels of illegal immigration. And the challenges facing our young people.”

Ffor people who are worried about the cost of the weekly shop, this deal will help, he said.

“By cutting the costs of exporting, it will help relieve pressure. At the moment, it can cost up to £1400 to export a single shipment of salmon. And obviously, that’s too high, and it will bring costs for business down.”

The deal would bring the cost of food down “and nd it opens up the possibility of lower electricity costs”.

There are so many businesses out there who are worried about the cost of doing business, Burnham said.

Burnham said that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey had “confirmed today that the UK Treasury has said that the deal struck here will add up to 0.5 per cent to UK GDP”.

“That is a £17 billion boost to the British economy. It is the single biggest growth measure that we could take in this Parliament,” Burnham said.

Brexit did take away opportunity from our young people, he said.

“And I can say to the young people of Britain, you will have, as a result of this deal, a new freedom. For anyone under 31, you will have much greater ease and ability to travel to any of the wonderful 27 member states of the European Union to live, to work, to study,” Burnham said.

“And that is such a positive note that we’ve been able to strike between ourselves so that the next generation can feel finally that people in our positions are directly doing something to recognise that they need more help and that they need more opportunity in their lives.”

Burnham said that a bill would be introduced in the British Parliament next week to implement this aspect of the deal.

(Photo: Council of the EU)

World.title: Two Russian missiles, Russian drone crash in Poland
World.content:
Two Russian missiles and a Russian drone have fallen in Poland, Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on November 20, as quoted by his ministry.

One missile exploded in Nowy Lipowiec, the other in Rudnik nad Sanem, and the drone in Mołodycz.

“This attack by the Russian Federation on Ukrainian territory, with its impact on the Republic of Poland, was one of the largest since the beginning of the full-scale war in Ukraine,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

He said that the missile that fell in Nowy Lipowiec, Biłgoraj County, was a Kh-101 missile.

“Throughout the night, our and allied pairs of on-duty jets operated – Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripens. Our pilots had a Dutch Air Force refueling aircraft at their disposal in the air. Our reconnaissance system, a Saab early reconnaissance aircraft, was also activated and operating in the Podkarpackie and Lublin Voivodeship,” he said.

Patriot systems located around Jasionka Airport in Rzeszów and near Świdnik in the Lublin region have been activated, as had the Poprad and Pilica+ ground systems.

Helicopters are also participating in the operation, as they continue to operate in the air, as are three brigades of the Territorial Defence Forces.

“We are dealing with another provocation by the Russian Federation,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“In my opinion, the date is not accidental. Today, the Coalition of the Willing exercises are taking place, involving several countries on Nowa Dęba near these locations,” he said.

“The Coalition of the Willing exercises, the presence of the Defence Ministers of France, Great Britain, and the Baltic states, eight chiefs of staff led by our most important allies. It seems the coincidence of these events is no coincidence,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“I will go to our allies, also with a request that they see what we have been facing here every day, every week, every month for four years. The threat to Nato and provocations from Russia are very serious. I will also request that the Alliance, the Secretary General, allocate additional forces and resources to support Operation Eastern Sentry. There are soldiers here from allied countries, for example, the Czech Republic, but more support is needed.”

We will not be intimidated, he said: “We will continue our actions, protecting above all our citizens, the Republic of Poland, and the strength of our Alliance”.

World.title: European prosecutors charge individual in 213.7M euro fraud probe into rail modernisation in Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Bulgaria has filed an indictment in the Sofia City Court against one suspect, following an investigation into a project for the modernisation of the Bulgarian railway infrastructure, EPPO said on November 19.

The project, which concerns parts of the railway section between Sofia and Plovdiv, is worth more than 213.7 million euro in EU financing.

The contract for the execution of the project was awarded to a consortium formed by three companies.

The accused is the legal representative of a company participating in the consortium.

According to the investigation, through the manager of the consortium, he submitted false information to the National Company Railway Infrastructure (NRIC) regarding the company he represented to illegally obtain EU funds.

His conduct enabled the consortium to be eligible to and to be awarded in 2019 the EU-funded grant agreement amounting to 213 714 235.14 euro.

Between 2019 and 2024, a total of 68 213 186.03 euro was paid out by the NRIC to the consortium, co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) and the national budget.

In particular, the accused used the manager of the consortium, who had no knowledge of the relevant criminal circumstances, to declare that the company was not subject to insolvency proceedings. In reality, based on the evidence, it was declared insolvent already in 2012.

The investigation was supported by Bulgaria’s Interior Ministry National Police General Directorate and the State Agency for National Security.

Numerous searches and seizures were carried out throughout the investigation across various locations in Bulgaria, including company headquarters and private residences. Documents concerning the tender procedure and its implementation were also seized.

The initial crime report was submitted by OLAF, which also conducted a complementary investigation, EPPO said.

(Archive photo: NRIC)

World.title: Arrests in Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Poland in probe into multimillion euro VAT fraud
World.content:
At the request of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Munich, three suspects were arrested this week in an investigation into a multimillion VAT fraud, EPPO said on November 19.

The arrests took place in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, and Poland. Searches and seizures were also carried out in those countries.

The criminal organisation under investigation is suspected of operating a cross-border VAT carousel fraud – a complex criminal scheme that takes advantage of EU rules on cross-border transactions between its member states, as these are exempt from value-added tax.

It is understood that they sold AirPods via companies and missing traders based in Germany and Bulgaria.

The activities of these suspects alone may have caused an estimated tax loss of 23 million euro in Germany.

With the support of national authorities from Bulgaria, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, searches were carried out at the premises of the suspects and companies under investigation.

These investigative measures are part of investigation Midas , targeting a transnational criminal organisation behind a 195 million euro VAT fraud scheme involving the sale of smartphones, small electronic devices and protective face masks.

(Archive photo: Interior Ministry)

World.title: EC opens two new infringement cases against Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Commission said on July 8 that it opened two new infringement cases against Bulgaria for failing to correctly transpose EU rules on deforestation and non-cash payments fraud.

In its latest infringements package, the EC said that it sent a letter of formal notice, the first stage in the infringement process, after Bulgaria failed to correctly implement the directive on non-cash payments fraud, which defines criminal offences and sanctions regarding fraud and counterfeiting of non-cash means of payment.

The Commission also found Bulgaria in breach of the EU Deforestation Regulation, which aims to ensure that key goods placed on the EU market do not contribute to deforestation and forest degradation, requiring member states to designate competent authorities responsible for implementing and enforcing the rules. Bulgaria did so for all commodities covered by the regulation, except rubber, the EC said.

Separately, the Commission also said that it was advancing an existing case by issuing a reasoned opinion, the second stage in the infringement process.

In that case, Bulgaria is accused of failing to correctly transpose the rules of the Seasonal Workers Directive, which outlines rules for the admission of third-country seasonal workers to the EU to meet seasonal labour demand.

World.title: FDI in Bulgaria in January-September 2026 was 3.96B euro
World.content:
Foreign direct investment in Bulgaria in the first nine months of the year stood at 3.96 billion euro, the equivalent of 3.1 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), statistics from the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) showed on November 19.

In January-September 2025, FDI was 2.38 billion euro, but the BNB originally reported 1.91 billion euro, which was revised upward later.

Investment in equity, including in the real estate sector, was 96.5 million euro (compared to an outflow of 10.5 million euro in January-September 2025) and the BNB figures showed 3.73 billion euro in re-invested earnings (compared to 3.33 billion euro for the first nine months of last year.)

Net receipts from real estate investments by foreign companies recorded an outflow of 11.1 million euro, compared to an outflow of 21.2 million euro in January-September 2025.

The central bank data showed 130.9 million euro in investment inflows as debt instruments, recorded as the change in the net liabilities of Bulgarian companies towards their foreign investor owners, compared to outflows of 935.3 million euro in the first nine months of 2025. Such financial flows include financial loans, suppliers’ credits and debt securities, BNB said.

By country, the largest direct investment in Bulgaria in the first three quarters of 2026 came from Greece (515.3 million euro), Luxembourg (487.1 million euro) and Switzerland (464.9 million euro). Notable net outflows were recorded towards the United States (-104.1 million euro) and Kazakhstan (-12.3 million euro).

According to preliminary figures, Bulgarian investment abroad increased by 406.8 million euro in January-September, compared to 379.2 million euro in the same period of last year, BNB said.

World.title: Why is Zagreb Airport Actually Losing Flights?
World.content:
November the 21st, 2026 – Zagreb Airport is losing flights, seeing foreign airlines either reduce flights or completely cut them. It all sounds very dramatic at first, but what’s actually going on?

Zagreb Airport received a record 4.72 million passengers last year, but in the first ten months of this year it recorded only 0.6 percent more passengers. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that the growth trend has slowed significantly and, since this summer, has completely reversed. From July to October, every month was weaker than it was back in 2025. At the same time, traffic at European airports grew by 3.4 percent in the third quarter of this year.

Some airlines, such as Austrian Airlines and British Airways, announced this autumn that they would no longer fly to Zagreb, while many others are cutting the number of flights or cancelling planned increases. Qatar Airways has significantly reduced capacity, Spanish Iberia has done the same, KLM has withdrawn its planned increase for next year, Turkish Airlines has reduced its schedule this year compared to last year, and Air France has removed some of the flights planned for 2027.

is the concessionaire looking to postpone their investment?

It should also be taken into account that Zagreb Airport has been applying a new schedule of charges for airlines since the 1st of June 2026. Some fees are higher by between 10 and 24 percent, and landing and take-off, passenger services, security screening and the use of airport infrastructure have all become more expensive. A comparison of airport charges in the region shows that Zagreb is more expensive than all of its competitors except Budapest. The question remains, however, whether the charges are the only or main reason for airlines withdrawing. Namely, the question has arisen whether there is a connection between the concessionaire’s business policy and its contractual obligation to expand the terminal. There is currently no concrete evidence for such a claim, but it is possible that the concessionaire is deliberately slowing down traffic in order to temporarily postpone the investment in the passenger terminal to which the contract obliges it once the airport reaches five million passengers per year.

zagreb airport is under the management of the franco-turkish consortium zaic

Zagreb Airport is publicly owned. Croatia as the state holds a 55 percent share, the City of Zagreb owns 35 percent, and Zagreb County and the City of Velika Gorica hold five percent each. Back in December 2013, the state handed over the management of the airport to a private concessionaire, the international consortium ZAIC, which includes the French companies Groupe ADP and Bouygues, Turkish TAV Airports and some other investors. The concession was concluded for 30 years and ends in 2042. The concessionaire took on the obligation to build a new terminal, maintain and manage the airport, and pay a concession fee to the public owners. The concession contract expressly obliges the concessionaire to expand the western part of the terminal with three new gates, the necessary associated facilities and an expansion of the apron once annual traffic reaches five million passengers.

The contract also provides for a final deadline for the start of the expansion of the 1st of January 2032, regardless of whether the five-million-passenger threshold is reached. It is clearly not a matter of indifference to the concessionaire whether it has to invest today or only in five years. The total cost for the concessionaire is measured in tens of millions of euros, and additional investments are also envisaged depending on traffic trends.

plans to reopen the old pleso terminal

Unofficially, however, we learn that the concessionaire is asking the Croatian Government to reopen the old Pleso passenger terminal instead of expanding the new terminal and to transfer low-cost traffic there, after which the number of passengers at the old and new terminals would be counted separately. In that case, traffic at the new terminal would fall by approximately 1.5 million passengers and would certainly not reach five million in the near future. Such counting is not in accordance with the existing contract. If the old Pleso terminal is opened for low-cost traffic, the arrival of Hungarian Wizz Air (which has transformed Bratislava Airport) is likely, as is a further expansion of Ryanair, which in recent years has been one of the main drivers of passenger growth in Zagreb, under significantly better conditions compared with full-service carriers. This would further complicate their operations in Zagreb and would also have a negative impact on Croatia Airlines.

For example, one of the reasons British Airways decided to leave Zagreb is that together with Croatia Airlines it carried only 68,303 passengers on the route to London Heathrow in the first nine months of 2026, or 5.5 percent less than a year earlier. At the same time, the wildly popular Ryanair carried 142,473 passengers on the Zagreb–London Stansted route, or 20.8 percent more, and for a much lower price for passengers.

incentives for opening new routes

In addition, since June 2026, Zagreb has had a special model for attracting airlines. For a new or poorly served year-round route that meets certain conditions, a 100 percent discount on the landing fee is provided in the first year, 50 percent in the second and 25 percent in the third, along with discounts on the passenger fee of 40, 20 and 10 percent. It has since been learned that the Croatian Government is getting closer to a positive response to the concessionaire’s request. After the global coronavirus pandemic, the concessionaire clearly did not make an effort to retain major carriers such as Emirates, Korean Air and Air Canada, but has mainly turned to the low-cost model.

Ideally, of course, a certain balance should be maintained between low-cost and traditional carriers, especially those hit by the sharp rise in fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East. By raising its charges, Zagreb Airport is losing competitiveness in the market and will find it difficult to compete with airports in the region that are expanding.

what will the government’s decision be?

Zagreb Airport has therefore found itself in an unusual situation: its traffic is falling precisely in the period when it is approaching the contractual threshold for a new major investment, while at the same time talks are under way about reopening the old terminal. The key question is whether that project will serve to increase capacity and attract new carriers, or whether it will be used to try to change the concessionaire’s contractual obligations. The answer depends on the conditions the government may eventually accept, particularly on whether all five million passengers will remain a single contractual threshold for the entire airport.

World.title: Zagreb to Purchase 20 New Trams at a Cost of Almost €70 Million
World.content:
November the 21st, 2026 – The City of Zagreb is set to purchase 20 new long low-floor trams at a cost of close to €70 million.

The City of Zagreb has now formally completed the public procurement for an additional 20 new long low-floor trams and selected Končar – Electric Vehicles as the most advantageous bidder with an offer worth €69.8 million excluding VAT. The delivery deadline for all trams is 36 months. Poslovni reports that these upcoming new trams will be 34.6 metres long and 2.3 metres wide. They will have 51 seats and a total capacity of up to 208 passengers. The low-floor design will make boarding and alighting easier for people with reduced mobility, parents with prams and more.

the trams will be produced in zagreb

Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević emphasised that trams are key to developing sustainable public transport, reducing traffic congestion and air pollution. “We’re especially proud that Zagreb’s trams are produced right here in Zagreb – few European cities can boast of that,” Tomašević said, according to the City of Zagreb. He added that the purchase of these trams is part of a broader investment cycle to modernise ZET. Between 2021 and 2026 the City has invested a total of €212.4 million excluding VAT and procured 258 buses and 39 trams. “In addition to purchasing new vehicles, we are also renewing the infrastructure, including the power grid, rectifier stations and turning loops. A further €164 million is being prepared for additional investments, so the total value of completed and planned investments reaches around €376 million excluding VAT,” the mayor stated.

100 new electric buses are also coming soon

The City of Zagreb also noted that the purchase of new trams had previously been awaited for 15 years. Of the 40 earlier contracted low-floor trams (worth €77.7 million excluding VAT, mostly financed from EU funds with €6 million from the state budget), 30 have already arrived, while delivery of the remaining 10 is underway. Alongside the additional 20 longer trams, the City is also preparing the modernisation of the existing Type 2200 trams, estimated at €10 million excluding VAT.

The new tram line on Sarajevska Road will soon open to traffic – the first new tram line built in Zagreb in more than 25 years. The City invested €11.7 million excluding VAT in it from its own budget. At the same time, the City is investing in the electrification of ZET’s bus fleet. After the opening of the charging station in Podsused this summer, 62 new electric buses have entered service, and the procurement of another 100 electric buses (estimated value €75 million excluding VAT) is in preparation. The modernisation of ZET also includes the renovation of the funicular, turning loops and power facilities, the purchase of vehicles for the transport of persons with disabilities, and the introduction of new systems for monitoring and ticket payment.

World.title: Scientists Warn About Mega Farms, Yet 24 are Planned in Croatia
World.content:
November the 21st, 2026 – Scientists are issuing stark warnings about mega farms, yet 24 of them are still being planned in Croatia.

A new scientific report by the European Commission (EC) is warning that huge quantities of animal manure from industrial livestock farming are seriously endangering European waters. Because of this, the association Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) is calling for a halt to the planned mega-farms in Croatia. Index writes that the report comes from the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission in 2026 and analyses the impact of livestock farming on water, soil and air. Scientists are now warning that the consequences of pollution can last for very many years.

nitrates from manure infiltrate the water

According to the report, large quantities of animal manure can lead to the pollution of groundwater and surface water with nitrates. In areas with intensive livestock farming, manure production sometimes exceeds the amounts that can be safely utilised.

Scientists warn that the existing limit value of 50 milligrams of nitrates per litre of water is not sufficient to protect aquatic ecosystems. Pollution can persist for years even after nitrate levels are reduced. Due to a possible increased risk of colorectal cancer, an international group of experts in Denmark has recommended lowering the permitted concentration of nitrates in drinking water from 50 to 6 milligrams per litre. The report also warns of phosphorus accumulation in the soil and ammonia emissions into the air. Ammonia pollution contributes to the formation of fine particulate matter, which increases the risk of respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.

24 mega farms are still being planned across croatia

Friends of Animals warn that two foreign investors have planned more than 20 large farms and slaughterhouses in four Croatian counties, with a total capacity of more than 200 million chickens per year. According to earlier data from environmental associations, there are 24 projects in total, of which 12 were stopped after public opposition. Some of the remaining projects have not yet been halted, and certain investors are announcing they will continue with their plans. They particularly highlight the Veliki Pažut farm, located within the UNESCO Mura-Drava-Danube Biosphere Reserve. The farm has begun trial operations, with a planned capacity of around 1.8 million chickens per year.

Residents of nearby settlements have already complained about unpleasant odours, damage to roads and houses, and the dumping of manure in the protected landscape of the Mura River. Associations are calling for the farm’s operations to be suspended and for the operating permit to be refused.

Friends of Animals claim that the environmental impact studies do not explain with sufficient precision how the investors will manage the large quantities of manure and wastewater, or at which locations this waste will be disposed of. They warn that waste management is often left to unspecified third parties and that no comprehensive assessment of the cumulative impact of all the planned farms and slaughterhouses on the environment and the local population has been carried out.

risks to public health

“The latest warning from European scientists confirms what citizens and associations have been pointing out for years: mega-farms generate huge amounts of waste and put a burden on water, soil and air that local ecosystems cannot bear, which also means risks to public health,” say Friends of Animals. The association believes there is still time to prevent the issuing of an operating permit for the Veliki Pažut farm. They emphasise that the other planned mega-farms and slaughterhouses have not yet been built and are calling for a response from the competent institutions. “We will not allow the resources that belong to all of us and to future generations to be permanently destroyed for the profit of a few investors,” Friends of Animals state, calling for new projects to be stopped.

scientists list recommendations, but will croatia follow them?

In the report, the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission notes that European rules on nitrates have reduced water pollution, but that the problem still exists in areas with a high concentration of livestock farms. Scientists recommend better manure management, a reduction in excess nitrogen, and more sustainable agricultural practices. They state that harmful impacts can be reduced in this way without a significant drop in agricultural yields.

World.title: Air France Reduces Number of Zagreb Flights
World.content:
November the 21st, 2026 – Air France has chosen to reduce the number of its Zagreb flights from Paris for the summer 2027 schedule.

French airline Air France has reduced the number of planned flights between Paris and Zagreb for the summer 2027 schedule. Index reports that the airline has withdrawn a total of 43 return flights from sale, cutting the number of available seats on the route by 9,460, according to the portal Croatian Aviation.

three weekly afternoon departures removed

The affected flights were planned for the period from the 28th of March to the 4th of July 2027. Air France has removed three weekly afternoon departures (on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays) from sale, so passengers can no longer book tickets for those flights.

During 2026 Air France operated these flights with Airbus A320-family aircraft. For summer 2027 it initially planned to switch to smaller Embraer E190 aircraft, which already meant a reduction in available seats. However, the company has now completely withdrawn all three weekly rotations from sale. This has further reduced the planned capacity on the Zagreb–Paris route, even though the flights had previously been included in the summer schedule.

around 9,500 fewer seats available

Under the original plan, there were to be 43 return flights (86 individual flights) between the 28th of March and the 4th July. With a planned capacity of 110 seats per flight, a total of 9,460 seats have been removed from sale. The reduction is significantly larger than originally planned, because Air France first intended only to replace larger aircraft with smaller ones. Now these afternoon flights have been completely removed from sale for the spring and the beginning of the summer season.

afternoon flights remain unchanged for autumn 2027

Air France has so far kept the three weekly afternoon rotations for the period from the end of August to the end of October 2027. The schedule can still change, however, so further adjustments to the number of flights cannot be ruled out. This latest cut fits into a broader trend of reduced planned capacity to Zagreb. British Airways and Austrian Airlines have already cancelled certain routes, while Qatar Airways and Spanish carrier Iberia have also significantly reduced their offering.

paris-dubrovnik remains unchanged

Unlike Zagreb, Air France has so far not reduced the number of planned flights between Paris and Dubrovnik. Capacity on that route for the period from the end of March to the end of June 2027 remains unchanged from the earlier plan. The changes to the Zagreb schedule concern planned capacities for 2027. Since several months remain until the start of the summer schedule, the airline can still make further adjustments to the timetable and number of flights.

World.title: Defining Luxury: RSVP Symposium Comes to Hvar
World.content:
November 6, 2026 – More international attention on Croatia’s premier island, as the prestigious RSVP Symposium comes to Hvar Town, hosted by Suncani Hvar Hotels.

Long known as Croatia’s premier island, the island of Hvar has been taking significant steps in recent years to cement and develop that image, as its tourism offer diversifies and targets the more elite market. Significant investment in the Suncani Hvar Hotels portfolio, including the first five-star hotel on a Dalmatian island (Palace Elisabeth, opened in 2019) has seen a surge in arrivals from the sought-after American market, which is now firmly number one in terms of both tourist arrivals and overnight stays.

All photos by Mihoci Studio

Success breeds success, and Hvar Town was the venue last month for the latest gathering of the influential RSVP Symposium, a global membership community for luxury event planners, wedding designers, creatives, and industry producers. The three-day event took place from October 5-8.

More than 150 professionals from over 30 countries came to Hvar to exchange knowledge and industry insights, build meaningful international partnerships, discover emerging luxury destinations, and to connect buyers with destinations, venues and suppliers.

After successful editions around the world, Croatia – and specifically Hvar – was chosen as the next destination to showcase its luxury hospitality, culture, gastronomy and event capabilities to an international audience. Full credit for this goes to Suncani Hvar Hotels, who not only hosted the three-day event, but were also instrumental who brought the event to Hvar.

The RSVP Croatia Experience was built around the concept of The Power of K(no)w, Shaped by Place, Informed by Heritage, Powered by Modernity. As such, Hvar was an incredible choice. The home of the gala dinner, 5-star Palace Elisabeth, lies on the spot where organised tourism in Europe began in 1868; across the main square lies the oldest public theatre in Europe, also an RSVP event venue, and no other island in the world in Europe has more UNESCO heritage, some of which was reflected in the UNESCO agave lace adorning the gala dinner tables. Experience inspired by authenticity.

The event was not just a celebration of the island of Hvar, but Croatia in general, and it was an opportunity also to celebrate one of the great symbols of innovation and modernity from years gone by – the genius of Nikola Tesla, who was born in what is now modern-day Croatia. Beach Celebration – Electric Enlightenment – Inspired by Nikola Tesla and invisible energy was a spectacular addition.

RSVP Symposium held several key events over the three days, hosted at the various Suncani Hvar hotels, each with its own theme and showcasing of the island’s diversity:

Knowledge of Place

After arrival in Hvar, there was an immersive destination welcome, followed by an Evening Cocktail Experience – 1001 Dalmatia, which was hosted by Hotel Adriana. Highlighted was a contemporary interpretation of the Dalmatian lifestyle, inspired by the contrast of white limestone and the Adriatic Sea.

Knowledge of Heritage

After a full educational programme and networking opportunity, the Signature Gala Dinner – Veiled Intentions – Inspired by UNESCO-protected Hvar agave lace, was held at Palace Elisabeth, a chance to see Hvar’s rich heritage presented through a contemporary luxury lens.

Knowledge of Modernity

After the final conference sessions and future-focused discussions, there was a beach celebration – Electric Enlightenment – Inspired by Nikola Tesla and invisible energy, hosted at Beach Club Hvar. The evening included dynamic lighting, music and immersive entertainment. A wonderful celebration of Croatia as an innovative and creative destination.

Three days of showcasing history, heritage, tradition and the Mediterranean lifestyle while networking, socialising and exchanging views, and delegates headed back to their corner of the world more informed, energised and impressed by Croatia and its luxury opportunities. The possibilities to expand and develop Croatia’s luxury tourism market, using its key ingredients of nature, gastronomy, heritage and tradition have always been plain to see, but hosting events such as the RSVP Symposium enable those possibilities to reach the right and influential audiences.

World.title: Croatia Draws Republic of Ireland in Nations League Play-Offs
World.content:
Croatia will face the Republic of Ireland in the Nations League play-offs, with their place in League A on the line. The draw was made on Friday at UEFA headquarters in Nyon.

Slaven Bilić’s side will play the first leg away and the return leg at home, both in March 2027. The winner stays in League A for the next edition of the competition, while the loser drops into League B.

The first legs can be played on March 25 or 27, and the return legs on March 28 or 30. UEFA will confirm the exact schedule after the draw. The Croatian Football Federation has not yet chosen a venue for the home leg, with Osijek’s Opus Arena, Zagreb’s Maksimir and Split’s Poljud all under consideration.

The tie is decided on aggregate over two legs. If the scores are level, two 15-minute periods of extra time follow, then penalties if needed. There is no away goals rule.

Croatia finished third in Group A3 behind England and Spain, and ahead of Czechia, collecting six points from six matches, with both wins coming against the Czechs. Only the two best third-placed sides, Greece and Italy, stayed in League A automatically, leaving Croatia and Denmark among the teams heading into the play-offs.

The other play-off ties

League A/B: Bosnia and Herzegovina v Denmark, Hungary v Serbia, Slovenia v Wales

League B/C: Cyprus v North Macedonia, Estonia v Romania, Faroe Islands v Georgia, Belarus v Israel

World.title: Foreign Workers Must Learn Croatian in 2027, But is That Really Integration?
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – Foreign workers must learn Croatian and be able to prove at least a basic level of it in 2027, but is that really integration into society? According to the law, it is, but according to experts, it’s far from enough.

You move from India, Bangladesh or Nepal to Croatia, an agency gets you a job, you learn about thirty basic phrases of its language, and according to the law, that’s enough to be considered “integrated.” Davor Kovacevic reports for Glas Slavonije that this is precisely what will be required of foreign workers in Croatia starting in 2027, as they will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at the A1.1 level in order to extend their residence and work permits.

However, is a basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, a senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is a clear “no,” and the data his institute collects shows that Croatia has only scratched the surface of a problem that will become increasingly complex.

there are more barriers than language

When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the daily lives of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out just one. Language barriers, inadequate housing, violations of labor rights, difficult access to healthcare, and social isolation, he says, are all intertwined, yet the common denominator of most of these problems is a lack of information. Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding to the new situation through regulations, though it remains an open question how much of it the administration manages to implement in practice. Stricter criteria for employers, for example, were meant to regulate the market, but they simultaneously increased the administrative burden, causing some workers to wait months for permit extensions.

The healthcare system is a particular problem, according to a November 2025 Institute survey conducted among 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously hampers regular healthcare. Language remains an obstacle even when workers try to find information on their own, as official institutional websites are often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of this, many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, and sometimes only, source of information becomes their employer or employment agency. “A series of very practical questions, from whether an employer can hold onto their passport, to whether they are entitled to unemployment benefits, to whom to contact if their rights are violated—remain without a reliable answer for a large number of workers. What Croatia lacks today is not primarily regulations. It lacks a system that will enable a foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” he pointed out.

acceptance from a society that was, until very recently, extremely homogenous

Balabanić views the obligation to pass the A1.1 exam simultaneously as an integration measure and an administrative condition, though he emphasised that its purpose should primarily be integration.

“Knowing the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first prerequisites for starting to feel like part of society. Still, such a low level of language proficiency does not in itself solve the issues of foreign workers’ legal security or their ability to navigate Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can genuinely exercise them,” Balabanić stated. Precisely for this reason, until a worker masters Croatian, information regarding residence, work, the healthcare system, and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and, Balabanić stresses, in one central place rather than scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mostly boils down to the relationship between worker and employer, the social dimension is equally important. Foreign workers need to become familiar with the norms and values of the society they are entering, while the local population must also accept that Croatia is becoming more culturally diverse.

Just how weak that readiness currently is was shown by a November 2025 survey by the Institute for Migration Research conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and only a negligible number of respondents as a family member.

“That is why I would say Croatia is still in the very early stages of integrating foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, accessible information, social contacts, and the readiness of the local population to accept new fellow citizens, we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić stated. When it comes to financing integration, Balabanić clearly points out that the state should bear the largest share of the costs.

a(nother) financial burden for employers

The Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK) pointed out that integrating a foreign worker places a serious financial burden on the employer. Through its own program “Welcome to Croatia,” HGK has so far included more than 400 foreign workers from 15 Croatian companies, while users of Croatian Employment Service (HZZ) vouchers for language learning are employed by 1,602 employers. According to HGK estimates, accommodation provided by the employer alone costs between 3,000 and 3,600 euros annually per worker, a language course costs between 300 and 500 euros, and administrative costs, such as residence and work permits, medical exams, and plane tickets, climb into the hundreds of euros. The new legal obligation will further increase costs, as the law stipulates that the cost of the standardised A1.1 exam is borne specifically by the employer.

taking responsibility

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily due to the needs of the domestic labour market and labour shortages in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest share of responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

This, he emphasised, doesn’t mean the responsibility must rest exclusively with the state. Local self-government plays an important role because integration happens within specific communities—the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, though Balabanić warns it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, as they already bear significant hiring costs. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have an obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the laws. It is precisely here that Balabanić sees a real danger of integration becoming something the state formally demands from a foreign worker without providing them the tools to actually fulfill that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration to be exclusively their personal problem,” he said. Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers facing overlapping adverse circumstances, those who went into debt just to reach Croatia through long chains of intermediaries, making it harder for them to refuse poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer upon whom they depend for their salary, accommodation, and information about their own rights.

the issue of language

Interestingly, employers themselves, according to an HGK survey on a sample of 572 companies, recognise the importance of language, with as many as 80 percent of respondents believing that learning Croatian would contribute most to easier integration of local and foreign workers in a shared work environment. However, HGK states that employers’ responsibility in practice already goes beyond merely paying for an exam. “It includes quality onboarding, mentorship support, and, where applicable, ensuring the adequacy of accommodation,” HGK stated. The Chamber believes that integration must remain a shared responsibility among institutions, employers, and workers.

World.title: Bjelovar Plans Extension of Brezovac Airport Following Wellovar Complex Completion
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – Bjelovar is planning the extension of the Brezovac Airport following the completion of the Wellovar complex. The desire is to attract more visitors to the newly opened facility.

The airport in the Bjelovar settlement of Brezovac could accommodate smaller passenger aircraft in the future, and its development opens up interesting opportunities for Bjelovar’s tourism. Ivan Karacony reports for Bjelovar Live that this is particularly relevant now given that the Wellovar geothermal complex in Veliko Korenovo is now completed and is just a few kilometres from the existing runway.

In its draft budget for 2027, the City of Bjelovar foresees the continued preparation of the airport expansion project, including a new runway and additional facilities. If realised, this project would expand the airport’s current sports purpose and enable the reception of smaller aircraft with a capacity of three to 10 passengers.

With the opening of Wellovar, a large geothermal sports and recreation complex featuring 10 indoor and outdoor pools, Bjelovar gained an attraction that, alongside the logical idea we might call “Operation Airport”—could draw additional visitors from Croatia and abroad. At least those who wish to reach their tourist destinations by plane and shorten their travel time. Of course, this does not involve large passenger airliners and regular commercial routes, but rather smaller private and business aircraft that could use the expanded airport in the future. In this context, the proximity of the Brezovac airport, located approximately 1.9 kilometres as the crow flies from Wellovar, and between 3.5 and four kilometres from the heart of Bjelovar, is particularly intriguing.

This opens up the possibility for the future airport to take on a specific tourism role alongside its sports function. The option of arriving via smaller private and business planes could be an added advantage for Wellovar visitors, as well as for business guests and other tourists coming to Bjelovar.

bjelovar’s more tourism-oriented future

This conclusion is backed by the official explanation of the city budget. The City of Bjelovar lists proximity to the city center, the planned Zagreb–Virovitica expressway, and Terme Bjelovar, Wellovar, as key advantages of the future airport expansion. The explanation highlights the potential for connecting air and road transport with tourist facilities, as well as introducing a passenger program for smaller aircraft. In other words, linking the airport and Wellovar stands out as one of the most interesting possibilities for Bjelovar’s future tourism development, although a concrete program for such a connection has not yet been presented. Thus, everything is still at the idea stage, albeit a good idea.

a newer runway for smaller passenger aircraft

The existing airport in Brezovac is currently used for sport aviation, and its infrastructure consists of a runway as well as business and auxiliary facilities used by the Bjelovar Aeroclub (Zrakoplovni klub Bjelovar). The planned expansion includes building a new runway and additional facilities to broaden airport activities. Clearly, this is a plan, or rather, an idea, to create conditions for accommodating smaller passenger planes, giving the airport new value and a new purpose.

For the Brezovac Airport expansion project, 33,000 euros were planned in the 2026 city budget for preparing project documentation, including the conceptual design, preliminary project, and environmental protection and parceling studies. Furthermore, according to the City of Bjelovar’s draft budget, another 33,000 euros are planned for the “Brezovac Airport” project in 2027. The projection for 2028 is 50,000 euros, while a significantly higher amount, 200,000 euros, is foreseen for 2029. When all is said and done, the sum of planned and projected amounts from 2026 to 2029 reaches 316,000 euros. It should be emphasised that this figure does not represent the total estimated cost of expanding the airport, but rather the funds listed in the budget documentation for that period. Additionally, this does not mean that all the stated money has already been spent or that all projected amounts will ultimately be realised.

Whether Brezovac will become an airport for smaller passenger planes in the future remains to be seen. However, given the proximity of Wellovar and the growth of the tourist offer, such infrastructure could gain new value far beyond its previous role in sport aviation. If Bjelovar already has a tourist attraction that might make someone want to arrive by plane, it is only logical to consider where that plane could actually land.

World.title: €2 million tender seeks developer of schools AI learning platform
World.content:
The AI-Leap Foundation is seeking a new developer for its ITI learning platform for Estonian students and teachers as its agreement with OpenAI nears expiration. The foundation has launched a tender worth up to €2 million for the platform's continued development through August 2028.

Last year, the AI-Leap (TI-Hüppe SA) signed a cooperation agreement with OpenAI to develop an AI-based learning platform for students. Distribution of the platform to 10th- and 11th-grade high school students began in January. This academic year, the program expanded to all high school grades, as well as vocational school students and teachers and lower secondary school teachers.

The agreement with OpenAI expires in February next year, prompting AI-Leap to seek a new technology provider whose platform will support the continued development of ITI for Estonian students.

"With the partner selected through the procurement process, we will continue the work we began during the first academic year in cooperation with OpenAI and Google. We are not procuring only user licenses but also educational adaptations, support and cooperation. The new service provider will be selected through the tender process," said AI-Leap communications manager Armas Riives.

The learning platform must meet the needs of Estonia's schools, be suitable for the Estonian language and cultural environment, and support learning. Teachers will receive an AI application designed to support classroom instruction.

According to Riives, large language models can be used across all subjects, both in class and for independent study.

"For example, to better understand the steps involved in solving a math problem, practice languages, explain a complex topic or receive feedback on one's work," Riives said. "Teachers can use AI to prepare lessons and create learning materials and assignments, among other things. How and how often it is used will remain up to teachers and students."

He added that ITI's goal is not to think on behalf of students but to help them think and learn independently. It must function in Estonian, account for the local context and, when necessary, direct users to local support and counseling services.

For students, the platform resembles ChatGPT, but behaves differently. It can offer tasks tailored to a student's level, help identify mistakes, support learning strategies and guide students to find answers in learning materials and formulate conclusions themselves.

"We will continue developing its connections to Estonian curricula and educational materials. Our long-term goal is to improve students' thinking and learning skills," Riives said, adding that a University of Tartu research team led by Jaan Aru, in cooperation with Stanford University, is studying whether and how the platform contributes to that goal.

The technology provider must initially provide user accounts for at least 20,000 students and 10,000 teachers, while being able to scale up if necessary to 42,000 students and 19,000 teachers.

The target audience includes high school and vocational school students, teachers, lower secondary school teachers for grades five through nine, and master's students in teacher training programs. The procurement does not include licenses for lower secondary school students.

The service provider may not use user data to train AI models, and educational institutions, teachers and system administrators may not have access to the content of users' conversations.

The maximum value of the procurement is €2 million, excluding value-added tax. The service period runs from March next year through the end of August 2028.

Delfi reported Friday that about 3,200 students actively use the AI-Leap learning platform each week, roughly one in six of those who have received licenses. Because the platform is still in its trial phase, the foundation considers that a solid result.

Students told the news portal that they prefer standard ChatGPT to the school's platform because it provides answers more quickly. The learning platform asks additional questions to guide students, but many students simply want an immediate answer or explanation and often return to familiar tools.

The tender is funded by the Ministry of Education together with private-sector support for the AI-Leap educational program.

World.title: Minister: Russia-backed murder plot in Denmark marks dangerous escalation
World.content:
In a press release, Tsahkna warned that Moscow's willingness to order political killings on European soil demands a united, concrete response beyond diplomatic condemnation, linking the threat directly to Estonia's decision to close its road border crossings with Russia next month.

"Denmark's attribution to Russia of the attempted murder that took place in September is extremely serious," Tsahkna said. "Attributing the ordering of political assassinations in Europe to Russia points to a new and particularly dangerous escalation of Russia's hostile activity. Europe must stand together to resist it," the minister went on.

Tsahkna stressed that the Kremlin's destabilization campaign extends well beyond its war in Ukraine.

"Russia's aggression is not limited to Ukraine," the foreign minister said. "Sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and the direct endangerment of lives are all part of Russia's broader efforts to undermine security across Europe."

He pointed to Tallinn's move earlier Friday to shut down road traffic at the Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa border checkpoints starting December 1 as a direct countermeasure against Moscow's hybrid operations.

"The Estonian Government's decision today to close the road border crossing points between Estonia and Russia from December 1 is a concrete response to Russia's continued hostile activities," Tsahkna said. "By protecting Estonia's border, we are also protecting the security of the European Union as a whole."

Estonia stands firmly with Denmark following its official attribution of the September assassination attempt to Russia and fully supports the countermeasures. Russia's aggression does not stop at Ukraine's borders. Across Europe, we have seen cyberattacks, sabotage and attacks on critical infrastructure organised by Russian security services. Now, even people are being directly targeted. These are not isolated incidents, but part of a wider pattern of Russian hostile activities threatening Europe's security. Condemnation alone is not enough. We must continue to call out Russia for these attacks and respond together with stronger pressure on Russia. Moscow cannot be allowed to exploit Europe's openness, intimidate our societies or divide us. — Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) November 20, 2026

Tsahkna added that European allies must pair evidence-based public attribution of hybrid attacks with tangible penalties. "Europe cannot limit its response to condemnation," he said. "We must publicly attribute Russia's attacks on the basis of evidence and ensure that they have concrete consequences."

According to the BBC, Danish authorities announced Friday that Russian intelligence services orchestrated a foiled September 25 plot to assassinate U.S.-Ukrainian rapper Albert Vasiliev, known as Kyivstoner, ahead of a concert near Copenhagen. Two suspects arrested with weapons near the venue have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, though both have pleaded not guilty. In response, Copenhagen expelled Russia's defense attaché and proposed halting non-essential Schengen visas for Russian citizens.
