World.title: Srikakulam releases 15,440 cusecs as inflows moderate after cyclone floods
World.content:
As many as 15,440 cusecs of water from the Bahuda River were discharged downstream on Saturday (November 21, 2026) morning as inflows continued from upstream, which witnessed heavy rains for the last few days with the impact of the Akvan cyclone.

The district administration heaved a sigh of relief as inflows are moderate compared to inflows of nearly one lakh cusecs one month ago due to the cyclone that caused havoc in Ichchapuram and other places. Irrigation officials released 3,600 cusecs from the Gotta barrage of Vamasadhara, and 3,100 cusecs of Nagavali water were discharged from Narayanpur Anicut.

Srikakulam collector Swapnil Dinakar Pundkar said that the situation was under control in spite temporary inundation of crops in Ichchapuram and other places. He said that agriculture officials will visit the fields and give necessary suggestions to farmers.

World.title: Strict action against drug peddlers to begin now, says U.P. CM Yogi
World.content:
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday (November 20, 2026) said the State government is now set to launch an extremely stringent crackdown on drug peddlers and urged young people to stay away from drugs. Mr. Adityanath warned that those who jeopardise the careers of the youth would be destroyed by the government.

“After crushing mafias and eliminating organised crime, the State government was now set to launch an extremely stringent crackdown on drug peddlers. The government would destroy those who jeopardise the careers of the youth,” said Mr. Adityanath in Gorakhpur, while distributing tablets to over 50,000 students and trainees from Gorakhpur, Deoria, Kushinagar and Maharajganj at a grand ceremony organized under the second phase of the Swami Vivekananda Yuva Sashaktikaran Yojana.

The Chief Minister described the incident in Gorakhpur two days ago, in which a Class 10 student was run over during an SP procession, as a blot on Uttar Pradesh’s identity. “The student, who was on his way to pick up his younger sister from school, was the great-grandson of Pujan Singh, a revolutionary associated with the Chauri Chaura incident. Anti-social elements who emerge from their hideouts and create trouble during elections would be crushed completely,” he said.

The U.P. CM added recruitment processes for 8,000 lekhpals, 32,000 police personnel and over 42,000 home guards have now been completed and appointment letters will be distributed at an average interval of every five to seven days until January 26. “Nearly 9.5 lakh government appointment letters had been issued over the past nine-and-a-half years. More than 16,000 appointments have recently been made in the Agriculture, Health, Education, Panchayati Raj, Police, Sports and Revenue departments. The recruitment processes for 8,000 lekhpals, 32,000 police personnel and over 42,000 home guards have now been completed. Appointment letters will be distributed at an average interval of every five to seven days until January 26,” said Mr. Adityanath.

“Recruitment examinations were earlier dominated by ‘Munna Bhai’ and the Saifai syndicate, whereas recruitment is now taking place swiftly and strictly on merit. This has been made possible by stringent laws prescribing life imprisonment, a ₹1 crore fine, and confiscation of property in cases of paper leaks. During the first phase, 60 lakh youths were provided with tablets and smartphones, with the benefits reaching nearly 3 crore people, according to an IIM Lucknow study. Under the second phase, 25 lakh tablets are being distributed. Equipped with more than 18,000 free courses offered by Infosys and the ‘Yuva Sathi App’, these tablets serve as mobile universities,” he said.

The Chief Minister advised young people to fact-check viral content, practice digital safety and devote three hours to skill development instead of spending time watching 30-second reels. He also urged them to use their tablets to complete the online self-enumeration process for Census 2027 and fill out Forms 6, 7 and 8 for the Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls.

Union Minister of State Kamlesh Paswan, Ministers Surya Pratap Shahi and Sanjay Nishad, MP Ravi Kishan Shukla, Mayor Dr Manglesh Srivastava, District Panchayat Chairperson Sadhana Singh, MLCs Dr Dharmendra Singh, Dr Ratanpal Singh and Dhruv Tripathi, MLAs Fateh Bahadur Singh, Vipin Singh, Shriram Chauhan, Mahendra Pal Singh, Pradeep Shukla, Rajesh Tripathi, Shravan Kumar Nishad, Sabha Kunwar, Manish Jaiswal, P.N. Pathak, Mohan Verma, Gyanendra Singh, Prem Sagar Patel and Jaimangal Kanujia, State Women’s Commission Vice-Chairperson Charu Chaudhary, BJP district president Janardan Tiwari, Chief Minister’s Advisor Awanish Awasthi and IIDC Alok Kumar, along with other public representatives and students, were present at the event.

World.title: Russia dusts off its pre-war demands as the U.S. raises discussing European security at Ukraine talks
World.content:
After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing a U.S. offer to discuss post-war European security, and Moscow is using that diplomatic opening to reaffirm the tough demands that President Vladimir Putin put forward before the start of his full-scale invasion.

The proposal to discuss broader security arrangements for Europe was floated by U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, and that has worried Ukraine and its Western allies, who fear it will play into Moscow's hands and weaken NATO.

The Kremlin strongly backed the U.S. idea, describing a review of the broader European security framework as vital for a settlement of Europe's most devastating conflict since World War II.

Mr. Putin discussed the Ukrainian conflict with Mr. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, their first trilateral meeting. That encounter had fuelled fears in Ukraine that they could discuss a possible settlement without Kyiv's participation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants a ceasefire to include a security framework to ensure that Russia does not attack his country again, and European leaders argue that such an architecture already exists in the form of NATO.

Russia's demands date back to 2021

In draft agreements submitted to the U.S. and NATO in December 2021, two months before the invasion, Russia demanded that Washington and its allies pledge to exclude NATO's expansion to Ukraine, Georgia or any other nation that was once part of the Soviet Union.

Moscow also demanded that the U.S. and its allies make a commitment to not deploy weapons or conduct any military activities in Ukraine and other ex-Soviet nations.

The documents also obliged the alliance not to station any troops in areas where they weren't present in 1997 — before NATO moved to incorporate former Soviet bloc countries and ex-Soviet republics.

They also suggested a freeze on patrols by Russian and U.S. warships and bombers near each other's borders. In addition, they called for efforts to reduce the risk of incidents involving Russia and NATO warships and aircraft, primarily in the Baltic and the Black seas; a reduction in the scope of military drills; and greater transparency and other confidence-building measures.

NATO allies have rejected the Russian demands as a nonstarter.

Mr. Putin described the West's refusal to consider these proposals as the main reason behind his decision to send troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, arguing that he had to act to fend off a major threat to Russia's national security. Ukraine and its allies denounce the invasion as an unprovoked act of aggression.

Moscow sees an opportunity to revive and expand its demands

Speaking after the meeting with the Chinese and U.S. Presidents, Mr. Putin reaffirmed his criticism of the West for failing to take Moscow's complaints about NATO's expansion into account.

"They just spat at our opinion,” he said.

Mr. Putin bluntly rejected the European response to Moscow's plans. He called it “political diarrhea” and “nonsense,” saying that “everybody understands that we don't strive for a war with Europe.”

He said Russia is open to discussing the continent's security arrangements with the Europeans as the U.S. has suggested, and scoffed at “hysterics in some European capitals" over Washington's offer.

“We understand that it makes no sense to discuss issues related to security in Europe without the Europeans,” Mr. Putin declared. He said Moscow invited a European delegation to visit and state its negotiating position before deciding on the date and format of Ukrainian talks.

Russia is ready to search for compromise, he said, but will not budge on its key demands. He has sternly warned that Russia will not accept the deployment of any European troops into Ukraine after the hostilities end and see them as a legitimate target.

Kremlin Foreign Affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said that during talks with Mr. Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Nov. 12 in the Kremlin, Mr. Putin reminded them of Moscow's 2021 security proposals, noting that they envisioned the pullback of NATO forces from Central and Eastern Europe.

Ushakov said the Kremlin would now update them with “fresh considerations.”

Some see room for compromise by Russia

While Mr. Vladimir Putin appears adamant on keeping Kyiv out of NATO and blocking any Western troops on Ukrainian soil, some observers say Moscow could be open to concessions on its other demands, including the rollback of NATO troops from Central and Eastern Europe.

Alexei Naumov, a pro-Kremlin political commentator, argued that Russian demands represented an initial bargaining position that could become more flexible during talks.

“Between maintaining the current status quo and the full realisation of Russia's demands, there is a vast space for compromise: mutual arms limitations, agreements regarding the deployment of military infrastructure, the parameters for a future Ukrainian military, security guarantees, and mechanisms to monitor their implementation,” he said in a commentary.

“Russia is currently negotiating from a position of strength, but that does not at all mean there will be no compromises.”

Tatiana Stanovaya, an expert at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that “for the first time since 2022, Moscow sees a concrete opening for negotiations that could address what it calls the root causes' of the war.”

“The Kremlin thinks the opportunity is worth pursuing, even though its expectations for this round are low,” she said. “If the talks fail, Russia is prepared to keep fighting until another opening presents itself.”

Russia expert Mark Galeotti, who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, said Moscow's set of demands could reflect “the classic attempt to start with a very, very exaggeratedly ambitious list of proposals with the expectation that you get haggled down.”

Vladimir Putin could be searching for a face-saving way to end the war without achieving the land gains in Ukraine that he had sought, Mr. Galeotti noted in a recent podcast.

Ukraine and its allies fear security talks will benefit Moscow

European leaders fear that Mr. Putin could persuade Donald Trump to support a peace settlement that would weaken not only Ukraine but broader European security.

The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Mr. Putin demands.

“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin earlier this month.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy also has warned that the U.S. proposal to discuss a new security framework for Europe before the war's end could be dangerous, arguing that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent's borders.

Jared Kushner, meanwhile, said after meeting with Mr. Zelenskyy and European leaders on Thursday (November 19, 2026) in Berlin that Mr. Trump wants to make a deal with Europe “by his side” and is not looking to impose a unilateral agreement. He also emphasised that Mr. Trump is “open” to NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, added that he believes Russia is “comfortable” with the allies offering such assurances to Kyiv.

Donald Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Mr. Kushner said.

Ms. Stanovaya noted that Putin wants Europe to accept that Russia will have to be part of any negotiation on European security and predicted that the prospective talks will fuel differences among the allies.

“I expect the process to deepen divisions within Europe, with little prospect of concrete results,” she said in a post on X.

World.title: Key takeaways from the Quad, ASEAN-India, and East Asia Summits in Manila | Explained
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi took part in three back-to-back multilateral meetings on the side-lines of the annual Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) summits in Manila this week. The summits, including the ASEAN-India Summit, East Asia Summit and then the Quad Summit along with U.S. President Donald Trump, Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi and Australian PM Anthony Alabanese ended with several concrete announcements. They also sent deeper underlying message on India’s broad-basing its ‘Act East’ and Indo-Pacific policies, even as the world turned its attention to the Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral later in the week.

In 2025, PM Modi had pulled out of attending the ASEAN Summits in Kuala Lumpur due to what was seen as a combination of domestic commitments around Diwali and trade friction with U.S. President Donald Trump. Ties with the Philippines have improved dramatically since President Bongbong Marcos’ visit to Delhi in August 2025, and hence it was doubly important for PM Modi to attend the two conferences hosted by him- the ASEAN- India summit, which includes Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam, as well as the East Asia Summit, which brings in U.S., Russia, China, Japan and South Korea. In addition, the invitation to the Quad Summit hosted by the U.S. and being held for the first time in Mr. Trump’s turbulent presidency was important to fit in, given concerns over his commitment to the Indo-Pacific grouping, and PM Modi ended his day with that.

World.title: One dies, four injured after a car plunges into gorge in Yercaud
World.content:
A 26-year-old man died and four persons sustained grievous injuries after a car plunged into a gorge in Yercaud on Friday (November 20, 2026) night.

The deceased, K. Sabareesh (26), a resident of Angalamman Kovil Street in Edappadi, worked at a jewellery shop in Edappadi. On Friday, he, along with his relatives K. Jeeva (26), N. Balaji (47), and P. Devan (55), all of whom are residents of Edappadi, went to Yercaud in a car. The car was driven by S. Alagiri, alias Alagesan (47), a resident of Edappadi. After visiting various spots in Yercaud, they headed to a resort at Keeraikadu. Around 10.30 p.m., when they were near Keeraikadu, the car went out of the driver’s control and plunged into a 100-foot-deep gorge along Yercaud-Kuppanur Ghat Road.

All five occupants sustained grievous injuries in the accident. On receiving the information, the Yercaud police rushed to the spot, rescued the five occupants and shifted them to Yercaud Government Hospital. They were later referred to Salem Government Hospital. However, Sabareesh died on the way to the hospital. The Yercaud police registered a case and are investigating further.

Police sources said that the condition of the car driver, Alagiri, was critical.

World.title: Telangana SAFE suspends FSSAI licences of four Hyderabad eateries over food safety violations
World.content:
The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has suspended the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) licences of four eateries in Hyderabad and ordered them to stop operations following inspections that revealed serious food safety and hygiene violations. The teams also closed two establishments for operating without FSSAI licenses or registrations.

The action followed a special inspection drive conducted by eight enforcement teams comprising food safety officers and police personnel at nine restaurants, hostels and other establishments across Hyderabad. The inspections were carried out based on consumer grievances.

Which Hyderabad establishments were asked to stop operations immediately?

The four establishments — whose FSSAI licences have been suspended are — Madhapur Bawarchi at Ayyappa Society, The Spice Kitchen in Kukatpally, Mataam Al Yamani Arabian Restaurant in Tolichowki and Annapurna Caterers in Chandanagar. The department has instructed them to immediately stop business operations in the interest of public health.

List of food safety and hygiene violations detected

Inspections at these establishments revealed cockroach infestation, rat droppings, unhygienic kitchen, improper segregation of vegetarian and non-vegetarian food, damaged flooring, use of synthetic food colours, smoke-stained walls and lack of medical examination records of food handlers.

The enforcement teams lifted eight food samples on suspicion of adulteration and seized or discarded approximately 135 kg of food articles during the drive. The enforcement teams also closed two establishments, Al Kareem Bakers in Tolichowki and Sri Lakshmi Luxury Men’s Hostel in Gowlidoddy, for operating without FSSAI licences or registrations in unhygienic conditions.

An improvement notice will be issued to Mehfil Restaurant in Balkampet, directing it to rectify the lapses identified during the inspection. Officials will conduct a reinspection to verify compliance before deciding on further action. Additionally, show-cause notices will also be issued to four establishments, including Raju Gari Biryani in Chaithanyapuri and Swaad Spicy in Nagole, over serious violations. The notices will also cover Al Kareem Bakers and Sri Lakshmi Luxury Men’s Hostel, which were closed for operating without the mandatory FSSAI licence or registration. Further action will be initiated to impose penalties.

Telangana SAFE to share suspension details with food delivery platforms

TG SAFE authorities said that they will share details of the four establishments whose licences have been suspended with online food delivery platforms Swiggy and Zomato, seeking their delisting until their FSSAI licences are restored.

World.title: In New Delhi, Musadik hails opportunity for multilateral dialogue
World.content:
KARACHI: After arriving in New Delhi to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) Civil­i­sational Dialogue Forum, Minister for Cli­mate Cha­nge Dr Musadik Malik hai­led the occasion as a “tremendous opportunity” to have a multilateral dialogue.

This is the first visit to India by a Pakistani minister since Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended the SCO meeting in the Indian state of Goa in May 2023, and comes two years after India’s External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar attended the bloc’s meeting in Islamabad.

Pakistan has assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term and is scheduled to host the organisation’s summit in Islamabad in August 2027.

The gathering in New Delhi brings together representatives from SCO member states to discuss issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultu­ral understanding, according to the Foreign Office.

“I think cultures and civilisations cut across boundaries, and it is fantastic that we are here and talking about our history, our geography, and our cultures and civilisations. It is a very welcoming sign,” Mr Malik told the ANI news agency.

Replying to a question regarding the improvement in Pakistan-India rel­ationships, he said, “I think all of our relationships will improve. The region is in flux, as you know. The plates underneath geopolitics are shifting very fast.

Mr Malik is expected to formally address the forum today (Saturday).

In a separate media int­eraction, when asked about action against terrorism, the minister said that the issues we face are not limited solely to those between our two nations; they have become far broader.

“When the time comes to address the issue of terrorism… we must ensure transparency. Both sides must bring forward evide­nce. Our objective is to est­ablish a transparent mechanism — a proposal we have put forward on several occasions. Such a mec­hanism would help res­tore trust and could lead to viable solutions,” he told ANI.

Highlighting how Pakis­tan suffered from terrorism, he acknowledged that India also experienced many such incidents.

“Our neighbourhood is a complicated one, and the challenges facing this ent­ire neighbourhood need to be addressed… Rather than focusing on a single incident or bilateral discussions — where the tenden­cy is often to point fingers at one another — it would be far better to address the problems of the entire reg­ion through a structured mechanism and based on con­­crete evidence.”

Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

World.title: Yemen’s Houthis launch strikes after Saudi coalition’s 'special operation'
World.content:
Yemen’s Houthis launched strikes on the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday, after vowing reprisals for a “special operation” by the Saudi-led coalition fighting them.

Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighbouring Yemen’s civil war this summer, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

An AFP journalist reported hearing two explosions shortly after authorities issued an alert, later lifted, saying the city was “under a hostile aerial threat”.

The coalition later said it had “intercepted and destroyed” three Houthi ballistic missiles headed for the capital.

The Houthis said on that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.

The strikes came after the Houthis vowed revenge for the coalition’s attack on the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets on Friday.

The “special operation” hit smuggling and weapons-transporting operations in Hodeida, the coalition said.

It also involved attacks on Sanaa, Saada and Taiz governorates, marking an uptick in violence after months of hostilities.

The Houthis had vowed to hit the Saudi city of Jeddah and other Red Sea ports if Hodeida was attacked, while warning airlines that Saudi airspace was “unsafe”. The group also threatened Riyadh’s financial district and a power station in Al-Shuqaiq.

Meanwhile, Prime minister Shahbaz Sharif strongly condemn the Houthi attack on the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh.

“Such acts of reckless aggression, targeting civilian infrastructure and economic facilities, are totally unacceptable and threaten regional peace and stability,” he said in a post on X.

Pakistan stands in unwavering solidarity with our brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people. We fully support the Kingdom’s right to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and to protect its citizens and residents, he said.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said its forces had “targeted operational capabilities at Hodeida port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles”.

The coalition also hit “military targets” in Sanaa, including missile and drone facilities and a supply depot, he said on X.

The Houthis claimed coalition strikes had killed 41 people in the previous 24 hours. Yemen’s Saudi-backed armed forces said dozens of airstrikes and drone attacks, as well as hundreds of artillery attacks, killed or wounded 193 Houthi fighters.

These figures were impossible to verify independently.

Two ballistic missiles were intercepted over the Jizan region near the Yemen border, the coalition spokesman said, with debris falling in Al-Shuqaiq.

The Houthi military spokesman said the group had targeted Al-Shuqaiq power station and Jizan port with “accurate and direct” strikes that caused “extensive damage”.

Images of a damaged power station in Mocha after a coalition air raid were broadcast by the Houthis’ Al-Masirah television.

The coalition strikes came after a Houthi attack struck a tower in Riyadh’s financial district, the latest high-profile blow against the world’s top oil exporter.

Witnesses told AFP that Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, housing Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, was damaged.

‘Airspace is unsafe’ -

After the coalition warned civilians to evacuate Hodeida port, the Houthis responded by threatening to hit Jeddah and other ports on the Saudi Red Sea coast.

The Houthis’ Humanitarian Operations Coordination Centre sent emails to shipping companies and other bodies using Jeddah port, warning them to evacuate.

The group warned “all airlines that Saudi airspace is unsafe, as it will be the theatre of our operations in the coming hours, except for the holy airspace over Makkah and Madina”.

They also told people to avoid Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, whose offices were evacuated weeks ago, calling it a “military target”.

The two sides have exchanged attacks since a four-year truce in Yemen’s civil war collapsed in July.

Early on Friday, the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking a civilian boat, killing 19 people.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces withdrew from areas near the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait this month, ceding territory to the Houthis, who launched a sweeping offensive in September.

The group has now advanced close to Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised government which fled the Houthis’ takeover of Sanaa in 2014.

The coalition intervened against the Houthis in early 2015, in a conflict that left hundreds of thousands dead and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

The United Nations expressed concern on Friday over the ongoing attacks.

World.title: Internet provider expects submarine cable repairs to be completed by Dec 6
World.content:
Internet service provider Transworld Associates has said repair work on an affected international submarine cable is expected to be completed by December 6, with users likely to experience slower internet speeds during peak hours until the work is finished.

In an email to customers, the company said repair operations were actively underway and that the tentative timeline for completion was Dec 6.

“Further to our earlier notice on November 18, 2026, repair operations for the affected international submarine cable system are actively underway,” the company said.

Transworld said it had also scheduled a maintenance window during which its technical teams would address the existing cable issue. It added that alternative routing arrangements had been made to maintain connectivity during the maintenance activity.

The development follows an earlier announcement by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) that a fault had been reported in the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system, approximately 11 kilometres from Pakistan’s coast.

The regulator warned that the fault could cause intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality for some internet users.

The PTA had said Transworld Associates was coordinating with the SMW5 consortium to identify the fault and determine the estimated time for restoration.

Meanwhile, internet traffic was being rerouted through alternative international links to minimise disruption and maintain service continuity, the regulator had added.

Internet monitoring organisation NetBlocks had also reported a decline in connectivity in Pakistan, saying the incident was consistent with a fault in the SMW5 international subsea cable system.

Submarine cables are a critical part of international telecommunications infrastructure, carrying data between countries and continents. Faults in these systems can affect internet speeds and connectivity, particularly when traffic has to be redirected through alternative routes.

Currently, seven submarine cables provide internet connectivity to Pakistan: Asia-Africa-Europe 1 ( AAE-1 ), South East Asia-Middle East-West Europe 4 (SMW4) and India-Middle East-Western Europe (IMEWE), operated by PTCL; and South-East Asia-Middle East-Western Europe 6 (SEA-ME-WE 6), South East Asia-Middle East-West Europe 5 (SMW5) and Transworld Associates 1 (TWA-1), operated by Transworld Associates.

Cyber Internet Services operates the seventh cable named Pak­istan and East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE).

In July this year, a fault in the same SMW5 cable system had caused widespread connectivity issues in Pakistan. The PTA subsequently announced that the fault had been repaired on July 3, following its detection on July 1.

World.title: Cummins wins Cricket Australia's 'unanimous support' to remain Test captain
World.content:
Cricket Australia threw its “unanimous support” behind Pat Cummins to remain Test captain Saturday, rejecting any suggestion his integrity had been compromised by the lingering “Sandpapergate” scandal.

Cummins has been under huge pressure since Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018.

He strenuously denied being aware of what was going on in a press conference last week, but his position was undermined when Cameron Bancroft backed Khawaja’s version of events.

Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.

With speculation over Cummins’ future rampant and a home four-Test series against New Zealand next month, CA moved to stamp out any further discussion about the 33-year-old’s fate after meeting him to check on his welfare.

It came after Josh Hazlewood earlier Saturday suggested he could quit if any action was taken against his long-time bowling partner.

CA expressed “its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain” following a board meeting.

“We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn,” said chairman David Boon.

“We’ve expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

“We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat’s integrity has been compromised.”

The retired Khawaja reignited the controversy in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by close friend Warner.

After Cummins’ denials, Bancroft dropped a bomb in a newspaper column by also claiming “it was the whole team” while saying he felt “angry and betrayed” by the Test skipper.

Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening its investigation but instead set up a forum for players to share their experiences about 2018.

Great leader

Cummins said being captain “carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly”.

“David and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018,” he added.

“I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say.

“There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth (at the first Test) will be my focus and priority.”

Hazlewood threw his support behind Cummins earlier Saturday and made a veiled threat to call it a day if he was removed as captain.

He reiterated that the bowling group at the time, which also included Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, were not part of the plan.

They jointly released a statement in 2021 denying any involvement.

“I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood told the Sydney Daily Telegraph in his first comments since the story blew up.

“He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.”

Asked if he would consider quitting in protest if Cummins was removed, Hazlewood said: “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah.”

Starc has also reinforced that he knew nothing in recent days. Lyon and Smith have yet to comment.

World.title: FBI, US Agriculture Department breached by hackers: reports
World.content:
The US Agriculture Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) were breached by hackers in cyberattacks, US media reported on Saturday, as concerns deepened over the recent spate of tech outages at key American institutions.

The incidents were first reported by NBC News and CNN, respectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.

Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the United States, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.

US President Donald Trump has sought to calm the public and urged people to “relax”, while officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyberattack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials.

The hackers may use the payments system as a backdoor to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.

The USDA deals with “a bunch of scary biologic issues” and “if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information… they could use our own research against us,” a former official was quoted as saying.

CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.

The federal agency was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Centre (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported, citing two people briefed on the probe.

The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.

“Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety,” a former FBI official told CNN.

The former official expressed concerns that hackers “could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

AFP has contacted the FBI and USDA for comment.

The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages like the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration.

In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.

The White House fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross this week as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.

World.title: Countries open path towards 'killer robots' pact
World.content:
Countries agreed on Saturday to open a path towards finding an international agreement on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems, though campaigners seeking to stop so-called killer robots were disappointed by the “watered-down” outcome.

After five days of gruelling talks at the United Nations, which ran into overtime, states agreed to open the door to building some form of pact over the next two years.

However, with warfare undergoing a radical transformation, spurred by artificial intelligence, non-governmental organisations wanted far swifter, legally binding rules on handing power over human life and death to autonomous machines.

Talks at the United Nations’ Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva stretched well into the early hours of Saturday.

The 128 countries party to the CCW “agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years”, conference president Julien Thoni told reporters afterwards.

The process to get there had been tricky, with countries at odds and full consensus required for any decision.

While a majority of states went in favour of a legally binding agreement, countries that have the technology, including the United States and Russia, are reluctant to have their hands tied.

The process ahead should flesh out “which weapons can be forbidden according to international humanitarian law, and which is not forbidden but can be regulated”, Thoni told AFP.

The Swiss diplomat said some countries had objected to the word negotiate, but had settled on elaborate instead.

Campaign groups said the outcome fell well short of expectations.

“States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument,” said the Stop Killer Robots (SKR) coalition.

“Autonomous weapons technology, including AI in the targeting cycle, is being deployed on the battlefield,” said Nicole van Rooijen, SKR’s executive director.

“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” Verity Coyle, the deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, branded the outcome “disappointing”.

“It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules — but the technology is racing ahead,” she said.

World.title: Wall Street ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
World.content:
US stocks extended their rout on Friday, and the S&P ​500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally.

All three major US equity ‌indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10 per cent below their record closing highs, confirming both indexes have entered a correction.

The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

The S&P 500 and the Dow logged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “liberation day” tariff package.

The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index has dipped into negative ​territory for the year.

“This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, it appears to be accelerating to a certain ​degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana.

“But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and ⁠sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.”

“Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic ​strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things.

Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as $2 trillion in market cap, failed to catch ​fire on Thursday, closing 17.1pc above its $83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session.

In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1pc; Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8pc.

The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology.

“Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate ​earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana.

“A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to ​some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.”

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6pc in ‌mid-June. That ⁠lustre has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7pc.

Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9pc, while Meta dropped 5.9pc.

Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1pc and its peer Nebius slid 16.1pc.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93pc, to 48,147.33; the S&P 50 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70pc, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28pc, to 22,617.73.

The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025.

World.title: Provinces cannot assume ‘unexercised’ federal powers: FCC
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitu­tional Court (FCC) has ruled that parliament’s failure to exercise a fiscal power does not mean that the subject has been transferred to the provinces.

“An identified conflict with a competent federal law attracts the consequence prescribed under Article 142 of the Constitution, meaning that the federal law will prevail whereas the provincial law becomes void to the extent of that conflict,” observed FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan in a 59-page judgement authored by him.

The ruling came as a two-judge FCC bench, consisting of the chief justice and Justice Aamer Farooq, issued its detailed judgement on a set of 568 challenges filed by different taxpayers against the provincial infrastructure development cess imposed by Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Following the verbal order issued a day earlier, the detailed FCC judgement explained that although the statutory schemes and procedural histories differed, the matters raised a common constitutional question for determination: whether the impugned levies, in their true nature and operation, fell within provincial legislative competence or encroached upon parliament’s exclusive authority over imports, exports and interprovincial trade.

Detailed order in provincial development cess case holds that federal law should prevail where it conflicts with provincial legislation

While allowing the civil appeals filed by the taxpayers, the FCC set aside the impugned judgements of the SHC and PHC and declared that the corresponding charging provisions, along with all dependent rules, notifications, assessments and recovery measures, were unconstitutional and without lawful authority.

“No demand, surcharge or penalty founded solely upon those charges shall be enforced,” the judgement said, adding that securities furnished solely for the invalid charges would be discharged upon verification and subject to any subsisting order governing their disposal.

However, the provinces remained free to enact constitutionally competent infrastructure or service charges on goods manufactured and consumed within their respective territories, the verdict ruled.

It explained that Article 160 of the Constitution and the applicable National Finance Commission arrangements distinguish between the power to levy a federal tax and entitlement to its proceeds.

“A province’s share does not authorise it to impose that tax independently. Equally, two competent levies are not unconstitutional merely because they affect the same goods. The defect in the present cases was legislative incompetence, not duplication; fiscal need could not supply the missing power,” the judgement said.

The FCC observed that the impugned judgements had given controlling weight to the infrastructure purpose, movement of goods and asserted compensatory character of the cess without first establishing provincial legislative competence.

None of these considerations provided an independent provincial basis for the challenged import, export and external-transit charges, it said.

The FCC further observed that the abolition of the Concurrent Legislative List through the 18th Amendment had expanded provincial competence but had not transferred subjects expressly retained in the federal domain.

Provincial autonomy must, therefore, be given full effect within its constitutional sphere while preserving parliament’s exclusive authority over matters reserved to it, the judgement said.

During the hearing, the taxpayers had contended that the levies encroached upon parliament’s exclusive legislative domain and could not be sustained as fees or compensatory charges merely because the goods used provincial infrastructure.

They had also challenged the collection arrangements, discriminatory treatment, restrictions on trade and retrospective validation.

The provinces, meanwhile, invoked their residual legislative powers, infrastructure responsibilities and services provided to commercial users, distinguishing the cess from customs duties.

Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
