World.title: Catching up with the relentless Ronnie Lazaro
World.content:
An old friend looks back on the quiet grit and gallantry of veteran Filipino actor Ronnie Lazaro

Who is the real Ronnie Lazaro?

After a few decades, Ronnie Lazaro shows up on my radar with an invitation to attend the opening of his mobile photography exhibit, Lies The Truth.

It was set in the Avellana Art Gallery in Pasay, and going through the charmingly wooded complex of the Henry Hotel with houses dating back to the ’50s, I am sent back to a place called Cool Malate in the ’80s.

No such place exists anymore, but it exists in every artist’s heart of that generation who used to hang out in Hobbit House, the Penguin Café, Coco Banana, and Bistro Remedios. And the ultimate survivor, Café Adriatico.

So, there’s Ronnie, at his exhibit opening, fussing about the white wine not being cold enough and why the red wine was in the cooler. He seems to be the same man running about the set of City After Dark, a determined art director keeping up with the demands of the director, Ishmael Bernal, and the production designer, Peque Gallaga.

City After Dark was originally titled Manila By Night, but Imelda Marcos objected to Manila being depicted as a decadent city with drugs, gay bars, and prostitution on just about every corner (which it was). This was Ronnie’s fifth assignment as art director.

Age has not done too much to Ronnie. Maybe he was leaner during the City After Dark days, but he looks down at me with the same soulful eyes. Or maybe he didn’t recognize me and was trying to place me in his memory?

Ronnie casually opens the exhibition. Friendly, but definitely in charge.

FAMILY FIRST. Ronnie Lazaro (left) with his wife Lola and son Gabriel. Contributed photo

One has to think about the message with this collection of photographs of artists covering their faces with both hands. Eyes are the mirror of the soul they say, but Ronnie’s subjects cover them up with both hands. Is it intimacy because they’re close-ups? Or the opposite, because they’re all covering their faces with their hands?

“The world is full of lies!” he moans.

Uprooting himself from his native Sagay, Negros Occidental, he set down to do the hard work in Manila. With a natural acting talent and an ability to adapt to any situation, Ronnie says, “I had to work hard. I could not go back a failure.”

So, coming up from the School of Hard Knocks, and living by his work philosophy, “Just show up,” Ronnie has certainly arrived.

“I went to every single art opening to learn, meet people, and also to eat. Hahaha,” he shakes his head, almost amused at himself thinking about those gritty days in the ’80s.

Needless to say, Peque was a major influence on Ronnie as an actor, but other artists like Cesare Syjuco and Jean Syjuco molded a new artist’s perspective in Ronnie, venturing out of his comfort zone and doing dozens of performance art around the city.

In Mendiola, he did Eto Ka, Eto Ako, Ngayon Na where he held up a mirror to each member of the audience. This was in 1984, if memory serves. We can certainly use some of that these days.

It’s not a surprise that the latest Fifth Wall Fest (@fifthwall.ph) invited him to comment on James Clar’s performance art centered around City After Dark.

“Bing, you have to come. Tayo na lang naiiwan (We’re the only ones left).”

After one production meeting for City After Dark, he gallantly escorted me to my car and we discovered I had a flat. Of course, he had to change the tire for me. Gallant as he was.

As he tightened the bolts, he said, “Ibig mo sabihin Bing, nakasalalay ang buhay mo sa akin? (Do you mean, Bing, that your life depends on me?)”

Well yes, I say.

“Then I better get this right.”

On another occasion, we were walking in Sagada, why there was only the two of us, I have no idea. Where was everyone? I was rattling on about some such nonsense, yadayadayada, when he stopped me in my tracks because a snake was crossing our path!

He was looking out for danger this whole time! (Or wasn’t listening at all).

Thank you for that, Ronnie.

Yes, a true galante (gallant) — somewhat soft spoken and introspective.

When you’ve had decades of work experience, it’s hard to name that defining moment. And yet, Ronnie says, the defining moment for him was when Mitch Valdez invited him to her group Reach for Inner Self, a spiritual workshop.

“That is where I learned to forgive and love myself.”

Ronnie hangs back for a beat, enjoying the memories this interview is bringing back. He talked about the time Mitch invited him to be on the board of OPM.

There was an awards night to be held in Tahiti. Everyone was busy so Ronnie had to take one for the team and attended the festival. He was to be a judge and Heber Bartolome was the talent. His eyes sparkled as he said, “Lots of nice girls there.”

His proudest moment, among several, was his directorial debut Edna (2014), with screenplay by Lally Bucoy. The film received glowing critical reviews as it moved away from the typical OFW story, but rather goes inward, exposing the tragic result of a family growing without a mother.

We both contemplate the depth of isolation and loneliness one feels when separated from family and home.

Ronnie has tackled his career as an actor like a man on a mission. In 2012, I reminded him, he had 11 projects listed in his filmography, not to mention the dizzying number of projects in television and theater.

Of note would be his Urian Award for Best Actor, Yanggaw (Affliction) in 2008, Urian Best Supporting Actor for Bagong Buwan (2001) and The Gospel of the Beast (2023).

Raymond Red’s Anino brought him to Cannes where it won Best Short Feature Film (2000), and in 2024, Ronnie attended the Venice International Film Festival as lead actor of Lav Diaz’s Phantosmia.

We put all of that aside for a moment and exchanged ideas for a new movie perhaps, exploring themes, fiction or non-fiction choices, perhaps a period piece. And just when I was saying to myself, how refreshing it was to just sit and shoot the creative breeze with someone so imaginative and passionate, a fire broke out!

Makati Cinema Square was on fire! I told him to quickly get out before the fire trucks completely blocked the road. No need to be galante this time. There were enough firemen to keep me safe. – Rappler.com

World.title: Abu Dhabi OFW turns to cleaning toilets for a living after losing job
World.content:
Dubbed ‘Banyo Boy’ online, a laid-off Filipino worker in Abu Dhabi cleans toilets for AED10 to afford a new visa — sparking an outpouring of community support alongside legal warnings

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates – An overseas Filipino worker (OFW) who recently lost his job has resorted to cleaning the toilets of fellow Filipinos for AED10 (P173.67) to raise funds for a new visa to stay in the country.

The good news is that 24-year-old Jaime Herrera (not his real name), who has until November 26 to legally remain in the United Arab Emirates, has been receiving numerous messages for toilet cleanups. Those he has serviced have been paying more than his asking rate and giving him groceries, he said. Others have been offering food and help finding a job.

The bad news is that under UAE law, it is illegal to engage in any form of work during a grace period after a visa has expired or been canceled unless the worker secures a new employment contract and visa.

A grace period, usually one month, only allows a foreign worker to legally remain in the country to process a status change, transition to a new employer, or exit the UAE. Working illegally during this window can result in daily overstay fines, legal action, or a reentry ban.

Herrera’s previous employment contract has been revoked.

A high school graduate, Herrera said he cannot risk becoming undocumented or flying home empty-handed.

Herrera, who hails from Dasmariñas in Cavite, has to exit to nearby Oman while a new two-month visa authorizing his stay in the UAE is processed. The entire process costs around AED4,000 – AED1,200 for the visa, and the rest for transportation and accommodation while waiting for his reentry document.

‘Too bad’

Herrera, who arrived in the UAE on July 4 this year, previously held an employment visa as a house cleaner in Dubai.

“Talagang sayang (It was really too bad),” said Herrera, adding that he was earning AED2,500 a month at that job.

He said he is currently only able to clean one toilet a day.

“Nakakapagod maglinis ng kubeta. Pero okay lang sa akin. Nagme-message sila (customers) sa akin, magko-conversation kami, ‘pag okay, kukunin ko,” Herrera shared.

“‘Yung unang customer ko, Dhs50 (P871) ang binayad sa akin, tapos binigyan ako ng mga prutas. Daming tumatawag, sa isang araw, may limang missed calls ako.”

(It’s tiring to clean a toilet, but I’m okay with that. Customers send me a message, we talk, and if it’s okay, I take the job. My first customer paid me Dhs50 and gave me some fruit. I’ve been getting lots of calls; I receive around five missed calls a day.)

Herrera said he started cleaning toilets in Abu Dhabi on October 26.

“Naghahanap ako ng trabaho. Okay naman dito. Dami kong nakikitang hiring. Nag-iipon ako ng pang-exit. Maganda rin dito sa UAE, pumalpak lang ang mga plano ko. Unang sahod ko, bumili ako ng scooter, naibenta rin, sayang,” he said.

(I’m looking for a job. It’s okay here. I see a lot of hiring. I’m saving up for my exit. Life is good here in the UAE; my plans just went wrong. I bought a scooter with my first paycheck, but I ended up selling it — what a waste.)

Talk of the town

Herrera became the talk of the town when a vlogger, Mercy Dimalanta (not her real name), came across his social media post offering toilet-cleaning services and shared it on her Facebook account.

“(K)ung may labis naman po kayong budget, ibigay ‘nyo na po ang paglilinis ng CR ‘nyo sa kanya dahil napakalaking tulong po sa kanya ang AED10 para makatawid siya sa araw-araw niyang pamumuhay dito sa Abu Dhabi. Higit na marangal ang ginagawa niya kumpara sa ginagawa ng iba. Noong nakita ko ang post niya, alam ko na kailangang-kailangan niya ng tulong kaya agad akong nag-message at ang bilis niyang nag-reply, patunay na abang na abang siya sa kung sinuman ang gusto magpalinis upang may pagkunan siya ng pagkain niya sa araw na ‘yun,” she wrote on Facebook.

(If you happen to have some extra budget, please consider hiring him to clean your bathroom; the AED10 would be a huge help for his daily survival here in Abu Dhabi. The work he does is far more honorable than what some others might resort to. When I saw his post, I knew he was in desperate need of help, so I reached out immediately. He replied right away — proof that he is eagerly waiting for anyone who might need cleaning services, just so he can afford a meal for the day.)

Dimalanta gave him the moniker “Banyo Boy.” And Herrera’s sudden influx of customer calls is largely attributed to her viral Facebook post.

“Tumutulo ang luha ko sa awa pero lamang ang paghanga. Kaya naman pagkatapos niyang maglinis, ibinigay ko ang bayad ko lakip ang munting grocery na dapat sana ay para sa amin,” she added.

“Naitanong ko rin kung may trabaho ba siya at sabi niya ay wala, kaya bukod sa pagpapalinis ng CR ‘nyo, inilalapit ko rin po na sana tulungan natin siya magkaroon ng trabaho.”

(Tears streamed down my face out of pity, but my admiration for him was even greater. So, after he finished cleaning, I handed him my payment, along with some small grocery items that were supposed to be for us. I also asked if he had a job, and he said he didn’t; so, aside from having him clean your bathrooms, I’m also appealing to everyone to help him find a job.) – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘A new imperial age’: Yuval Harari warns Philippines of foreign AI dependence
World.content:
FUTURE. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and historian Yuval Noah Harari talk about the future of AI for humanity.

The best-selling author of 'Sapiens' and 'Nexus' warns that AI could usher in a new age of empires and leave countries like the Philippines dependent on foreign powers

MANILA, Philippines – As the Philippines finds its place in the global artificial intelligence (AI) industry, historian and best-selling author Yuval Noah Harari warned that countries outside the world’s leading technology powers risk losing control of critical infrastructure unless they develop their own capabilities or cooperate with regional partners.

Speaking with Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa at a pre-recorded conversation for the 2026 Social Good Summit, Harari said the concentration of AI technology in superpowers like the United States and China could usher in a new era of economic and political dependence.

“We are entering a new imperial age,” Harari said. “The empires are back.”

And this time, he warned, could be even worse. Consider how the Romans and the British – powerful as their empires were – remained constrained by geography and physical resources. But now with AI, control of its infrastructure and frontier models could concentrate economic and military power in ways previously impossible.

As lesser powers become dependent on foreign AI systems to run hospitals, airports, and military equipment, that could raise their vulnerability to decisions made abroad.

“In that situation, you’re no longer independent, you are a vassal state,” Harari said.

For the Philippines, which Ressa described as having been a testing ground for social media platforms, the concern revives many old fears.

“We were the petri dish for social media,” Ressa said, recalling how Facebook became a breeding ground for disinformation and political manipulation during Rodrigo Duterte’s rise to power in 2016.

Could the specter of what Harari calls “data colonialism” be coming back to haunt the Philippines, this time through its ambitions under Pax Silica?

Where should the Philippines stand?

The US-led initiative promises to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, and AI technologies. After joining the initiative in April 2026, the Philippines unveiled plans for a roughly 1,600-hectare advanced manufacturing hub in New Clark City, Tarlac. As of November, Manila and Washington were still working toward a framework agreement. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has sought to allay concerns by saying no data centers would be built in the area.

But beyond concerns over its energy and water use is another question often missing from discussions on Pax Silica. Would joining global AI supply chains give the Philippines greater control over the technology, or merely a role in manufacturing it?

For Harari, countries outside the US and China face three choices. They could remain dependent on foreign AI infrastructure, spend enormous sums building their own, or pool resources with other countries to develop shared capabilities.

He suggested the last option for the Philippines—working alongside partners such as Japan and Australia. Such cooperation could be cheaper than developing independent infrastructure, but would require closer political coordination.

‘Too late for politics?’

Harari rejected the argument that AI development was already beyond political intervention.

“What the companies are now trying to do is to convince us that it’s too late to do politics,” he said. “It’s not yet deterministic, it’s not inevitable, there are still choices to be made.”

AI, Harari said, is particularly dangerous because an agent is capable of making decisions, rather than being just a tool fully controlled by humans. And that leash used to keep autonomous AI under human control has already begun to slip.

In July 2026, agents powered by OpenAI models broke out of a restricted test environment and accessed live systems at AI platform Hugging Face, apparently seeking answers to a cybersecurity evaluation.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, also reported that its models had gone rouge and hacked computer systems of other organizations. Months later, that same company went on to raise $81 billion in the world’s largest IPO in November, beating the record that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had set just months earlier.

In light of all this, Harari argued that governments need not halt AI development outright, but should reconsider the race toward superintelligence and invest more in safety. He urged greater focus on practical uses in healthcare, education, transportation, and public services.

“A product which is not safe is just not useful,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?
World.content:
PART 1 | Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

PART 2 | Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?

The Ambani brothers got what they wanted in 2005: the freedom to run their businesses without having to answer to each other. Their mother, Kokilaben, helped divide the Reliance empire founded by their father, Dhirubhai Ambani. Mukesh, the elder brother, took control of the oil, petrochemicals, and refining businesses. Anil, the younger, received interests in telecommunications, power, and financial services.

More than two decades later, the brothers’ business fortunes could hardly be more different. Mukesh built Reliance Industries into one of India’s largest companies, expanding into telecommunications through Jio and consumer businesses through Reliance Retail. Anil’s business empire, once valued in the billions of dollars, suffered heavy debts, corporate insolvencies, and the collapse of some of its most prominent enterprises. Both brothers gained independence, but only one turned that freedom into a sustained expansion.

That 20-year history offers a sobering preview for Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, Federico “Piki” Lopez, and the other third generation heirs now unbundling their own family family empire in the Philippines. Following Gabby’s P11.56-billion exit from Lopez Inc. in August, Piki’s September board consolidation at Lopez Holdings and FPH, and FPH’s November approval to sell Rockwell Land to Gabby’s Crème Investment Corp. for almost P16 billion, the Lopezes are moving toward separate corporate spheres. (Click these links below for the author’s special reports on these developments:

Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

Part 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles

Part 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

The cousins are not dividing their group in the exact same way the Ambanis did, nor is their separation complete. Yet the questions hanging over both families are remarkably similar: Will the businesses become stronger when the relatives no longer have to agree on how they should be run? Will the separation end the fighting? And what happens to the shareholders, employees, and younger heirs who must live with the consequences?

The real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements.

The first two installments of this series examined why business families fight, whether they should stay together or separate, and how they can negotiate a division of their interests. This final installment looks at what happened to families that went through the process years earlier.

After all, the real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements.

Freedom has its price

The Ambanis offer one of the clearest long-term tests of a family-business separation because enough time has passed to examine what each brother did with the businesses he controlled. In the financial year ending March 2026, Reliance Industries reported consolidated revenue of ₹11.76 trillion and profit after tax of about ₹95,754 crore. Its telecommunications business served more than 524 million subscribers, while its retail operations had grown to more than 20,000 stores. Mukesh had not merely preserved the oil and petrochemicals businesses he inherited, he had used their financial strength to build major new businesses in industries that barely figured in the family’s original empire.

Anil’s experience was very different. Reliance Communications, once a major competitor in India’s telecommunications industry, entered insolvency proceedings after accumulating debts it could not service. The company became subject to a court-supervised resolution process, and Anil resigned from its board in 2019. Other businesses associated with his group also underwent financial difficulties and restructuring. The Reliance Group even emphasized that Reliance Communications is no longer under Anil’s management and that its remaining operating companies should be assessed separately.

It would be convenient to conclude that Mukesh made the right choices and Anil made the wrong ones. But that would oversimplify what happened. Telecommunications changed dramatically as competition intensified, particularly after Mukesh’s Jio entered the market in 2016. Financing decisions, accumulated debt, industry regulation, and the timing of investments all influenced the brothers’ fortunes. The 2005 division gave them freedom to make those decisions. It did not determine how those decisions would turn out.

There is also another question: Did the separation actually end their disputes? Not entirely. The brothers subsequently fought over the supply and pricing of natural gas, a disagreement that reached India’s Supreme Court. Their businesses were separate, but they still had commercial interests that brought them into conflict. Later reports of Mukesh helping Anil meet a financial obligation suggested that the relationship was more complicated than an unbroken feud, although such episodes cannot establish the state of their private relationship.

The Ambanis’ experience illustrates the difference between settling a family dispute and succeeding in business afterward. The brothers gained control of their respective enterprises. What they accomplished with that control was another matter.

Different businesses, different fortunes

The Bajaj family’s experience reinforces the point. The division of its business interests gave different branches greater independence, but the companies that emerged from the arrangement did not enjoy identical fortunes.

Bajaj Auto has become one of India’s major motorcycle and three-wheeler manufacturers. In the financial year ending March 2026, it reported record standalone revenue of ₹58,732 crore and profit after tax of ₹9,825 crore, an increase of more than 20% from the previous year. The wider Bajaj financial-services businesses have also expanded significantly. Bajaj Finance reported assets under management exceeding ₹5 trillion in the same financial year.

Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar, associated with Shishir Bajaj’s branch, experienced a more difficult period. Its 2026 annual report described financial pressures arising from high sugarcane procurement costs, relatively flat sugar prices, and difficulties servicing debt. The company reported a loss of ₹751 crore for the previous financial year before returning to a reported profit of about ₹138 crore in the year ending March 2026. Its November 2026 financial disclosures continued to discuss restructuring arrangements and the need to manage liquidity.

The difference is striking, but it is not proof that the Bajaj separation benefited one branch at the expense of another. Motorcycles, financial services, and sugar are very different businesses. They face different markets, regulatory requirements, and operating risks. Sugar producers in India, for example, are affected by government policies governing cane prices and sugar sales, factors that have little to do with disagreements among shareholders.

What the Bajaj experience does demonstrate is that once relatives gain control of their respective businesses, their fortunes increasingly depend on the companies they manage and the industries in which they operate.

The separation may have settled who controlled the businesses, but it did not guarantee how those businesses would perform.

Independence beyond the family

Not every family dispute ends with relatives dividing an entire conglomerate. Sometimes independence means leaving the management of a business while building another enterprise.

Walter Kwok, the eldest of three brothers who inherited Hong Kong property developer Sun Hung Kai Properties, lost his leadership position following a prolonged dispute with his brothers. He subsequently established Empire Group Holdings, pursuing property development outside the company his father had founded.

Walter died in 2018, but Empire continued operating. The privately held company has undertaken residential, commercial, and hospitality developments, demonstrating that Walter established a substantial business outside Sun Hung Kai. That does not establish whether he became wealthier than he would have been had he remained in charge of the family company.

But his experience illustrates something important about family-business disputes: ownership, management, and independence are not necessarily the same thing. A family member may lose the right to run a company without losing all financial interests in it. Another may choose to surrender a position in an established enterprise to pursue opportunities elsewhere.

The question is not always who gets to keep the family company. It can also be whether the relatives are better able to pursue their ambitions without constantly contesting control.

Corporate peace, family wounds

There is another measure of success that cannot be found in a company’s financial statements: whether the relatives themselves are able to move beyond the conflict.

The Ambani brothers’ dispute over natural gas showed that dividing ownership does not necessarily eliminate commercial disagreements. Even after companies have been separated, relatives may remain connected through contracts, investments, obligations, and the history of decisions made when the businesses were still together.

Other family disputes have demonstrated how difficult it can be to separate corporate disagreements from personal relationships. In the Philippines, the Ilusorio family’s conflict extended into disputes over family authority and the care of elderly parents. The Yanson family’s disagreement over the Vallacar Transit group involved competing claims to management and ownership that produced years of legal proceedings. Those histories were discussed in Part 1 and 2 of this series.

But a separation need not restore close personal relationships to succeed as a business arrangement. Relatives who can no longer work together may prefer to run their businesses independently and maintain a more distant personal relationship. That may be preferable than remaining partners in an enterprise where every major decision becomes another family confrontation.

Corporate peace, however, should not be confused with family peace.

The distinction becomes especially important when the relatives belong to a family whose businesses have been associated with its identity for generations. Disagreements over corporate control can become disagreements over legacy: who deserves to lead, whose contribution matters most, and who has the right to decide what happens to the assets accumulated by parents and grandparents.

A separation may reduce the occasions for corporate disagreement. Whether it changes the relationships among relatives is a different question.

What the children inherit

A family settlement can be satisfactory to the relatives who negotiated it and still create problems for their children.

The Ambani family’s experience offers an opportunity to examine the next stage. Mukesh’s children—Isha, Akash, and Anant—have assumed increasingly prominent responsibilities in the Reliance businesses. Akash chairs Reliance Jio Infocomm, Isha has played a leading role in retail, and Anant has taken on responsibilities in the group’s energy and other businesses. The family’s succession arrangements are being developed within the enterprise Mukesh expanded after the 2005 separation.

That development is significant because the original division did more than establish which brother controlled which assets. It created separate business structures within which their descendants would eventually exercise ownership and management responsibilities.

The Bajaj family offers another example of business interests passing to younger generations after an earlier division. But a clear separation among branches does not automatically resolve every future succession question. Children and grandchildren may eventually disagree among themselves over who should manage a company, how profits should be distributed, or whether particular assets should be sold.

Family-business advisers Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer have written about how family feuds can threaten businesses when money, authority, and personal relationships become intertwined. Their work is a useful reminder that removing one source of conflict does not necessarily eliminate the conditions that produced it.

Asian family business adviser Enrique Soriano makes a related point about inheritance: He argued that passing ownership to the next generation does not necessarily mean passing on a business capable of functioning successfully under its new owners. Inheriting shares and being equipped to manage a company are different matters. His point raises another way of judging family settlements: Should success be measured by what the relatives accomplish immediately after separating, or by what happens when their children and grandchildren take over? (READ: If great business dynasties can fracture, why would your family be any different?)

For the Lopezes, that question may be answered only 10 or 20 years from now. Their younger heirs will inherit not only the businesses that Gabby, Piki, and their third generation cousins choose to retain, but also the ownership arrangements, financial obligations, and family relationships left by the current dispute. Whether those arrangements prove durable may ultimately be a more meaningful measure of success than the agreements reached today.

The longer-term test of a family settlement may therefore come when the next generation begins exercising the ownership and leadership rights established by their parents.

The people outside the family

When business families fight, the headlines usually focus on the relatives: who controls the company, who gets the assets, and how much each branch receives. But the consequences extend to people who did not participate in the dispute and have little influence over its outcome.

Reliance Communications’ insolvency left creditors dealing with a court-supervised resolution process. Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar’s financial difficulties required negotiations with lenders over debt and liquidity. Neither company’s difficulties can simply be blamed on its family’s earlier separation. They nevertheless demonstrate that the financial decisions of controlling shareholders and managers can have consequences far beyond their own fortunes.

For the Lopez group, the changes have also been felt in its boardrooms and executive offices. Long-serving executives have left positions they held for years, while changes in shareholdings have brought new directors and altered the composition of boards. One significant departure was Salvador Tirona. He had worked with the Lopezes since early 2000s-and served as president, chief operating officer, and chief finance officer of Lopez Holdings. At the September 14 annual meeting, Piki’s brother Jay Lopez took over Tirona’s executive positions. Tirona also resigned from ABS-CBN Holdings, where he had served as chairman and held senior executive posts.

Another longtime corporate officer, Enrique Quiason, resigned as corporate secretary of First Philippine Holdings in November after nearly 34 years with the company. Both Tirona and Quiason resigned—not retired—during a period of major changes in ownership and leadership, although neither cited the family feud as the reason for leaving.

Earlier, when the cousins were exchanging increasingly hostile public statements, two independent directors of Lopez Holdings also stepped down. Roberto Panlilio resigned effective May 1, followed by Consuelo Garcia on May 5. Both cited personal reasons. Their departures left the seven-member board with only one independent director at the time.

The family conflict was also being discussed directly with employees. At a First Gen town hall on April 17, Piki acknowledged the dispute but urged employees not to become involved in choosing between the warring relatives. “There’s no need for you to take sides,” he said. He described the fight as a shareholder conflict that would eventually work itself out. His message was to remain professional and continue doing their jobs.

At ABS-CBN, employees received a more difficult message. During a September 15 town hall, president and CEO Carlo Katigbak announced another round of retrenchments—around 200 employees, or 7% of its workforce—even as the company was preparing to receive P6 billion in fresh capital from the Lopez family and other investors. Katigbak told employees that this would be the last retrenchment program under his leadership, but it followed years of job cuts since ABS-CBN lost its broadcast franchise in 2020, when about 5,000 employees were retrenched.

The contrast between the new investments and the latest job losses was difficult to ignore. The additional capital was intended to help ABS-CBN recover, but it did not remove the need to reduce expenses. In its September statement, the company cited weak advertising and consumer spending, inflation, and difficult conditions in the content industry.

The retrenchments cannot be solely attributed to the bitter Lopez family feud. ABS-CBN’s financial difficulties began years before the cousins’ dispute became public. But the layoffs demonstrate why the outcome of the family’s business decisions matters to people outside the family. For employees, a successful turnaround is not simply a stronger balance sheet or the arrival of new investors. It is a company capable of sustaining jobs and paying the people who work for it. (READ: Banks, retirees, the business: Where will ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue go?)

Creditors have their own concerns. ABS-CBN must demonstrate that it can generate enough cash to meet its obligations, including loans that may require refinancing or extensions. Banks will have to assess whether the company’s recovery plans provide a credible basis for continued lending.

Minority shareholders also have a stake in what happens next. Rockwell’s public shareholders face a proposed change in control. FPH’s November disclosure states that the transaction requires, among other conditions, a mandatory tender offer by Crème to other Rockwell shareholders. The terms of that offer will matter to investors who did not participate in the family’s negotiations.

For employees, the test is whether the businesses can sustain jobs. For creditors, it is whether debts are repaid. For minority shareholders, it is whether their investments are protected and rewarded.

These interests do not always coincide with those of the relatives negotiating a settlement. They cannot be left out when judging whether a corporate divorce worked.

Two cousins, two big bets

The experiences of the Ambanis and Bajajs bring us back to the Lopezes. Their separations gave different family branches the freedom to pursue their own business strategies. But the results depended on what businesses they controlled, the investments they made, the risks they took, and their ability to finance those decisions.

For Federico “Piki” Lopez, the future increasingly depends on energy. His group is committing enormous resources to renewable power and infrastructure projects that may take years to complete and even longer to recover their investment costs.

Geothermal energy, pumped-storage hydropower, and other large projects require substantial capital upfront. They involve technical studies, regulatory approvals, financing, construction, and agreements for selling the electricity they will eventually produce. Delays can increase costs, while changes in electricity prices and financing conditions can affect returns.

The Lopez group has decades of experience in the power business. But experience does not remove the risks of committing large amounts of capital to projects whose expected earnings lie years, if not decades, ahead.

The question is whether Piki is making the right investments now to secure substantial earnings years from today. Will the projects produce enough cash to justify their cost? Can the group finance the years of development without taking on excessive debt? And will selling Rockwell, an established property business, prove a worthwhile exchange for the capital needed to pursue those ambitions?

FPH has told the stock exchange that selling Rockwell would allow it to redirect resources toward energy, infrastructure, and other businesses where it sees opportunities. The proposed transaction would bring in nearly P16 billion, but the amount of cash raised is only one measure of its value. The more important test is what FPH eventually earns from the investments it makes with that money.

For Gabby Lopez and the majority cousins, the challenge is almost the opposite. They are committing resources to ABS-CBN at a time when the economics of the media industry are being rewritten.

Before losing its franchise, ABS-CBN produced television programs and distributed them through its own nationwide broadcast network. It controlled much of the process, from creating shows to delivering them to viewers and selling advertising around those audiences. Today, ABS-CBN remains a content producer but relies on broadcast partners, streaming services, and digital platforms to reach audiences. It must negotiate distribution arrangements, compete for attention across multiple platforms, and find ways to earn enough from its content in a market where viewers and advertisers have more choices. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The P6-billion capital infusion may provide breathing room, but it cannot by itself establish a profitable business model. Can ABS-CBN consistently earn more from its content than it spends producing and distributing it? Can it control costs without sacrificing the talent and production capabilities that remain its principal strengths? And can it generate sufficient cash to meet its obligations rather than depend on repeated financial support?

The proposed acquisition of Rockwell adds another dimension to Gabby’s bet. Rockwell has established assets and earnings, but acquiring it requires substantial capital. Its cash flows must first support its own operations, development projects, financing requirements, and shareholders. How much, if anything, could eventually be available to support the other investments of Gabby’s branch?

Nor should Rockwell’s profits automatically be treated as money available to ABS-CBN. The two companies have different shareholders, creditors, and financial obligations. Rockwell’s ability to distribute cash to its owners depends on its own financial condition and corporate requirements. Whether Gabby’s branch can use such distributions to support ABS-CBN will also depend on how the Rockwell acquisition is financed and which entities receive the dividends.

That brings both sides to a question that rarely features prominently in accounts of family feuds: Will their bankers continue to have confidence in them?

Piki’s group must finance projects whose expected returns lie years ahead. Gabby’s branch must manage the cost of a major acquisition while supporting a media business still searching for sustainable profitability.

For ABS-CBN, the debt question is particularly pressing. Its ability to meet repayment schedules, refinance obligations, and retain access to bank credit will depend partly on whether its operating performance improves.

Extending loan maturities can be a normal part of corporate financing. But when a business repeatedly needs more time because it cannot generate enough cash to meet its obligations, lenders must reassess the risks.

The relevant questions are not simply how much debt ABS-CBN owes, but when its loans fall due, how much interest it must pay, whether its operations generate enough cash, and what security or guarantees its lenders hold. Those obligations must also be distinguished from any financing arrangements used by Crème or other companies to acquire Rockwell.

Banks have their own reasons for supporting companies through difficult periods. They may prefer a workable restructuring to an immediate default. But their willingness to extend credit is not unlimited. A turnaround must eventually demonstrate that the borrower can repay what it owes.

The separation may give each cousin greater control over the businesses he believes in. It also makes the consequences of those choices more clearly his responsibility.

The Lopezes may eventually discover what the Ambanis learned after their own division: freedom to pursue a business strategy and success in carrying it out are two very different things.

The verdict takes years

The experiences of other families offer no guarantee that the Lopez separation will work. The Ambanis demonstrate that independence can produce dramatically different business fortunes. The Bajajs show that the industries and financial circumstances inherited by each branch matter enormously. Walter Kwok’s experience shows that leaving an established family enterprise need not mean the end of a business career.

None of these examples proves that separation is always preferable to remaining together. They demonstrate that settling ownership is one achievement. Making the resulting businesses successful is another.

For the Lopezes, the immediate questions concern whether the proposed transactions are completed and whether the new ownership arrangements establish more stable control. But the harder questions will take much longer to answer.

Will Piki’s large investments in energy generate the returns needed to justify their cost? Can Gabby’s branch build a sustainable future for ABS-CBN in an industry whose business model is still changing? Will Rockwell prove a valuable investment without becoming an excessive financial burden? And can both sides generate enough cash to repay creditors, finance their ambitions, and reward shareholders?

And when the next generation takes over, will it inherit companies capable of prospering under the arrangements made today—or another set of disputes over ownership and control?

A family settlement can end the argument over who owns what and who gets to run the business. It cannot guarantee that the companies will prosper, that the relatives will reconcile, or that their children will be spared another fight.

For the Lopezes, the separation may finally give each branch greater freedom to pursue its own ambitions. Whether that freedom produces stronger businesses, healthier relationships, and a better future for the next generation will take years to discover. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

NEW BOND. The Piccadilly Circus screen displays an announcement that British actor Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond in an upcoming film from Amazon MGM Studios, in London, Britain, on November 16, 2026. PHOTO BY FELIX URSELL/OCEAN OUTDOOR VIA REUTERS

A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

MANILA, Philippines — Leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and United States President Donald Trump, arrived in Manila for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

On November 14, regional leaders signed the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), the first region-wide agreement of its kind. The milestone established common rules for digital trade and payments. The bloc also advanced initiatives on maritime cooperation, disaster response, online scams, and child protection.

The 49th ASEAN Summit resulted in over a hundred outcome documents but failed to resolve ongoing issues such as the civil war in Myanmar and the South China Sea Code of Conduct negotiations.

“I would say that it was a success simply because of the work that we were able to achieve. The one thing I did not want to do was to waste an opportunity such as this by just doing this hosting,” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. told the media following the summit’s closing ceremony on November 17.

Meanwhile, activists opposing Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s visit gathered on November 15 to protest. Police blocked their march resulting in skirmishes and arrests. Nearly 300 were detained in Manila and Las Pinas City. On November 18, the demonstrators were released due to lack of evidence.

World.title: In Bago City, a Hiligaynon storybook addresses history gaps, reading struggles
World.content:
STORY TIME. Bago City Mayor Mayette Javellana-Yao proudly presents the hard copy of a book on Tan Juan that she envisioned almost a decade ago.

Through bright illustrations and simple Hiligaynon dialogue, Bago City’s new children's book tackles two urgent local challenges — improving early reading skills and keeping the legacy of Al Cinco de Noviembre alive

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – It takes just 32 glossy pages, simple Hiligaynon dialogue, and bright illustrations to reintroduce a 19th-century revolutionary hero to a young child.

Launched on November 5 alongside the 128th anniversary of Negros Occidental’s bloodless revolution, Al Cinco de Noviembre, Bago City’s new children’s book — Ang Kanyon ni Juan (The Cannon of Juan) — hopes to address the growing generation gap and the struggles of young readers.

For Bago Mayor Mayette Javellana-Yao, the problem was impossible to ignore. Most of the city’s younger generation, she candidly admitted, do not really know who the late General Juan Anacleto Araneta (Tan Juan) is — one of the two heroes who put Negros Occidental on the map of Philippine history by leading a bloodless uprising against Spanish colonizers on November 5, 1898.

At the same time, literacy numbers weighed heavily on her mind. The 2025–2026 End-of-School-Year Reading Profile for Grades 4 to 10 in English and Filipino, alongside the Comprehensive Literacy Assessment for Grades 1 to 3, revealed a troubling picture.

Using the Philippine Informal Reading Inventory (Phil-IRI) methodology, assessments showed that the city still has many frustrated readers.

To tackle both challenges at once, the city government teamed up early this year with the Department of Education (DepEd) Schools Division of Bago and the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) Federation to bring Tan Juan’s story to life for young readers.

The mayor requested that the book be written in Hiligaynon, featuring simple paragraphs and an accessible layout so that even a five-year-old child can easily grasp its message. Each 8×8-inch page pairs a large illustration of the characters with a four-paragraph dialogue centered on Tan Juan.

Bringing the pages to life were two creatives from DepEd-Bago: education program specialist II Roxan “Dondon” del Castillo as author, and art teacher Jullienne Castillo as illustrator.

For Del Castillo, the project was deeply personal — he is a fourth-generation descendant of Tan Juan’s clan.

Meanwhile, the SK Federation of Bago spearheaded the printing. Fifty copies were presented to guests during the launch, with mass production set to follow soon, the mayor said.

For Javellana-Yao, seeing the book come to fruition was the fulfillment of a dream years in the making. “Actually, I have envisioned this book since I entered politics in 2018 as a councilor,” she confided.

“Really,” the mayor said, “it pains me to hear and see children passing by the monument of Tan Juan in front of the Bago City Coliseum saying, ‘Who is he?'”

A former campus journalist at St. John’s Institute in Bacolod City during high school and at the University of the Philippines Visayas in Miag-ao, Iloilo during college, Javellana-Yao had long felt an inner drive to publish a book about Tan Juan once she had the means to do so. When she was elected mayor in May 2025 and took office in July, making that book a reality became one of her top priorities.

Sixteen months into her term, that vision finally took shape — born out of a practical question she had asked herself for years.

“I always ask myself, if the city government is spending so much every November 5 to commemorate Al Cinco de Noviembre, why can’t we publish a book — a series, at that — that will last forever?” Javellana-Yao said.

And after 128 years, this marks the first time Al Cinco de Noviembre and Tan Juan have a book published right here in Bago — not bulky, yet truly educational and inspirational, she added.

The urgency behind the project is underscored by Bago’s recent Phil-IRI End-of-School-Year Reading Profile results. The neophyte mayor said she was disturbed to learn that from Grades 4 to 10, many students across the city remain frustrated readers:

Grade 4: 20.37% in English, 16.76% in Filipino

20.37% in English, 16.76% in Filipino Grade 5: 19.47% in English, 15.93% in Filipino

19.47% in English, 15.93% in Filipino Grade 6: 17.48% in English, 16.51% in Filipino

17.48% in English, 16.51% in Filipino Grade 7: 14.60% in English, 6.06% in Filipino

14.60% in English, 6.06% in Filipino Grade 8: 14.00% in English, 5.47% in Filipino

14.00% in English, 5.47% in Filipino Grade 9: 12.26% in English, 4.23% in Filipino

12.26% in English, 4.23% in Filipino Grade 10: 6.70% in English, 2.90% in Filipino

A similar picture emerged from the 2025–2026 End-of-School-Year Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment for Grades 1 to 3, which evaluated 8,551 students:

8.77% (750 students) are low emerging readers

(750 students) are low emerging readers 19.03% (1,628 students) are developing readers

(1,628 students) are developing readers 4.84% (414 students) are high developing readers

(414 students) are high developing readers 33.70% (2,882 students) are transitioning readers

(2,882 students) are transitioning readers 33.60% (2,874 students) are reading at grade level

Faced with these numbers, the mayor is convinced that early intervention is critical — and that a simple storybook could help turn the tide.

“That’s why I want the book to be simple and written in Hiligaynon, so it can be easily understood by students at the day care and kindergarten levels,” the mayor explained. Once children learn to read starting in day care through their mother tongue, she stressed, they can build a lasting reading habit and smoothly advance to higher grades.

Ang Kanyon ni Juan is only the beginning. According to Javellana-Yao, five more sequels are planned, starting with Requinto: Ang Kabayo ni Tan Juan, which is already in the pipeline.

To help sustain the series and defray printing costs, senior tourism supervising officer Mae Ann Furtos said the city will also coordinate with the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) to see if the book qualifies for publishing grants. – Rappler.com

World.title: All about MUNI, a platform turning online conversations into real-world action
World.content:
MUNI, launched by Rappler in 2026, is a digital space where verified information and trusted voices are given prominence – an antidote to opaque algorithms that have turned social media platforms into toxic places

In September 2026, Rappler launched MUNI, a community platform that aims to carve out a corner of the internet that can still do good.

With AI slop, disinformation, deepfakes, uncontrolled AI scraping, and opaque algorithms turning off many from the internet of today, Rappler envisioned an alternative digital space where facts dominate feeds and people can more easily find trusted voices and trustworthy information with which to make decisions.

MUNI is that space. It comes from the Filipino word “muni-muni,” which means to reflect or think deeply. It is also at the heart of the word “community,” which is what the platform aims to build.

What is MUNI?

MUNI is a digital space, accessible on both mobile and desktop devices, where you can find various public and private chat rooms run by civil society groups, community leaders, journalists, and institutions.

Unlike other social media platforms where anyone can create a chat room, MUNI gives prominence to trusted voices and groups that all agree to only share facts and verified information. Groups on MUNI abide by a constitution and set of community guidelines that enforce this. Leaders in these groups are given green shield badges beside their usernames to help people on MUNI identify them.

Play Video

MUNI, as a platform, is accessible through multiple platforms, not just one app or website. Participating groups in MUNI can put MUNI on their websites or apps. Rappler, for instance, has a MUNI tab on our free app (download it here). The concept is that MUNI is one corridor, reachable through many doors. Or one corridor through which you can enter many doors, many communities.

It’s built on the Matrix Protocol, a digital infrastructure for decentralized and secure communications. It prioritizes privacy and security, and is end-to-end encrypted like Signal and Telegram. But it provides an additional layer of protection because of its decentralized nature, which makes it less vulnerable to surveillance or attacks compared to a centralized system. Also, unlike Telegram or Signal that requires a phone number to create an account, you can communicate with the Matrix Protocol with just a username.

How to join MUNI

Download the Rappler app for free from the App Store or Google Play Store. Once inside the app, tap the MUNI tab at the bottom of your screen to explore communities and chat rooms.

MUNI is also visible on the websites of newsgroups like Daily Guardian, an Iloilo-based news outlet, and SunStar Cebu, a newsroom based in Cebu, among others.

What can you do in MUNI?

Muni gives you or your organization more than just another communication channel. It’s a space to bring people together, strengthen relationships, and turn shared interests into meaningful action.

Here’s what you can do:

Build your community . Bring your members, supporters, and audiences together in one dedicated space where they can connect, interact, and feel more involved in your organization’s work.

Keep your community informed about your latest news, activities, announcements, events, and initiatives. Make sure the people who matter to your organization stay in the loop.

Encourage meaningful discussions, exchange ideas, ask questions, and gather feedback. Allow your community to participate and make their voices heard.

Connect with people beyond your existing network. Through Muni’s growing community of organizations and individuals, you can introduce your work to new audiences and build valuable connections.

Share knowledge. Give your community easier access to relevant stories, trusted information, and expert voices. Help them stay informed about the issues and interests that matter to your organization.

Encourage action. Bring your advocacies and initiatives closer to the people who care. Share volunteer opportunities, calls for participation, and community activities that turn shared goals into real-world action.

Bring your advocacies and initiatives closer to the people who care. Share volunteer opportunities, calls for participation, and community activities that turn shared goals into real-world action. Grow beyond your own network. Become part of a wider community of newsrooms, civic organizations, experts, and like-minded groups. Discover opportunities to collaborate, learn from others, and create connections that extend beyond your own chat room.

Muni is more than a place to exchange messages. It’s an opportunity to bring your community closer to your mission and help your organization grow.

Play Video

How to set up your profile in MUNI

Before joining your organization’s chat room as a moderator, make sure your profile is ready!

Use your real name. We encourage all moderators and members of partner organizations to use their real names. Muni is built around real people having meaningful conversations, and using your real name helps build trust, familiarity, and accountability within the community.

Add a profile photo. Adding a profile photo is optional but highly encouraged! It helps other members recognize you and makes interactions feel more personal.

Follow the recommended name format. For moderators and members representing partner organizations, we encourage using this format for your display name:

Name – Organization

Example: Juan Dela Cruz – ABC Foundation

This helps other members easily identify who they’re talking to and which organization they represent.

Muni features

Muni gives your organization the tools to create, manage, and nurture your own community. Here’s a look at the features that can help you make the most of your space.

Moderator powers

Moderators are identified by a special green shield badge displayed beside their names, making them easily recognizable to other members. They can also manage conversations, moderate their chat room, and help maintain a welcoming community space. Pinned messages

Keep important announcements, reminders, and updates visible by pinning them in your chat room. This makes essential information easier for members to find. Moderators have the power to pin messages. Threaded conversations

Keep discussions organized with threaded replies. Members can respond to specific messages without cluttering the main conversation. Notifications

Help members stay updated on new messages and important conversations through notifications. In-chat video playback

Share videos that members can watch directly within the chat room, without needing to switch to another app or browser. Curated Rappler news updates

Request automated delivery of specific types of Rappler stories to your chat room based on your organization’s interests, advocacies, or community needs. Keep your members informed with relevant news and trusted information. Website integration

Make your organization’s Muni chat room accessible through your own website. This allows your existing audience to discover and join your community without having to rely solely on the Rappler app.

Muni brings together different communities, organizations, and individuals through dedicated chat rooms within the Rappler app. Explore spaces covering news, public affairs, education, local initiatives, and various advocacies, and find conversations and communities that interest you.

Rappler chat rooms in MUNI

Education Share insights on news and issues related to the Philippine education sector. Everyday Tech Keep up with the fast-paced tech world and weigh in on what’s new and what’s hot. FactsFirstPH Connect and champion truth in the ongoing fight against disinformation. Front Page Get the latest news and updates from Rappler. Justice and Crime Stay updated on matters related to justice and human rights in the Philippines. Send leads and tips for future investigations here. Live Jam Get to know fellow music lovers and stay updated on upcoming Live Jam sessions. Liveable Cities Share updates about your city or town and get updates on urban liveability and local governance. Oragon Bicol A space connecting Bicolanos and those passionate about Bicol to share stories of resilience, learn about their heritage, discuss community issues, and collaborate on seeking solutions to issues affecting the region. Philippine Politics Stay in the know about the latest developments in national and local politics. Project Agos Get weather, volcano, and earthquake alerts, and share your situation during a disaster. Rai Ask questions on current news and issues to Rai, Rappler’s AI-enabled chatbot. RappLearn A chat room connecting RappLearn participants and teachers. Rappler+ An exclusive chat room for Rappler+ members featuring special announcements and discussions about events and articles. Security and Global Affairs Be updated with the latest news on the Philippines’ foreign and security policy. Volunteer Opportunities Discover ways to be involved in advocacies and campaigns. Voter Hotline Share your concerns about the Philippine elections directly with the Comelec.

Partner chat rooms on MUNI

Bangsamoro Voices Get updates or join discussions about the Bangsamoro region. Daily Guardian Iloilo Catch up on the latest news, stories, and local issues in Iloilo and join conversations with the Daily Guardian community. Padayon Cebu A hub for local civic action that brings citizens together to discuss local issues, collaborate on solutions, and keep Cebu moving forward. The chat room is managed by Cebu Citizens Initiatives. Philippine Press Institute Discover stories that matter from trusted community newsrooms across the Philippines. Scam Alert A space to report scams and find practical guidance on how to respond, warn others, and flag incidents to the relevant authorities. World.title: Watching alone wasn’t enough, so these Filipino YouTube fans found each other offline
World.content:
Discovering YouTube creators like Dan and Phil and Smosh was a solitary experience. Filipino fans are making it a communal one.

Alone in the glow of the computer screen — that’s how many who grew up watching YouTube started.

In 2005, when the platform was conceived, it was geared to be a dating website where people could upload videos “talking about the partner of their dreams.” More than two decades later, video reigns social media, and YouTube is the second-most-visited website in the world.

It’s hard to imagine that the first few YouTube creators knew they could make a career out of the website when it began. Many have since stepped away. But some, including Dan and Phil and the Smosh channel, were able to build fandoms that have stuck with them for well over a decade.

“When I first started watching them, I didn’t even have a concept of stanning people,” recalled Wayne Pontalba, an admin of Dan and Phil Manila, who got into the fandom in the early 2010s.

Even back then, Daniel Howell and Philip Lester went only by their nicknames, always in tandem: Dan and Phil. They were among the first famous YouTubers, rising right as the platform boomed, and viewers “shipping” them together fueled much of their popularity.

A promotional photo for Dan and Phil’s Hard Launch podcast. Photo from Daniel Howell’s Instagram page.

Wayne was one of these fans, and she found only one other comrade in her class. They became best friends.

“We were the two weirdest people in the classroom,” she said. They weren’t quiet about their interest in these British YouTubers, even mimicking their videos in a school talent segment while barely understanding the words.

Meanwhile, Reese Reyes, an admin of Smosh Philippines Fans, didn’t have her own computer at ten years old, so she’d march her way to her neighbor’s house to watch Smosh on YouTube.

“I was the only one addicted to YouTube,” she said. “Unsupervised, as a kid,” she added.

Back then, Ian and Anthony were just two loud teenagers posting lip-sync videos online, but they would go on to become YouTube’s most subscribed channel in their heyday.

Reese’s interest in them waxed and waned as the channel evolved, with companies buying the Smosh channel out, new faces being brought in, and one half of the duo, Anthony, leaving. She’d fall right back in when the original duo bought the company back and geared their content towards their new motto.

A photo of Smosh’s current cast. Photo from Smosh’s Instagram page.

“Their motto is ‘comedy rooted in friendship,’ and I can see it as a viewer,” Reese remarked. “I’m thankful for YouTube because it gave me a little space of solace to fangirl.”

Now, with fan events happening left and right, that little space of solace no longer belongs to just the screen.

Live, in person

For Marj Castro of Dan and Phil Manila, the first event she organized was out of necessity.

“Dan and Phil skipped the Philippines in their 2024 tour, and I felt how sad the fanbase was about it,” she said.

She organized it all by herself. After an interest check drew 30 responses, she booked a cafe that could cater to that size, dolled up the place, and warmly greeted everyone who walked in. The event was a success, so much so that four more admins joined the team after it.

“It was a communal way to say [to Dan and Phil] that, ‘Hey, we’re still here!’” said James Mortilla, one of the new admins, about why he joined the planning of their latest event.

I was there for it on the afternoon of October 18. The Recto cafe’s brutalist interior was hidden well under purple nylon balloons and animated drawings of the internet couple.

Participants find their seats as Dan and Phil Manila’s Howlter High cupsleeve event begins in Kape Light Recto, Sampaloc, Manila, on October 18, 2026. All photos by Aidan Bernales/Rappler.

Throughout the afternoon, attendees in bedazzled outfits came up to give away stickers of their Dan and Phil fan art. I asked one of them if the organizers had commissioned her. She said no: the stickers were free, she had printed them herself, and she brought enough for everyone in the room.

“It is such an honor to be a medium for fans to interact with each other in real life,” Wayne commented. “It’s not every day you see someone who watches the same YouTuber that you do.”

A Howlter High attendee poses with standees of YouTubers Dan and Phil, illustrated by another Filipino fan.

Smosh Philippines Fans began the same way, with fans who couldn’t be where the creators were. It started as a Discord server, Bahay ni Ian, in 2025 with around 30 to 50 fans who’d found each other through other social media platforms. When Smosh held a live show, the server pooled donations toward a livestream ticket and streamed it for a watch party.

The server has since grown past 600 members and spilled out of the online sphere.

At an October 24 board game event in a cafe in España, I met a group of six friends who became close, thanks to Smosh Philippines Fans.

“Smosh’s motto is ‘comedy rooted in friendship,’ right? That’s also what happened to us,” said Hywel Jintalan, one of the attendees. The group barely fit on the small couch, so one of them sprawled across the others’ legs like a baby. They had “yearned for a friendship” like this: hanging out after school and work, playing the board games they’d only ever enjoyed vicariously through Smosh.

Smosh fans prepare for a round of Blood on the Clocktower during Smosh Philippines Fans’ board game event at Coffee + Co, Sampaloc, Manila on October 24, 2026.

The games are a nod to Smosh Games, one of the channel’s most popular offshoots, which is devoted to games of all sorts. Tables were littered with board game pieces and players screaming in jest. In a conference room, players spoke in low voices and cast suspicious glances at each other over a roleplaying game. A Dress To Impress contest, a live reenactment of the Roblox fashion game, was held. The winning fit? A lifeguard costume with a floatie, a nod to a Smosh summer series.

Smosh fans, dressed up as lifeguards, man the sign-ups for Last Splash of Blood.

Whether you’re extroverted or introverted, Kiki Langahid, Smosh Philippines Fans’ social media manager, says it doesn’t matter. “It doesn’t hinder anyone from playing games,” she remarked. “It’s people who love playing board games and having a good time with their friends.”

A special shoutout

The creators they gather for are entire continents away, but the internet does this funny thing where it closes the distance.

At another cupsleeve event last year, Dan and Phil surprised attendees with a video message.

“To all the Filipino fans, we appreciate you out there where it’s nice and warm,” Dan said, looking over at Phil for an extra comment. “Enjoy the meetup!” Phil exclaimed.

Surprise! Some familiar faces had a special message for us during the #TerriblyInPHluencedCSE 😁👋



Maraming salamat @danielhowell and @AmazingPhil for making our day extra special 💙#DNPMNLCSE2025 pic.twitter.com/uZmB3Z8ED8 — Dan and Phil Manila (@DanAndPhilMNL) October 18, 2025

“It was one of the hardest secrets I had to keep,” Marj said. It was a complete shot in the dark when she sent that email to Dan and Phil’s manager; she couldn’t believe her eyes when they responded.

The pair’s manager stayed in contact with the team afterward, even sponsoring the merchandise giveaways for the next fan meet. Attendees who won the games the admins organized went home with signed photo cards.

Dan and Phil fans pose with their signed photo cards after winning a game during Howlter High.

This December, Dan and Phil themselves are coming. They’re bringing their Hard Launch World Tour to Manila on December 4. It will be their first Philippine show since 2018.

Smosh hasn’t announced any plans yet to come here, but Kiki has made it her goal to bring them.

She recalls an event where attendees dressed as characters played by Smosh cast member Amanda Lehan-Canto, just as a Filipino producer of the show was visiting the country. They invited her, but she was out of town spending time with family.

Nevertheless, they persisted. Their flashiest effort yet is one you might have seen: an LED birthday greeting for Lehan-Canto that ran for a whole day in Guadalupe, EDSA.

She reacted to it on a Smosh podcast she co-hosts. “They had a bigger celebration for your birthday than you did!” fellow cast member Shayne Topp joked.

The people who get it

It’s easy for these events to be all about the creators. But really, it’s about the people there.

For Mikhail Valdez, the Smosh events are special. “It’s one of the few times I get to socialize,” he said.

He wouldn’t consider Smosh “niche” now, but when he started watching them, he couldn’t find anyone to talk about their videos with. Then he met two people who were also interested, and they became close.

“It became bigger and bigger to the point that I get to attend social events like these,” he said. Nearly 30 people filled that cafe in España. For Mikhail, it was a long way from two friends.

Mikhail Valdez and fellow game participants pose with their role chips after completing a round of Blood on the Clocktower.

Noeri David and Cielo Fortin, who attended the Dan and Phil event, reconnected only recently.

“We stopped communicating because of our high school lives,” Noeri told me. “But when Dan and Phil hard launched last year, I reached out to [Cielo] again. I didn’t even anticipate that she’d reply back.”

All Noeri wanted was to tell Cielo she appreciated their time together, since Dan and Phil’s relationship had brought those memories back. Fortunately, Cielo replied, and their friendship picked up again.

“I’ve met so many people in this fandom that helped me survive,” Noeri said.

Cielo Fortin and Noeri David, Dan and Phil fans, holding literal Dan and Phil fans.

Discovering these creators, whether two decades ago or just yesterday, was a solitary experience. But a singular decision to press play can bloom into a Saturday night of board games, sharing your art with strangers, and reigniting dormant friendships.

Joo Mondia, one of the Dan and Phil Manila admins, put it this way: “If there are those who don’t understand why you love these guys, there are over 200 people right now who will tell you otherwise.” — Rappler.com

Quotes translated to English for brevity.

World.title: Army unit sharpens frontline trauma care for combat, disasters
World.content:
Medical personnel of the Army’s 4th Infantry Division and Joint Task Force Diamond treat a soldier’s arm inside a field tent during the Forward Treatment Unit readiness training at Camp Edilberto Evangelista in Barangay Patag, Cagayan de Oro City, held from Nov. 11 to 19, 2026. —Photo courtesy of the 4th Infantry Division Public Affairs Office

CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY, Philippines — When a soldier goes down far from a hospital, survival is measured in minutes.

To close that gap, the Army’s 4th Infantry Division (4ID) put its frontline medical teams through a nine-day readiness drill at Camp Edilberto Evangelista here, sharpening their ability to keep wounded troops alive in combat and disaster zones.

The Forward Treatment Unit (FTU) Readiness Training ran from Nov. 11 to 19 at the 4ID headquarters in Barangay Patag, division spokesman Lt. Col. Joe Patrick Martinez told the Inquirer on Saturday, Nov. 21.

Article continues after this 

READ: PH Army holds medical mission in Lanao del Norte

Martinez thanked the training staff for honing the skills of frontline responders and urged soldiers in the field to fight with confidence, assuring them that the medical team is right behind them to keep them alive and bring them home.]

“To the people we serve, our commitment to protect you remains steadfast,” he said.

Speaking at the closing ceremony, Col. Robert Rosqueta, commanding officer of the Camp Evangelista Station Hospital, stressed the urgency of quick medical response as the Armed Forces of the Philippines builds up its territorial defense.

“We must recognize that in military operations, particularly in situations where medical facilities are not readily accessible, every minute matters,” the 4ID advisory quoted Rosqueta as saying.

Article continues after this 

He added that finishing the course is only the beginning.

“The completion of this training does not mean that we are already fully mission-ready. This is only one step toward developing and sustaining that readiness,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Run by the 4th Service Support Battalion under Lt. Col. Milner Taglinao through its Forward Support Medical Company, the course prepares medical teams for combat, disaster response, and territorial defense emergencies.

Acting as a mobile field hospital, the FTU bridges the gap between basic battlefield first aid and full-scale hospitals. It provides emergency life-saving care and stabilizes wounded personnel before evacuation, cutting preventable deaths and keeping units ready to fight.

READ: The urgency of air rescue in the West Philippine Sea

Trainees drilled on unit setup, medical evacuation, battlefield first aid, patient tracking, and handling victims of chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear exposure. They also practiced setting up operating rooms, sterilizing gear, preventing infections, managing pain and sedation, and providing psychological first aid for combat stress.

Hands-on exercises covered emergency trauma surgery and resuscitation, rapid ultrasound scans, burn and crush injuries, triage, and maintaining medical equipment in the field.
