World.title: Eyre Peninsula residents worried about further blackouts
World.content:
Eyre Peninsula residents say they are counting on temporary fixes to the power grid to carry them through the next few weeks.

About 24,000 properties were without power on Thursday during a mass blackout.

The region is now temporarily being serviced by the mothballed Port Lincoln power station and reconfigured power lines.

An intense storm damaged three transmission towers, which operator ElectraNet said crippled the "radial line" powering much of the peninsula, including Port Lincoln.

Storm clouds above grain fields on the Eyre Peninsula where wild weather lashed the region on Thursday afternoon (Supplied: Benjamin Wandel)

The company is investigating whether any structural defects were to blame but said that it is unlikely.

'Can't be without power'

Port Lincoln mayor Diana Mislov acknowledged the severe weather was "an unexpected event" but wanted assurances that the construction requirements were met.

"I think the whole line needs to be looked at and more work undertaken to ensure that this doesn't happen again," Ms Mislov said.

Port Lincoln's Mayor Diana Mislov said she was putting her faith in the people operating the regional city's mothballed power station. (Robert Lang)

"I understand the cost-benefit analysis that needs to happen with some of this decision-making, but we can't afford to allow our communities to be without power."

The nearby power plant, which is privately owned and will shut down permanently in 2028, will be used for several days, according to ElectraNet.

Ms Mislov wanted to see the plant maintained long-term as a back-up option.

"The fact we were able to fire up the power station … and get it back into action for our communities is incredibly important," she said.

She also urged people who had lost power to switch off their solar panels, in line with SA Police's instructions, to avoid overloading the grid.

Multi-day blackout 'wouldn't be good'

On Friday, Premier Peter Malinauskas also warned that predicted storm events and hot weather on Sunday could further strain the grid.

The Bureau of Meteorology is predicting early thunderstorms and temperatures to reach around 30 on the Lower Eyre Peninsula.

Restaurant owner Craig McCathie, of the Fresh Fish Place, said he was concerned about more blackouts over the next few weeks while repairs are underway.

The venue's back-up generator kicked in, but Mr McCathie said a blackout running into several days – such as in 2016 – "wouldn't be a good scenario" if the town's reserves run out.

"It does cause a bit of a stress because of what's happened in the past," he said.

Fresh Fish Place owner Craig McCathie said businesses and industry in the region are dependent on reliable power. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

"We keep enough [fuel] for about 20 hours, but when the town is down, the diesel pumps are down too, so we haven't got a back-up plan for when we run out of our storage."

There is still no timeline for when the damaged towers will be permanently replaced, but temporary structures are expected to go up within days, which will bolster energy reliability.

Speaking to 891 Adelaide, ElectraNet's Alex Trento said the company was confident its designs were structurally sound.

"Depending on the investigation, that'll determine whether we go down the path of looking at a different design," Mr Trento said.

"But at this point in time we're of the strong view that the design is adequate, tested to the requirements of the Australian standards ... and constructed by very competent contractors, with ElectraNet personnel overseeing [them]".

World.title: Aussie bowlers no longer in control of public perception of legacies
World.content:
Three days ago — an eon in the context of Australian cricket's most embarrassing and avoidable omnishambles — former Australian wicketkeeper Ian Healy offered a reasonable take on Australia's famed bowling group.

"I would say it taints their personal legacies … I don't think it's going to taint their performance legacies," Healy said. "Personally now, they're not as credible as they once were, unless they change something drastically in the next few days."

Healy's personal stake in this is self-evident: his niece is married to Mitchell Starc. And in a fast-evolving crisis, his qualifiers were understandable, although we will get to Josh Hazlewood's version of drastic intervention later.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

Healy was right to differentiate between the professional and personal: one need not disparage all the hard work, all the joy, all the winning they have given Australians, by admitting that Australia's bowlers have, in recent times, irreparably damaged their own and Australia's credibility.

The bowlers also surely must concede that the precise and absolute truth of what happened in 2018 no longer matters to most fans. In fact, their carefully-worded prevarications and collective obsession with semantic distinctions project an air of guilt almost comically out of proportion with the original offence.

No matter what they saw or heard, barely anyone believes what they are saying about it.

Even if players have publicly approved of Cricket Australia's "truth forum", the rest of us surely agree it is as likely to establish an agreed and convincing set of facts as it is to locate Jimmy Hoffa.

So, to extend Healy's thought, what is their legacy, exactly?

They can hardly blame us for pondering it now in unflattering light. Because the obsession with the "legacy" of Australia's bowlers predates Usman Khawaja's book.

In the past 12 months, the idea has been fairly rammed down our throats as justification for keeping the gang together for a marathon 12 months of Test engagements against South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. The last hurrah for a golden generation, they said.

The legacy of Australia's veteran group of bowlers remains up in the air amid the recent sandpaper furore. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It could be argued that the very concept was rendered pointless weeks ago, before Sandpapergate's flare-up, on Australia's disastrous recent tour of South Africa.

It is one of the ironies of the present crisis engulfing the bowlers: it has precluded lengthier analysis of their deep and abject failure in the most recent Cape Town Test.

All the noise coming from within the team, of course, suggested this was a mere setback: South Africa are world champions for a reason, ya know? Geez, I guess we shouldn't have bowled first. Oh well, onward and upward, eh?

Actually, it was proof not just of muddled selection priorities and dwindling returns from old stagers, but a deeper crisis of philosophy and proof that the bowlers, in particular, were not operating in a meritocracy.

Having played out of his skin in the second Test, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon, who was in turn out-bowled by Simon Harmer, an off-spinner most Australians had previously thought of as a glorified clubbie.

Nathan Lyon was brutally out-bowled by South Africa's Simon Harner in Australia's most recent Test performance. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

And Harmer didn't merely take wickets. He publicly called out and dismantled the Australian captain in a manner that should have caused far more alarm than whatever Cummins did or didn't see as a 24-year-old.

To delve into another modern-day obsession — being "aura" — the loss went far deeper than a 2-1 scoreline. Before its present distraction, Australian cricket pretended otherwise, but symbolic damage was done on a scale we will see more clearly in a few years.

Which brings us to Josh Hazlewood. On a very simple level, his claim yesterday that he would "review" his place in the Australian team if Cummins lost the captaincy was an impassioned if artless expression of loyalty and solidarity with the skipper in times of disloyalty.

More so, it smacked of the cart being placed a hell of a long way in front of the horse. It was an expression of entitlement that brought to mind another unflattering scene from a year ago, of an "absolutely filthy" Nathan Lyon sulking away to a sideline TV reporter after being omitted from last December's pink-ball Test. There have been others.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

For a long time now — long before Sandpapergate reared up again — there has been an inescapable sense that Australia's senior players see themselves not as members of a team chosen by an independent selection panel, nor as merely a self-selecting elite within that team, but as the self-appointed bosses of Australian Test cricket.

It is hard to escape the feeling that it is this self-absorbed culture of entitlement and the desire to control its own narrative — much more so than anything that happened in 2018 — that now defines what the public thinks of Australia's bowlers.

And yes, it is true that those who've thrown their weight around like this are, by most definitions, indisputably Australia's best. And it is also true that they have sometimes needed to exercise their collective power for the benefit of others, too, as in their pay negotiations.

But what is the average fan — who, by the time the Perth Test rolls around in nine days, will have been subjected to weeks of a melodrama which is only a paternity test and a few exploding boats away from a Home and Away plot — to make of a 35-year-old multi-millionaire threatening to take his ball and go home if his mate's not in charge?

Australia's bowling 'cartel' has always been inseparable, particularly in the years following the infamous 2018 South Africa tour. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

"The cartel". It has always had a faintly sinister ring to it, don't you think? Some of the behaviour is, frankly, gangsterism, albeit in the territory mined by Martin Scorsese and David Chase — the petty spats over matters of honour and respect, the fragile egos and wounded pride.

In this light, we now see Cameron Bancroft as the hapless 'Spider', egged on and then assassinated. Perhaps we suddenly respect Steve Smith a little more for silently doing all that time for crimes he didn't commit.

Which leaves us with how Australia proceeds in the short-term. Cricket Australia, more to blame for the mess than any player, confirmed on Saturday that Cummins would be retained as captain. It was the most predictable and probably the most sensible course of action based on a sober appraisal of all relevant facts, but it did also have the unfortunate effect of validating Hazlewood's veiled threat.

Even granting the need to extinguish a tabloid bin-fire, and acknowledging the overwhelming good Cummins has done for Australian cricket, there is an irony in this: backing him in as leader guarantees him a higher work and stress load than he would ideally be shouldering at this point of his career. In an ideal world, free of this scandal, honest conversations about succession planning would already be happening.

Hazlewood's defence of Cummins came after Mitchell Starc had also previously whacked down claims of knowing about the plot to ball tamper in 2018. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Hazlewood's interjection and the self-conferred gravitas of his Test spot, meanwhile, sit somewhat at odds with the prevailing views of his contemporaries. Only a week ago, players' union boss Paul Marsh admitted there was "decreasing" support among players for the idea of Test cricket as the pinnacle of the sport.

Fans, by extension, are now buffeted by administrators who care too little about Test cricket and a few players who care too much.

In the time since Sandpapergate, Cricket Australia has had six chairmen, four CEOs, three men's head coaches and capped 21 new Test players. That a few mainstays attained an over-mighty status is perhaps natural enough, but it is surely time that senior players are reminded that Test selection is not their birthright.

Australia's next 15 Tests would have been brutally difficult in any context. Against such a draining and unpleasant backdrop, the degree of difficulty for an aging and now embittered group of old hands has only increased.

And that really is the stuff of "legacy" — not just everything in totality, but the aftertaste left by the final few bites.

World.title: Victoria Point woman waited seven hours for ambulance before death
World.content:
The ABC understands a woman who died in Brisbane last month was left waiting almost seven hours for an ambulance.

The 63-year-old woman died at Victoria Point after repeated calls for an ambulance.

At least six Queenslanders have died in recent weeks, with some people waiting as long as 18 hours for an ambulance.

Queensland health minister Tim Nicholls said last week the government was pulling "every possible lever" to deliver more hospital beds, while also calling on the Commonwealth to provide more aged care beds.

Premier David Crisafulli has said the health system's issues could be resolved "overnight" with more federal funding.

Federal frontbencher Murray Watt has pushed back against calls for more Commonwealth health funding. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

But federal frontbencher Murray Watt said the Queensland government needed to "take responsibility" for managing public health.

Minister Watt said state premiers had always "sought to blame Canberra for their woes".

"Running public hospitals and ambulance services is the responsibility of the state government and the state government needs to take responsibility for that here," he said.

" It's an absolute tragedy that we've seen Queenslanders lose their lives in recent times waiting for ambulances. The premier and his health minister need to step up and solve this. "

Opposition leader Steven Miles said: "Nobody deserves to die helpless and in agony".

"Sadly, that's what we've learned has been the end-of-life experience for seven Queenslanders over just the last few weeks," he said.

The Queensland Ambulance Service said the death of any patient is a tragedy and that it is providing support to the woman's family.

World.title: Man in hospital after stabbing in Melbourne's CBD
World.content:
A man has been taken to hospital with serious injuries after a stabbing in Melbourne's CBD this afternoon.

Police believe the 24-year-old was stabbed by another man on Bourke Street, near the corner of Elizabeth Street, about 2.30pm.

The men are not believed to know each other, police say.

Police are looking for a Caucasian man, aged about 30, with a beard and a dishevelled appearance, who they say approached a man and a woman 'without provocation'.

"[There was] an altercation between a couple and an unknown male who assaulted the male victim and [it] ended up in a stab wound to the chest," Inspector Dale Huntington said.

Victoria Police Inspector Dale Huntington says the victim was stabbed in the chest. (Supplied: Braden Taemin Nam)

Police are making inquiries into the whereabouts of the alleged offender, who they say ran off along Elizabeth Street towards Little Bourke Street.

"We have a good idea who we're looking for," Inspector Huntington said.

Police believe the man often frequents the CBD and may have been sleeping rough.

Inspector Huntington said a sleeping bag was believed to have been involved in the altercation.

Paramedics took the injured 24-year-old man to the Royal Melbourne Hospital in a critical condition with upper body injuries.

"He's in surgery at the moment. It's not life-threatening, but as I said... we don't want this occurring to anyone," Inspector Huntington said.

Police do not believe the two men are known to each other. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Police are appealing for anyone with information or footage to come forward.

"It is a very dynamic area... we've got people coming and going, a lot of shoppers, it's Christmas time," Inspector Huntington said.

Police defend city's safety, as concerns mount

Inspector Huntington said police were not expecting a further incident, as they continued their search.

"This really rarely occurs in the CBD in Melbourne. It's an issue that doesn't come up every day," Inspector Huntington said.

"Yes, we do have many homeless people that maybe defend themselves and maybe carry some implements... so we work with the service providers and we really walk around and make sure that doesn't occur."

He said the victim was believed to have been in Melbourne to partake in activities happening in the city, noting that the Myer Christmas windows were just around the corner.

"We really want to encourage people to come in and enjoy the city," Inspector Huntington said.

Emergency services were called to Bourke Street about 2.30pm. (Supplied)

Harry, a university student in Melbourne, was nearby and saw 'so many' police officers, taking pictures as they rushed towards H&M in Bourke Street.

"I feel that Melbourne's public safety is terrible," Harry told the ABC.

"The main issue is the lack of effective measures to deter crime.

" Feels like something is happening every single day lately. "

A Melbourne resident says more police patrols would help him feel safer living in the CBD. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Ryu has lived in the Melbourne CBD for almost four years and says he has started avoiding parts of the city because of violent crime.

"I don't feel safe anymore living here," he says.

He says an increase in police patrols in the city would help him feel safer.

"Whenever I see the police I feel safe because there's cover for me to walk safely without worrying about whether I'm going to get stabbed."

Police are urging anyone with information about the stabbing or footage to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Teen critical after being shot by arrow
World.content:
A 15-year-old boy left fighting for life after being struck with an arrow remains in a critical condition in hospital, after several incidents in a northern New South Wales unit block.

Police said they were called to the area in Kempsey around 6pm on Thursday for a welfare check, where they were told several people armed with machetes had entered a home.

"We believe that a group have attended, some armed with machetes, one potentially with a bow and arrow," Mid North Coast Police District crime manager Detective Inspector Mark Rogers said.

Police seized an arrow from the scene. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

He said officers were unable to make contact with the unit's residents, leaving the scene after making enquiries.

Around 7.30pm, police were called back to the unit block to reports a woman had been struck with a machete, sustaining superficial injuries.

Shortly after, they received a call a teenager had presented to Kempsey District Hospital with an arrow wound.

He was flown to John Hunter Hospital in Newcastle where he remains in a critical condition.

"We believe that he has an injury around his neck and another injury to his torso. The details of how the injuries have occurred will form part of the investigation," Detective Inspector Rogers said.

Police are urging anyone with information to come forward to assist with investigations. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

"The police have engaged with the boy's family.

"We're yet to have the opportunity to speak to the boy."

A crime scene was established, with an arrow seized by police for forensic examination.

Detective Inspector Rogers said officers were not ruling out gang-related activity, calling on the community to assist with any information.

Detective Inspector Mark Rogers said the incident was "appalling" and "shocking". (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

"It would be irresponsible to rule out any possibilities like that at this early stage of the investigation," he said.

"However, I can assure the community we have a team of police that are going to be working on this and they'll be making every attempt to identify the offenders and bring some justice to the family.

"It's certainly a shocking incident and I think anyone in the community would be similarly appalled, which is why I urge those with information to assist our detectives and come forward with any information."

World.title: Roos survive Swans scare to book trip to fourth straight AFLW decider
World.content:
North Melbourne is within touching distance of an AFLW premiership "three-peat" after fighting out a 32-point victory over a Chloe Molloy-inspired Sydney in their preliminary final.

Ash Riddell and veteran Emma Kearney were centre stage as the Kangaroos kicked six goals clear in the first half before holding off a brave Swans challenge in the 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51) triumph at Princes Park on Saturday.

Darren Crocker's all-conquering side is into a fourth consecutive grand final, with the chance to complete the first flag hat-trick in the history of the women's competition.

North will take on the winner of Saturday's second preliminary final between Melbourne and Carlton.

But there is some concern over ruck Kim Rennie, who spent some time on the turf in the final quarter and eventually hobbled off with what appeared to be a right knee injury.

Riddell (29 disposals) and Eilish Sheerin (22) were outstanding, while superstar Jasmine Garner finished with three goals from 18 disposals despite attention from Swans tagger Tanya Kennedy.

Tahlia Randall and Blaithin Bogue kicked two each for the Kangaroos.

Kearney (15 disposals) was dependable as always on managed minutes in her return from a hamstring injury, and got under her opponents' skin in trademark fashion.

Molloy (three goals) did her best to lift Sydney, sparking a second-quarter fightback, but North had a greater number of contributors across the ground.

Laura Gardner (25 disposals), Zippy Fish (18) and Cynthia Hamilton (two goals) also fought hard for the gallant Swans.

A global Ticketmaster outage caused long queues for frustrated fans outside the ground, but those lucky enough to get in early witnessed a slice of history.

Hamilton opened the scoring for Sydney with the fastest AFLW goal, finishing well on the run just 21 seconds into the contest.

But Garner responded within a minute, and the opening term belonged to North, who led 4.2 to 2.1 at the first break.

Garner added her second early in the second quarter and it opened the floodgates, with the Kangaroos piling on another four consecutive goals.

Molloy breathed life back into the contest with three of Sydney's four goals in a nine-minute burst before half-time.

The Swans' superstar caught both Riddell and Kearney holding the ball, and kicked team-lifting goals against the tide.

The North duo demonstrably disputed the decisions with umpires but were not penalised further for dissent.

Kearney also sparked a melee when she riled her opponents by sarcastically joining in the Swans' celebrations.

Molloy's third major cut what was a 36-point margin back to 18 by half-time, with North leading 9.2 to 6.2 at the main break.

It was one goal apiece in a tight third quarter and the Swans got within a couple of kicks when Maddie Quinn (two goals) kicked the first major of the final term.

But North held firm and Garner kicked the sealer when she snapped her third major with less than four minutes left on the clock.

AAP

World.title: Spirit IV ferry docks late again after 'technical issue'
World.content:
One of the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries has once again docked hours behind schedule because of a "technical issue" with its primary navigational system.

Spirit IV was heading towards Geelong when the issue occurred early on Saturday morning, resulting in a tugboat being called to escort the vessel and passengers being dropped off four hours late.

A track map shows the ferry started to perform a series of loops within Port Phillip Bay from about 4.40am, with the vessel only resuming its course towards Geelong about 8am.

The Spirit of Tasmania IV spent more than three hours performing a series of loops early on Saturday morning. (Supplied: MarineTraffic)

TT-Line chief executive Chris Carbone apologised for the inconvenience to passengers but said "safety is a more important consideration than meeting schedule".

"We experienced a minor technical issue with the primary navigational system, but at no point was Spirit of Tasmania IV at risk," Mr Carbone said.

"The secondary system performed as designed and the Master acted in accordance with his training."

The ABC understands the issue was related to the same steering fault that previously caused the Spirit IV to arrive four hours late into Geelong on November 5.

This is the second time the Spirit of Tasmania IV has been escorted into Geelong by a tugboat, following a similar incident in early November. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

One passenger posted on social media that the vessel was roughly on time before they were advised it "requires assistance from a tugboat", while another said it was "another day, another technical hitch" for Spirit IV.

Mr Carbone said the incident was "reported to the relevant authorities" and there was not expected to be any delay to the departure time for the Spirit IV's journey from Geelong to Devonport on Saturday night.

As a result of the incident in early November, TT-Line announced it had suspended the use of autopilot on the new vessels within Port Phillip Bay while it probed the steering faults.

That incident is being investigated by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, which is also looking into a separate steering fault which affected the Spirit V on a trial voyage in October.

The two vessels started ferrying passengers between Devonport and Geelong last month when they replaced the Spirit of Tasmania I and II.

World.title: The 4am Christmas Eve tradition this family can’t live without
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCity life The 4am Christmas Eve tradition this family can’t live without Rachael Ward November 21, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. By 4am on Christmas Eve morning, a family of self-described “carols fanatics” will have already secured prime position for Melbourne’s biggest carols concert. Well, that might not be the complete truth. It could be much earlier. “We don’t actually tell people because they try and beat us,” Nada Poke said with a laugh. “Our standard answer is 4am.” Hala Austin, Nada Poke, Paytn , Lilian Poke and Ashtyn are part of a family who arrives for Carols by Candlelight at 4am on Christmas Eve. Simon Schluter



Armed with blankets, chairs, games and enough food to last (at least) 12 hours until the gates open, Poke’s family has been first in line for Carols by Candlelight for more than a decade. Scoring a coveted spot as close to the stage as possible at the front of the lawn is the goal. Carols by candlelight rehearsal in 1947. The Age Their arrival 16 hours before the first song is sung has become part of their Christmas tradition, designed to be a reprieve from frantic festive preparations. Their numbers swell to more than 30 throughout the day, taking time to catch up with each other and their extended “carols family” made of other fans they only see in line once a year – although other groups tend to rock up after sunrise. While Poke and her mother, Lilian, have attended 27 concerts together, younger sister Hala Austin has been to 26. One Christmas Eve she went into labour and gave birth 45 minutes before the opening note, offering just enough time for a quick FaceTime call to induct her newborn daughter into the family ritual. “Christmas Eve is definitely more important than Christmas Day for us,” Austin said. “It just brings so much peace to our family, and we always look forward to it.



“It’s just for family, there’s no rushing, nothing to do. We just sit there and enjoy the moment together and listen to the music.” While hosts and the full list of performers have yet to be announced, the cast of The Shawshank Redemption stage production – Rodger Corser, David Berry and Bert LaBonté – will appear along with regular performers Marina Prior, Silvie Paladino, Denis Walter, David Hobson and Michael Paynter. A Christmas fixture in Melbourne since 1938, when the first concert was staged at Alexandra Gardens, Carols by Candlelight had an estimated 175,000-strong crowd in 1956, before the event shifted to the Sidney Myer Music Bowl in 1959. Claudia Gemes and son Finn, who is one of the thousands of children supported by Vision Australia. Joe Armao Nowadays, numbers are capped at 10,000. The concert aims to raise more than $2 million for children and young people connected to Vision Australia, including those not yet able to secure NDIS funding but in need of support.



One of them is Finn Gemes, a happy, loud three-year-old who loves playing, experimenting and moving around as much as possible. Finn Gemes is supported by Vision Australia and its Carols by Candlelight. Joe Armao He was born blind, but it took until after his first birthday for his genetic diagnosis to come back and his NDIS support to come through, so the family leant on Vision Australia during his early months. Finn Gemes uses a cane to navigate through the world. Joe Armao His mother, Claudia Gemes, said: “Unless you’re in it, you don’t really fully understand it and what it means, and how families, if that funding’s not there, how they are expected to navigate to support their children.”



Vision Australia NDIS funding specialist Caitlin McMorrow said that not all children were eligible for government funding, and when they were it could take months to access, but it’s important children receive assistance as early as possible. “Sometimes [with] the diagnosis, they haven’t managed to get one yet, or if they’re quite little, we might not always be sure what the degree of their vision impairment is yet,” she said. Finn is making quick progress and confidently walks around with his cane. Claudia has noticed a lack of awareness of how people, particularly children, with low vision or blindness navigate the world and appreciates the help from Vision Australia. “They just need that little bit of support. They might do things a little bit differently, but they always get there,” she said. Carols by Candlelight is at the Sidney Myer Music Bowl on December 24 and will be televised by Nine, the owner of this masthead. World.title: Teenage boy charged with orchestrating Melbourne bar wars firebombings
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Teenage boy charged with orchestrating Melbourne bar wars firebombings Hannah Hammoud and Rachael Ward Updated November 21, 2026 — 6:48pm ,first published 1:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A 17-year-old accused of operating the “Onepercent” account and directing a string of crimes linked to Melbourne’s so-called bar wars has been charged following a police investigation. The teenager was arrested on Friday after police appealed for information about the identity behind the online handle “Onepercent”. Police allege an arson attack on a Williamstown ice cream store was tasked out, with the business sustaining more than $600,000 worth of damage. Chris Hopkins Police allege the account was used to task and co-ordinate crimes through encrypted messaging apps, including arson attacks, a home invasion and a kidnapping. The 17-year-old, who was already on bail for other offences, has been charged with extortion, making threats to kill, criminal damage by fire, armed home invasion and trafficking drugs including cocaine, human growth hormone, testosterone and peptides.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Nightclub promoter believed to be intended target of botched kidnapping Detectives allege “Onepercent” was responsible for directing several incidents linked to attacks on Melbourne licensed venues and other properties earlier this year, including arson attacks in South Melbourne, Williamstown and Moonee Ponds, as well as a home invasion and mistaken identity kidnapping in Springvale. Police executed a search warrant at the teenager’s home, seizing a trafficable amount of cocaine, three mobile phones and cash. He did not apply for bail as he faced court on Saturday. Charge sheets released to media detail allegations he made a demand on a family in Epping on January 28 that if they did not repay an outstanding debt on behalf of their son then he would burn the house down and made threats to kill.



The document states a threat to kill was allegedly made “intending that the [redacted] family would fear such a threat would be carried out or being reckless as to whether or not the [redacted] family would fear that the said threat would be carried out,” the court document states. He is also charged with destroying Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on March 22 by arson, setting fire to two cars in Moonee Ponds on March 29 – including a $124,000 Land Rover Defender – and trespassing in the Springvale home on April 18 armed with a knife with intent to assault someone he knew was present. On Saturday, a court heard he has been diagnosed with ADHD, has mild asthma and a severe allergy to grass and dust mites. Operation Eclipse was established on April 27 to target serious and organised crime syndicates believed to be behind a series of offences linked to Melbourne’s hospitality industry. The operation is led by specialist detectives from the Gang Crime Squad, Armed Crime Squad and Arson and Explosives Squad, working alongside local police and regional investigators.



Related Article Exclusive

Organised crime Alleged ‘bar wars’ shot caller was released early from youth detention Detective Inspector Graham Banks, from Operation Eclipse, said the arrest highlighted the concerning use of encrypted applications to co-ordinate serious violence. “Offences such as arson and kidnapping are not low-level offences. They are violent crimes that can have life-changing consequences for victims and create fear within our community,” he said. “Following our appeal for information we’ve been able to progress the investigation, and we would like to thank members of the public and the media for their assistance. “Victoria Police will continue to identify, target and dismantle the activity of those responsible for serious criminal activity and hold them to account for the harm they cause to our community.”



Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or submit a confidential report at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Beware who you jettison, PM
World.content:
If Paul Sakkal is right about Labor factions seeking to marginalise Jim Chalmers, and I very much doubt he is, Anthony Albanese will be making the biggest mistake of his career (“Fractured Albanese-Chalmers ties force Labor to consider policy reset”, November 15). It was Chalmers who persuaded the prime minister to alter the unfair tax reforms of the Coalition and to ensure that lower income groups were also looked after, and the electorate rewarded Labor for breaking a promise and emerging with a fairer policy by giving the party its greatest victory since federation. Now Albanese has joined Chalmers in agreeing to rectify the very lopsided benefits that asset-rich investors have over everyday first home buyers, some bed-wetters in the Labor caucus think it’s a step too far. It is a long-overdue reform and still kind to investors, allowing them to keep what they have, but, unlike John Howard’s lopsided largesse to many investors, it will immensely increase the chances of many long sought to have their own home. Chalmers is our best treasurer since Paul Keating, and if Albanese jettisons him, he can say goodbye to the next general election. Frank Carroll, Moorooka (Qld)

They must speak up, we must listen

Noting that male political leaders Matt Canavan and Angus Taylor passed up the opportunity to support consent education, Jacqueline Maley throws the enormous challenge to all of us: empower children to know and speak up when they are being abused and sensitise adults to listen to little people (“Time to create a culture that will close the book on sex predators”, November 15). And teach little girls and boys to blather, to be open and not keep secrets! Frederika Steen, Chapel Hill (Qld)

This article asks how serious we are about child safety. Do writers of children’s books even have a Working with Children Check (WWCC) processed? It has long baffled me how it seems anyone can write a children’s book without scrutiny, yet you need a WWCC to volunteer at your child’s canteen. Also, let’s stop sports players from bringing their children onfield or being interviewed post-match. It is irrelevant and unnecessary. And in an environment of gambling and alcohol, it is inappropriate. Jenny Stephenson, Wollongong

Equal pay for teachers

The placement of two articles on one page (“New approach helping schools to protect students from bullying” and “Top Sydney private schools poised for huge fee increases”, November 15) captured the dark irony of Australia’s school system. The second described overfunded, high-fee independent schools behaving like bullies: using their financial clout to grab more than their fair share of teachers, at the expense of under-funded schools where students need them more. Parents are advised that this is necessary if they want to ensure their own children have the supply and quality of teaching they need to maintain their advantage. These schools often blame inflation for their fee hikes, but their increases frequently exceed it. They also fail to mention that government grants are indexed annually to the Schooling Resource Standard, preserving their real value. Australia has among the highest teacher shortages in the OECD. Independent schools are now the fastest growing part of our school system and the sector that contributes most to the unfair distribution of teachers. Catholic systems are not the problem here, setting their salary rates largely in line with public schools. But while public schools in particular are being starved of teachers, wealthier independent schools celebrate their surplus. The Commonwealth should act immediately, requiring states and territories to make the registration of private schools conditional on paying teachers the same salaries as award salaries for teachers in public schools … no more and no less! Lyndsay Connors, Ashfield

World.title: Roos, Demons storm into AFLW grand final after Ticketmaster outage wreaks havoc for fans
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFLW Roos, Demons storm into AFLW grand final after Ticketmaster outage wreaks havoc for fans Hannah Kennelly Updated November 21, 2026 — 6:21pm ,first published 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

North Melbourne outlasted a valiant Sydney to book their place in a fourth consecutive grand final, storming to a 32-point victory in front of a roaring crowd at Ikon Park, 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51). A global Ticketmaster outage initially wrought havoc on Saturday’s AFLW preliminary final double-header, with long queues of frustrated footy fans left waiting to get into the stadium midway through the first quarter. View post on X Fans took to social media to complain about the outage, with a Ticketmaster spokesperson confirming the team was “actively looking into it” and would “share updates as soon as they are available”. An AFL spokesperson confirmed the global Ticketmaster outage to this masthead.



The Swans got off to a blistering start, with Cynthia Hamilton booting the game’s opening goal in just 21 seconds – one of the fastest opening goals in AFLW history. Backed by a roaring blue-and-white crowd, the North juggernaut kicked into gear, with Jasmine Garner kick-starting a string of goals. Suddenly, the Swans were in trouble, staring down the barrel of a 36-point deficit in the second term. View post on X But, just like in last week’s breathtaking final against Geelong, Swans superstar Chloe Molloy was a telling standout. Molloy kicked her first goal of the game in the second term, becoming the first player in AFLW history to kick 20 goals in a seven-game stretch, breaking the record of 19 set by Aishling Moloney in 2024.



Tensions flared in the second quarter after Roos veteran Emma Kearney (a columnist for this masthead) was caught holding the ball, giving away a free kick to Molloy, who converted. When the star Swan celebrated, Kearney ran up to mock celebrate alongside the Sydney crew, with a few jumper grabs and push and shoves included for good measure. It only seemed to inspire Molloy, who kicked her third consecutive goal moments later. Emma Kearney assesses her options down the ground in North’s clash with Sydney. AFL Photos After another pivotal goal from Hamilton in the third, the Swans found themselves within 12 points of the Roos and with all the momentum. A soccer-like goal from Blaithin Bogue kept the two-time reigning premiers ahead, but the Swans hit back with a goal in the opening minute of the final term from young star Maddie Quinn. As the clock ticked down, both sides wrestled for momentum and amped up the pressure. But, seemingly as always, the Roos remained one step ahead, with Garner and Bella Eddey slotting goals to extinguish Sydney’s hopes of a maiden grand final berth.



Swans coach Colin O’Riordan said while the result was a disappointing one for his group, he was proud of their ability to face adversity throughout the season – on-field and off. “[We’re] pretty disappointed, that’s a given,” he said. Emma Kearney (left) and the Roos belt out their famous song. AFL Photos “You’ve just lost a brilliant final, so yeah, the group is shattered.” Kearney was at her hard-nosed best for the Roos, while league medallist Ash Riddell finished with a game-high 29 touches to go with her seven clearances and 337 metres gained.



A beaming North Melbourne coach Darren Crocker said his group would not discuss the potential of a historic three-peat, instead remaining process-focused in the build-up to the decider. “The Swans brought some things that troubled us,” he said in his post-match press conference. “So we’ll need to actually have a drill-down. We’ll have a good look at those, but for us, it’ll be what does our best footy look like? … We have a great opportunity to try to bring that best football one more time for this season.” Ahead of Monday night’s AFLW best-and-fairest award count, Crocker was asked about Garner’s chances of taking out the top gong. Despite being one of the best players in the competition, the 32-year-old has never won the league’s highest honour, losing out to teammate Riddell last year. “I think she’s [Garner is] a generational player,” Crocker said simply.



“We’ll be talking about her in a number of years’ time, about this period of AFLW and its infancy, but I know that that would be the furthest thing from her mind. All she would be focusing on is, how does she help the team win next week?” Despite Kim Rennie limping off the field, North Melbourne stressed it was just a cramp. Demons far too good for depleted Blues When the siren blared, Melbourne captain Kate Hore threw her hands in the air and rushed to embrace her teammates. On a sun-soaked Saturday afternoon, Hore and the Demons delivered a third quarter to remember, booking a spot in Friday night’s grand final against North Melbourne with a 30-point win over the besieged Blues, 10.15 (75) to 6.9 (45).



It was a low-scoring first half, with the only goal of the opening term belonging to Hore, but the Blues leapt to live in the second, thanks to dependable Irishwoman Erone Fitzpatrick, followed by another from Nell Morris-Dalton. The Demons entered this preliminary final as favourites, but the Blues were putting up a real fight, with Fitzpatrick stealing another goal in the dying seconds of the second quarter. Tyla Hanks celebrates a goal with Kate Hore. Getty Images Cue the Melbourne goal onslaught. First came Tayla Harris, then Alyssa Bannan, another from Hore, and a goal from Maggie Mahony in the third. The three-quarter-time siren went, and the Blues found themselves looking at a bleak scoreboard and a 26-point deficit.



A goal from former rising star nominee Poppy Scholz breathed life back into Carlton’s grand final dreams, but two dribbling goals from Megan Fitzsimon quickly snuffed that out as the Demons booked their first grand final appearance since 2022. View post on X On Saturday, the AFL announced Brisbane indie group The Jungle Giants as the pre-game entertainment for the grand final, with Australian songstress Kate Miller-Heidke to perform the national anthem. The Demons and Roos last faced each other in round seven, with Melbourne losing the highly anticipated clash by 31 points. However, first-year Melbourne coach Tom Wilson said North Melbourne should prepare to encounter a changed Demons side in the grand final.



“We’re probably a different side now than what we were back in round seven. Ultimately, you keep evolving, don’t you,” he said. “They’ve [North Melbourne] got the runs on the board, but I’m really proud of our playing group. I’m really confident in our playing group, I’ll back our playing group in every day of the week.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Gringotts bangs Gong for third time to set Big Dance record straight
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Gringotts bangs Gong for third time to set Big Dance record straight Craig Kerry November 21, 2026 — 5:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Ciaron Maher camp could spell Gringotts and look to the $2 million All Star Mile after the seven-year-old bounced back from a luckless Big Dance run to claim a hat-trick of victories in the $1 million The Gong (1600m) at Kembla. Gringotts, a $2.30 favourite carting 61 kilograms from an ideal draw in two, raced just off front-runners Formal Display and Perfumist under Nash Rawiller before taking over at the 100m to score a one-and-a-quarter-length win. Nash Rawiller salutes on Gringotts in The Gong. Getty Images Annabel and Rob Archibald-trained Formal Display, which was first across the line in the $3 million Big Dance before losing a protest to fourth-placed Gringotts for interference at the 600m, stuck on for second. Kris Lees-trained Tavi Time was third. The win, Gringotts’ first since last year’s Gong, was a satisfying one for Rawiller and connections after the Big Dance protest, which has been much debated.



“It’s hard to know last start what should have happened,” Maher assistant trainer Johann Gerard-Dubord said. “Nash was pretty adamant he would have won, but you just wouldn’t know. Today there was no excuse there. He ended up in a good spot and he was just too good for them.” Nash Rawiller after winning on Gringotts. Getty Images The victory took Gringotts to $7.5 million in earnings and qualifies him again for November’s Big Dance, which he won in 2024 and 2025. Rawiller won the Gong on Gringotts last year, while Tommy Berry rode him in 2024. The victory gave Maher four consecutive Gong titles, after Detonator Jack won in 2023. Gerard-Dubord said Gringotts would be back for the Gong next year, while the All Star Mile in March at Flemington could be a new target.



“We’ll see how he comes through it,” he said. “He’s run in the Ingham [three weeks later] the last two years. Both times, probably a bit of a pass. “We could stop now, and then there’s some good races in the autumn. “There’s a race like the All-Star Mile, which obviously he’s never run in because he’s been going to the Ingham, so we could save him for that, but it’s job done to get that win today. “It’s been a frustrating prep. He’s been going really well. Obviously, the Big Dance was his main target and he didn’t get much luck. “He’s just a marvel. He keeps showing up. He’s been so consistent. He obviously loves this track, loves this day and great for the owners to win today.



“Obviously, he hasn’t won for 12 months. He’s been contesting some top-grade races. He’s been racing against the best weight-for-age horses.” Rawiller, who earlier won on Graffiti Tycoon, won the last on Ripley to give himself a treble and Maher a double on the day. Reece Jones was suspended for three meetings but will not miss a Saturday meeting after pleading guilty to careless riding at the 50m of the Gong on seventh-placed Matias when it shifted ground. Exciting Queenslander goes the distance It was third time lucky at Kembla in a huge way for Queensland trainer Jack Bruce after Earn To Burn proved himself in open company and gave his trainer his richest race win with an impressive performance in the $300,000 The Warra (1000m).



Bruce, who worked for leading trainers Bjorn Baker, Chris Waller, Ciaron Maher and John O’Shea before going out on his own in 2022, opted to bring the promising four-year-old on the long road to Kembla instead of the listed Swiss Plate at the Sunshine Coast for his first-up assignment after back-to-back listed Queensland wins in three-year-old races last preparation. His faith in Earn To Burn, a $2.05 favourite, was rewarded as Kerrin McEvoy settled him in third spot before he motored past the leaders late for a one-length victory over the fast-finishing The Black Cloud, which was also second in the Warra last year. Fire Star was third. Earn To Burn wins The Warra. Getty Images “I brought a stayer down once here who didn’t run any good and I ran one in an Inglis bonus race, but he drew wide and was off the track the whole way,” Bruce said of his past runners at Kembla. “You need a bit of luck in this game.



Jack Bruce. Getty Images “When they went out quick and [Earn To Burn] had to take a sit, I was a little bit concerned, but once he got balanced up, that’s when he really hit top gear, and that’s what’s helped on the big track at Kembla. He likes that space to move and he got that today.” Bruce said the main aim now with Earn To Burn was the $1 million Magic Million Snippets (1200m) at the Gold Coast in January. “The road there’s not easy because you’re going back to the summer carnival against the A-graders in Brisbane, but somehow, we’ll pick our path through,” he said. “It’s a long way to come [for the Warra], but it’s going to be good for him in the long run. Maybe less ideal coming down now, but to season them up and to turn them into the horse that he needs to be, that’s what he needs to do. He needs to be able to do this.



“He’s always been a raw talent ... and now we’re starting to see the finished product.” Warra prospect a boost for Baker camp The Bjorn Baker camp was looking to the $300,000 Warra (1000m) next year after Compensation claimed the benchmark 78 handicap over the trip on Saturday as part of a morale-boosting double for the Warwick Farm stable. Fading to fourth first-up at Randwick, Compensation led this time under Rachel King and kicked clear before Cassiel fell just short with a late charge. “He’s just jump and run, and that’s all he is,” Baker foreman Glen Lobb said.



“I think [apprentice] Amber [Riddell] last time riding, she just had trouble holding him, and they went 9.4 or something the first furlong after the initial jump and he just got tired late. “Rach rides him great and I thought today she might be the difference.” Baker, who earlier won with Horseshoe Hill, was inconsolable this week after the loss of Melbourne Cup runner So You Are to colic on Monday, then the fallout from footage of the five-year-old’s body in a skip bin on Tuesday at the Cleanaway Lucas Heights waste facility, where it was disposed by a contractor for Randwick Equine Centre. Tycoon puts writing on the wall Co-trainer Tom Charlton was looking to Big Dance qualifiers, potentially starting with the Mudgee Cup (1600m) on December 4, with Graffiti Tycoon after the four-year-old powered away late for a third consecutive win.



The $1.70 favourite, second in all three starts as a three-year-old, jumped well and sat second under Nash Rawiller in the 1400m benchmark 78 handicap before easily holding off Fiddlers Green and Bella Khadijah. “What a polished individual he’s turning out to be, and full credit to everyone who’s been a part of that, because he wasn’t very straightforward and he still has his quirks,” Charlton said. “So to see him put a performance there where he just did everything, jumped in front. I mean, who would have thought that during the winter, so fantastic. And to do that grade-wise, a maiden, 64, 78, and with a kilo over. He’s got a massive cruising speed and he’s a nice horse.” Charlton said the 2027 $3 million Big Dance (1600m) in November at Randwick had been talked about as a possible target. Jamberoo, with Dylan Gibbons aboard, gave Charlton and co-trainer John O’Shea a double when it caused a boilover at $31 in the 1600m benchmark 88 handicap.



Thompson times run to perfection Randwick trainer John Thompson and jockey Kerrin McEvoy made all the right moves with Picture Perfect to score a timely win for ailing owner and Hall of Fame trainer Neville Begg in the Midway Handicap. The five-year-old mare, second-up off a seventh over 1200m at Rosehill, stormed down the centre of the track late to beat local long-shot Audenzia ($81) by half a length in the 1400m benchmark 72. Thompson said Picture Perfect needed the first up run, the addition of blinkers helped and she got the tempo she needed to finish off on Saturday in what was a second win in five starts for his stable since coming from Begg’s son, Grahame, in Victoria. He hoped the victory would give 95-year-old Begg a boost.



“Neville wanted a few horses up here to race and it’s pretty timely, it might give him a bit of a lift,” Thompson said. Related Article Opinion

Horse racing The disposal of So You Are has shocked the racing industry just as much as the public Kim Waugh Australian horse trainer “He’s not very well at all and is in hospital, so hopefully that cheers him up.” McEvoy, who found the best ground down the centre of the track after a start in gate 12 of 15, also gave a shout-out to Begg. To apprentice Siena Grima won the first, a class 3 Highway Handicap (1400m), on Todd Howlett-trained Athena’s Treasure in almost identical, but more dominant, style from a wide gate. Tommy Berry repeated the dose on Chris Waller-trained Donatello in the third, a 2000m benchmark 78. James McDonald showed there was a path to victory closer to the inside fence when Baker-trained favourite Horseshoe Hill, starting in gate one, surged between runners for a two-length win. It was McDonald’s first time riding at the Gong meeting since 2023, when he had a win with Unanimous.

World.title: Australia vs England LIVE updates: Fox Cricket stand down Khawaja, Warner ahead of T20 as Sandpapergate swirls
World.content:
Retired Test greats David Warner and Usman Khawaja have been removed from the Fox Sports’ cricket commentary team until the fall-out over the sandpaper ball-tampering scandal has eased.

Fox Sports managing director Steve Crawley confirmed to this masthead on Saturday that Warner and Khawaja, central figures in the drama which has enveloped Australian cricket for a fortnight, were unlikely to be on camera for their own best interests during Australia’s Twenty20 series against England.

Usman Khawaja and David Warner have been openly critical of Pat Cummins’ statements about who knew what in Cape Town. They have been temporarily removed from Fox Sports’ commentary team. Getty

Warner and Khawaja were absent from Saturday night’s opening clash at the MCG, but it’s hoped they return in time for next month’s home Test series against New Zealand.

“In light of recent events both Usman and Davey will be rested from our broadcasts over the next few weeks,” Crawley said.

“While we always support all members of our commentary team and welcome a diversity of views which is a feature of our summer of cricket we also understand the pressure they are under to respond to each and every new comment.

“We think it is increasingly difficult to focus on the game while the situation continues to unfold and think it is unfair on both commentators to put them in that position.

“Our focus remains on providing our viewers with the best broadcast of Australia’s summer of cricket. We will continue to monitor the situation.″⁣

Khawaja relit the Sandpapergate firestorm by declaring in his just-released autobiography that all players in the infamous Cape Town Test against South Africa in 2018 knew about the ball tampering, contradicting now captain Pat Cummins and his fellow bowlers, who have maintained their innocence.

Warner has backed Khawaja’s version of events, each adding fuel to the fire with their comments during Fox Sports’ coverage of the just-completed one-day international series, which England won 2-1.

World.title: Why Cricket Australia board provided ‘unanimous support’ for Cummins to remain as Test captain
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Why Cricket Australia board provided ‘unanimous support’ for Cummins to remain as Test captain Tom Decent and Hannah Hammoud Updated November 21, 2026 — 5:16pm ,first published November 21, 2026 — 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cricket Australia chairman David Boon wants the latest Sandpapergate saga put to bed before the first Test in Perth, as his board rallied in solidarity behind Pat Cummins following a turbulent fortnight, throwing its unequivocal support behind him to remain captain. The CA board met several times this week to discuss the fallout from Australia’s infamous 2018 tour of South Africa. On Thursday evening the board agreed that there was no reason to reconsider Cummins’ position despite explosive allegations from Cameron Bancroft that everyone in the team knew of the ball-tampering plot eight years ago. Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood during NSW Blues training in Sydney on Thursday. Kate Geraghty Boon flew to Sydney with CA chief executive Todd Greenberg for a meeting on Friday with Cummins and his manager Neil Maxwell at a “private location”, according to the former Australian batsman, to personally convey the board’s unanimous support and check on the welfare of the under-pressure fast bowler. Sources not authorised to comment publicly on the matter said the meeting was at a house in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. On Saturday, CA confirmed this masthead’s report that Cummins would remain in charge of Australia’s Test team for the opening match of the summer against New Zealand in Perth on December 9.



“[The CA board] chatted it out for quite a considerable amount of time,” Boon told this masthead. “My belief [is] we need solidarity and we need stability. Pat has without a doubt over the last five years been an outstanding leader and he has been a focal point of a rebuild of the culture in the Australian cricket team. “We saw absolutely no reason to reconsider his role. Every single board member backs his leadership and integrity. Loading “My strong feeling is that there’s a lot of people out there who love the game of cricket and might be a little bit over this [saga]. We know there are things that have got to happen for it to be finally put to bed and we are trying to ensure that occurs over the next short period of time. Hopefully, it settles down right now before the first Test starts in Perth.” Central to that process is the establishment of an independent forum, announced by CA earlier this week, to allow players and staff involved in the 2018 tour to give their accounts of what happened. Further details are expected in the coming days, with several prominent players indicating their willingness to participate.



Cummins confirmed on Saturday, in a statement released by CA, that he would attend the forum and share his recollections of 2018, which differ from accounts given by the likes of Usman Khawaja, David Warner, Bancroft and Chadd Sayers. “I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there,” Cummins said. “All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Loading “Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority. “It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly.”



Boon said the willingness of Cummins, Khawaja and Bancroft to participate was encouraging, but all eyes will be on whether Warner attends. “I think that’s a great show of faith in the process that we’re establishing,” Boon said. “We’re extremely respectful of all opinions and all views. It’s up to us to take responsibility, take ownership, and sort this out as best we possibly can with the interests of Australian cricket at the forefront of mind.” Pat Cummins answered questions for well over an hour. Sam Mooy Boon admitted he had been saddened by the events of the past fortnight and said player welfare was a major consideration behind Friday’s meeting with Cummins, who has had reporters stationed outside his Sydney home. Other members of the 2018 team, including Steve Smith, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, have also found themselves under scrutiny as fresh questions emerge about what happened in South Africa. The bowlers’ accounts differ from Bancroft, Khawaja and Warner.



“They’re all feeling the pressure,” Boon said. “What we think is paramount in anything like this is the welfare of our players – not only Pat – but the rest of the team and expressing the fact that we support them in every way. “Our support for the whole team is unequivocally strong and this includes supporting Steve Smith, Mitch Marsh, all the team members, and the staff.” Asked if Cummins had indicated he wanted to remain Test captain, Boon said: “Yeah, I sensed that. I think Pat is extremely proud to be the Australian captain and he wants to continue to do that. “We want Australian cricket to be what it should be. That’s a national sport for everybody and the pride of the nation. The game needs to unite. It needs to move on together and we need to do everything in our power to make that happen.” The announcement of Australia’s Test squad for the New Zealand series has been delayed amid the controversy – that is expected some time next week after the upcoming round of Sheffield Shield – while some players have been shielded from facing the media as CA attempts to contain the fallout.



Despite the turmoil, and Australia’s 2-1 series defeat in South Africa last month, Boon is confident the team will be ready for the opening Test in Perth. “We’re in a position with the support that’s provided, the talent that we have, that we can move forward and be ready to play by that time,” he said. Loading It comes as Hazlewood broke his silence over the ball-tampering scandal and launched a strong defence of Cummins. Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood rejected suggestions that Australia’s bowling attack knew about the use of sandpaper during the third Test against South Africa, insisting he had no involvement in, or knowledge of, any plan to alter the condition of the ball.



Hazlewood admitted he would reconsider his place in the Test side, should Cummins lose the captaincy. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Pat Cummins is under siege. His manager blames ‘hysteria unfounded in reality’ Hazlewood said while he was sympathetic about the “ridiculous” suspensions Bancroft, Smith and Warner received for their part in the scandal, there was a distinction between assuming teammates knew about the ball-tampering operation and having actual knowledge of it. “Assuming everyone knows and actually knowing everyone knows – that gap is huge. That’s a big chasm,” Hazlewood said. His comments come after Bancroft reignited the controversy through a recent column detailing his recollections of the scandal and questioning the extent of the bowling group’s knowledge.



Hazlewood acknowledged that Australia’s team environment was fractured at the time, with divisions between batsmen and bowlers contributing to a toxic dressing-room culture. But he rejected claims that the entire team was aware of what was happening. “No [I had no knowledge of ball tampering taking place in that series]. We were interviewed straight after [Cape Town] and I trust what I said in that two-three hour interrogation more than anything because it was in the day or two after,” Hazlewood said. “It was fresh in my mind at that point. Two things stand out for me from what’s been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field? “The answer is no. When it boils down to it, I think those two points are crucial.” The experienced fast bowler also threw his support behind Cummins, praising the Australian captain for transforming the team’s culture following the events of 2018.



“It feels like it’s been a bit of a pile-on the last few days from different people. I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood said. Related Article Opinion

Australian cricket Cummins’ captaincy in peril after Bancroft’s sandpaper revelations Daniel Brettig Chief cricket writer “To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again – I think is just a remarkable job. He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.” Hazlewood went on to warn that stripping Cummins of the captaincy would plunge the Australian team into turmoil. When pressed on whether he might walk away from the Test team in protest, he conceded it was a scenario he would carefully weigh. “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah,” he said.



Addressing the original allegations, Hazlewood insisted he had no knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper, including suggestions that those discussions took place in the Port Elizabeth dressing room before Bancroft carried out the act. Tea breaks, he said, were generally busy periods for bowlers, who were preparing their equipment and getting back onto the field, often without engaging in conversations among other players. “As bowlers in a tea break. You’ve only got 20 minutes, so I’m probably changing all my gear, and I’m getting out on the field earlier to bowl to whoever wants to catch, probably the fielding coach,” he said. “It’s a lot different to lunch where you sit down and touch on things about how the game is going. Tea breaks are a very busy time.” Hazlewood also dismissed suggestions that bowlers should have recognised the ball had been illegally altered. Explaining that his usual routine was to receive the ball shortly before beginning his run-up, briefly check its condition and then bowl.

Police are appealing for witnesses to a random daylight stabbing in Melbourne’s Bourke Street Mall that has left a 24-year-old man in critical condition. Police at the site of a stabbing in the Melbourne CBD on Saturday. Shelby Brooks The young man, who was understood to be enjoying a day out in the CBD with his partner, was stabbed once in the chest while outside the H&M store near the corner of Elizabeth Street about 2.30pm on Saturday, police say. The attack was “without provocation” and the alleged offender was last seen running north along Elizabeth Street towards Little Bourke Street, Inspector Dale Huntington said. Police are scouring the streets for the alleged offender, who has been described as a “dishevelled”-looking 30-year-old Caucasian male, with a beard and white T-shirt.



Huntington said the alleged offender was known to police and CCTV was being used to track him down but asked the public to call 000 if they recognised him. Anyone who witnessed the altercation has been asked to call Crimestoppers on 1800 333 000. Police want to speak to a man regarding a knife attack in Bourke Street Mall. Victoria Police The man might have changed his appearance by putting on more clothing and might have been holding a sleeping bag, Huntington said. Investigators are asking for Evan Liatsas, or anyone who may know his whereabouts, to contact police.



Huntington stressed that random stabbings were rare. The victim was taken to Royal Melbourne Hospital with upper body injuries and was in critical condition, an Ambulance Victoria spokesperson confirmed. A witness who said he had arrived at the scene shortly after the incident said he saw a young man sat on the steps of H&M on Elizabeth Street holding his chest. Blood could be seen on the steps of the GPO building on Elizabeth St. Christopher Hopkins “There was quite a bit of commotion. There was a lot of chaos and stress obviously,” the witness said.



The man said the victim “did a good job at staying calm”. The witness went on to say he saw a man “hopping” away from the scene in a sleeping bag. Peter Vadiveloo was busking on the corner of Bourke and Elizabeth streets for most of the day and said he heard yelling coming from behind him. Peter Vadiveloo was busking on the corner of Bourke and Elizabeth streets when a young man was stabbed. Shelby Brooks He said it was not unusual for a commotion to occur at the popular intersection.



He carried on playing while waves of police and ambulance arrived at the scene. “If I stopped playing every time something happened, I’d never finish a song,” he said. “I play a lot on the street, and you just see lots of people [experiencing homelessness] around, and they’re often my greatest fans. They sit on these steps, and for them, this is free music. They can’t afford to go to a pub and pay.” More to come

World.title: The 4am Christmas Eve tradition this family can’t live without
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCity life The 4am Christmas Eve tradition this family can’t live without Rachael Ward November 21, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. By 4am on Christmas Eve morning, a family of self-described “carols fanatics” will have already secured prime position for Melbourne’s biggest carols concert. Well, that might not be the complete truth. It could be much earlier. “We don’t actually tell people because they try and beat us,” Nada Poke said with a laugh. “Our standard answer is 4am.” Hala Austin, Nada Poke, Paytn , Lilian Poke and Ashtyn are part of a family who arrives for Carols by Candlelight at 4am on Christmas Eve. Simon Schluter



Armed with blankets, chairs, games and enough food to last (at least) 12 hours until the gates open, Poke’s family has been first in line for Carols by Candlelight for more than a decade. Scoring a coveted spot as close to the stage as possible at the front of the lawn is the goal. Carols by candlelight rehearsal in 1947. The Age Their arrival 16 hours before the first song is sung has become part of their Christmas tradition, designed to be a reprieve from frantic festive preparations. Their numbers swell to more than 30 throughout the day, taking time to catch up with each other and their extended “carols family” made of other fans they only see in line once a year – although other groups tend to rock up after sunrise. While Poke and her mother, Lilian, have attended 27 concerts together, younger sister Hala Austin has been to 26. One Christmas Eve she went into labour and gave birth 45 minutes before the opening note, offering just enough time for a quick FaceTime call to induct her newborn daughter into the family ritual. “Christmas Eve is definitely more important than Christmas Day for us,” Austin said. “It just brings so much peace to our family, and we always look forward to it.



“It’s just for family, there’s no rushing, nothing to do. We just sit there and enjoy the moment together and listen to the music.” While hosts and the full list of performers have yet to be announced, the cast of The Shawshank Redemption stage production – Rodger Corser, David Berry and Bert LaBonté – will appear along with regular performers Marina Prior, Silvie Paladino, Denis Walter, David Hobson and Michael Paynter. A Christmas fixture in Melbourne since 1938, when the first concert was staged at Alexandra Gardens, Carols by Candlelight had an estimated 175,000-strong crowd in 1956, before the event shifted to the Sidney Myer Music Bowl in 1959. Claudia Gemes and son Finn, who is one of the thousands of children supported by Vision Australia. Joe Armao Nowadays, numbers are capped at 10,000. The concert aims to raise more than $2 million for children and young people connected to Vision Australia, including those not yet able to secure NDIS funding but in need of support.



One of them is Finn Gemes, a happy, loud three-year-old who loves playing, experimenting and moving around as much as possible. Finn Gemes is supported by Vision Australia and its Carols by Candlelight. Joe Armao He was born blind, but it took until after his first birthday for his genetic diagnosis to come back and his NDIS support to come through, so the family leant on Vision Australia during his early months. Finn Gemes uses a cane to navigate through the world. Joe Armao His mother, Claudia Gemes, said: “Unless you’re in it, you don’t really fully understand it and what it means, and how families, if that funding’s not there, how they are expected to navigate to support their children.”



Vision Australia NDIS funding specialist Caitlin McMorrow said that not all children were eligible for government funding, and when they were it could take months to access, but it’s important children receive assistance as early as possible. “Sometimes [with] the diagnosis, they haven’t managed to get one yet, or if they’re quite little, we might not always be sure what the degree of their vision impairment is yet,” she said. Finn is making quick progress and confidently walks around with his cane. Claudia has noticed a lack of awareness of how people, particularly children, with low vision or blindness navigate the world and appreciates the help from Vision Australia. “They just need that little bit of support. They might do things a little bit differently, but they always get there,” she said. Carols by Candlelight is at the Sidney Myer Music Bowl on December 24 and will be televised by Nine, the owner of this masthead. World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Teenage boy charged with orchestrating Melbourne bar wars firebombings Hannah Hammoud and Rachael Ward Updated November 21, 2026 — 6:48pm ,first published 1:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
