World.title: Half of Kiwi adults are skipping the dentist
World.content:
The latest health survey shows half of adults aren't going to the dentist when they should.

An advocate for free dental care says the lack of access to dentists is a public health crisis, and New Zealand risks billions in lost productivity and quality of life.

Dental for All campaigner Hana Pilkinton-Ching said the survey showed 52 percent of New Zealanders aren't attending check-ups.

"Around the half of the population either never goes to the dentist, or only goes when there's problems, which shows that there's a really large part of the population which isn't getting the preventative care they need," she said.

"That lack of access to care directly impacts the rest of people's health and wellbeing, and does add more strain to the health system."

The NZ Health Survey also showed that 42.6 percent of adults reported an unmet need for dental care due to its cost.

Pilkinton-Ching said that statistic had persisted over several years.

"Sadly it's already been this way for many years, more than four in 10 adults not accessing dental care due to cost for more than five years now," she said.

"Which should be taken seriously by the Government and seen as a crisis in access to oral healthcare."

She noted 75.3 percent of adults had reported their oral health was "good, very good or excellent", but this was down from 79.6 percent in 2020/21.

Ignoring the issue carried an economic cost, she said.

World.title: Southland storm review has 'done nothing to restore public trust' - farmer
World.content:
A Southland Federated Farmers board member says he has no confidence the local Emergency Management response has improved on the response to a storm seen last year.

In October 2025, a destructive storm with winds up to 180km/h caused widespread damage and power cuts.

A review of Emergency Management Southland's response found a number of problems, including poor communication and stretched staffing.

Southland Federated Farmers executive member Chris Dillon says Emergency Management ignored people with local knowledge and failed to take timely action.

"What they've done in the review is got one of their bureaucratic mates to do the review and to make sure that they covered their own arses.

"They haven't addressed any of the main shortcomings in the whole event and that's why they've done nothing to restore public trust."

Formal emergency procedures were largely followed, the review found.

But it also found that people in governance roles during the emergency were not getting the right information at the right time, or in the right format to do their jobs effectively.

The review made several recommendations, including:

increasing the pool of trained, competent staff genuinely available to work in the Emergency Coordination Centre

updating plans and policies to reflect the Emergency Management Act 2026

introducing an operational system providing real-time information, coordination and record-keeping that approved councils and agencies could access.

World.title: Caution urged as more travel booking sites hacked
World.content:
The Travel Agents' Association is urging travellers to be vigilant after an influx of scams using data from the likes of Expedia and Booking.com.

Travel booking companies Bookit, Booking.com and most recently Expedia have each confirmed data breaches in recent months.

Travel Agents' Association chief executive Julie White said that data had allowed scammers to make convincing phishing attempts.

"The thing is, they're so sophisticated. Most will actually know your name, the dates you're travelling," she said.

"What's common is 'please update your card details, we've had an error in the system.' You should not be asked that."

University of Auckland Professor of Commercial Law Alex Sims said scammers were also using AI to generate websites that looked very similar to legitimate providers.

"There's websites with AI now that look really convincing, and people are booking directly, thinking they're booking with a legitimate accommodation provider," she said.

"Yes, you know it's a real hotel, but you don't realise you're actually dealing with a fake website."

Julie White said travellers should consider booking with local providers or travel agents to make sure they would be protected by New Zealand's consumer rights laws.

"There's very little recourse if travellers have booked with an offshore third party. New Zealand law does not cross over into other jurisdictions," she said.

World.title: NZ lamb 'complementary' to US production, exporters insist
World.content:
A longstanding New Zealand lamb exporter is echoing descriptions of sheepmeat exports as "complementary" to United States-grown lamb, where it is considered a minority meat.

It came as Australia and New Zealand's sheepmeat industries faced increased scrutiny, among other lamb exporting nations, from US officials looking to protect their domestic industry from imports.

For nearly four decades, Atkins Ranch has exported lamb from New Zealand farms to the US, where it has a processing plant and a retail team.

Audio player for " Morning rural news for 16 November 2026 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2720289%2Fnz-lamb-complementary-to-us-production-exporters-insist

Morning rural news for 16 November 2026 Rural News Download MP3 4m

Now collecting carcasses from 150 farms, its product range and retail presence have continued to grow there over the years.

It had worked with its major customer natural foods giant Whole Foods Market since the early 1990s.

Atkins Ranch chief executive Pat Maher. Supplied / Atkins Ranch

Chief executive Pat Maher said the New Zealand company saw significant growth in US sales year-on-year in both value and volume.

"We view ourselves as complementary to the US lamb that's grown, and we fill the gaps that they can't," he said.

"They only harvest two million lambs a year in the States, so they've got to get their lamb racks and their other cuts from somewhere else, and that's where Australia and ourselves help out."

Maher said it was actually trying to get American consumers to eat more lamb, and grow the market.

"Our focus is for consumers to eat more lamb because it's still a minority protein in the States, it's less than three to four percent of meat sales in America, so there's room to grow."

NZ pushes back on alleged harm from exports

Representatives from New Zealand's sheepmeat sectors were defending their US exports, as part of a safeguard investigation launched by the US International Trade Commission in July.

Last week, the commission decided to progress its investigation into possible harm lamb imports were causing to its domestic farming industry, following a hearings process in October.

Commissioners were split in their decision, however. Australia was singled out as a substantial cause of serious injury or threat to the local industry.

Next, in the early New Year, it would recommend possible remedies - or not - to the administration, which could include further tariffs.

New Zealand lamb faced a similar protectionist investigation in the late 1990s.

Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay. RNZ / Nick Monro

Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay said New Zealand's share of US lamb consumption had remained stable over the past 20 years.

He said New Zealand was disappointed the commission would move the investigation to the next stage.

"New Zealand lamb exports do not harm US producers. Our lamb complements US production and helps meet growing consumer demand."

Beef and Lamb New Zealand's chairperson Kate Acland said while the outcome last week was "disappointing", its case was strengthened by some of the commissioners supporting New Zealand's case, and that imposing further import restrictions was unjustified.

"New Zealand farmers have faced the same challenges as the US domestic industry, such as declining sheep numbers, and have responded through sustained investment in genetics, research and farm management," she said.

"These are pressures on the whole sector, not the result of New Zealand lamb imports."

Beef and Lamb New Zealand's chairperson Kate Acland. © Clare Toia-Bailey / www.image-central.co.nz

New Zealand Trade and Enterprise's head of export customers, Dan Taylor, said there were always levels of uncertainty around global trade, but it, alongside the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, were supporting exporters.

He said red meat exporters capitalised on their high-quality, sustainable products including lamb, allowing them to command a premium on prices too.

"The US remains our biggest red meat export market, over $3.5 billion in the year to June 2026, and it really does complement their local production, which I think is an important part of the story, and meets that consumer demand for really high quality nutrient dense protein.

"I think that New Zealand has a role to play and New Zealand has a place in the market, finding those niches and delivering against them."

Meanwhile, Maher said Atkins Ranch was trying to capitalise on big demand for grass-fed red meat from US consumers, even looking to gradually grow its supply into the US.

"We are after more farmers to satisfy market needs," he said.

"We're in a bit of a growth patch at the moment, despite all the geopolitical headwinds that we're sort of facing, lamb continues to sell well."

These days Atkins specialised in regeneratively farmed sheep and other sustainability credentials and attributes.

Maher said it aimed for the higher end of the meat market, so while its farmers had to "jump through a few more hoops" to meet requirements like certified regenerative, it was worth it for greater returns.

"Generally those customers pay more for attributes, so animal welfare, grass fed, free range, GMO-free has been a big one in America," he said.

"And now we've moved into regenerative, better for the planet, so yeah, we're looking to target those conscious consumers."

In the year to June, the European Union was New Zealand's largest lamb export market, followed next by China and the US. The US market was worth around $600 million for New Zealand lamb in 2025.

Meanwhile, StatsNZ figures showed New Zealand's global lamb exports had increased to $5.19 billion in the year to June.

New Zealand officials and representatives would return to Washington DC for the remedy hearing on 1 December.

World.title: Cyclone-hit community gets revamped fire station to bolster disaster resilience
World.content:
A rural farming community in Hawke's Bay will be better prepared for any future weather crisis with the opening of an improved fire station.

Rissington, northwest of Napier, was cut off for several weeks when the bridge over the Mangaone River washed away during Cyclone Gabrielle.

Hawke's Bay Assistant District Commander Hamish Smith, from the Rissington Volunteer Fire Brigade, said the community was caught out quite badly when the extreme weather struck.

The emergency response was run out of a basic shed with no bathroom or meeting room, and everyone had a story about the position they were left in, he told RNZ.

"I think the instant isolation and the fact that the bridge washed away was high on that list for a number of the community, because that was their access to Napier and Hastings, that was their access to employment, that was their access for all their needs around food, welfare, doctor services, pharmacies, supermarkets.

"Some people were even more affected because they went to the end of their driveway and the road had either washed away or there had been slips of land, so they couldn't leave home for a number of days."

Smith said the new hub was purpose-built.

Multiple fire brigades will have access to the new facility. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

"Instead of a shed with fire appliances they've got toilets, which they never had before, showers, plenty of water storage and a meeting room, so they can actually use it as a hub and they can coordinate a response to any emergency," Smith said.

The improved building also had a kitchenette, office and training room. It could also accommodate community groups which wanted to hold meetings.

Smith said most of the building's costs were met by Fire and Emergency New Zealand, but the Rissington brigade put in $67,000 of its own saved funds. The project also had significant support from other organisations and the local community.

The Rissington Volunteer Fire Brigade has 10 firefighters and three supporting roles.

It's one of three brigades along the 50-kilometre-long Puketitiri Road, stretching inland between Napier and Kaweka Forest Park.

Smith said the Patoka and Puketitiri brigades provide essential emergency services in the area, such as firefighting, medical response and support during natural disasters.

All three brigades will use the new facility for training and other brigade meetings.

World.title: Khawaja and Warner taken off commentary as CA backs Cummins' captaincy
World.content:
Usman Khawaja and David Warner have been removed from Fox Cricket's commentary team as another day of developments in the sandpaper saga saw Cricket Australia back captain Pat Cummins.

Khawaja and Warner will miss Australia's T20 series against England but are expected to return for next month's Test series against New Zealand.

"In light of recent events both Usman and Davey will be rested from our broadcasts over the next few weeks," Fox Sports managing director Steve Crawley said.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

"While we always support all members of our commentary team and welcome a diversity of views which is a feature of our summer of cricket, we also understand the pressure they are under to respond to each and every new comment.

"We think it is increasingly difficult to focus on the game while the situation continues to unfold and think it is unfair on both commentators to put them in that position.

"Our focus remains on providing our viewers with the best broadcast of Australia's summer of cricket. We will continue to monitor the situation.''

Fox's decision to sideline Khawaja and Warner comes as Cricket Australia threw its support behind embattled Test and one-day captain Pat Cummins on Saturday afternoon.

Cummins was unanimously backed by the CA board to continue as captain after meeting with CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg on Friday in Sydney, with Cummins saying the meeting "meant a lot" amid the ongoing speculation

Pat Cummins will remain the captain of Australia's men's cricket team amid ongoing speculation. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

His captaincy had been questioned following claims by former Test batters Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft that knowledge of the sandpaper plot during the 2018 South Africa tour was widely known.

"Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly," Cummins said in a statement on Saturday.

"David and Todd have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this, and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins has come under fire for his denials made in a 68-minute press conference on November 13. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cummins encountered several reporters at his house this week after Bancroft broke his silence on the sandpaper saga with a 4,500-word statement.

In the statement, Bancroft said he was left feeling "angry, betrayed and alone" by Cummins's lengthy press conference where he denied any knowledge of sandpaper being brought onto the field.

Among the issues discussed in the meeting between Cummins, Boon and Greenberg were Cummins's welfare and the support required for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn," Boon said in the same CA statement.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon (pictured) says CA "unequivocally" rejects suggestions Cummins's integrity has been compromised. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )

"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about, and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there. We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins has been Australia's Test captain since 2021 and is also the captain of the one-day team, having led Australia to the 2023 50-over World Cup title.

World.title: Hazlewood backs Cummins as sandpaper saga continues
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has thrown his support behind Pat Cummins to remain Australian men's captain following the resurfacing of the ball-tampering scandal.

Speculation about Cummins's future in the role has intensified since Cameron Bancroft alleged the entire Australian cricket team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Cummins has maintained he and the Australian bowling unit did not know sandpaper was being used on the field during the infamous Test series in South Africa.

He was not Australia's captain at the time.

Cummins spoke at length in a media conference last week and released a statement via his management following Bancroft's allegation on Wednesday night.

Several former international Test players, including retired Australian fast bowler Mitchell Johnson, have publicly questioned whether Cummins could continue as captain.

Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood, who played alongside Cummins in Cape Town, said he had no knowledge of ball-tampering being used in the series against the Proteas.

Hazlewood said he supported Cummins remaining Australia's captain.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile-on the last few days from different people," Hazlewood said.

"I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

"To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again — I think is just a remarkable job."

Hazlewood said Cummins was an outstanding captain.

"He's a great leader," Hazlewood said.

"If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.

"I think if we turned up for the first Test [against New Zealand] and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Pat Cummins has maintained his stance on the ball-tampering allegations. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hazlewood said he might reconsider his position in the Australian squad if Cummins was removed as captain.

Last week, Cummins held a 70-minute media conference in response to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations, which were published in his memoir, Sabr.

"When he [Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told reporters in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

World.title: The key takeaways from 2026 AFL Draft
World.content:
The AFL Draft occupies a unique space for footy fans: one of hope and ambition.

It's when the stars of tomorrow take their first steps in the professional footballing landscape, even if exactly who they are is unclear.

All 18 clubs have stocked up for the future, with each looking at how their future can be set up (and be Tasmania Devils-proofed) for the next decade.

The surest bet of this year's crop is second-generation Port Adelaide player Dougie Cochrane.

The youngster joins his brother at the club he loves most. Despite playing no junior football this year, Cochrane's potential is almost limitless: tall, agile, smart and skilful.

To some draft watchers, his potential is reminiscent of names like Adam Goodes, Matthew Pavlich or Anthony Koutoufides.

But Cochrane is far from the only prize from this year's crop.

This year's draft is considered to be particularly deep, with names such as Cody Walker, Ethan Drever, Harry Van Hattum, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody set to dominate footballing discourse over coming years.

The home state of football

Ask a football fan where the home of football is, and you'll get a different answer based on your location.

The passion for the game spreads throughout the nation, with several places holding strong claims to being the spiritual home of the sport.

While the draft attracted nominees from right across this country, it was one state in particular that continued to be tapped as the source of the league's future talent.

Victorians again dominated the draft with 13 of the top 20 picks and 58 per cent of all new draftees.

While not quite as dominant as Victoria's 2024 draft showing, it represents a shift back from some stronger years for other states in recent years, such as Queensland's big haul last year.

The strong draft year for Victoria comes off the back of yet another Under 18 National Championships victory for Vic Metro.

Despite this, the first two Victorian players chosen, Walker and Drever, come from the Vic Country zone.

It's also worth noting the top 10 was spread much further, with five states represented and only four Victorians among their ranks.

An absence in the middle

The draft is often topped by those who dominate traffic in the middle.

But just seven midfielders were taken in the first 20 picks, the equal lowest since 2023.

Across the whole draft, only 25 midfielders were tabbed.

Draft watchers have a couple of different theories on why this might be the case.

The simplest one is that each crop has a different shape, with some stronger in some parts and weaker in others.

Another theory is that because this year's draft was considered to be particularly deep and even, clubs focused on drafting for need more than pure talent.

One further theory posits that clubs are looking to target players who can perform in a defined role rather than those who need to be moulded.

Success stories such as Nick Watson have provided a pathway for young talents looking to maximise their chances of making a quick impact at AFL level.

There's only a small number of dedicated midfield roles in any best 23, so drafting for difference-makers elsewhere may have come back into vogue.

This year's average draftee also stood about 2 centimetres taller than their counterpart last year, an indication of where the strength of this year's crop lay.

North Melbourne had the tallest group of draftees at 194cm on average, while the Bulldogs and Cats had the shortest at around 182cm.

First Nations representation

Earlier this year, the AFL acknowledged the declining numbers of First Nations players in the AFL, saying there was plenty of work ahead to address the fall.

In recent seasons the number of First Nations players at the top level has dropped almost 30 per cent from 87 in 2019 to 62 this year.

But there are signs that the short-term prospects might be shifting even before new AFL-led measures take full effect.

This year's draft saw a number of records achieved for First Nations players.

For the first time two of the first three selections involved First Nations players (Cochrane and Walker).

Five of the first 14 picks involved Indigenous players.

By the end of the National Draft seven First Nations players were selected by clubs.

If each club uses their new dedicated list spot, this would mean 25 additional First Nations players will be on AFL lists this year compared with last season.

But, as Dillon noted in May, recruitment was not the only issue.

"It's not only just about identifying [talent]," Dillon said.

"It's then that the players are on a list. How can we make sure that the Indigenous player stays on the list as long as any other player?"

Time will tell if the tide has really turned.

Bidding wars

The talk of night one of the draft was the selection of Brisbane Academy player Caylen Murray by Sydney, with the Swans pouncing on a series of moves by the Lions that left him ripe to be poached.

The Lions have been aggressive in maximising the value of their picks under the various iterations of the draft points bidding systems.

But Sydney has perhaps had more experience testing other clubs' willingness to match.

Later in the draft, Geelong embarked on the longest streak of bids yet seen, racking up five in quick succession, eventually hitting on Adelaide's unwillingness to match for Anthony Long.

The Cats forced several clubs to draft players they may have been hoping to slide onto the rookie list.

Murray is the first top-10 bid to go unmatched, but there has been an uptick in clubs letting tied players go in recent years.

A third of the successful (unmatched) bids since 2015 came in the last two drafts. While many of these draftees were fringe prospects, the higher points value has now forced clubs to prioritise more strictly.

Last year, Sydney's Lachlan Carmichael (pick 21) and Brisbane's Tyan Prindable (pick 32) both went unmatched due to a focus on another prospect.

Previously, Sydney's refusal to match the Bulldogs' bid for Josh Dunkley in 2015 was famous as a rare occurrence.

The bidding wars have also created opportunities for arbitrage against other clubs' very short-term needs. Many trades saw future draft picks swapped for small changes of draft position.

Of particular note is that Brisbane (2027), Port Adelaide (2027) and Sydney (2028) added to an extensive slew of extra first- and second-round picks in a specific upcoming draft.

With the next two drafts set to be dominated by the Tasmania Devils, this year's draft might be the last chance some clubs have to tap into the best young talent pool for a while.

World.title: Canberra United star on 'reclaiming the narrative' as she marks 200 games
World.content:
If there ever were a mountain top to reach in Australian women's domestic football, there is no doubt Michelle Heyman would stand at the top, alone with all the accolades one could dream of.

Today, the 38-year-old will add yet another accomplishment to her already glittering resume, becoming just the first A-League Women's player to reach 200 games for a single club, Canberra United.

It is a point Heyman herself did not think she would ever reach.

"It's a really proud moment," she said.

"I've been thinking about it a lot lately. Did I think this day was ever going to come? Definitely not."

Michelle Heyman will play her 200th game for Canberra United this weekend. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Along with the goals, the national team call-ups and Olympics, in 2019 her football journey was put on hold, and she was forced to find her love of the game — and herself —again.

"I had to leave Canberra … play in Adelaide and have a year away, which was a terrible season for myself," Heyman said.

"I just wasn't feeling good. I didn't like who I was as a person. I wasn't getting the best out of my football, so I thought, 'This is it, this is time.'

" For me, having that time away from football, at the time I didn't think it was going to be so important, but it actually changed the way I viewed the game. "

After rejoining the competition in the 2020/21 season, Heyman returned as if she never left — winning that season's Julie Dolan medal, the highest individual honour in the league.

Michelle Heyman has been part of the competition since its inception. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

The return to the league was not just about proving something to herself; for the star striker, it was also about "reclaiming the narrative".

"The last five, six years have been probably the most important journey that I've ever had within football," Heyman said.

"I think that amount of time is probably better than the first 10 years that I had playing the game.

" So, for me, I was lucky enough to get a second chance. "

Having been a part of the competition since its inception, the 38-year-old has seen and done it all: a two-time premiership winner, multiple Julie Dolan medals and golden boots, and watching the league expand from 10 games to 20.

Michelle Heyman started playing at Canberra United in 2010. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

But the one thing she says has not changed is the league's professional status.

"I'm not going to lie, I don't think a lot of things have changed; we just play more games. I still think we still have the exact same problems as we did back then," Heyman said.

"People might judge me for saying that, but I still think we've got a long way to go to make it a more professional league.

" You look over what's happening in England, in America, and I'm like, 'Why are we so far behind?' So if we can copy them, I think we can improve and make it an incredible league. "

Though her time in the league will eventually come — now being closer to the end of her chapter as a footballer than the start — her legacy will forever remain solidified not only at Canberra United but in A-League Women.

Michelle Heyman has not decided when she will retire, but says it will be on her terms. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

That legacy is something her coach Antoni Jagarinec believes cannot be overstated.

"You talk about people being part of the furniture, and I've heard that a lot this week," Jagarinec said.

" She's not [part of the furniture]. She's the whole house. "

While Heyman has not set a date for when her time in football will end, she said she "won't be around in five years' time, that's for sure".

But one thing is certain — she will do it the way she has always done it: on her terms.

"I don't want them to tell me that I need to retire because it's their opinions on me. I want to do it because I want to do it," Heyman said.

World.title: Alcaraz wears elastic band on injured thigh to beat Cobolli at ATP Finals
World.content:
Seven-time major singles champion Carlos Alcaraz has eased concerns about a hamstring injury by cruising past Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli 6-4, 6-1 at the ATP Finals in Turin.

Wearing an elastic black band on his injured left thigh and a strip of tape on his right knee, Alcaraz completed an unbeaten group-stage campaign ahead of the semifinals.

The Spaniard had already booked his place in the last four ‌after victories over American seventh seed Frances Tiafoe and Daniil Medvedev.

But his fitness came under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy strapping on his left leg following his win over Medvedev, who was the 2020 ATP Finals champion.

Any doubts were quickly ‌dispelled as Alcaraz broke the already-eliminated Cobolli in the opening game and surged into a 2-0 lead.

The 23-year-old ⁠delivered an efficient display, keeping rallies short and dictating play without putting unnecessary strain ‌on his body.

Carlos Alcaraz's left thigh was heavily bandaged during his match against Flavio Cobolli. (Reuters: Guglielmo Mangiapane)

He carried that momentum into the second set, breaking for a 2-0 ‌lead and again to move 4-1 ahead before closing out a 65-minute victory.

Alcaraz finished with 29 winners to Cobolli's nine.

"It was a difficult match to see how I was going to feel on court and playing against Flavio is not easy," Alcaraz said.

"He is a great player and person off the court.

"I tried to play as ‌aggressively as I can, hit the ball as hard as I can.

"The way I felt on court today was incredible. I am getting more confident after every match and hopefully I can keep it going."

Alcaraz had already secured a place in the semifinals against Ben Shelton at the elite eight-player event.

The semifinal will be a re-match of the US Open quarterfinal between Shelton and Alcaraz.

While Shelton won that five-set clash in New York, Alcaraz recently got revenge in the Paris Masters final.

In the other semifinal, top-ranked Alexander Zverev will face either Medvedev or Tiafoe.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Sidelined Swans star on making first prelim in a 'really tough year'
World.content:
Right after Sydney upset Geelong in the AFLW semifinals last weekend, a photo was taken that perfectly encapsulated the moment for the Swans.

In it, injured star Ally Morphett is crying while holding a beaming Lexi Hamilton.

"I mean, [at] first glance, I hated the photo," Morphett laughed to ABC Sport. "I thought I looked absolutely terrible. But there's so much meaning and emotion behind it.

"I just care so much about the girls … I was so proud of them once they won because it was just an unbelievable game. I think it was one of the best games of the year."

Sydney booked its first preliminary final in the AFLW competition with an upset win over Geelong. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

With the victory, the Swans booked a spot in their first preliminary women's final in head coach Colin O'Riordan's first year at the helm.

Some AFLW pundits had questioned whether the Swans could go deep in finals without Morphett, who did her ACL in round 8.

"It's very bittersweet to be watching on the sidelines because all you want to do is be out there," Morphett said, adding it had been "probably the most emotional year of my life".

"But I was just so incredibly happy for all the girls. I think the difference in the way we play this year compared to previous years is we do it for each other, rather than worrying about how you personally play."

Chloe Molloy was the leading AFLW goal kicker for the 2026 season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

The success has come while the club was repeatedly in headlines due to male players under a police investigation for allegations of a sexual assault and breaching club standards. The investigation is over and players will not be charged.

The saga has added extra emotional weight, Morphett said, but strengthened their bonds internally in the AFLW program.

"It's been a really tough year. Not just for our program, but also women amongst the whole organisation," Morphett said.

"When you go through adversity like that, it brings you closer together compared to other teams who don't really go through something like that and as significant as that.

"But I think vulnerability is such a massive strength, especially around strong women and so many of us, and that happening has brought us so much closer.

Ally Morphett says this year has made the Sydney Swans AFLW side even closer. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

"It's just brought so much care amongst the group between Colin, all the staff and the players. And all together as a whole program, we just care so much about everyone.

"It's been a massive [emotional] roller coaster. As for the football side of things and how we're performing, our connection has gone onto the field and the way that we go about it."

With the rehab group not travelling to Melbourne, Morphett will now have the tough task of watching her side face North Melbourne from home.

When the pair faced each other in round eight this year, the two-time reigning premiers in the Kangaroos won by 51 points.

Morphett knows it will be a huge challenge for the Swans, but also knows finals footy is a different game.

Sydney went down by 51 points when they played North Melbourne earlier this year. (Getty: Robert Cianflone/AFL Photos)

"Yes they're nervous, but I think everyone's more geed up than nervous. It makes us hungry, the fact that they're going for a three-peat, and we want to be the ones to stop them," she said.

"If we played how we did last weekend against the Cats, I think that it is very achievable.

"Finals footy is very much grit and desire, and we aren't the number one pressure team in the comp for no reason. So I think … Bloods [Swans] footy is finals footy, really. So I'm really excited to watch it."

World.title: Tim Tszyu hunting 'legacy-defining' win on Gold Coast
World.content:
Tim Tszyu knows all about the highs boxing can deliver.

He knows a fair bit about the lows, too.

Three years ago, Tszyu, the WBO junior middleweight world title holder, was eyeing up unification and US domination.

Three defeats in four fights later, his career was on the trash heap.

"You learn more about your character," Tszyu told ABC Sport from his Rockdale gym.

"You realise life isn't just going to go on an upward scale. It goes up and down. You've got to ride through the waves.

"One thing I learned was don't get too high from your wins, don't get too low from your losses, maintain a stable way of living and keep approaching every day with the foundation of something to work towards.

"That's how it's always been for me."

Tim Tszyu is headlining the event, with Jermell Charlo lower on the card. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Three wins later, including against American legend Errol Spence Jr, the 32-year-old is fighting for another world title, this time at the 160-pound-limit against WBA middleweight champion Erislandy Lara.

Not everyone is happy about Tszyu's return to the top.

"We all know he don't deserve a world title fight," American fighter Jermell Charlo told media on Wednesday via Zoom link from the United States.

"You didn't work your way up [at middleweight] for real. He fought a 147-pounder [welterweight] that just happened to overlap 154 [junior middleweight].

"Errol Spence wasn't the Errol Spence we all know, right?

"He can't beat Lara. Styles make fights, and this is just stylistically a bad fight for Tim.

"Lara's going to destroy Tszyu."

Tim Tszyu is leaving no stone unturned in his bid for glory. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Charlo, a former unified champion in Tszyu's former weight division, light middleweight, may have a vested interest in shooting down Tszyu's chances.

Tszyu was supposed to face Charlo in January 2023, but the bout collapsed after Charlo broke his hand in sparring.

Despite Tszyu still being keen, Charlo wanted to hunt bigger fish and stepped up two weight divisions to take on Canelo Álvarez in a big-money blockbuster.

The WBO were not amused, stripping Charlo of his title the second he stepped into the ring, elevating Tszyu.

Tszyu has rebuilt his reputation since, while Charlo has stagnated.

Tim Tszyu knows the threat Erislandy Lara poses. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Charlo has not fought since losing to Canelo, returning as the third-billed fight on December's spectacular Gold Coast card.

"Don't forget that, Charlo," Tszyu said, mockingly.

"You're on my undercard."

Tszyu's resurrection into a world title challenger has been nothing short of remarkable.

And although Lara will pose an enormous test of Tszyu's resilience, "He's going to present a lot of challenges," Tszyu noted, with the Australian backing himself to claim victory.

A big part of Tszyu's recovery has been his partnership with former three-weight world champion Jeff Fenech.

"He just came on board at a time where I really needed it," Tszyu said.

Tim Tszyu has been training with Jeff Fenech and Billy Hussein. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Despite that, Fenech has been dealing with several health challenges of late, including a third heart operation in October.

"I wouldn't say it impacted my training camp. I was more impacted personally because I felt like a lot was missing from Jeff," Tszyu said.

"But then when Billy [Hussein] came on board, we just started flowing with things, and we've just been working ever since."

Fenech is one of just two Australian male fighters to win championships in different weight classes (IBF bantamweight, WBC super-bantamweight and WBC featherweight), the other being Liam Paro (IBF super lightweight and welterweight titles).

"Playing it safe all the time is not the way I do things," Tszyu said.

"You got to chase the hard stuff. The tricky stuff. The legacy-defining type stuff."

World.title: An ex-Queensland premier's cherished link to legendary Wallabies family
World.content:
Holding the future Queen Elizabeth II when she was a toddler and joining King George V to shoot pheasants aren't stories every Australian rugby union player gets to tell.

Nor is sending British newspapers into a frenzy over a rumoured engagement to marry.

But for Jim and Arnold Tancred, these were some of the tales they shared during their rugby careers a century ago.

Jim, a mobile prop, and younger brother Arnold, an aggressive back-rower, were members of the legendary 1927/28 NSW Waratahs, which captivated the rugby world on their tour of Great Britain, Ireland and France (as well as Sri Lanka and Canada).

One of their older siblings, Harry, also played for NSW during his career.

The trio was posthumously recognised as Australian representatives and awarded Wallaby numbers 192 (Harry), 231 (Jim) and 241 (Arnold) following a decision to grant Test status to the Waratahs' matches against international teams between 1920 and 1928.

Jim Tancred's playing career was celebrated at the Sydney Bledisloe Cup Test last month. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

To celebrate 100 years since Jim (christened James) played for the Waratahs against the All Blacks, 22 of his direct descendants, along with spouses and friends, attended last month's Bledisloe Cup Test in Sydney.

Among those commemorating the milestone was Jim's granddaughter, former Queensland premier Anna Bligh.

"We had caps made. We all sat together in the stands. It was great," Anna tells ABC Sport.

Anna's brother, Stephen Tancred, adds: "We rounded up the family from Perth, Melbourne, Sydney, Darwin and country Queensland.

"We had three of Jim's daughters there. They're all in their 80s, and we had a great-great-great-grandchild who was 13."

It wasn't the only occasion Jim's descendants came together to remember his career.

Jim and Arnold Tancred were welcomed home by their family following the 1927/28 Waratahs tour. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

Anna and Stephen's mother, Frances, was one of nine children born to Jim and his wife Mary, and a coveted family photo was recreated to coincide with her 90th birthday.

The original image captured Jim and Arnold's family outside their home in the Sydney suburb of Rozelle as they welcomed the brothers back from the Waratahs' tour in early 1928.

The Tancreds' return to Rozelle was recently recreated by Jim's descendants. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

"It was such a proud moment for the family," Anna says.

"The photo is quite precious."

Playing for the Waratahs

When writing about the Tancred brothers, Australian rugby historian Jack Pollard noted they were "sometimes described mistakenly as New Zealanders".

Born in Sydney, they spent part of their childhood in New Zealand after parents Thomas and Anna moved the family of 10 children to the Shaky Isles.

Much of their rugby education took place across the Tasman.

Harry Tancred was the first of the brothers to play for the Waratahs. (Supplied: Rugby Australia/Classic Wallabies)

Harry even represented New Zealand in rugby league but was permitted to rejoin the union ranks.

Once the family returned to Australia, it was Harry, a robust number eight, who first represented the Waratahs when he twice faced the New Zealand Māori (now Māori All Blacks) in 1923.

Jim, who like Harry and Arnold played for the Glebe-Balmain club in Sydney, made his Waratahs debut in 1926, appearing in two internationals against the All Blacks.

A caricature of Jim Tancred appeared in The Daily Telegraph in 1928. (Supplied: The Daily Telegraph)

But the highlight of Jim's playing days was his selection alongside Arnold for the 1927/28 Waratahs tour.

The Waratahs, away from Sydney for 252 days, dazzled crowds in Great Britain, Ireland and France with a breathtaking display of "running rugby".

They won three of their five internationals and played more than 30 matches in total.

"It was such a big thing in those days to represent your country and tour internationally," Anna Bligh says.

"It meant being away for many weeks at a time because they travelled by ship."

Jim played the third and final international of his career against France, with the Waratahs winning 11-8 in Paris.

He was headbutted by opposition prop Jean Morère during the match, only for Waratahs teammate Ted "Bluey" Greatorex to violently square up with the Frenchman.

The Waratahs captivated spectators with their attacking brand of rugby. (Supplied: Official 1927/28 Waratahs Report)

Standing at 5'10" (1.78 metres) and weighing 78 kilograms, Jim would be considered a small front-rower by today's standards.

His modest physique, though, complemented the Waratahs' attacking game.

"The Waratahs' forwards were mobile," says Stephen Tancred, who played for the Stanthorpe Kookaburras during a proud bush rugby career.

"They would have the set-play and then join in with the backs. That was the essence of running rugby."

Arnold Tancred appeared in three internationals for the Waratahs. (Rugby Australia/Classic Wallabies)

All three of Arnold's internationals came on tour, against Ireland, Wales and Scotland.

A dislocated shoulder ended his tour early, meaning he and Jim never played an international together.

Waratahs Tour (internationals) Won 5-3 vs Ireland

Won 18-8 vs Wales

Lost 10-8 vs Scotland

Lost 18-11 vs England

Won 11-8 vs France

Arnold's ferocious tackling shocked spectators, especially in England, where rugby was regarded as a "gentlemen's game".

"Even though the Waratahs were known for running rugby, they had some really good defenders," Arnold's grandson Toby Tancred says.

"Dad [Arnold's son John] has told me stories about them getting booed at games because of the hard defence.

"That was Arnold's forte."

Meeting the royals

It wasn't just rugby keeping the Waratahs busy on tour.

While in England, they enjoyed afternoon tea with the Duke (who would become King George VI) and Duchess of York at their Piccadilly residence.

The Waratahs' meeting with Princess Elizabeth made newspaper headlines. (Supplied: The Arrow)

The Waratahs were introduced to the duke and duchess's one-year-old daughter, Elizabeth, who 24 years later would be crowned queen of the United Kingdom.

Jim Tancred was among the players to take a shine to "Baby Betty".

"The family story is he jiggled Elizabeth on his knee," Anna Bligh laughs.

Another meeting with the royal family involved pheasant shooting with King George V at his Sandringham estate.

Arnold Tancred (left) and his teammates met King George V (third from left). (Supplied: Toby Tancred)

According to the official tour report, written by manager E Gordon Shaw and captain Johnnie Wallace, the king "gave us each a pheasant from the day's bag".

So what happened to the pheasants?

This was a topic of conversation when Jim's descendants came together at the Sydney Bledisloe Cup Test a month ago.

They were joined by the daughter of star 1927/28 Waratahs centre Cyril Towers, Marguerite Howard, whose husband Jake and son Pat played for the Wallabies.

Anna Bligh (left) with Marguerite Howard at the Sydney Bledisloe Cup Test. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

"Marguerite asked, 'Does your family have the pheasant?'" Anna recalls.

"We said, 'What pheasant?'

"She said, 'The king apparently gave all the players stuffed pheasants in a glass case. My mother claimed it was the ugliest thing she had ever seen.'"

The Waratahs fraternised with more than royals while abroad.

Arnold Tancred was rumoured to have become engaged on the Waratahs tour. (Supplied: South Wales Argus)

Arnold Tancred sent tongues wagging among the British press when it was reported he was engaged to marry Vera Morgan, whom he met at a dance in Swansea, Wales.

"The marriage will probably take place in a year's time, when Miss Morgan will go out to Australia," the South Wales Argus newspaper reported on January 6, 1928.

Alas, it wasn't to be.

"There is nothing at all in our friendship," Arnold told London's The Evening Standard.

"And there is no likelihood of our becoming engaged."

Business giants

Given rugby was amateur at the time, Jim, Arnold and Harry cut their playing careers short because of their business interests.

As a family of butchers, they helped established Tancred Brothers in the 1920s, quickly becoming giants of Australia's meat industry.

Arnold and Harry remained in Sydney while Jim ran the Queensland arm of the business, which went public in 1955, after moving his family to Toowoomba.

"They had a fair bit of go about them," Stephen Tancred says.

"They pioneered slaughtering in the country and shipping chilled meat to the city."

Arnold managed and coached the Wallabies on their 1947/48 tour of Great Britain, Ireland and France.

Arnold Tancred (second from right) training with the 1947/48 Wallabies squad. (Supplied: Toby Tancred)

Newspaper reporters following the tour suggested he was prickly, and his players considered him tough on the training paddock.

"I think what was more notable than his playing career is he was the coach of the 1947/48 Wallabies," Toby Tancred says.

"He trained them like bastards."

The Tancred name lives on in rugby, with Toby's three sons showing promise.

The eldest, Arnie, was a member of the Waratahs' 2024 preseason squad, George represented Australian Schoolboys last year, while Tomma played in the Riverview first XV, which was named AAGPS co-premiers in August.

Arnie (left), George (centre) and Tomma Tancred are making names for themselves in rugby. (Supplied: Toby Tancred)

A well-known racehorse owner, Harry, who was christened Henry Eugene, served as Sydney Turf Club chairman (1953-59), with the prestigious H E Tancred Stakes named in his honour.

Jim stayed connected to rugby in Toowoomba and, like Harry, racehorses were among his passions.

He was a punter, too, once betting 1,000 pounds on the horse he owned, On Cor, when it won the 1948 February Handicap at Doomben.

"We knew he liked the GGs [horses] and a flutter," Anna Bligh says admiringly.

Tragically, Jim died suddenly of a heart attack at his home in 1965, at the age of 62.

His brothers Arnold and Harry also died from heart-related conditions, aged 59 and 64 respectively.

Anna, who was five at the time of Jim's death, remembers her grandfather as "larger than life" and a family man "taken from them far too young".

She learned more about Jim during her political career, especially his generosity.

Anna Bligh was Queensland premier between 2007-12. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

A chance meeting with Wallabies great, prominent businessman and ex-lord mayor of Sydney, the late Sir Nicholas Shehadie, left Anna beaming with pride.

"When Shehadie finished his rugby career, he was very keen to go into business and couldn't find a bank that would give him money without someone going guarantor for him," Anna says.

"My grandfather offered to do it.

"Shehadie said, 'I owe my success to your grandfather being prepared to back me', which has always made me feel good about my grandfather.

"It's nice when you hear a story like that."

Tech.title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.

The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California, judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.

Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

Tech.title: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79 billion in its first day
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day of sales, which set “a new record for entertainment across any medium,” according to an announcement from Rockstar Games. The game also sold 32.5 million preorder copies.

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.” Rockstar claims that the game’s release, which happened Thursday, was “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

The news follows leaks, delays, and a huge amount of interest ahead of GTA VI’s launch. (Many other games steered clear of GTA VI to get their time in the sun.) But even with the weight of anticipation placed upon GTA VI, it actually lived up to the hype, my colleague Andrew Webster said in his review.

Tech.title: Eufy’s Omni C28 is 53 percent off ahead of Black Friday
Tech.content:
Hosting Thanksgiving can be fun, but cleaning up afterwards? Not so much. Eufy’s Omni C28 robot vacuum / mop hybrid can help, and thanks to an early Black Friday deal, you can pick it up at a new low price of $379.99 ($420 off its original price) at Amazon, Best Buy, or directly from Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1). While this model has dropped to around $499.99 a few times before, it commonly sells for a lot more, making now a great time to consider buying one.

The Verge’s smart home reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy named the Eufy Omni C28 one of her top picks after testing 16 robot vacuum mops. She thinks it’s a particularly great fit for apartments and smaller homes. It offers features typically found in pricier flagship models, including a multifunction dock that automatically washes the mop roller with hot water and dries it with hot air, yet it doesn’t take up too much space. The robot itself is also relatively narrow and maneuvers easily around furniture and into tight spaces. It boasts excellent navigation, and had no trouble climbing over the legs of Jen’s lounger, which have tripped up many of the more expensive models she’s tested.

The Omni C28 also does a great job cleaning with its mops, particularly on hardwood floors. Surprisingly, it’s powerful enough to lift up dried oatmeal. Unlike most other robot vacuums Jen’s tested, this one lacks a camera, making it a good option if you’re concerned about privacy. Unfortunately, the trade-off is mediocre obstacle detection, so you’ll want to pick up socks and cables before running it.

Tech.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
Tech.content:
Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.

We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.

So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

Tech.title: Multiplying your Switch 2’s storage costs less than usual right now
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards, while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds. Thankfully, Samsung’s 256GB model has dropped to $44.99 at Amazon ahead of Black Friday, which is a few bucks off its usual price but still well below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk, if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason.

For those who don’t want to think about upgrading their Switch 2’s storage again, both brands’ 512GB microSD Express cards are selling for a fair $99.99 on Amazon. That gives you double the storage for roughly twice the price of a 256GB card, as it should be.

I suspect the 256GB option will be enough for most Switch 2 players, unless you buy a lot of games. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, for example. Other Nintendo-developed games tend to be similar in install size, though it’s all over the place for third-party game makers; Resident Evil Requiem (which also recently dropped to $39.99 on Amazon) is relatively small at 28.7 gigs, while The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is about 50. Some games take up even more storage.

Tech.title: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.

The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.

The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.

Gemini for Home was announced last year, so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.
